ingredients.name: flatbreads or thick slices of bread

steps.t: Beat the eggs with the salt until no clear streaks remain; unbeaten whites set into rubbery ribbons before the yolks catch up.
Heat a wide frying pan until a slice of onion hisses sharply, then add the oil, onion and pepper; if the pan is timid, the vegetables stew and taste watery.
Stir-fry hard until the onion tips are bronze and the pepper skins blister in small freckles; pale onion keeps the whole pan sweet but flat.
Push the vegetables aside, fry the tomato paste in the bare oil with pul biber and dried mint until it darkens brick-red and smells toasted; raw paste tastes tinny.
Pour in the eggs and stir in broad sweeps over high heat, dragging set curds from the base while leaving glossy streaks on top; tiny frantic stirring makes dry crumbs.
Pull the pan off while the eggs still look a shade underdone, because the metal keeps cooking them; waiting until they look finished in the pan makes them chalky on the plate.
Scatter with parsley and scoop up with bread straight away; if it sits, the onions weep and loosen the eggs.

note: Cheap, fast and built for one pan; double it only in a wider pan, not a crowded one.

name: Hanoi Pickle-Dressed Beef Shin Bowls
hook: Pickle snap over anise-rich beef

steps.t: Put the beef shin in a snug pan with sliced ginger, star anise and 10 ml fish sauce, then cover with 1.2 litres cold water; bring it up slowly and skim the grey foam, because a hard boil traps scum and makes the broth taste flat.
Simmer with the lid slightly ajar until a fork slides through the beef with almost no push; if the water drops below the meat, top it up, or the exposed side dries before the centre softens.
Cut the carrot and daikon into fine matchsticks, then scrunch with rice vinegar, 15 g sugar and a good pinch of salt until glossy; thick pieces stay woody, so keep them slender.
Lift out the beef and strain the broth; discard ginger and star anise, because leaving them in keeps extracting bitterness.
Stir the remaining fish sauce and sugar with the lime juice and 4 tbsp hot broth to make a dressing; taste for sharp-salty balance now, as cold noodles will mute it.
Cook the rice noodles until bendy but not swollen, then rinse briefly under warm water; if they sit hot and undressed, they clump into one slab.
Shred the warm beef, toss it with half the dressing, then bowl it with noodles, hot broth, pickles, herbs and the remaining dressing; cold beef repels the dressing, so do not let it fully chill.

note: For extra comfort, warm the serving bowls with boiling water before assembling.

name: Calabrian Sunrise Halloumi Egg Bake
hook: Runny eggs under salty golden halloumi

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C and put the olive oil in a medium baking dish while it warms; a cold dish makes the tomatoes leak before they blister.

Add sliced red onion, whole cherry tomatoes, oregano and chilli flakes, then roast until the tomato skins split and the onion tips darken; if the onions are piled up, they steam sharp instead of sweetening.
Stir in torn roasted peppers and cannellini beans, scraping the sticky tomato juices through them; if the beans sit dry on top, they toughen in the heat.
Tear the ciabatta into rough crumbs, tuck them around the edges and lay sliced halloumi across the middle; buried bread turns soggy, so keep some jagged bits exposed.
Make four hollows, crack in the eggs and bake until the whites are set but the yolks still wobble; underbaked whites are unsafe and overbaked yolks lose the breakfast drama.
Rest for 3 minutes, scatter with torn basil and spoon from the dish; serving straight from the oven makes the tomato sauce spit and the eggs tear.

note: Use a shallow dish so the eggs cook before the halloumi hardens.

name: Kashmiri Saffron-Braised Tofu Rogan
hook: Silken spice, saffron, serious table presence

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in kitchen paper and press it under a board until the surface feels dry; wet tofu spits in the pan and waters down the braise.
Cut the tofu into large cubes and brown them in half the oil until the corners turn honey-gold; crowding the pan makes the cubes tear and steam, so work in batches if needed.
Cook finely sliced onions in the remaining oil with a pinch of salt until they collapse to deep caramel strands; pale onions leave the gravy harsh and thin.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste, Kashmiri chilli and garam masala until the oil stains red and smells rounded; if the paste catches black, the whole sauce will taste bitter.
Blend the cashews with 150 ml boiling water, then stir in yoghurt and passata off the heat; adding yoghurt to a fierce pan splits it into grainy flecks.
Return the pan to low heat, add the cashew mixture, saffron and 250 ml water, then nestle in the tofu; the sauce should sigh, not boil, or the tofu toughens at the edges.
Uncover, crumble in the kasuri methi and braise until the gravy clings heavily to a spoon; stop before oil puddles aggressively, or it will eat too rich.
Rest for 10 minutes, then finish with chopped coriander; serving immediately hides the saffron, while resting lets the perfume come forward.

note: Serve with saffron rice or hot naan for a proper centrepiece.

name: Bangkok Tamarind Lamb & Green Bean Stew
hook: Sour broth, tender lamb, bright herbs

steps.t: Trim obvious hard fat from the lamb and pat the pieces dry; leaving slick fat on makes the stew greasy instead of summery.
Heat the oil and stir the curry paste until it darkens slightly and smells roasted; if it scorches, the broth turns acrid, so keep it moving.
Add the lamb and turn it through the paste until every piece is stained red, not browned hard; a dark crust muddies the clear tamarind broth.
Bruise the lemongrass, tear the lime leaves and add both with 900 ml water, tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar; unbruised lemongrass gives almost nothing back.
Simmer gently until the lamb yields when pressed with a spoon; a rolling boil tightens the meat and throws scum through the broth.
Add halved cherry tomatoes, green beans and sliced courgette, then simmer until the beans are bright and just tender; overcooking turns the whole stew army-green.
Tear in Thai basil off the heat and skim any orange oil from the surface; boiling basil makes it black and medicinal.

note: Serve in shallow bowls with jasmine rice and extra herbs rather than a heavy garnish.

name: Osaka Miso-Roasted Whole Chickpeas with Nori Salt
hook: Crisp miso shells for passing round

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C and rub the chickpeas dry in a tea towel until their skins feel papery; damp pulses steam and never crisp.
Toss the whole chickpeas with rapeseed oil and spread them on a wide tray with space between them; crowding gives soft centres and leathery skins.
Whisk miso, mirin and soy sauce in a bowl while the chickpeas roast; glazing from the start burns the sugars before the insides dry.
Tip the hot chickpeas into the miso glaze, add sesame seeds, then return them to the tray; if they sit in the bowl, the glaze slides off and pools.
Roast until the coating is speckled bronze and the tray smells nutty, not blackened; pull them early if the miso darkens too fast.
Crumble nori over the warm chickpeas with shichimi and finely sliced spring onions; covering them while hot traps steam and softens the crisp shells.

note: Best eaten warm as part of a table of pickles, rice and grilled vegetables.

name: Asturian Saffron Lentil Pot
hook: Steam-soft lentils under smoky saffron broth

steps.t: Warm the oil in a heavy lidded pan and sweat the onion and carrot with a pinch of salt until the onion turns glossy and slack; if it catches now, the broth will taste bitter rather than sweet.
Add the chorizo and cook until orange oil beads around the slices and the edges tighten; do not rush with high heat or the paprika in the sausage will scorch.
Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika and saffron for about 30 seconds, just until the pan smells smoky and floral; any longer on a dry base and the spices turn dusty.

Add the lentils, bay leaves and stock, bring to a lively simmer, then cover tightly and turn the heat low so the pot steams rather than boils hard; a rattling boil splits the lentils and muddies the broth.
Check the lentils: they should squash gently against the side of the pan but still hold their skins. If the pan looks dry before that, add a splash of hot water so the bottom does not glue on.
Remove the lid and simmer for a few minutes until the broth coats a spoon lightly; stop before it becomes stodgy, because the lentils thicken as they sit.
Finish with sherry vinegar and enough salt to make the chorizo taste round rather than sharp; pull out the bay leaves before serving in deep bowls.

note: A crusty loaf and a bitter green salad make this feel properly northern Spanish.

name: Charcoal Garlic Mushroom Tartines
hook: Smoke, butter, yolk and crisp bread

steps.t: Light a small bed of coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no tall flames; flames lick mushrooms black before their centres go juicy.
Mash the butter with garlic, mustard, thyme and a pinch of salt until smooth; if the garlic stays in lumps, one bite will shout while the next says nothing.

Toss the mushrooms with olive oil, salt and pepper, then grill in a basket or on a fine grate until they slump, squeak less, and show dark freckles at the edges; crowding traps steam and makes them rubbery.
Grill the bread beside them until the ridges are crisp and lightly charred, not brittle all the way through; bread that is too dry will steal the yolk instead of carrying it.
Poach the eggs in barely trembling water with the vinegar until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble under a spoon; boiling water shreds the whites into rags.
Spread the hot toast with garlic butter so it melts into the holes, pile on the mushrooms, then set an egg on each pair of tartines.
Scatter with parsley and a little black pepper, and serve while the butter is still running into the toast.

note: If cooking indoors, use a smoking-hot ridged grill pan; you lose some smoke but keep the breakfast spirit.

name: Maine Scallop Crudo with Corn Butter
hook: Cold scallops, sweet corn, clean heat

ingredients.name: very fresh dry-packed scallops, from a trusted fishmonger
crushed ice, for chilling the serving plate

steps.t: Put the serving plate over crushed ice to chill hard; warm plates soften scallops and make the dressing taste greasy.
Melt the butter gently, add the corn kernels and cook until they turn glossy and smell like popcorn, but do not let the butter brown or it will bully the scallops.
Blend the corn butter with lime juice, lime zest and a pinch of salt, then strain if you want it sleek; leaving coarse skins is fine, but watery unblended butter will split on the plate.
Pat the scallops dry with kitchen paper and slice them horizontally into thin coins with a sharp knife; sawing with a dull blade tears the flesh and makes the crudo look tired.
Spoon a thin layer of corn butter onto the chilled plate, lay the scallops in a single layer and keep them cold; stacking them warms the centre and spoils the clean snap.
Dress with olive oil, shallot, jalapeño, chives and flaky salt just before serving; salt too early draws out liquid and turns the plate milky.

note: Serve only if the scallops are explicitly suitable to eat raw; when in doubt, choose another dish.

name: Mendoza Halloumi Peach Saltado
hook: Hot squeaky cheese, cool herb brightness

ingredients.name: ají molido or mild chilli flakes

steps.t: Dry the halloumi batons thoroughly with kitchen paper; if they go in damp, they steam, stick and lose the golden crust you need.
Heat a wok or wide frying pan until a drop of water skips away, then add the oil; warm metal gives you sweating vegetables rather than a quick saltado.
Stir-fry the halloumi for a minute or two until the long edges are deep gold and the cheese bends slightly; leave it too long and it toughens like a rubber band.
Lift the halloumi out, then throw in the onion and red pepper, tossing until the onion edges char in spots but the pepper still snaps; soft peppers make the plate heavy.
Add the peaches and ají molido for a fast toss, just until the cut sides gloss and catch a little heat; overcooked peaches collapse into jam.
Return the halloumi with red wine vinegar and lemon juice, tossing once so the acid hisses and coats everything; boiling the vinegar away leaves only salt and oil.
Fold through coriander and parsley off the heat, then serve spread out on a platter so the herbs stay green and the cheese keeps its crust.

note: Good with chilled Torrontés, tomato salad, or both.

name: Bahian Pork Tapioca Coalhos
hook: Crisp pork tucked into chewy cassava

ingredients.name: queijo coalho or firm halloumi, grated

steps.t: Mix the pork with lime juice, garlic, cumin, paprika, chilli, cachaça and salt, then leave it while you set up the griddle; skipping this short rest gives pork that tastes seasoned only on the outside.
Heat a flat griddle or heavy frying pan until a little tapioca starch turns opaque on contact; if the pan is only warm, the beiju dries out before it binds.

Sieve a thin, even layer of hydrated tapioca starch into the dry pan to make a small round, then cook until the grains fuse into a flexible white pancake; press gently, but do not add oil or it turns sandy.
Sprinkle a little queijo coalho over half the beiju, fold it, and griddle until the outside has pale toast marks and the cheese softens; hard browning makes tapioca brittle.
Repeat to make 8 small folded beiju, stacking them under a clean tea towel so they stay pliable; uncovered ones curl and crack before filling.
Oil the hot griddle, spread the pork in a single layer and leave it until the underside forms crisp brown bits before tossing; constant stirring makes grey mince with no savoury edge.
Cook until no pink remains and the juices run clear, then fold through coriander off the heat; undercooked pork is unsafe, while overcooked pork turns dry and pebbly.
Open the warm beiju slightly, spoon in crisp pork, and send them out on one platter with lime wedges if you like.

note: Small, hot and hand-held: ideal beside olives, pickles and cold beer.

name: Chipotle Mushroom Chilaquiles Bake
hook: Crisp edges, smoky sauce, molten cheese

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Put the mushrooms, oil and chipotle paste in a medium baking dish and toss hard enough to coat the gills; dry patches roast flat and bland instead of smoky.
Bake the mushrooms until they have shrunk and the dish has a dark, sticky film at the corners; if they still look swollen and wet, the bake will turn soupy.
Stir in the salsa, black beans and sweetcorn, scraping the chipotle film off the dish into the sauce. If you leave that stuck-on paste behind, the heat tastes harsh rather than rounded.
Fold through half the tortilla chips so they are sauced but not crushed to crumbs, then stand the rest upright on top. Flat chips steam soft; exposed edges go properly crisp.
Scatter over the cheddar and bake until the sauce bubbles through the middle and the tortilla tips are lace-brown, not just pale and warm.
Rest for 3 minutes so the sauce grips the chips; spooning straight away makes a runny pile. Finish with soured cream, lime and coriander.

note: Use sturdy tortilla chips; very thin ones collapse before the cheese browns.

name: Wine-Dark Beef Cheek Stifado
hook: Sticky onions, cinnamon, spoon-soft beef

ingredients.name: beef cheeks, trimmed and cut into large chunks

steps.t: Pat the beef cheeks very dry and season them. Brown in the oil in a heavy casserole until the corners are crusted dark mahogany; if the pan hisses weakly and fills with juice, stop adding meat and work in smaller batches.
Lift the beef out, add the shallots and cook until their skins of colour catch in spots. Pale onions taste boiled after three hours, so give them a little patience now.
Stir in the garlic for 30 seconds, then pour in the wine and scrape until the base feels smooth under the spoon. Any blackened bits left stuck down will turn the sauce bitter.
Add the tomatoes, vinegar, cinnamon, bay, allspice and the beef with its resting juices. The liquid should come about two-thirds up the meat; drown it and the sauce will never turn glossy.
Cover with a tight lid and braise on the lowest hob setting, turning the beef once or twice, until a spoon pushes through a chunk with almost no resistance.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce coats the shallots like lacquer. If the fat pools heavily, skim it now rather than stirring it back into a greasy finish.
Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, then pull out the cinnamon and bay. Shower with parsley so the stew smells lifted, not just dark and sweet.

note: Best with orzo, mashed potatoes or crusty bread to catch the thick wine sauce.

name: Sumac Mackerel & Chickpea Yahni
hook: Bright tomatoes around rich, flaky fish

steps.t: Salt the mackerel lightly and leave it on a plate while you start the stew. This firms the flesh; unsalted oily fish breaks into ragged flakes the moment it hits tomato.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion and pepper until the onion bends softly and the pepper loses its raw snap. Rushing this leaves the stew tasting like hot salad.
Add the garlic and tomato paste, stirring until the paste darkens to brick-red and smells roasted. If it stays bright red, it will taste tinny in the finished broth.
Pour in the chopped tomatoes, chickpeas, pul biber and 150ml water. Simmer until the bubbles look thick and lazy around the chickpeas, not watery and sharp.
Lay the mackerel skin-side up in the stew and spoon sauce over the edges without burying it. Hard boiling tightens the fish and pushes out white protein, so keep the surface at a gentle tremble.
When the thickest part flakes under a fork and is fully opaque, turn off the heat. Stirring now will shred the fillets, so shake the pan instead if sauce needs moving.
Finish with sumac, parsley and lemon juice. Add these off the heat, otherwise the sumac dulls and the parsley tastes grassy.

note: Serve as it is for a lower-carb bowl, or add bulgur if you are training hard.

name: Orange-Blossom Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Silky custard, pistachio, floral syrup

steps.t: Set four small heatproof cups in a wide lidded pan on a folded tea towel. Add hot water to come halfway up the cups; without the towel, the cups rattle and the custard steams unevenly.
Whisk the eggs just until the yolks disappear, then whisk in the milk, sugar, orange blossom water, cardamom and salt. Frothing hard traps bubbles that set as little holes.
Strain the mixture into a jug, then pour into the cups. Do not skip the sieve; stringy egg white is what makes steamed custard taste like breakfast, not dessert.
Cover each cup tightly with foil and bring the water to the gentlest simmer, where only small bubbles touch the sides. A rolling boil gives rubbery edges before the centre sets.
Cover the pan and steam until the custards wobble like soft jelly and a knife at the edge comes out clean. If the centre sloshes, give it longer; under-set egg will taste raw.
Lift the cups out and rest for 5 minutes, still covered, so carry-over heat finishes the middle without overcooking the surface.
Mix the date syrup with rose water, spoon it over the warm custards and scatter with pistachios. Add the nuts at the end so they stay crisp against the silk.

note: Lovely warm, but also good chilled for two hours if you want a firmer finish.

name: Tea-Smoked Lamb & Lentil Harira
hook: Campfire lamb over tomato-red lentils

steps.t: Mix the lamb mince with 1 tablespoon ras el hanout and a good pinch of salt, then roll into small walnut-sized balls. Pack them firmly; loose meatballs crack in the smoker and leak fat onto the tea.
Line a wok or deep pan with foil and add the tea leaves, rice and brown sugar. Set a rack or steamer insert above it, leaving space below so the smoking mix can smoulder rather than touch the lamb.

Put the lamb balls on the rack, cover tightly and heat until a thin stream of smoke appears, then smoke gently. They should turn bronze and smell like toasted mint; they are not fully cooked yet, so do not taste them.
Meanwhile, in a saucepan, cook the onion and carrot in the oil until the onion is soft and sweet at the edges. If the carrot is still hard now, it will stay oddly crunchy in the quick stew.
Stir in the remaining ras el hanout until it darkens and clings to the vegetables. Add the lentils, tomatoes and stock, scraping the base so the spices do not scorch.
Slide in the smoked lamb balls and simmer until the sauce thickens and the lamb is cooked through to the centre, with no pink remaining. A fierce boil will break the meatballs into mince.
Taste for salt, then finish with coriander. Let it stand for 2 minutes so the smoke settles into the broth instead of hitting the nose too sharply.

note: The smoking mix is for flavouring only; discard the foil and spent tea-rice mixture after cooking.

name: Sizzling Tadka Paneer Winter Chaat
hook: Sizzling ghee softens paneer into winter luxury

steps.t: Put the paneer in a wide shallow bowl, not a deep one; piled-up cubes stay cold in the middle and the hot tadka cannot kiss every edge.
Whisk the yoghurt with lemon juice, honey and a good pinch of salt until glossy. If it looks grainy, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water or it will cling in chalky patches.
Fold the yoghurt through the paneer with the pomegranate, coriander and half the walnuts. Use a spatula, not a spoon, so the paneer stays in plush cubes rather than rubble.
Heat the ghee in a small pan over medium heat, add the cumin and mustard seeds, and cook until the mustard pops and the cumin smells nutty; pull it early and the spices taste dusty.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chilli and garam masala, then immediately pour the foaming ghee over the paneer. Leave it too long in the pan and the chilli turns bitter.
Scatter over the remaining walnuts and serve at once, while the ghee is still fragrant and the paneer is only just warmed through.

note: Barely cooked by the hot spice ghee, so use fresh paneer and serve straight away.

name: Bangkok Basil Wok Eggs
hook: Crisp egg curds, chilli, morning basil

ingredients.name: spring onions, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.t: Beat the eggs with fish sauce, chilli jam and lime juice until no clear streaks remain; streaky whites set into rubbery threads in the wok.
Put the rice in bowls before you heat the wok. This dish waits for nothing, and cold bowls steal the steam from the eggs.
Heat the wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add the oil. If the oil only shimmers gently, the eggs will stew instead of puffing at the edges.
Add garlic and spring onions, stir-fry just until the garlic smells sweet and the onion tips blister; browned garlic will bully the basil.
Pour in the eggs and push them from the edge to the centre in big scoops. Stop when the curds are glossy and torn-looking, because dry curds keep cooking on the way to the bowl.
Toss through the tomatoes and Thai basil for a few seconds only, until the basil collapses and the tomatoes shine but do not dump their juice.
Slide the wok eggs over the hot rice, scraping out the chilli-stained oil from the bottom because that is the breakfast-making part.

note: Have every ingredient cut and measured before the wok goes on; high heat exposes hesitation.

name: Golden Dashimaki Tamago with Yuzu Daikon
hook: Silky rolled layers with a savoury sheen

steps.t: Beat the eggs gently with dashi, soy, mirin and sugar, then strain into a jug. Skip the straining and the white knots drag through the layers like elastic.
Grate the daikon, squeeze it lightly, and season with yuzu juice and a pinch of salt. If it is dripping wet, it will flood the plate beside the tamago.
Heat a rectangular tamago pan or small non-stick griddle over medium-low heat and wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Too much oil gives greasy blisters instead of satin layers.
Pour in a thin veil of egg, just enough to cover the base, and cook until the surface is softly set but still shiny. If it goes matte, the roll will crack.
Roll the egg towards you with chopsticks or a spatula, push it back to the far side, oil the bare pan, then add another thin veil so it runs under the roll.
Repeat until all the egg is used, keeping the heat gentle; fierce heat browns the outside before the centre layers can fuse.
Press the roll in a bamboo mat or clean tea towel for neat sides, then rest until warm rather than hot, because slicing a steaming roll squeezes out the dashi.
Slice into thick pieces and finish with yuzu daikon, nori threads and sesame, arranging the cut faces upward so guests see the fine layers.

note: A small non-stick frying pan works if you fold the sides in as you roll.

name: Crisp Courgette and Perilla Jeon
hook: Lace-crisp greens with a cool soy dip

steps.t: Toss the courgette with the salt and leave until it bends without snapping; if you skip this, the water leaks into the pan and the jeon turns flabby.
Squeeze the courgette firmly in a clean tea towel until it feels damp, not wet. Do not crush it to mush or you lose the clean summer bite.
Mix flour, potato starch and gochugaru, then whisk in the sparkling water only until lumpy. A smooth, overworked batter fries up tough rather than lacy.
Fold in the courgette, spring onions and perilla so everything is barely coated; batter pooling in the bowl means heavy pancakes.
Heat a film of oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat, then drop in small loose handfuls and press them thin. Thick mounds steam before they crisp.
Shallow fry until the edges go lace-brown and the underside releases cleanly, then turn once. Fiddling early tears the crust from the vegetables.
Fry the second side until crisp and audibly scratchy against the spatula, then drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, which traps steam underneath.
Stir soy sauce, rice vinegar and sesame seeds together, and serve the jeon hot with the dip on the side so the crisp edges stay sharp.

note: Perilla gives the most Korean fragrance; shiso or mint can stand in if needed.

name: Chinkiang-Pickled Cod with Ginger Oil
hook: Cool white flakes in black vinegar perfume

ingredients.name: fresh ginger, half sliced and half finely shredded
spring onions, whites bruised and greens finely sliced

steps.t: Season the fish with salt and Shaoxing wine, then lay it on a heatproof plate with the sliced ginger and bruised spring onion whites. Uneven seasoning leaves the flakes tasting flat after chilling.
Steam over briskly boiling water until the fish is opaque and flakes at the thickest point; undercooked fish is not safe for this cold plate, and overcooked fish turns woolly.
Lift the fish from the steamer, discard the ginger and onion, and cool for 10 minutes. Do not pour the steaming juices into the pickle or it will taste muddy.
Whisk Chinkiang vinegar, soy sauce and sugar until the sugar dissolves. If grains remain, the dressing catches harshly on the tongue.
Break the fish into large flakes, spoon over half the vinegar dressing, and chill until cool and lightly pickled; tiny flakes absorb too much acid and become sharp.
Arrange cucumber on a small platter, then place the pickled fish on top with its juices. Keep the cucumber underneath so it stays crisp rather than soaking limp.
Finish with shredded ginger, spring onion greens, chilli oil and sesame oil, then spoon over the remaining dressing at the table for a bright black-vinegar hit.

note: The fish is cooked before pickling, making it safe for a chilled shared plate.

name: Griddled Butternut with Za’atar Butter and Molasses Onions
hook: Charred edges, sweet-sour winter warmth.

ingredients.name: butternut squash, peeled and cut into 1.5 cm wedges
red onions, cut into thick petals

steps.t: Steam the squash wedges for 8 minutes, just until a knife goes in with a little resistance; take them too far and they will collapse on the griddle instead of charring.
Toss the warm squash and onion petals with the olive oil, cumin and salt, coating every cut face; dry patches scorch black before the middle warms through.
Heat a ridged griddle until a flick of water snaps away, then lay in the squash without crowding; if the pan is only warm, the squash sweats and turns woolly.
Griddle the squash in batches for about 3 minutes a side, until the ridges are dark and the edges look sticky, then move to a warm platter.
Griddle the onion petals until their tips blister and the centres slump; pull them early and they taste sharp rather than jammy.
Melt the butter with the za’atar, pomegranate molasses and a squeeze of lemon, then spoon it over the vegetables; boiling the molasses hard makes it bitter and tarry.
Finish with parsley and extra lemon zest, serving while the butter still shines; once it dulls, the dish loses its cosy gloss.

note: A warming vegetable centrepiece for cold evenings; good with warm flatbreads if you want a fuller plate.

name: Harissa Pork Breakfast Cakes with Runny Eggs
hook: Craggy potato crust, yolk, chilli warmth.

ingredients.name: preserved lemon, flesh discarded and rind finely chopped

steps.t: Boil the potatoes in salted water until the corners crumble and the centres are tender; undercooked chunks make the cakes split when they hit the oil.
Drain the potatoes and leave them in the hot pan for 2 minutes so steam escapes; wet mash gives you a soft, greasy crust.
Fry the pork mince with the onion, garlic, ras el hanout and harissa until the pan is dry and there is no pink meat left; any moisture left here will burst through the cakes later.
Roughly crush the potatoes, then fold in the cooked pork, preserved lemon, coriander and 1 beaten egg; mash too smooth and you lose the craggy edges that crisp best.
Shape into 8 squat cakes and dust lightly with flour, knocking off excess; a thick flour coat tastes pasty before it browns.
Shallow fry the cakes in hot sunflower oil until deep golden and crisp on both sides, lowering the heat if the harissa darkens before the middle is hot.
Fry the remaining eggs in the same pan and serve on top; keep the yolks soft, because they are the sauce for the spiced crust.

note: The Moroccan spicing is bold and breakfast-friendly, while the pork is fully cooked before the final crisping.

name: Sherry-Pickled King Oysters with Almond Picada
hook: Glossy mushrooms, sharp sherry, almond crunch.

steps.t: Slice the mushrooms lengthways into 5 mm planks; cut them thicker and the pickle only seasons the outside.
Sear the planks in a dry, wide pan until tan freckles appear and they bend without snapping; crowd the pan and they leak water instead of taking colour.
Bring the sherry vinegar, dry sherry, water, garlic, bay and salt to a brief simmer; boiling it hard drives off the sherry aroma you want to keep.
Pour the hot pickle over the mushrooms in a shallow dish and press them under the liquid; exposed pieces dry at the edges and look tired on the plate.
Chop the almonds with parsley, orange zest and smoked paprika, then stir through the olive oil; add the paprika to hot oil and it can turn bitter in seconds.
Lift the mushrooms from the pickle, lay them in glossy folds, and spoon the almond dressing over the top; drowning them in pickle makes the dressing slide off.
Finish with a little orange juice if the vinegar feels blunt; the final bite should be sharp first, then nutty.

note: Make the mushrooms a few hours ahead, but dress them close to serving so the almonds stay crisp.

name: Provençal Beef, Courgette and Tomato Gratin
hook: Juicy tomatoes keep lean beef tender.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C and oil a shallow baking dish; a deep dish traps steam and turns the gratin soupy.
Toss the tomatoes, courgettes and onion with 2 tbsp olive oil, half the salt and the herbes de Provence, then spread them in loose layers; tight stacks stay raw in the middle.
Bake the vegetables until tomato juices bubble at the edges and the courgettes just soften; adding the beef now would overcook it before the vegetables relax.
Rub the steaks with Dijon, garlic, the remaining oil and salt, then cut into broad ribbons across the grain; long fibres chew tough even when the beef is pink.
Nestle the beef ribbons into the hot tomato juices, leaving a few edges exposed; bury them completely and they stew grey instead of staying tender.
Scatter over the breadcrumbs and Comté, then bake until the crumbs are gold and the beef springs lightly when pressed.
Rest for 5 minutes and tear basil over the top; serving straight from the oven sends all the tomato juices across the plate.

note: Use ripe summer tomatoes rather than tinned ones; their acidity keeps the beef dish bright.

name: Old Bay Tomato-Braised Mackerel with Saltines
hook: Silky fish, peppery tomato, salty crunch.

steps.t: Pat the mackerel dry and check for pin bones with your fingertips; hidden bones are much harder to find once the fish is sauced.
Soften the onion and celery in olive oil until glossy and sweet-smelling, not brown; browned celery makes the braise taste muddy.
Add the garlic and Old Bay for 30 seconds, just until fragrant; let the spice catch on the pan and it turns harsh.
Stir in the tomatoes, lager, cider vinegar and brown sugar, then simmer until the beer foam disappears and the sauce tastes rounded rather than raw.
Slide in the mackerel skin-side down, spoon sauce over it, cover and braise on the lowest heat until the thickest flakes are opaque; a hard boil tightens the fish and leaks its oil into the sauce.
Rest off the heat, covered, so the fish relaxes and takes on the tomato seasoning; stirring now will break it into shreds.
Spoon into a shallow serving bowl, scatter with dill and pile saltines alongside; the crackers matter because the braise is soft, rich and made for scooping.

note: Serve warm rather than piping hot, as the mackerel tastes silkier once the tomato braise has settled.

name: Pampas Tofu Locro
hook: Smoky squash, corn and golden tofu

ingredients.name: butternut squash, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: Pat the tofu very dry, then tear it into rough thumb-sized pieces; damp tofu turns spongy in the stew instead of holding golden edges.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan and sear the tofu until the torn edges are chestnut-speckled; crowding the pan makes it steam and shed water.
Lift out the tofu, add the remaining oil, onion, pepper and garlic, and cook until the onion smells sweet and the pepper softens; rushing this leaves the stew harsh and raw-tasting.
Stir in the squash, paprika, cumin and salt until the cubes are brick-red and glossy; dry spices left on the pan base scorch bitterly within seconds.
Add the stock, beans, sweetcorn and tofu, then simmer gently until the squash edges crush easily against the spoon; a hard boil breaks the tofu and makes the squash woolly.
Mash a ladleful of squash and beans against the side of the pan, stir it back through and serve thick; skipping this leaves a brothy soup rather than a locro-style stew.

note: Fast, smoky and filling, with tofu taking the place of the usual cured meats.

name: Bahian Orange-Rubbed Whole Lamb Leg
hook: Citrus smoke, sticky edges, tender slices

steps.t: Blend the garlic, orange zest and juice, lime juice, cachaça, oil, coriander, cumin, paprika and salt to a vivid orange paste; under-salting now means the centre of the lamb stays flat however good the crust looks.
Make deep, narrow cuts all over the whole lamb leg and work the paste right into them, then cover and chill; shallow slashes only season the surface and leave bland grey tunnels inside.
Take the lamb out of the fridge and leave it covered on the counter for an hour; roasting it fridge-cold tightens the outside before the heat reaches the bone.
Set the potatoes in a deep roasting tin, put the lamb on top, scrape over every drop of marinade and cover tightly with foil; exposed garlic paste burns black before the meat has softened.
Roast at 150°C until the meat gives when pressed and the potatoes are sitting in orange lamb juices; if the tray looks dry, add a splash of water or the sugars will weld to the tin.
Remove the foil, raise the oven to 220°C and roast until the fat is lacquered and the potato corners are sticky-dark; pulling it before this stage makes the joint taste steamed rather than roasted.
Rest the whole leg loosely covered, then carve across the grain in broad slices; carving straight from the oven sends the juices over the board instead of through the meat.

note: A Brazilian-leaning celebration roast built around cachaça, citrus and garlic, sized for leftovers.

name: Dhungar Chana Dal Bowl
hook: Charcoal perfume over thick, peppery dal

steps.t: Rinse the chana dal and red lentils until the water is only faintly cloudy; leaving the starch on gives a foamy, dusty-tasting pot.
Simmer the pulses with the turmeric in 1 litre of water until the red lentils collapse and the chana dal is tender but still nubbly; a hard boil bursts the outside while the centres stay chalky.
Meanwhile fry the onion in the oil until the edges are deep gold and slightly frilled; pale onion leaves the finished dal sweet and canteen-like.
Add the ginger-garlic paste, tomatoes, chillies and coriander-cumin, then cook until the tomatoes slump and the oil freckles the surface; watery masala makes the dal taste raw and thin.
Stir the masala and salt into the pulses and simmer to a spoon-coating thickness; if you let the base get too thick now, it catches on the bottom and tastes scorched.
Heat the natural charcoal until ashed over, sit it in a small foil cup on top of the dal, drip on a few drops of oil and cover; do not use self-lighting briquettes or let charcoal touch the food.
Remove the charcoal, swirl in the yoghurt off the heat and serve while glossy; boiling after the yoghurt goes in can split it into grainy flecks.

note: Chana dal, red lentils and yoghurt make this a sturdy post-training bowl without relying on meat.

name: Saigon Coffee Caramel Egg Custards
hook: Bitter coffee, wobbling satin custard

steps.t: Cook the sugar and water in a small pan until the syrup turns clear copper and smells nutty; pale caramel tastes flat, while black caramel will dominate the custard with bitterness.
Immediately divide the caramel between six ramekins and tilt to coat the bases; if you hesitate, it sets in a thick puddle before it spreads.
Warm the milk, condensed milk and coffee until steaming, not boiling; boiling dairy poured onto eggs gives sweet scrambled egg strands.
Whisk the eggs, yolks and salt gently, then slowly whisk in the warm coffee milk; beating in too much air leaves pockmarks instead of a satin wobble.
Strain the custard into the ramekins and cover each with foil; unstrained egg whites and bubbles show up as lumps on the spoon.
Steam over the lowest steady heat until the centres tremble like soft jelly; a raging boil honeycombs the custard and makes it weep.
Chill until cold, then loosen the edges and turn out onto plates; unmoulding warm custards makes them slump and spill the caramel unevenly.

note: This is in the spirit of Vietnamese bánh flan, with coffee folded into the custard rather than just poured over.

name: Sicilian Coal-Grilled Mussels with Lemon Crumbs
hook: Briny shells, hot crumbs, lemon smoke

ingredients.name: lemon, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Light the coals and let them settle to a grey, medium-hot bed; flames lick soot onto the shells and scorch the crumbs before the mussels open.
Scrub and debeard the mussels, discarding cracked ones and any open shells that do not close when tapped; keeping doubtful mussels is not worth the food-safety risk.
Pulse the bread, garlic, lemon zest, parsley, chilli, oil and salt into damp rough crumbs; dry crumbs fall through the grate and burn instead of crisping.
Set a cast-iron pan or grill tray over the coals, add the mussels and tomatoes, cover with a lid and shake once; leaving them uncovered makes them open slowly and turn rubbery.
When most shells have opened, scatter over the crumbs and grill uncovered until the crumbs are crisp and the tomato juices hiss; discard any mussels that stay shut.
Squeeze over lemon and eat straight from the pan with the smoky crumbs; letting cooked mussels sit around makes them shrink and toughen.

note: Mussels keep the cost student-friendly while still feeling like a proper coal-grilled supper.

name: Lahori Crisp Egg Shami Patties
hook: Golden edges, cumin heat, soft egg centres

steps.t: Put 3 eggs in a small pan, cover with cold water and bring to a boil; once bubbling, set a timer for firm yolks, because soft yolks make the patties split in the pan.
Cool the boiled eggs under running water, peel and chop them into pea-sized pieces; do not mash them to paste or the filling turns rubbery instead of softly chunky.

Mash the chickpeas in a bowl until mostly crushed with a few rough bits left, then mix in onion, chilli, coriander, cumin, garam masala, salt, gram flour and the chopped eggs; if it feels wet and slumps, add another spoon of gram flour or it will shed crumbs in the oil.
Beat the remaining egg in a shallow bowl, shape the mixture into 6 squat patties, and brush or dip them lightly with the beaten egg; thick egg coating burns before the middle warms through.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat until a crumb sizzles straight away, then lay in the patties with space between them; crowding drops the heat and gives you greasy, pale sides.
Fry until the undersides are deep golden with crisp, lace-brown edges, then turn once and cook the second side; keep flipping and they will crack before a crust forms.
Drain on kitchen paper for 1 minute, then serve with lemon wedges while the crust still taps under a fork; leave them stacked and the steam softens all your work.

note: Good with plain yoghurt and sliced cucumber if you want to stretch it into a bigger dinner.

name: Kerala Steamed Cardamom Caramel Custard
hook: Silky wobble, dark caramel, warm cardamom

steps.t: Put the sugar and water in a small pan and cook over medium heat without stirring until the syrup turns deep amber at the edges; stirring throws crystals up the sides and gives you gritty caramel.
Immediately pour the caramel into a 1 litre heatproof pudding basin and swirl to coat the base; wait too long and it sets in one thick lump.
Whisk the eggs just until the yolks and whites disappear together, not until foamy; foam steams into bubbles and ruins the smooth wobble.
Warm the milk, condensed milk, cardamom, vanilla and salt until hand-hot, then whisk it slowly into the eggs; boiling milk will scramble the eggs into sweet flecks.
Strain the custard into the caramel-lined basin and cover tightly with foil; unstrained chalazae and cardamom husks spoil the silkiness.
Set the basin on a trivet in a large pan with simmering water halfway up the sides, cover the pan, and steam gently until the custard has a soft central wobble; a hard boil punches holes through it.
Cool for 30 minutes, then chill until fully cold before turning out; unmoulding warm custard makes the caramel run thin and the sides slump.

note: Make it the day before if you can; the caramel melts into a better sauce overnight.

name: Bangkok Beef & Cabbage Pot Stew
hook: Peppery broth, tender beef, sweet cabbage

ingredients.name: beef shin or stewing beef, cut into 3 cm chunks
white cabbage, cut into thick wedges

steps.t: Pat the beef dry and season lightly, then brown it in the oil in a heavy pan until the corners are dark and sticky; damp beef boils grey and leaves the stew tasting flat.
Lower the heat, add garlic, crushed pepper and curry paste, and fry until the paste stains the oil red and smells roasted; if it catches black, the whole pot turns bitter.
Add fish sauce, dark soy, sugar and 900 ml water, scraping the browned bits from the base; leave those stuck on the pan and you lose the cheap flavour boost.
Cover and simmer gently until the beef can be pressed with a spoon but is not falling apart; a rolling boil tightens shin into dry strings.
Add potatoes and cabbage wedges, pushing them under the broth as much as possible; if the cabbage sits dry on top, it stays squeaky and raw-tasting.
Simmer uncovered until the potatoes are tender and the cabbage has gone sweet at the thick ribs, while the broth reduces slightly.
Taste before serving, then sharpen with lime and scatter over coriander; adding lime early cooks away its lift and makes the stew taste muddy.

note: Serve with rice if you need more portions; the broth is built to stretch.

name: Aleppo Butter Prawn Saç Tava
hook: Hot pan, sweet prawns, peppery butter

ingredients.name: raw king prawns, peeled and deveined

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry and salt them lightly; if they go into the pan wet, they steam grey instead of catching sweet bronze spots.
Heat a wide frying pan or wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add the olive oil; a lukewarm pan gives you rubbery prawns and soft vegetables.
Throw in the pepper and onion and stir-fry hard until the onion edges blister and the pepper skins wrinkle, keeping everything moving so the garlic later has room to fry rather than burn.
Add the garlic, tomato paste and pul biber, scraping the paste across the hot metal until it darkens brick-red; stop before the garlic turns bitter brown.
Add the prawns in one layer and stir-fry until they curl into loose Cs and turn opaque at the thickest part; tight Os mean they have gone too far.

Drop in the butter and toss until it foams into a glossy red sauce clinging to the prawns, then squeeze over lemon and fold through parsley; if the butter splits, the pan was left raging too long after the prawns were cooked.

note: Serve straight away with bread or rice; prawns wait for nobody.

name: Sumac Onion Halloumi Taboon
hook: Smoky cheese over pillowy warm bread

steps.t: Mix flour, yeast, salt, 2 tbsp olive oil and warm water into a shaggy dough, then knead until it feels smooth and elastic; if it tears like wet paper, it needs more kneading, not more flour.
Cover and leave the dough until doubled and puffy, with a finger dent that slowly springs back; if it has not risen, the breads will griddle dense and leathery.
Cook the onions gently in 2 tbsp olive oil with a pinch of salt until soft, jammy and pale gold, then stir in the sumac off the heat; rushing this gives harsh onion rather than sweet musakhan depth.
Divide the dough into four balls, rest them briefly, then roll into thin ovals; if you roll without resting, they snap back and cook thick in the middle.
Griddle each bread on a very hot dry pan until bubbled, smoky-spotted and cooked through, flipping once; pale floppy patches mean raw dough, black dust means the pan is too fierce.
Griddle the halloumi until the ridges are deep gold and the centres slump slightly; move it too early and the crust tears onto the pan.

Spread yoghurt over the breads, pile on sumac onions and halloumi, then finish with lemon juice, parsley and pomegranate molasses; adding the yoghurt before the breads cool a touch makes it split and run.

note: The weekend part is the bread and onions; the final griddle is quick and theatrical.

name: Chermoula Pork Schnitzel Bowl
hook: Crisp edges, lean heat, herby lift

steps.t: Put the pork between baking paper and bash to an even 7 mm thickness; thick patches stay tough and under-seasoned while thin patches overcook.
Mix cumin, paprika, ground coriander, lemon zest, garlic, chopped coriander and a good pinch of salt into the breadcrumbs; if the seasoning sits only on the meat, most of it falls off in the oil.
Beat the egg in a shallow bowl, dip the pork, then press firmly into the spiced crumbs until every wet patch is covered; bare spots fry hard and dry instead of crisp.
Heat the oil in a frying pan until a breadcrumb fizzes immediately, then lay in the pork away from you; cold oil soaks the coating, smoking oil scorches the spices.
Shallow fry until the underside is crisp and deep golden at the edges, then turn once and cook until the pork is just cooked through with no pink centre, or 63°C if using a thermometer.
Rest the schnitzels on a rack, not kitchen paper, so steam escapes; trapping them on paper softens the crust you worked for.
Fluff the couscous with lemon juice, cucumber and a little salt, then slice the pork on top; cutting before resting floods the board and dries the meat.

note: Lean loin keeps the protein high; the shallow fry is for crunch, not greasiness.

name: Orange Caramel Steamed Flan
hook: Silky custard under bitter orange caramel

steps.t: Put 120 g sugar and the water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup turns deep amber at the edges; stirring makes it crystallise into sandy lumps.
Swirl in a squeeze of orange juice if you like, then divide the caramel between four ramekins, tilting quickly before it sets glass-hard; touch nothing with fingers, caramel burns viciously.
Warm the milk with the orange zest until steaming and fragrant, then let it stand off the heat; boiling milk gives the flan a cooked, eggy smell later.
Whisk eggs, yolks, 60 g sugar, vanilla and salt just until smooth, then slowly whisk in the warm milk; frothing hard traps bubbles that steam into little holes.
Strain the custard into the caramel ramekins and cover each with foil; unstrained zest and egg strands spoil the silky set.
Set the ramekins in a steamer over barely simmering water and steam until the edges are set but the centres wobble like soft jelly; a hard boil makes the custard curdle and weep.
Cool, then chill before unmoulding with a thin knife; turning out while warm makes the flan slump instead of standing cleanly in its caramel.

note: Classic flan texture comes from gentle steam, not speed.

name: Snow-Day Milk-Braised Cod with Leeks and Potatoes
hook: Soft cod, sweet leeks, woolly warmth

ingredients.name: thick cod loin or haddock fillet, skinless
waxy potatoes, cut into 2 cm chunks
lemon, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Melt the butter in a wide casserole over a low-medium heat, then add the leeks, celery and a pinch of salt. Cook until the leeks slump glossy and smell sweet; if they catch brown now, the braise will taste scorched rather than cosy.
Stir in the potatoes, bay and thyme, coating every piece in the leeky butter. Let the potatoes turn shiny at the edges; skipping this leaves them tasting boiled and separate from the pot.
Pour in the milk and stock, then bring just to a lazy simmer with small bubbles at the edge. Do not boil hard or the milk can split and the fish will later toughen.

Cover with the lid slightly ajar and braise gently until a potato chunk crushes easily against the side of the pan. Keep the surface barely trembling; a rolling boil will make the potatoes ragged and grainy.
Whisk a ladleful of hot liquid with the Dijon, then stir it back into the pot. Adding mustard straight in can clump and give sharp little pockets instead of mellow warmth.

Season the cod with salt, lay it on top of the potatoes, cover and cook until the flakes part with a spoon but still look pearly in the centre. If you wait until it looks dry-white all through, it is already overcooked.
Lift out the bay and thyme, fold in parsley and lemon zest, then rest off the heat for 3 minutes before serving with lemon wedges. Stirring hard at the end will break the cod into stringy shreds.

note: For a thicker bowl, crush a few potato pieces into the milk before adding the fish.

name: Rio Whole-Roasted Picanha with Lime Farofa Crust
hook: Carved pink, crackling fat, citrus crumbs

ingredients.name: whole picanha beef joint, fat cap intact
small red chilli, deseeded and finely chopped

steps.t: Take the picanha out of the fridge and pat it very dry, especially the fat cap. Wet beef steams before it roasts, so the prized cap stays rubbery instead of blistering.
Score the fat cap in a shallow diamond pattern without cutting into the meat, then rub all over with salt, pepper, garlic and olive oil. Cut too deep and the juices run out through the score marks.
Heat the oven to 220°C and set the beef fat-side up on a rack over a tray. The rack matters: sitting in its own juices makes the underside grey and flabby.
Roast until the fat cap is sizzling and patched deep gold, then lower the oven to 160°C. If the cap is still pale at this point, the final roast will not rescue it.
Continue roasting until the centre reaches 52°C for medium-rare, checking with a probe in the thickest part, not the fat. Guessing by colour from the outside is how good picanha becomes dry picanha.

Rest the beef loosely under foil while you make the farofa: melt the butter, stir in cassava flour, lime zest and chilli, and toast until sandy and nut-brown. Stop while it still smells buttery; over-toasted cassava tastes like burnt popcorn.
Slice the picanha across the grain into thick rosy slices, spoon over lime juice and scatter with coriander and farofa. Slicing with the grain leaves even perfect beef chewy.

note: A probe thermometer is the difference between impressive and apologetic here.

name: Lahore Dhungar Mackerel Kachumber Plate
hook: Cool crunch, smoky chilli, silver fish

steps.t: Rub the mackerel with oil, chilli, coriander, cumin, salt and half the lemon juice, then leave it while the grill heats. Do not marinate for ages; the lemon starts curing the surface and makes the fish woolly.
Mix cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, mint, the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Dress it just before serving if your tomatoes are very ripe, because early salt can flood the plate.

Grill the mackerel skin-side up first until the flesh turns opaque at the edges, then flip and crisp the skin until it blisters. If you start skin-side down on a weak grill, it welds itself to the bars.
Move the cooked fish to a wide lidded pan or heatproof bowl, leaving space in the middle for a small metal cup. Keep the fillets in one layer; stacking them traps steam and softens the skin.
Heat the charcoal over a gas flame or with a blowtorch until one edge glows red and ashy. Do not use self-lighting barbecue coals indoors; they give off chemical smoke you do not want on food.

Set the hot charcoal in the metal cup, spoon the ghee onto it, and cover the pan immediately so the smoke stays with the fish, not your ceiling. A loose lid gives you fragrance in the kitchen and almost none on the mackerel.
Lift the fish onto the kachumber, spoon over any smoky juices, and serve while the salad is still cold against the warm fish. Waiting too long turns the crisp summer plate oily and dull.

note: If charcoal smoking is impractical, use plain hot-smoked mackerel and warm it briefly, but the dhungar aroma will be softer.

name: Saigon Steamed Silken Tofu with Ginger Scallion Oil
hook: Quivering tofu, hot ginger, bright soy

ingredients.name: silken tofu, drained in one block if possible
fresh ginger, cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: Slide the tofu onto a shallow heatproof plate and blot the top gently with kitchen paper. Pressing hard cracks it, and those cracks leak water into the sauce.
Set the plate in a steamer over simmering water, cover, and steam until the tofu is hot and trembling all the way through. A violent boil splashes water onto the plate and dilutes everything.
Meanwhile stir soy sauce, lime juice, sugar and rice vinegar until the sugar disappears. If grains remain, the dressing tastes sharp in one spoonful and sweet in the next.
Carefully pour away the clear water that has gathered around the tofu. Skip this and the finished plate tastes washed-out, no matter how good the oil is.
Scatter spring onions and ginger over the tofu, keeping a small mound in the centre so the hot oil hits it properly. Spread too thin and the aromatics warm rather than sizzle.

Heat the neutral oil and sesame oil until the surface shimmers and a ginger strand dropped in fizzes at once. If the oil smokes heavily it will taste burnt; if it is too cool, the ginger stays raw and harsh.

Spoon the hot oil over the ginger and spring onions, then pour the soy-lime dressing around the tofu, not directly over the top. Finish with chilli and coriander so the herbs stay vivid instead of wilting black.

note: Serve with small spoons so everyone gets tofu, aromatic oil and dressing in one scoop.

name: Coal-Kissed Lamb Scottadito with Anchovy Beans
hook: Smoke, lemon, lamb fat, done fast

steps.t: Light a small bed of charcoal first; if the coals are still black and flaming, the lamb will taste sooty rather than smoky.
Rub the lamb with 1 tbsp oil, garlic, rosemary, lemon zest, salt and pepper; do not leave thick clumps of garlic on the meat or they will burn bitter on the grill.
Warm the beans in a small pan with the remaining oil, anchovy and a splash of water until creamy at the edges; if they look dry and separate, add another spoon of water and mash a few beans.
Grill the cutlets over ash-grey coals until the fat hisses and the edges are darkly freckled, turning once; move them aside if flames lick the meat or the fat will scorch.
Rest the lamb on a warm plate with the cut lemon halves squeezed over; cutting straight away sends the juices onto the board instead of into the meat.
Spoon the anchovy beans onto plates, fold rocket through at the last second so it wilts but stays peppery, then sit the lamb on top.

note: Best with thin lamb cutlets; thick chops push this beyond weeknight speed.

name: Malabar Lime-Cured Scallop Chaat with Coconut and Green Mango
hook: Cool scallops, mustard crackle, mango bite

ingredients.name: green mango, peeled and finely diced

steps.t: Buy scallops sold for raw eating, keep them fridge-cold, and smell them before you start; if they smell fishy or ammoniac, do not try to rescue them with lime.
Mix salt and sugar, coat the scallops lightly, cover and chill; too much cure time makes the outside tight and hammy while the centre stays bland.
Rinse the scallops quickly in iced water, pat completely dry, then chill uncovered on a plate; if they are wet, the lime dressing will turn watery.
Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil, add mustard seeds and curry leaves, and pull the pan off once the seeds pop and the leaves go glassy; take them dark and the whole chaat tastes burnt.

Dice the scallops into neat nuggets and fold with lime juice, coconut, mango, onion, chilli, coriander and the cooled tempering; dress them no more than 10 minutes before serving or the acid will chalk the flesh.
Fold in puffed rice right at the end so it crackles; if it sits in the bowl, it collapses into damp cereal.

note: Use only scallops specifically suitable for raw consumption and keep everything very cold.

name: Lean Thai Basil Chicken Wok with Crunchy Beans
hook: Hot basil steam, clean chilli heat

ingredients.name: green beans, cut into short lengths

steps.t: Stir fish sauce, oyster sauce and sugar together before the wok heats; hunting for bottles later means the chicken overcooks while you hesitate.
Blot the chicken dry and spread it in a thin layer on a tray; damp strips steam grey instead of searing cleanly.
Heat the wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add oil, garlic and chilli; if the garlic turns chestnut before the chicken goes in, tip it out and start again because it will be bitter.
Add chicken in one layer and leave it until the underside turns opaque with golden catches; stirring too soon makes it leak juices and toughen.
Throw in the beans and toss hard over the highest heat until they are bright green with blistered spots; limp olive beans mean the pan was crowded or too cool.
Pour in the sauce and toss until it clings in shiny streaks, not a puddle; boil it too long and the breast meat dries fast.
Turn off the heat, fold through Thai basil until just collapsed, and serve with lime; cooking the basil on the flame kills its aniseed lift.

note: Eat as is for a lean bowl, or add cooked jasmine rice if you need more carbs.

name: Silken Matcha Egg Custard with Black Sugar Syrup
hook: Soft green custard, dark caramel gloss

steps.t: Whisk matcha with a spoonful of warm milk to a smooth paste first; dry lumps never disappear once the eggs are in.
Warm milk, cream, caster sugar and vanilla until steaming but not bubbling, then whisk into the eggs slowly; boiling dairy scrambles the eggs into sweet soup.
Strain the custard into four small cups and skim off foam; bubbles left on top set into pockmarks rather than a lacquered surface.
Cover each cup with foil, set in a steamer over the gentlest simmer, and keep the lid slightly ajar; furious steam makes the custard split and honeycomb.
Check by nudging a cup: the centre should wobble like soft jelly, not slosh; if it ripples wetly, steam a little longer.
Simmer muscovado sugar with water until glossy and lightly thickened; take it too far and it sets like treacle on the cold custard.
Cool the custards for at least 10 minutes, then spoon over syrup and strawberries; adding fruit while hot makes it bleed and slump.

note: Serve barely warm for the softest texture, or chill for a firmer pudding.

name: Crisp Gochujang Paneer Coins with Sesame Cabbage
hook: Sticky red edges, squeaky golden centres

steps.t: Pat the paneer dry, then dust every side with cornflour; wet paneer sheds its crust and spits oil across the hob.
Stir gochujang, soy, honey, garlic and 2 tbsp water into a loose glaze; if it is thick like paste, it will burn before it coats.
Toss cabbage, spring onions and sesame seeds in a bowl with a spoon of the glaze; drowning the cabbage now makes the plate soggy.
Heat oil in a frying pan until a pinch of cornflour fizzes, then lay in the paneer with space between pieces; crowding drops the heat and gives you rubbery white cubes.
Fry until the undersides are crisp and biscuit-gold, then turn once and repeat; keep flipping and the crust tears off.
Pour off excess oil, lower the heat, add the glaze and roll the paneer until the edges go sticky and brick-red; high heat at this point scorches the chilli paste.
Pile sesame cabbage into bowls and top with the paneer while it still crackles; wait too long and the sauce softens the crust.

note: Paneer is cheapest from South Asian grocers; halloumi also works but costs more and tastes saltier.

name: Miso-Butter Whole Mackerel with Winter Daikon
hook: Rich smoke, sweet daikon, lacquered winter fish

ingredients.name: mackerel, gutted and scaled, about 350 g each

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan and put a heavy roasting tray inside; a cold tray steams the fish before the skin has a chance to tighten and crisp.
Score each mackerel three times on both sides, then rub the fish and belly cavities with 1 tsp salt. Cut right to the bone, not just the skin, or the fish curls and cooks unevenly.

Toss the daikon with the remaining salt and spread it on the hot tray. Roast until the undersides are honey-gold and the centres give slightly to a knife; pale daikon will taste watery under the fish.
Mash the miso, butter, mirin, soy and ginger into a glossy paste. If the butter is fridge-cold, the glaze sits in lumps and scorches in patches.
Lay the whole mackerel on the daikon and roast until the eyes turn opaque and the skin is taut and blistered at the scores. If the belly still looks glassy, it is not ready for glazing.
Brush the miso butter over the fish and roast again until the glaze bubbles at the edges like caramel. Take it too far and the miso turns bitter before the flesh benefits.
Rest the fish on the tray, then scatter with spring onions and serve with lemon. Move it too soon and the soft belly flesh tears away from the bones.

note: Best with hot rice and a bowl of miso soup; lift the fillets away from the backbone at the table.

name: Gochujang-Smoked Mackerel Breakfast Rice
hook: Warm rice, smoky fish, sharp kimchi

steps.t: Rub the mackerel with salt, sugar and gochugaru, then leave it skin-side up. This short cure seasons the oily flesh; leave it much longer and it eats tight and hammy.
Rinse the fillets briefly and pat them very dry with kitchen paper. Wet fish makes sour, dirty smoke and the skin sticks to the rack.
Line a wok with foil, add the smoking chips and set a rack above them. Heat until a thin blue smoke appears; thick grey smoke means the chips are burning too hard and will taste acrid.

Put the mackerel on the rack, cover tightly and hot-smoke over medium heat until the thickest part is opaque and flakes cleanly. If the lid leaks, the fish cooks patchily and your kitchen gets the smoke instead.
Turn off the heat and rest the covered fish so the smoke settles into the flesh. Opening straight away lets the aroma vanish and leaves the surface harsh.
Fry the eggs until the whites are set with crisp lacy edges. If the pan is too cool, the whites turn rubbery before the edges colour.
Divide the hot rice between bowls, add kimchi, the smoked mackerel, eggs, spring onions, sesame oil, soy and sesame seeds. Flake the fish at the last moment so it stays juicy, not chalky.

note: Use a well-ventilated kitchen and check the fish is fully opaque before serving.

name: Lotus-Steamed Cumin Lamb with Pearl Rice
hook: Silken lamb under a lotus-scented veil

ingredients.name: boneless lamb shoulder, sliced 5 mm thick across the grain

steps.t: Soak the lotus leaves in hot water until pliable and tea-green. If they stay brittle, they crack in the steamer and the perfume escapes with the steam.
Toast the glutinous rice with cumin seeds and five-spice in a dry pan until the grains smell nutty and turn ivory at the tips. Burnt rice makes the whole dish taste dusty.
Pulse the toasted rice to coarse crumbs, stopping before it becomes flour. Powder turns into glue around the lamb instead of a pearly coating.
Mix lamb with doubanjiang, soy, Shaoxing wine, ginger, garlic and sugar, then fold in the rice crumbs until every slice is speckled. Bare patches steam grey and taste under-seasoned.
Line a wide steamer basket with the softened lotus leaves, pile in the lamb loosely and fold the leaves over the top. Pack it flat and tight and the centre stays chewy while the edges overcook.
Steam over a steady simmer until the lamb is tender enough to pinch apart and the rice coating has swollen translucent. Let the pan boil dry and the lotus leaf scorches bitterly.
Tuck the pak choi around the parcel for the final few minutes, then open the lotus leaves at the table. Add the greens too early and they collapse into khaki threads.

note: Serve with black vinegar and chilli oil on the side for guests who want a sharper finish.

name: Coal-Blackened Broad Beans with Lime Crema
hook: Charred pods, cool lime, sunny crunch

ingredients.name: fresh broad beans in their pods

steps.t: Light the charcoal and wait until the coals are glowing with a grey ash coat. Flames lick the pods black before the beans inside have softened.
Toss the broad bean pods with olive oil and salt so they shine lightly, not drip. Too much oil flares on the coals and tastes sooty.
Grill the pods in a single layer, turning often, until the skins blister, the seams slacken and the beans inside feel plump when pressed. Crowding them makes them steam rather than char.
Stir lime zest, half the lime juice, soured cream and jalapeño into a loose crema. If it is mixed too early with all the lime, it can split and taste sharp rather than bright.
Split the hot pods and pop the beans into a bowl; peel only the largest grey skins if they feel leathery. Peeling every bean makes the plate fussy and cold.
Fold the beans with cotija, coriander, epazote, radishes and the remaining lime juice. Crush them and you lose the summer snap that keeps the dish light.
Spoon the lime crema over a platter and tumble the warm beans on top. Serve while the char still smells sweet, before the herbs wilt.

note: Choose young broad beans if you can; older pods still work, but peel more of the inner skins.

name: Ouzo-Cured Mackerel with Cucumber and Dill
hook: Cold mackerel, ouzo lift, lemony snap

ingredients.name: previously frozen sashimi-grade mackerel fillets, skinless and pin-boned
small red onion, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Keep the mackerel fridge-cold while you check again for pin bones. Do not use never-frozen fresh mackerel for this raw cure, as oily fish can carry parasites.
Mix salt, sugar and lemon zest, then coat the fillets evenly and set them on a cold plate. Thin spots over-cure quickly, so do not mound the cure at the tail ends.
Rinse the cure off quickly under cold water and pat the fish completely dry. Lingering grains make the first bite harsh and wet fish dilutes the dressing.
Slice the mackerel on a shallow angle into glossy 5 mm pieces. Sawing straight down bruises the flesh and gives ragged, metallic-tasting edges.
Whisk lemon juice, ouzo and olive oil, then fold in red onion and capers briefly. Leave the fish sitting in this too long and the acid bleaches it chalky.
Arrange cucumber, mackerel slices, dill and barley rusks on a shared plate, then spoon over the ouzo dressing. Dress the rusks at the end or they turn to paste before they reach the table.

note: Serve the same day, well chilled, with olives and small glasses of the remaining ouzo.

name: Crisp Moroccan Beef Kefta Coins
hook: Spiced edges, juicy middles, lemon snap

steps.t: Squeeze the grated onion hard in your fist over the sink; if it goes in wet, the kefta mixture steams and splits instead of crisping.
Mix beef, squeezed onion, garlic, parsley, spices, flour and 1 tsp salt with your fingers just until tacky; overworking makes the coins bouncy rather than tender.
Shape into 10 small, flat coins about 1 cm thick; thick patties brown outside before the centre is hot enough.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat until a pinch of mixture sizzles immediately; if the oil is quiet, the meat will shed juice and boil.
Fry the coins in one layer until the undersides are deep chestnut with crisp lacy edges, then turn once; crowding the pan drops the heat and gives grey kefta.
Cook the second side until firm with a little spring and no raw softness in the centre; keep flipping and they will lose their crust.
Rest on kitchen paper for 2 minutes, then squeeze over lemon at the table; lemon too early softens the crust you just made.

note: Serve with warm flatbread, yoghurt and a chopped tomato salad if you want to stretch it.

name: Weekend Escabeche Steamed Mackerel
hook: Silky fish under sharp saffron oil

steps.t: Salt the mackerel on both sides and chill uncovered; this firms the flesh, while skipping it leaves the fish fragile and watery in the steamer.
Warm the olive oil in a saucepan, then soften onion, carrot, garlic and bay until glossy and sweet-smelling without browning; browned garlic turns the escabeche bitter.
Stir in paprika and saffron for 20 seconds only, then add wine and vinegar; frying paprika longer makes it dusty and burnt.
Simmer the marinade until the onion is floppy and the vinegar sting mellows but still pricks your nose; reducing it too far makes the fish taste harshly salty.
Set the mackerel skin-side down in a steamer, cover and steam gently until the flakes separate when nudged at the thick end; a rolling boil knocks the oily fish apart.
Lift the hot fillets into a shallow dish and spoon the warm escabeche over them; pouring cold marinade on hot fish makes the oil sit separately instead of soaking in.
Leave at room temperature for 1 hour, then chill for at least 45 minutes; eating it straight away misses the point, because the acid needs time to season the fish through.
Bring back to cool room temperature, scatter with parsley and spoon over the orange oil; fridge-cold mackerel tastes waxy and muted.

note: Best with boiled potatoes, crusty bread and a slow weekend appetite.

name: Coal-Grilled Dijon Tofu Steaks
hook: Smoke, mustard crust, clean protein bite

steps.t: Press the tofu between towels under a heavy pan until the towels are damp; unpressed tofu steams on the grill and never takes smoke properly.
Cut the tofu into 4 thick steaks and whisk mustard, soy, oil, lemon, maple syrup, garlic and herbs into a paste; a runny marinade drips into the coals before it flavours anything.
Coat the tofu and leave it while the coals burn down to a white ash with no tall flames; cooking over flames scorches the mustard before the centre warms.
Oil the grill bars lightly, then lay on the tofu and do not move it until dark grill marks release cleanly; prying early tears off the crust.
Turn with a thin spatula and grill the second side until the edges look dry and lightly blistered; if the tofu still looks wet, it will taste bland and cold inside.
At the same time, grill the green beans in a perforated tray until blistered in spots but still squeaky; leave them too long and they collapse to khaki strings.
Rest the tofu for 3 minutes, then top with chopped cornichons and any remaining mustard paste kept separate from raw tofu contact; cutting immediately spills moisture onto the plate.

note: Add boiled new potatoes if you need more post-training carbohydrates.

name: Bourbon Vanilla Steamed Custard Cups
hook: Soft wobble, caramel warmth, satin spoonfuls

steps.t: Put caster sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until amber like strong tea; stirring throws crystals up the sides and makes the caramel grainy.
Divide the caramel between 4 heatproof ramekins, swirling just enough to cover the bases; touching it with a finger or tasting now will burn badly.
Warm milk and cream until steaming at the edge, not boiling; boiled dairy gives the custard a cooked, cabbagey smell.
Whisk eggs, yolks, brown sugar, vanilla, bourbon and salt until smooth, then slowly whisk in the hot dairy; adding it all at once scrambles the eggs.
Strain into the ramekins and cover each tightly with foil; unstrained chalazae and foam leave white flecks and bubbles in the finished custard.
Steam over a gentle simmer until the edges are set and the centres tremble like jelly, not liquid; hard boiling makes tunnels and a rubbery texture.
Rest off the heat, still covered, so the centres finish softly; uncovering straight away drops water onto the custards.
Chill, then run a thin knife round each cup and invert; forcing them out warm breaks the custard before the caramel loosens.

note: Use apple juice instead of bourbon if you prefer an alcohol-free dessert.

name: High-Heat Chimichurri Lentil Skillet
hook: Charred pulses, vinegar herbs, student-proof

ingredients.name: cooked green lentils, drained very well

steps.t: Drain the lentils hard in a sieve and shake until no liquid drips; wet lentils hiss, steam and turn the stir-fry to soup.
Mix vinegar, parsley, oregano, olive oil, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt into a rough chimichurri; cooking these herbs would dull their sharp green bite.
Heat a large frying pan or wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add sunflower oil; a lukewarm pan gives soft lentils with no char.
Stir-fry onion and pepper until the edges blacken in tiny patches but the strips still bend, not collapse; too much time makes them sweet and limp.
Add garlic, paprika and chilli flakes and stir for a few seconds until fragrant; burnt garlic tastes metallic and will ruin the whole cheap pan.
Tip in the lentils, spread them out, then leave them alone until the bottom layer crackles and picks up dark spots; constant stirring prevents the high-heat crust.
Toss once or twice until hot through, then take off the heat and fold in the chimichurri; adding it on the flame drives off the vinegar and greys the parsley.
Finish with more lemon and salt while the lentils are hot; seasoning cold pulses leaves the centres flat and beany.

note: Eat with rice, toast or a fried egg if your budget and appetite allow.

name: Black Vinegar Pickle-Dressed Pork
hook: Sticky pork, sharp greens, winter heat

ingredients.name: Chinese pickled mustard greens, rinsed and chopped

steps.t: Put the pork belly, ginger and enough cold water to cover in a pan. Bring up slowly and skim the grey foam; if you boil it hard from cold, the meat tightens and the broth tastes muddy.
Simmer the pork at a lazy bubble until a chopstick slides through the lean part with only slight resistance; keep the water just trembling or the fat turns woolly rather than soft.
Lift the pork out and rest it on a board until it stops steaming fiercely. Slice across the grain into thick bite-sized pieces; cut too soon and the juices run out across the board.
Stir black vinegar, both soy sauces, chilli oil, grated garlic and sugar in a large bowl until the sugar no longer crunches under the spoon; undissolved sugar leaves sharp pockets in the dressing.
Fold in the chopped pickled mustard greens and sliced pork while the meat is still warm. Leave it to drink in the dressing until the edges of the pork look lacquered, not wet.
Cook the noodles in boiling water until springy in the centre, then drain well. Watery noodles thin the dressing and make the bowl taste flat.
Toss the hot noodles through the pork and pickles, loosening with a splash of pork broth if needed. Finish with spring onions; add them earlier and they lose their clean bite.

note: Rinsing the mustard greens keeps the dish bright rather than punishingly salty.

name: Chipotle Black Bean Breakfast Bake
hook: Smoky beans under just-set eggs

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Oil a medium baking dish; if the beans sit in a dry corner, they catch before the eggs are ready.
Warm the oil in the dish on the hob or in a frying pan, then soften the onion until it bends without browning. Burnt onion makes the whole bake taste bitter, especially with chipotle.
Add the garlic, cumin and chipotle paste and stir until the oil turns brick-red and smells smoky. Do not walk away here; scorched spices taste dusty.
Stir in the black beans, tomatoes and a pinch of salt, then simmer until thick enough that a spoon dragged through leaves a brief trail. If it is soupy, the tortilla chips collapse into sludge.
Fold in the crushed tortilla chips, tip everything into the baking dish if needed, and make four deep hollows. Shallow hollows let the eggs slide to the edges and overcook.
Crack an egg into each hollow, scatter over feta and bake until the whites are opaque but the yolks still wobble when the dish is nudged.
Rest for 3 minutes, then squeeze over lime and scatter with coriander. Serve too fast and the beans burn mouths while the eggs keep cooking underneath.

note: For firmer yolks, add another 2 minutes in the oven.

name: Saffron Lemon Artichoke Braise
hook: Silky vegetables in golden lemon oil

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Choose a wide casserole with a tight lid; cramped vegetables steam into mush instead of braising in neat layers.
Warm the olive oil, then cook the onion and fennel until glossy and sweet-smelling but not brown. If they colour hard now, the braise loses its pale Greek elegance.
Add the garlic and saffron and stir until the garlic smells mellow. Keep it moving; browned garlic will shout over the lemon.
Nestle in the potatoes, carrots and artichokes, seasoning each layer lightly. Pour in the wine and let it bubble until the sharp alcohol smell has gone.
Add the stock, lemon zest and half the lemon juice. The liquid should come halfway up the vegetables; drowning them makes soup, too little leaves leathery artichokes.
Cover and braise in the oven until the potatoes take a knife easily and the artichokes look satin-soft at the edges.
Uncover and cook until the oil rises in golden beads and the juices reduce to a spoonable glaze. Stop while there is still gloss in the pan, or the potatoes will stick and tear.
Rest for 10 minutes, then finish with dill and the remaining lemon juice. Dill added before the rest turns dull and swampy.

note: Serve warm rather than piping hot so the saffron, lemon and olive oil come forward.
