Mix in the gram flour and rice flour with your fingers until every strip looks sandy and uneven, not pasty; dry crags are what fry into crisp corners.
Heat 1 cm oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of coating fizzes hard and rises straight away; if it only sighs, the pork will drink oil before it crisps.
Fry half the pork in a single layer, turning once, until the ridges are deep brick-red and the centres are piping hot with no raw pink patches; crowding the pan drops the heat and makes steamed pork.
Lift onto a rack or crumpled kitchen paper and fry the second batch the same way; a flat plate traps steam underneath and softens the underside.
Scatter with the raw onion while the pork is still crackling-hot so the onion just wilts at the edges; leave it buried too long and the crust loses its snap.

note: Excellent with warm roti, a squeeze of lemon and plain yoghurt for cooling the achari heat.

name: Saigon Steamed Egg Terrine
hook: Silky egg, peppery pork, savoury steam

steps.t: Soak the wood ear mushrooms and glass noodles in hot water until bendy, then drain hard and chop small; long wet strands make the terrine slump and weep when sliced.
Separate 2 eggs, keeping those yolks for the top, then beat the remaining 4 whole eggs plus 2 whites just until loose; frothy eggs steam into little bubbles instead of a clean, satiny face.
Mix pork, mushrooms, noodles, carrot, shallots, fish sauce, sugar, pepper and spring onions until the pork feels sticky, then fold in the beaten egg; under-mixed pork breaks into crumbly pockets.
Oil a small loaf tin or heatproof dish and line the base with baking paper, leaving no wrinkles; folds print into the custard and catch slices as you lift them out.
Set the dish in a steamer over a gentle simmer, cover the lid with a tea towel and steam until the middle feels springy, not liquid under the spoon; a hard boil pocks the sides with holes.
Beat the reserved yolks with a teaspoon of water, brush over the top and steam uncovered until glossy and set like lacquer; put the lid back on now and condensation will spot the yellow surface.
Rest in the tin until the juices settle, then unmould and slice with a wet knife; cutting it roaring hot makes the pork juices run and the layers tear.
Finish with coriander leaves and serve warm or room temperature; if serving later, chill it quickly and reheat slices until steaming hot.

note: A patient weekend version of chả trứng hấp, good with rice, cucumber and nước chấm.

name: Saffron Steamed Caramel Egg Mishti
hook: Saffron steam and wobbling caramel silk

steps.t: Put the sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until it turns the colour of strong tea; stirring throws crystals up the sides and gives you gritty caramel.
Divide the caramel between 4 ramekins and swirl just to coat the bases; hesitate too long and it sets in one thick puddle that will not unmould cleanly.
Warm the milk with saffron and cardamom until steaming at the edge, then take it off the heat; boiling milk gives the custard a cooked-skin flavour before it even steams.
Whisk eggs, condensed milk and rosewater gently, then whisk in the warm milk in a thin stream; dumping hot milk in at once scrambles the eggs into sweet threads.
Strain the mixture into the ramekins and cover each tightly with foil; unstrained chalazae and bubbles show up as lumps in the final wobble.
Steam over the lowest steady simmer until the custards tremble as one piece when nudged, with no liquid ripple in the centre; fierce steam honeycombs them like a sponge.
Cool to room temperature, then chill until the caramel loosens into sauce and the custard holds its shape; unmoulding warm custard collapses the sides.
Run a thin knife around each ramekin, invert onto plates and scatter with pistachios; saw at the edge and you will scar the smooth saffron face.

note: A steamed Indian caramel custard with mithai flavours, best made before dinner.

name: Krapao Mushroom Student Wok
hook: Hot wok mushrooms, basil, salty gloss

ingredients.name: mixed mushrooms, torn or thickly sliced

steps.t: Spread the cooked rice on plates before you start, because the stir-fry is too fast to pause for bowls; waiting with mushrooms in the wok turns them soggy.
Crush the garlic and chillies into a rough paste, not a purée; a fine paste burns before the mushrooms have taken colour.
Stir oyster sauce, soy sauce, fish sauce and sugar in a cup so it is ready to throw in; measuring at the stove means the wok cools and the mushrooms leak water.
Heat the wok until a drop of water skates and vanishes, then add oil and the mushrooms in one loose layer; if the pan is only warm, they boil in their own juice.
Stir-fry hard until the mushrooms shrink, squeak against the wok and show bronze patches at the edges; stop at pale beige and they will taste damp.
Add the chilli-garlic paste and toss until it smells sharp and savoury, keeping it moving so the garlic freckles rather than blackens.
Pour in the sauce and toss until it clings in a shiny coat with almost no liquid left at the bottom; too much sauce left behind will soak the rice instead of glazing it.
Kill the heat, fold through the Thai basil until just wilted, and spoon straight over the rice; cooking basil hard makes it dark and medicinal.

note: Use the cheapest mushrooms you can find; tearing them gives better crispy edges than neat slices.

name: Miso Butter Teppan Beef with Snowy Cabbage
hook: Hot iron, sweet miso, melting beef

ingredients.name: sirloin steak, thinly sliced across the grain
sweetheart cabbage, cut into thick wedges
spring onions, cut into 4 cm lengths

steps.t: Stir the butter, miso, mirin, soy and ginger into a smooth paste; if it stays streaky, the miso clumps will scorch on the hot iron before they glaze the beef.
Pat the beef dry and let it lose its fridge chill while you heat a cast-iron griddle until a flick of water skips; if the pan is only warm, the beef and cabbage will steam grey.

Rub the cabbage and shiitake with sesame oil, then griddle them cut-side down until the cabbage edges go lace-brown and the mushrooms squeak when nudged; if you keep moving them, they never build that wintery char.
Push the vegetables to the cooler side and lay the beef down in a single layer; if the slices overlap, they dump juice and turn chewy instead of searing.
Add the miso butter and spring onions, then toss hard until everything is glossy and the sauce smells nutty; if you leave it sitting, the miso catches and the beef tightens.
Spoon the hot rice into bowls and slide the beef, cabbage and pan juices over the top straight away; if you wait, the rice drinks the butter and the cabbage loses its snap.

note: Best with very hot rice and a small bowl of pickles to cut the butter.

name: Crisp Kimchi Mung Bean Breakfast Cakes
hook: Crackly edges, sour kimchi, soft centres

steps.t: Rinse the mung beans until the water runs clear, then soak them in plenty of cold water; if they are under-soaked, the centres stay gritty no matter how crisp the outside gets.
Drain the beans very well, then blend with the water, egg, soy and sesame oil to a coarse batter with tiny nubs left; if you blitz it smooth, the cakes fry up dense and pasty.
Fold in the kimchi, spring onions, rice flour and gochugaru with a spoon; if you beat the batter, the kimchi leaks too much brine and the cakes spread raggedly.
Heat the rapeseed oil in a wide frying pan until a dot of batter sizzles immediately; if the oil is quiet, the first cake will drink fat and taste heavy.

Fry spoonfuls of batter in batches, leaving space between them, until the edges are frilled and chestnut-brown before turning; if you crowd the pan, the oil temperature drops and the crust never crackles.
Drain the cakes on a wire rack, not flat on kitchen paper; if steam is trapped underneath, the breakfast you got up for goes soft in two minutes.

note: Serve with extra kimchi juice mixed with a little soy for dipping.

name: Black Vinegar Pickled Silken Tofu with Cucumber Ribbons
hook: Cool silk under glossy sour heat

steps.t: Slide the tofu onto a tilted plate and let it drain in the fridge; if you press it, the block cracks and looks tired before guests see it.
Peel the cucumber into ribbons, thinly slice the radishes, then toss both with the salt, sugar and half the black vinegar; if the slices are thick, they taste raw rather than sharply pickled.
Stir the soy, remaining black vinegar, chilli oil, sesame oil and grated garlic into a glossy dressing; if the garlic sits in a lump, one bite will be harsh and the rest flat.
Blot the tofu gently, slide it onto a cold platter and score it into large diamonds with a wet knife; if you cut too small, the silken curds collapse under the dressing.
Lift the pickled cucumber and radish from their brine and shake them off before piling them around the tofu; if you pour the brine on too, it thins the dressing and floods the plate.
Spoon the dressing around and partly over the tofu, then finish with sesame seeds and coriander; if you dress it early, the tofu weeps and the colours dull.

note: Chill the platter first for a cleaner, restaurant-style finish.

name: Lime-Chipotle Lamb Traybake with Courgette and Corn
hook: Bright lamb juices, sweet summer vegetables

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C, or 200°C fan, with a wide baking dish inside; if the dish starts cold, the lamb leaks before it browns.
Mix the lamb, egg, breadcrumbs, chipotle paste, oregano, lime zest and a good pinch of salt just until combined; if you knead it like dough, the meatballs turn bouncy.
Roll the mixture into 16 small meatballs with damp hands; if they are much larger, the vegetables will overcook before the lamb is safely done in the centre.
Toss the courgettes, tomatoes, corn and red onion with olive oil in the hot dish, spreading them into one layer; if they sit in a heap, they stew pale instead of roasting sweet.
Nestle the lamb meatballs among the vegetables and bake until the tomato skins split and the meatballs colour on top; if you cover the dish, you trap steam and lose the light traybake feel.
Shake the dish, then bake again until the lamb juices run clear and the centres reach 70°C; if any meatball is still pink inside, return the whole dish to the oven.
Squeeze over the lime juice, scatter with coriander and rest briefly before serving; if you skip the rest, the juices run across the plate instead of dressing the vegetables.

note: Keep the dish wide and shallow so it eats bright, not heavy.

name: Orange-Dill Braised Gigantes with Whipped Feta
hook: Soft beans, olive oil, sunny herbs

ingredients.name: drained jarred or tinned butter beans

steps.t: Warm most of the olive oil in a heavy pan and soften the onion slowly until it turns translucent and sweet; if you rush this stage, the finished beans taste sharp and raw.
Add the garlic, bay leaves and orange zest, stirring just until the garlic smells mellow; if the garlic browns, its bitterness carries through the whole braise.
Stir in the butter beans, passata, orange juice and water, then bring it only to a lazy simmer; if it boils hard now, the bean skins split before the sauce thickens.
Cover and braise on the lowest heat, nudging the pan now and then rather than stirring hard; if you scrape aggressively, the beans break into a paste.
Uncover and simmer until the tomato sauce clings to the beans in glossy patches; if you stop while it is watery, it will run across the meze table.
Whip the feta with the yoghurt and a spoon of olive oil until spreadable; if you leave it chunky, it fights the soft beans instead of cooling them.
Fold the vinegar and most of the dill through the beans off the heat, then spoon over the whipped feta and remaining dill; if the dill cooks for long, it turns khaki and loses its lift.

note: Serve warm rather than hot, with bread, olives and sliced tomatoes.

name: Pesto Tofu Gnocchi Al Forno
hook: Crisp corners, basil oil, molten mozzarella

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Use a metal roasting dish if you can; a deep ceramic dish steams the gnocchi instead of giving you crisp edges.
Tear the tofu into walnut-sized chunks, then pat it dry hard with kitchen paper. If it goes in wet, it turns bouncy rather than catching at the corners.
In the dish, toss gnocchi, tofu, tomatoes, olive oil, oregano and salt until everything is glossy. Spread it into one layer; piling it up leaves the middle pale and stodgy.
Bake until the gnocchi edges blister and the tomatoes split into sticky puddles.
Stir through the pesto and vinegar, scraping the basil oil into the hot tomato juices. Do this before adding cheese, or the mozzarella glues everything into clumps.
Tear over the mozzarella and shower with parmesan, then bake until the cheese bubbles and the exposed tofu tips go golden.
Rest for 3 minutes before serving; straight from the oven the sauce is too loose and will run off the gnocchi.

note: A fast tray-style bake with tofu standing in for chicken, built around supermarket gnocchi and pesto.

name: Black Cardamom Lamb Nihari
hook: Silken lamb, dark spice, marrow-rich gravy

ingredients.name: lamb shoulder on the bone, in large pieces

steps.t: Salt the lamb generously while you slice the onions. If the meat is fridge-cold and unsalted, it tightens before the seasoning reaches the bone.
Heat the ghee in a heavy casserole and brown the lamb in batches until the fat edges are mahogany, not grey. Crowding the pot drops the heat and gives you boiled lamb smell.
Lower the heat and cook the onions in the same ghee until deep gold and soft at the edges. Stop at pale beige and the gravy will taste sweet but flat.
Stir in ginger and garlic until the raw sting fades, then add chilli, coriander, cumin, cardamom and cinnamon. Keep the spices moving; scorched chilli turns bitter fast.
Return the lamb, pour in the stock, and scrape the base until it feels smooth under the spoon. Any stuck spice left behind will burn during the long braise.
Cover and braise very gently until the lamb can be pressed apart with a spoon and the bones look clean at the ends. A rolling boil makes the meat stringy and clouds the sauce.

Whisk the flour with 150 ml cold water, stir it into the pot, then simmer uncovered until the gravy coats the back of a spoon in a shiny layer. Pouring dry flour straight in gives dumpling-like lumps.
Rest off the heat for 20 minutes, then skim only the harsh orange fat, leaving a little sheen. Skimming it bone-dry steals the spice aroma.

note: Serve with naan, lime and sliced ginger; it is even better after a night in the fridge.

name: Thai Red Lentil Peanut Stew
hook: Thick coconut broth with gym-bag protein

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide saucepan and fry the curry paste until it darkens slightly and smells toasted. If it only dissolves in liquid later, the stew tastes raw and dusty.
Stir in the lentils so they are stained red and glossy. Dry lentils added after the liquid clump on the bottom and catch.
Pour in the stock and coconut milk, scraping the pan clean, then bring to a steady simmer. Do not hard-boil it; coconut milk can split and the lentils foam over.
Simmer until the lentils collapse into a thick orange base with only a few intact grains left. If they still look separate, the stew will eat watery rather than creamy.
Stir in chickpeas, peanut butter, soy sauce and green beans. Add the peanut butter in spoonfuls; one big lump hides at the bottom and scorches.
Simmer until the beans are bright green and just tender, and the stew drops slowly from the spoon. Take it further and the beans go army-green and squeaky.
Finish with lime juice and torn herbs off the heat. Boiling the herbs dulls the clean Thai lift you need against the peanuts.

note: Built for meal prep: lentils and chickpeas keep the protein high without needing meat.

name: Black Sesame Caramel Chawanmushi
hook: Wobbling custard, smoky sesame, bitter caramel

steps.t: Put four small heatproof cups in a steamer setup and check the lid closes. If the cups touch the lid, condensation will drip straight into the custard.
Cook 70 g sugar with the water in a small pan until it turns dark amber and smells faintly bitter, then divide it between the cups. Pull it while pale and the dessert tastes like syrup, not caramel.
Whisk eggs, milk, cream, 45 g sugar, sesame paste, vanilla and salt until smooth but not foamy. Beating in lots of air leaves pinholes instead of a silk surface.
Strain the mixture into a jug, pressing the sesame through the sieve. Skipping this leaves egg threads and gritty paste at the bottom.
Pour into the cups and cover each tightly with foil. Loose foil lets steam puddle on top and gives you watery craters.
Steam over low heat, with the water barely murmuring, until the custards tremble as one piece when nudged. Vigorous steam makes them puff, split and taste eggy.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving warm, or chill until cold. Digging in immediately breaks the caramel layer before it loosens into sauce.

note: A dessert take on chawanmushi: gentle steam is the whole technique.

name: Smoked Mussel Kimchi Jumeokbap
hook: Briny smoke, sticky rice, chilli crunch

steps.t: Warm the rice until it is hot and sticky, not steaming wet. Cold rice will not bind, while soggy rice makes the balls paste-like.
Chop the kimchi finely and squeeze out a spoonful of excess juice. If it goes in too wet, the rice falls apart before it reaches your mouth.
Flake the smoked mussels with a fork, checking for any hard bits of shell. Leaving them whole makes salty pockets instead of smoke running through the rice.
Mix gochujang, soy sauce, sesame oil and rice vinegar in a bowl until glossy. If the gochujang stays in lumps, every bite lands differently hot.
Fold in rice, kimchi, mussels, spring onions, seaweed and sesame seeds with a rice paddle or wet spoon. Mash too hard and you lose the separate, chewy grains.
Wet your hands, then press into 6 compact triangles or balls until the surface looks shiny and tight. A loose squeeze crumbles; a crushing grip turns the middle gummy.
Eat at room temperature, or pan-toast the sides in a dry non-stick pan until the seaweed freckles dark. Walk away and the gochujang sugars catch quickly.

note: Tinned smoked mussels keep it cheap, safe and dorm-friendly without needing a smoker.

name: Istanbul Lemon Chicken and Butter Bean Stew
hook: Silky beans, bright lemon, tender chicken

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into large bites

steps.t: Season the chicken lightly and keep the pieces chunky; tiny pieces cook fast but turn stringy before the stew has body.
Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft and glossy at the edges; if it catches now, the stew will taste bitter instead of sweet.
Stir in garlic, tomato purée, pul biber and cumin until the oil turns brick-red and smells toasted; stop before the garlic browns or it will dominate the lemon.
Add the chicken and turn it through the paste until the outside loses its raw shine; hard browning is not the aim, as it makes the quick simmer tougher.
Pour in tomatoes and stock, scrape the base clean, then add the beans and simmer gently until the chicken is opaque and tender; a rolling boil will split the beans and dry the meat.
Stir in lemon zest, a squeeze of juice and parsley, then rest off the heat so the beans drink in the sauce; skipping the rest leaves the stew watery on the plate.

note: Serve with flatbread or a spoonful of thick yoghurt if you want it softer.

name: Aleppo Butter Whole Prawns with Walnut Tarator
hook: Shells blister, butter runs red

ingredients.name: whole raw king prawns, shell-on and head-on

steps.t: Snip along each prawn back with kitchen scissors and lift out the dark vein while leaving heads and shells attached; if you skip this, the roast can eat gritty.
Blend walnuts, tahini, yoghurt, half the lemon juice and a splash of water to a spoonable tarator; stop when it looks satin-smooth, because overworking walnuts makes the sauce oily.
Mash butter with olive oil, garlic, Aleppo pepper, za’atar, lemon zest and a little lemon juice; add too much juice now and the butter slides off the shells instead of clinging.
Coat the prawns in the spiced butter, cover and chill so the shells take on the seasoning; leaving them much longer than an hour firms the flesh before it reaches the oven.
Heat the oven to 230°C with a large roasting tray inside until the tray is fiercely hot; a cool tray makes the prawns steam grey rather than roast rosy.
Spread the prawns in one layer on the hot tray and roast until the shells are lacquer-red and the thickest flesh is pearly opaque; if they are piled up, the lower ones stay undercooked.
Finish with sumac, parsley and the remaining lemon juice, then serve at once with tarator; letting roasted prawns sit makes the shells cling and the meat tighten.

note: Put a bowl out for shells and keep the tarator cool until serving.

name: Chermoula-Smoked Halloumi Lentil Bowl
hook: Smoky slabs over lemony pulses

steps.t: Soak the smoking chips, then drain them well; bone-dry chips flare and wet chips smother the heat, so aim for damp and fragrant.
Mix olive oil, lemon zest, garlic, ras el hanout and cumin, then rub a little over the halloumi; do not add salt, as halloumi is already carrying plenty.
Set a lidded barbecue for indirect heat, add the chips to the coals, and place the halloumi away from the fiercest heat; direct flames scorch the outside before smoke gets in.
Meanwhile warm lentils and chickpeas in a pan with the remaining spice oil until they smell nutty; if they boil or dry out, the bowl turns chalky instead of hearty.
Fold tomatoes, spinach, lemon juice and most of the coriander through the warm pulses until the spinach just slumps; cook it hard and you lose the fresh gym-meal lift.
Sear the smoked halloumi briefly over the hot side until striped and soft-centred; more than a minute a side makes it squeak and toughen.
Pile pulses into bowls, top with halloumi and the last coriander; plate straight away because smoked cheese firms as it cools.

note: If using an indoor smoker, keep the heat moderate and ventilate well.

name: Seville Orange Tocino de Cielo
hook: Caramel glass, satin golden custard

steps.t: Cook 80 g of the sugar with 30 ml water and the lemon juice until it turns deep amber at the edges; stirring after it dissolves can crystallise it into sand.
Pour the caramel into six small metal moulds and tilt to coat the bases; move quickly, because set caramel clumps instead of forming a clean glassy layer.
Simmer the remaining sugar with 150 ml water and the orange zest until lightly syrupy, then cool until just warm; hot syrup scrambles eggs on contact.
Whisk yolks, whole eggs, vanilla and salt just until smooth, then stream in the syrup slowly; frothing the mixture gives the finished custard pockmarks.
Strain into the caramel moulds and cover each with foil; unstrained egg strands set into rubbery flecks.
Steam over the gentlest simmer until the centres wobble like set jelly, not liquid; boiling water punches holes through the custard.
Chill fully before unmoulding, running a thin knife round the edge; turning it out warm makes the custard slump and tear.

note: Use the leftover whites for meringues or an omelette.

name: Charcoal Baguette Oeufs Cocotte
hook: Runny yolks in smoky toasted bread

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are grey-edged rather than flaming; live flames blacken the bread before the eggs have a chance to set.
Cut a long trench from the top of the baguette and press the crumb down, leaving a firm base and walls; cut through the bottom and the filling leaks into the fire.
Butter the inside, then mix crème fraîche, mustard, emmental, spring onions and thyme; dry bread without the butter turns brittle instead of custardy underneath.
Set the baguette on doubled foil, spoon in the cream mixture and crack in the eggs one at a time; rushing them in from height breaks yolks and spills whites over the sides.
Grill over indirect coals under a lid or upturned roasting tin until the whites are milky-set and the yolks still wobble; direct heat gives you a burnt base and raw tops.
Rest off the heat before slicing into two messy boats; cutting immediately sends the hot filling running across the board.

note: A cheap bag of salad on the side is enough to make it dinner.

name: Ginger-Steam Paneer Shiitake Bowl
hook: soft curds, dark broth, winter heat

ingredients.name: fresh ginger, cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: Cover the dried shiitake with 200 ml just-boiled water and put a plate on top; if they bob above the water the centres stay leathery.
Lift out the mushrooms, squeeze them firmly and slice them. Keep 120 ml of the soaking liquor, stopping before the gritty last spoonful or the sauce will crunch.
Pack the Chinese leaf into a shallow heatproof bowl, scatter over the shiitake, then lay the paneer slabs on top in a single layer; stacked paneer steams unevenly and turns rubbery at the edges.
Mix the mushroom liquor with soy, Shaoxing, oyster sauce, garlic, half the ginger and the sesame oil. Spoon it over the paneer, letting some run down into the cabbage rather than pooling only on top.
Steam over a lively simmer until the cabbage has slumped and the paneer feels hot and springy in the centre; a weak simmer leaves the bowl watery and lukewarm.
Rest the bowl off the heat so the paneer drinks in the broth; serving straight away makes the sauce taste thin.
Finish with chilli oil, spring onions and the remaining ginger, making sure the hot broth catches the raw ginger so it blooms instead of tasting harsh.

note: Use firm paneer rather than soft fresh paneer, which can crumble under steam.

name: Ember-Cecina Pork Breakfast Tacos
hook: smoke, yolk, lime, early sunshine

steps.t: Light the coals first; you want a glowing bed with a thin grey coat, not tall flames that scorch the marinade bitter before the pork cooks.
Beat together orange juice, achiote, chipotle, garlic, oregano and salt, then rub it hard into the pork. If the paste sits in blobs, those spots burn black and salty.
Let the pork sit while the coals settle; this short cure is enough for thin steaks and keeps the breakfast moving.

Grill the pork directly over the coals until the edges char in little rusty patches and the thickest piece is safely cooked through; move pieces away from flare-ups or the orange sugar will turn acrid.
Rest the pork on a warm plate, loosely covered. Cutting straight from the grill spills the juices and makes the taco filling dry.
Warm the tortillas on the cooler side of the grill until they puff and freckle; if they go stiff, you have left them too long and they will split around the filling.
Fry the eggs in a small pan set over the grill or hob until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble; under-set whites make messy tacos, hard yolks lose the breakfast richness.
Slice the pork across the grain, pile into tortillas with avocado, egg, coriander and lime. Cut against the grain or even good pork will chew stringy.

note: If your pork steaks are thicker than 1 cm, butterfly them before marinating so they cook safely before the glaze burns.

name: Aegean Lemon-Cured Bass with Caper Grapes
hook: cool silk with salty green sparkle

ingredients.name: skinless sea bass fillet, pin-boned and suitable for raw eating
small fennel bulb, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Chill the serving plates and keep the bass in the fridge until the moment you slice it; warm raw fish loses its clean snap and looks dull.
Check the fillet with your fingertips for bones, then slice across the grain into thin, even pieces. Ragged thick slices cure patchily and look clumsy on the plate.
Whisk lemon juice, orange juice, ouzo, lemon zest, salt and olive oil until glossy; if the oil floats in big beads, the first slices will taste sharp while the last taste greasy.
Lay the bass in a single layer and spoon over half the dressing. Cure only until the edges turn milky but the centres still look translucent; longer makes the fish chalky, not safer.
Toss fennel and cucumber with a spoonful of dressing so they bend without flooding the plate; wet vegetables make the fish slide around.
Arrange the bass on the chilled plates, then tuck in fennel, cucumber, capers and olives. Do not heap everything on top or you hide the clean slices you worked for.
Finish with dill, black pepper and the remaining dressing just before serving; dill bruises and darkens if it sits in the acid.

note: Buy fish specifically sold as suitable for raw eating, keep it cold, and serve the dish immediately after curing.

name: Istanbul Market Courgette Sizzle
hook: smoky edges, lemon-bright juices

ingredients.name: red onion, cut into thin wedges

steps.t: Cut all the vegetables before the pan goes on; high-heat cooking gives you no time to hunt for a tomato while the garlic burns.
Heat a wide wok or frying pan until a courgette piece hisses the second it lands. If the pan is only warm, the vegetables stew and lose their summer snap.
Add half the oil and the courgettes in one layer, leaving them alone until the cut faces get dark freckles. Stir too early and you trade char for watery softness.
Add peppers and onion with the remaining oil, then toss hard so the edges blister while the centres stay bright. A crowded pan drops heat, so use two batches if needed.
Stir in garlic and pul biber for a few seconds until fragrant; if the garlic goes brown now it will taste bitter through the whole plate.
Add tomatoes, sumac, pomegranate molasses and lemon juice, tossing just until the tomato skins wrinkle and release a little gloss. Cook them to collapse and the dish turns into sauce.
Tip onto a platter and scatter with mint while still warm; leaving it in the pan keeps cooking the courgettes past tender-crisp.

note: Serve warm rather than piping hot, when the lemon and mint read brightest.

name: Sumac-Griddled Cod with Pickle Tarator
hook: crisp fish, nutty sauce, sharp pickles

ingredients.name: cod loin, cut into chunky fingers

steps.t: Stir tahini with garlic, half the lemon juice and enough cold water to make a spoonable sauce. Add the water slowly; too much at once makes it seize into a grainy paste before it loosens.
Fold pickled cucumbers, radishes and parsley through half the tarator, keeping the rest plain for drizzling. If everything goes in one bowl, the fish has nowhere creamy to land.
Pat the cod very dry, then coat with olive oil, za’atar and sumac. Damp fish sticks to the griddle and tears before it browns.
Heat the griddle until a drop of water skates off fast, then oil the ridges lightly. A lukewarm griddle gives pale fish and no Levantine grill flavour.
Lay on the cod and do not move it until the underside releases with clear dark bars; forcing it early leaves the crust welded to the pan.
Turn once and cook until the flakes part easily and the centre is opaque and hot. Keep turning and the fingers break into scraps.
Warm the flatbreads on the griddle until soft and striped, not crisp like crackers.
Spread plain tarator on a platter, add the cod, spoon over pickle tarator and finish with the remaining lemon juice. Serve straight away while the crust still crackles at the edges.

note: Hake or pollock loin works well if cod is expensive; choose thick pieces so they survive the griddle.

name: Orange-Olive Mackerel Plaki
hook: Silky fish under wintry tomato oil

steps.t: Heat the oven to 170°C. Salt the mackerel inside and out, then leave it while you start the base; if it goes in unsalted, the flesh tastes flat no matter how good the sauce is.
In a wide flameproof casserole, soften the onions in the olive oil with a pinch of salt until they slump and turn translucent, not brown; scorched onion will make the braise bitter.
Add the garlic, oregano, orange zest, tomatoes and potatoes. Simmer until the tomato oil separates in red beads at the edge, because watery sauce will steam the fish instead of braising it.

Pour in the orange juice and 150 ml water, tuck the potatoes under the sauce, cover and bake until a knife slides into them with only a little resistance; hard potatoes will not catch up once the fish is added.
Nestle the mackerel into the hot sauce, spooning some over the backs, then scatter in the olives. Cover and return to the oven until the flesh lifts cleanly from the backbone at the thickest part.
Rest uncovered for 8 minutes so the oil settles glossy on top; if you serve straight away, the fish breaks raggedly and the sauce tastes sharp.
Finish with chopped parsley and a final spoon of the orange-red oil from the dish.

note: Serve with thick bread or bitter greens for proper cold-weather comfort.

name: Sucuk Mushroom Breakfast Güveç
hook: Peppery mushrooms, eggs, bubbling tomato

steps.t: Put the olive oil and sucuk in a small deep pan over medium heat until the fat stains the oil brick-red; if the heat is fierce, the slices curl hard before flavouring the stew.
Add the onion and pepper and cook until the onion looks glassy and the pepper softens at the edges; crunchy onion gives the breakfast a raw bite.
Stir in the mushrooms with a pinch of salt and cook until they first flood the pan, then the liquid mostly disappears; stopping at the wet stage makes the güveç thin.
Add the pepper paste and pul biber and stir until the paste darkens and smells sweet, not dusty; raw paste leaves a metallic taste.
Pour in the grated tomatoes and simmer until the stew blips slowly and a spoon dragged through leaves a brief trail.
Make two hollows, crack in the eggs, cover and cook until the whites are set but the yolks still tremble; uncovered eggs set unevenly and the yolks go chalky while the tops stay clear.
Scatter parsley over the pan and eat straight from the table with warm pide, scraping the thick mushroom sauce from the sides.

note: For a meat-free version, skip the sucuk and add 1 teaspoon smoked paprika with the pepper paste.

name: Pomegranate Baharat Lamb Shoulder
hook: A whole roast, lacquered and fragrant

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C. Mix the olive oil, garlic, baharat, pomegranate molasses, lemon zest and salt, then rub it all over the lamb, especially into the seams; bare patches roast grey rather than lacquered.
Lay the onions in a roasting tin, set the shoulder on top and pour the stock around, not over, the lamb; washing the rub off now means the crust never forms.
Cover the tin tightly with foil and roast until the shoulder gives when pressed through the foil and the bone starts to loosen; a loose foil tent lets steam escape and leaves the meat stubborn.
Remove the foil, baste with the dark pan juices and roast hotter at 210°C until the top is sticky, mahogany and slightly crisp at the edges.
Lift the lamb to a warm board and rest it under loose foil; carving too soon sends the juices across the board instead of through the meat.
Meanwhile simmer the freekeh in the roasting tin juices until tender and smoky-green, adding a splash of water if the pan looks dry; if the grains catch, they taste burnt rather than nutty.
Brighten the freekeh with lemon juice, fold through pine nuts and torn mint, then serve the whole shoulder on top for guests to pull apart.

note: A whole shoulder is dramatic, forgiving and easier to cook evenly than a full leg.

name: Smoked Chickpea, Lentil and Carrot Salad
hook: Cool pulses with a charcoal whisper

steps.t: Soak the smoking chips in water while you prep; dry chips flare instead of smoulder and make the pulses acrid.
Steam the carrots until bendy but still bright orange, then cool them quickly on a plate; overcooked carrots turn the salad soft and sweet like mash.
Toss chickpeas and lentils with olive oil, cumin, paprika, harissa and a good pinch of salt so every pulse is lightly stained; unseasoned lentils taste dull once chilled.
Line a heavy pan with foil, add the drained chips, set a small rack or steamer insert above them and spread the pulses on a perforated tray. Cover tightly and heat until smoke curls from the rim.
Smoke the pulses over medium heat until they smell gently woody, not like a bonfire; longer smoking will swamp the lemon and herbs.
Tip the smoked pulses onto a tray to cool, then toss with carrots, lemon juice and coriander; dressing them hot bruises the herbs black.
Spoon yoghurt onto a platter, pile the salad over it and finish with a thin thread of olive oil.

note: Use only food-safe smoking chips, and keep the smoking pan covered until the smoke has settled.

name: Saffron-Steam Chicken Banderillas
hook: Tender bites for passing around

steps.t: Cut the chicken into large bite-sized pieces and toss with garlic, smoked paprika, lemon zest, olive oil and salt; pieces that are too small tighten before they turn juicy.
Warm the sherry with saffron just until fragrant, then pour it into the base of a steamer pan; boiling it hard drives off the aroma you want in the steam.
Spread the chicken in a single layer in the steamer basket, leaving gaps for steam to move; piled chicken cooks grey outside and underdone in the middle.
Steam over a steady simmer until the thickest piece is opaque all the way through and reaches 75°C, with clear juices when pierced.
Lift the chicken onto a plate and spoon over a little of the saffron sherry from the pan; leaving it dry now makes the surface tacky as it cools.
Thread warm chicken onto skewers with roasted pepper strips and olives, keeping each banderilla small enough to eat in two bites.
Finish with lemon juice and chopped parsley just before serving; add them earlier and the herbs wilt while the citrus flattens the saffron.

note: Serve as part of a tapas spread with almonds, bread and chilled fino.

name: Wok-Torn Thai Basil Eggs
hook: Peppery basil, lacy eggs, hot wok smoke

ingredients.name: green beans, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.t: Beat the eggs with the fish sauce, soy and sugar just until streaky; if you whisk them foamy they puff then collapse instead of setting in soft torn sheets.
Heat a wok until a drop of water skitters and vanishes, then add the oil; if the wok is only warm, the eggs drink the oil and turn heavy.
Pour in the eggs and leave them for 20 seconds until the rim frills and goes lace-gold, then fold into large pieces; stirring too soon makes wet crumbs.
Push the eggs to one side, add garlic, chilli and shallot to the bare oil, and toss until the garlic smells sweet rather than raw; let it go dark brown and the whole dish tastes bitter.
Add the green beans and stir-fry hard until they turn glossy bright green with tiny blistered spots; if they slump, the wok was overcrowded or too cool.
Fold the eggs back through with the Thai basil until the leaves just wilt and perfume the pan; cooking the basil longer dulls its peppery lift.
Plate immediately with lime wedges, because this is best while the egg edges are still crisp and the centre is custardy.

note: Cook rice before you start; the stir-fry itself waits for nobody.

name: Miso-Griddled Daikon Steaks with Charred Negi Oil
hook: Deep miso edges, sweet radish centres

ingredients.name: daikon radish, peeled and cut into 3 cm rounds
spring onions, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.t: Score one face of each daikon round in a shallow cross-hatch; cut deeper than 5 mm and the rounds split on the griddle instead of staying steak-like.
Put the daikon and kombu in a wide pan, cover with cold water and bring to a bare simmer until a skewer slides through with only a little resistance; a rolling boil makes the edges woolly.
Lift the daikon onto a rack, salt lightly and leave until the surfaces look dry and slightly tacky; wet rounds steam on the griddle and never take colour.
Stir miso, mirin, sake and sugar into a smooth glaze; if lumps remain, they scorch before the daikon is seasoned evenly.
Heat a heavy griddle over medium-high heat, oil it, and cook the daikon scored-side down until the grooves are dark gold and the edges smell nutty; moving them early tears the crust away.
Turn, brush the browned side with glaze, then flip briefly to lacquer until the miso bubbles in tiny blisters; leave it too long and the sugar burns black.
Griddle the spring onions beside the daikon until striped and floppy, then chop and stir with sesame oil; raw centres taste harsh against the sweet radish.
Serve the daikon with charred negi oil and sesame seeds, spooning over any sticky glaze left on the board.

note: Most of the time is gentle cooking and drying, which is what gives daikon a meaty bite without adding protein.

name: Crisp Gochugaru Cod Jeon with Cucumber Soy
hook: Lean white fish, crackly chilli-gold edges

ingredients.name: skinless cod loin, cut into 2 cm thick fingers

steps.t: Pat the cod dry until kitchen paper comes away almost clean, then salt it; surface water thins the coating and makes the fish spit in the pan.
Mix flour, potato starch and gochugaru on a plate, and beat the egg in a shallow bowl; unmixed starch leaves chalky white patches after frying.
Dust each cod piece lightly, shake off the excess, dip in egg, then dust again; a thick flour jacket goes pasty before the fish cooks through.
Heat the oil in a frying pan until a pinch of coating sizzles at once, then lay in the fish with space between pieces; crowding drops the heat and gives you steamed fish in a soggy coat.
Shallow fry until the underside is crisp and chilli-gold, then turn once and cook until the flakes just separate under gentle pressure; repeated turning breaks lean cod apart.
Stir cucumber, soy, vinegar, sesame seeds and spring onion into a sharp dipping sauce; if you make it too early, the cucumber dumps water and tastes flat.
Drain the jeon on a rack, not paper, for two minutes so steam can escape; paper traps moisture and softens the crust you worked for.

note: Cod keeps this lean and protein-heavy; serve with rice if you want a bigger training-day meal.

name: Ginger Rock Sugar Steamed Egg Custard
hook: Silky spoonfuls with warm ginger sweetness

steps.t: Warm the milk with rock sugar, ginger and salt until the sugar dissolves and the milk smells gently gingery; boiling it gives the custard a cooked-milk skin.
Take the pan off the heat and let the ginger steep until the milk is warm, not hot; pour hot milk onto eggs and you will scramble them at the edges.
Beat the eggs lightly with vanilla, then strain in the ginger milk and stir slowly; vigorous whisking traps bubbles that become pockmarks.
Strain the mixture into four small heatproof bowls and skim off surface foam; skipping this is why steamed custard looks cratered rather than glassy.
Cover each bowl tightly with foil and set in a steamer over a gentle simmer, not a hard boil; violent steam makes the custard split into honeycomb.
Steam until the centres wobble like soft jelly and a spoon touched to the surface comes away clean, then turn off the heat; pushing it firm makes it watery around the sides.
Rest covered for five minutes before serving warm, so the heat finishes the centre without toughening the rim.

note: For a colder finish, chill the covered bowls and serve with a little extra ginger syrup.

name: Chipotle Beef, Bean and Rice Bake
hook: Smoky beef, bubbling rice, crisp cheese corners

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan and set a deep baking dish or ovenproof pan over medium-high heat with the oil; starting cold makes the mince boil before it browns.
Fry the beef mince, breaking it up, until the water has vanished and the meat catches in dark speckles; stop while it is grey and the bake tastes flat.
Add onion and garlic and cook until the onion looks glossy and soft at the edges; raw onion stays harsh because the rice stage is too wet to fry it properly.
Stir in chipotle paste and cumin until they stain the fat brick-red and smell smoky; adding liquids too soon leaves the spices dusty.
Add rice, beans, tomatoes, stock and sweetcorn, scrape the browned bits from the base, and level the rice under the liquid; exposed grains bake hard and chalky.
Cover tightly with foil and bake until the rice has swollen and there is no soupy liquid sloshing at the edges; a loose cover lets steam escape and leaves the centre crunchy.
Scatter over cheddar and bake uncovered until the corners bubble and the cheese blisters brown; taking it out pale misses the cheap-but-great crispy bits.
Rest for five minutes before spooning out, because straight-from-oven rice collapses into wet rubble instead of neat, steamy scoops.

note: Use the baking dish on the hob only if it is hob-safe; otherwise brown the beef in a pan and transfer once the liquid is added.

name: Feijoada-Roasted Whole Pumpkin
hook: Black beans under sweet collapsing pumpkin

ingredients.name: black beans, drained, 150 ml liquid reserved

steps.t: Heat the oven to 190°C. Cut a neat lid from the pumpkin and scoop out every stringy seed; leave strands behind and they steam into wet ropes rather than sweet flesh.
Rub the inside and skin with 1 tbsp oil and salt. Roast the pumpkin and lid cut-side down until a knife meets only gentle resistance at the thickest wall, not until it slumps open.
Meanwhile soften the onion in the remaining oil until glossy and straw-gold at the edges; if it catches dark now, the bean filling will taste bitter rather than deep.
Add garlic, paprika and cumin and stir until the pan smells smoky and warm, about 30 seconds; spices left dry for longer scorch fast.
Fold in the beans, reserved bean liquid, orange zest and juice. Simmer until the spoon leaves a brief trail through the beans; too loose and it floods the pumpkin when carved.
Turn the pumpkin upright, spoon in the beans, sprinkle with cassava flour, and return uncovered until the top is crusty and the pumpkin skin wrinkles like paper.
Rest for 10 minutes, then finish with coriander and carve in wedges; cutting straight away makes the filling run instead of settling into the flesh.

note: Use a pumpkin with firm, dry flesh such as kabocha, onion squash or Hokkaido.

name: Coal-Smoked Lahori Masala Eggs
hook: Soft eggs wrapped in breakfast smoke

steps.t: Beat the eggs with a good pinch of salt until no clear streaks remain; half-mixed eggs set in rubbery white patches.
Heat 1 tbsp ghee and cook the onion until the tips turn caramel-brown while the centres stay soft; pale onion tastes raw once the eggs go in.
Add chilli, tomato, coriander, chilli powder and turmeric. Cook until the tomato collapses and the ghee beads orange at the edge; watery masala makes loose, grainy eggs.
Lower the heat, pour in the eggs and push them slowly from the edge to the centre until they are softly folded and still glossy; if they look dry in the pan, they will be tough on the plate.
Heat the charcoal over a gas flame or with a kitchen torch until one side is glowing red, then put it in a small heatproof metal cup set inside the pan; do not let charcoal touch the eggs.
Drop the remaining ghee onto the coal, cover immediately, and smoke until the eggs smell like a tandoor but not an ashtray.
Remove the coal cup, fold through fresh coriander and serve at once with hot paratha or toast; leaving the lid on traps condensation and dulls the smoke.

note: Use natural untreated charcoal only, and keep the smoking cup heatproof and stable.

name: Saigon Lemongrass-Steamed Clams
hook: Briny shells, lime steam, chilli heat

steps.t: Rinse the clams in cold water and discard any cracked ones or open shells that do not close when tapped; no sauce can rescue bad shellfish.
Put lemongrass, lime leaves, garlic, chilli, lager, fish sauce and sugar in a wide lidded pan. Bring it to a hard, fragrant boil so the steam is ready before the clams arrive.
Tip in the clams, clamp on the lid and shake the pan once; a crowded, unmoved pile opens unevenly and the bottom layer overcooks.
Lift the lid and pull out clams as they spring open, glossy and plump. Leave stubborn ones for another minute, but discard any still shut after that.
Boil the liquor uncovered until it tastes clean and punchy, not thin and beery; if grit has settled, pour carefully and leave the last spoonful behind.
Add lime juice off the heat, then pour the hot liquor over the clams and scatter with herbs; boiling lime juice turns its perfume flat.
Serve in a warmed wide bowl with small spoons for the broth; cold bowls steal the drama from the steam at the table.

note: Buy clams the day you cook them and keep them chilled, uncovered or loosely covered.

name: Coal-Grilled Halloumi with Sicilian Peach Fennel
hook: Salty char against cold anise crunch

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no tall flames; live flames blacken halloumi before the centre warms.
Whisk lemon zest, half the juice, olive oil and oregano with a pinch of salt. It should smell bright and grassy, not sharply sour.
Toss fennel with the remaining lemon juice and a little salt, squeezing once with your hands until it bends rather than snaps; unsalted fennel stays hard and separate.
Pat the halloumi dry and brush lightly with the dressing. Wet cheese steams and sticks instead of taking clean grill marks.
Grill the halloumi over direct coals until the bars are deep bronze and the edges begin to puff, then turn once; repeated flipping tears the crust away.
Grill the peach wedges just until striped and warm but still holding their shape; take them too far and they collapse into jam on the grate.
Arrange rocket, fennel, peaches and halloumi on a platter. Spoon over the remaining dressing, then finish with pistachios and mint so the nuts stay crisp.

note: If your halloumi is very salty, soak the slabs in cold water for 15 minutes, then dry thoroughly.

name: Kokum-Cured Mackerel Chaat
hook: Cold silver fish, sour spice snap

ingredients.name: sashimi-grade mackerel fillets, pin-boned and skinned

steps.t: Keep the mackerel chilled and slice it across the grain into 5 mm pieces with a sharp knife; ragged cuts warm up and turn mushy at the edges.
Soak the kokum in 3 tbsp hot water until the liquid turns deep rose and sharply fruity, then squeeze the petals well; weak kokum gives colour without the sour backbone.
Stir kokum liquid with lime juice, jaggery, cumin, chilli and salt until the sugar dissolves; gritty jaggery clings in sweet spots rather than seasoning the fish.
Fold the cold mackerel through the cure and spread it in a shallow layer. Chill until the surface turns slightly opaque but the centre still looks glossy.
Drain off excess cure, then gently mix in onion, cucumber and coriander; stirring hard breaks the oily fish into paste.
Taste one piece and adjust with a few drops of lime or a pinch of salt; the flavour should hit sour first, then chilli, then rich fish.
Pile onto a cold plate and scatter sev over at the last second; add it early and the crunch disappears before the platter reaches the table.

note: Use fish explicitly sold for raw consumption, previously frozen to parasite-safe standards, and eat the dish the day it is made.

name: Crisp Chermoula Mushrooms with Lemon Couscous
hook: Crackly mushrooms, cool garlic yoghurt

steps.t: Put the couscous in a bowl with a pinch of salt, cover with 170ml boiling water and a plate, then leave it to swell; if you prod it early, the grains turn claggy instead of fluffy.

Finely grate the garlic and lemon zest, then mix half of each with the yoghurt, a squeeze of lemon and chopped coriander stalks; keep the leaves for later, because they go dull if stirred in too soon.
Wipe the mushrooms dry and halve only the big ones. Do not rinse them under the tap, or they steam in the pan and throw off the coating.

Mix the flour, semolina, ras el hanout, paprika and salt in one bowl, and beat the egg in another. Dip the mushrooms in egg, then the dry mix, pressing into the gills; bare patches fry soft, not crisp.

Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of coating fizzes straight away. Fry the mushrooms in two batches, turning when the edges go deep gold and gritty; crowding the pan drops the heat and makes them greasy.

Drain the mushrooms on kitchen paper, fluff the couscous with lemon juice and coriander leaves, then plate with the garlic yoghurt. Salt the mushrooms while hot, or the seasoning bounces off the crust.

note: Best eaten straight from the pan; the crust softens as it sits.

name: Andalusian Escabeche Beef Cheek with Olive-Pepper Dressing
hook: Silky beef, sharp sherry bite

steps.t: Season the beef cheeks well and brown them in a heavy casserole with a little of the olive oil until the outside is mahogany in patches; pale meat will taste boiled even after the pickle.
Add the onions, carrots, garlic and bay leaves, then cook until the onion edges soften and catch lightly; if the vegetables scorch black, the escabeche will taste bitter.
Stir in the paprika for a few seconds, then pour in the wine, 150ml vinegar and enough water to barely cover. Keep the paprika moving, because burnt paprika goes harsh fast.
Cover and simmer gently until a spoon can press into the cheeks with almost no resistance. A rolling boil tightens the meat before the collagen melts.

Lift the cheeks into a shallow dish. Strain 500ml cooking liquor over them, stir in the remaining vinegar and enough olive oil to gloss the surface, then cool quickly before refrigerating; leaving warm beef out too long is unsafe.
Chill the beef in its sharp liquor overnight, turning once if you remember. This is where the pickle moves through the meat rather than just seasoning the outside.
Slice the cold cheeks thickly across the grain. If the knife drags and shreds them, let the meat warm for ten minutes rather than forcing ragged slices.
Dress with chopped olives, roasted peppers, parsley, a spoonful of pickle liquor and the last olive oil. Taste for salt at the end, because olives and reduced liquor can push it over.

note: Serve cool or just below room temperature with bread and a bitter salad.

name: Provençal Mackerel, Bean and Tomato Bake
hook: Oily fish, blistered tomatoes, clean protein

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Use a roasting dish big enough for the beans to sit in a shallow layer; a cramped dish traps steam and stops the tomatoes blistering.
In the dish, toss the beans, tomatoes, courgette, onion, garlic, capers, thyme, olive oil, salt and pepper. Spread it flat so the onion tips can char rather than sweat.
Bake until the tomatoes split and the beans look dry at the edges, not soupy in the middle.
Whisk the mustard with lemon zest and a squeeze of juice, then brush it over the flesh side of the mackerel. Keep the layer thin, or it slides off and burns in the tray.
Lay the mackerel skin-side up on the hot beans and return the dish to the oven until the skin tightens and the thickest part flakes cleanly. Overbake it and the fish oil turns heavy.
Rest for three minutes, then spoon the lemony tray juices over the fish. If you serve immediately, the beans taste flat because they have not drunk in the juices.

note: High protein without a separate sauce or pan.

name: Steamed Maple Custard Cups with Pecan Salt
hook: Soft custard, maple smoke, salted crunch

steps.t: Set a steamer or wide lidded pan with a rack over a low simmer. The water should murmur, not thump, or the custards will bubble and split.
Whisk the eggs, milk, cream, maple syrup, brown sugar, vanilla and salt just until smooth. Do not beat in froth, because those bubbles set as little craters.
Strain the custard into four heatproof ramekins, then skim any foam from the top. Straining catches egg threads that would otherwise cook into rubbery flecks.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil and place them in the steamer. Keep the lid slightly wrapped in a tea towel if it drips, as water spots make the tops pitted.
Steam gently until the custards wobble as one piece and the centre is no longer liquid. If the water boils hard, lower the heat before adding more time.
Toast the pecans in a dry pan until they smell like maple wood, then chop with a pinch more salt; stop before they darken at the edges, because burnt pecans taste metallic.
Rest the custards for five minutes, then finish with pecan salt. Serve warm for softness or chill for a firmer diner-style set.

note: The custard is fully cooked when softly set, not runny in the centre.

name: Patagonian Lamb Neck and Pumpkin Guiso
hook: Tender lamb, smoky broth, soft pumpkin

ingredients.name: aji molido or mild chilli flakes

steps.t: Heat the oil in a large saucepan and brown the lamb neck chops on both sides until the fat smells nutty. If you skip this, the stew tastes thin no matter how long it simmers.
Add the onion and carrot with a pinch of salt, cooking until the onion turns glossy and the browned bits loosen. If the pan looks dry and black, splash in water before it burns.
Stir in the garlic, aji molido and oregano for thirty seconds only; the garlic should smell sweet, not sharp and scorched.
Add the tomatoes, stock cube and 900ml water, scraping the base clean. Simmer with the lid half on until the lamb starts pulling from the bone.
Stir in the potatoes, pumpkin and rinsed lentils. Keep the simmer lazy, because a hard boil breaks the pumpkin into sludge before the potatoes are tender.
Lift out the lamb chops, pull the meat from the bones and return the meat to the pot. Do this while it is hot enough to shred easily, but check carefully for small bones.
Simmer uncovered until the lentils thicken the broth and the spoon leaves a brief trail through the stew. If it gets too thick before the potatoes soften, add water in small splashes.

note: Built for cheap cuts: the lentils stretch the lamb without making it feel sparse.

name: Charcoal Mussels with Pastis Persillade
hook: Briny shells, anise butter, smoky bread

steps.t: Light a small chimney of charcoal first; if the coals are still black when the mussels go on, they will stew in smoke rather than snap open cleanly.
Check the mussels while the fire settles: discard cracked shells and any open ones that do not close after a firm tap, because dead mussels are not worth gambling on.
Mash butter with garlic, parsley, shallot, pastis, lemon and salt until it smells sharp and green; leave lumps of plain butter and they will melt unevenly into greasy pools.
Brush the baguette with olive oil and grill cut-side down until the ridges are dark gold and brittle; pull it before the edges go black or the smoke will bully the mussels.

Tip the mussels into a grill basket or a shallow cast-iron pan over the hottest coals, close the lid and shake once halfway; they are ready when most shells gape wide and the liquor hisses at the bottom.
Immediately toss the hot mussels with the pastis persillade so the butter melts into the shell liquor; wait too long and the mussels tighten and lose their sweetness.
Pile into warm bowls with the charred baguette, discarding any mussels that stay shut after cooking.

note: Keep the mussels cold until cooking and never force open a closed cooked shell.

name: Everything-Bagel Halloumi Pickle Board
hook: Salty squeak, sharp grapes, dill crunch

steps.t: Stir vinegar, sugar and mustard seeds until the sugar no longer rasps on the bowl, then fold in the grapes; if the sugar sits at the bottom, the pickles taste harsh instead of rounded.
Cover and refrigerate the grapes overnight until their skins look taut and ruby-bright; rush this and they stay flatly sweet, not pickle-sharp.
Slice the halloumi as thinly as you can with a sharp knife; thick slabs eat rubbery and hide the lemon.
Dress the halloumi with lemon zest, lemon juice and olive oil, then chill it for at least 2 hours so the edges soften; skip the rest and the cheese tastes only salty.
Drain the grapes well before serving; watery pickle liquor will soak the crackers and turn the board tired in minutes.
Layer halloumi, grapes, radishes and cucumber on a cold platter, scattering dill and everything-bagel seasoning as you go so every bite gets crunch and acidity.
Serve with rye crackers right at the end; put them out early and they lose their snap beside the pickles.

note: This is a no-cook weekend board built on cured, pickled and raw textures; halloumi is safe to eat uncooked.

name: Chimichurri Pork Wok with Charred Peppers
hook: Lean pork, hot pan, green bite

ingredients.name: pork fillet, trimmed and sliced into thin strips

steps.t: Pat the pork dry and spread it on a plate with paprika, oregano, half the garlic and a good pinch of salt; damp meat drops the wok temperature and turns grey before it browns.
Stir parsley, vinegar, chilli flakes, remaining garlic and 1 tablespoon olive oil into a rough chimichurri; make it early so the garlic loses its raw sting.
Heat a wok or heavy frying pan until a drop of water skitters away, then add the remaining oil; if the oil only sits there, wait or the peppers will soften without charring.
Stir-fry peppers and onion hard until blistered at the tips but still loud when they hit the spoon; limp vegetables make the bowl taste like leftovers.
Lift the vegetables out, reheat the pan until smoking lightly, then fry the pork in two batches so each strip sears at the edges; crowd it and you will boil the fillet.
Return everything to the pan for a final toss, just until the pork is cooked through and the juices run clear; keep going past that point and lean fillet dries fast.
Spoon over hot brown rice and finish with chimichurri off the heat, because frying the parsley sauce dulls its clean green punch.

note: Slice the pork thinly across the grain for fast cooking and a tender, high-protein bowl.

name: Steamed Coconut Pudim Cups
hook: Silky caramel, coconut warmth, clean wobble

steps.t: Put sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup turns deep amber at the edges; stir it and it may crystallise into a sandy block.
Pour the caramel into six ramekins and swirl quickly to coat the bases; hesitate and the caramel sets in one thick patch.
Whisk condensed milk, coconut milk, eggs, yolks, vanilla, lime zest and salt until smooth but not foamy; too much froth bakes into bubbles instead of silk.
Strain the custard into a jug, then divide it over the caramel; skipping the sieve leaves little cords of egg white in the finished pudim.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil and set in a steamer over barely simmering water; a rolling boil rattles the cups and makes the custard grainy.
Steam until the edges are set and the centres tremble like soft jelly when nudged, topping up the pan with hot water if it runs low.
Cool, then chill until the caramel loosens into a glossy sauce; unmould too warm and the custard slumps instead of standing proud.
Run a thin knife around each cup and invert onto plates, letting the caramel spill over the top.

note: Use gentle steam, not aggressive boiling, for the smooth Brazilian pudim texture.

name: Lahori Lace-Edge Aloo Pakora
hook: Crisp potato ribbons, chilli, tangy salt

steps.t: Grate the potatoes into thin ribbons and squeeze them hard in a clean tea towel; leave them wet and the pakoras spit oil and turn leathery.

Mix potato, onion, cabbage, chilli, coriander, gram flour, rice flour, cumin, turmeric and salt with just enough cold water to make a sticky clump; a pourable batter gives heavy pancakes, not lace-edged pakoras.
Heat 1 cm oil in a frying pan until a shred of potato bubbles at once; if it sinks quietly, the first batch will drink oil.
Drop in small forkfuls and flatten them slightly so ragged edges stick out; smooth balls stay doughy in the middle before the outside crisps.
Fry until the undersides are deep golden and the onion tips look mahogany, then turn once; fiddling early tears off the crust.
Fry the second side until the pakoras sound scratchy when moved across the pan, then drain on a rack rather than paper so steam does not soften them.
Dust with chaat masala while hot and eat straight away, before the potato ribbons lose their brittle edges.

note: A cheap vegetable-led fry-up with no meat, eggs or dairy; keep the batter thick for real crunch.

name: Za’atar Griddled Pork with Tahini Apples
hook: Charred edges, warm spice, cool apple.

steps.t: Pat the pork very dry, then rub with za’atar, cumin, salt and 1 tbsp oil. If the surface is damp, it steams and the spice crust turns muddy instead of toasty.
Whisk tahini, lemon juice, garlic and 3–4 tbsp cold water until pale and spoonable. Add the water gradually; too much at once makes the tahini seize into a chalky lump.
Heat a griddle pan until a drop of water skitters off fast, then oil it lightly. If the pan is only warm, the pork will leak juice before it chars.
Griddle the pork until dark stripes form and the edges start to curl, about 4 minutes per side depending on thickness. Use a timer for the first side; moving it early tears off the crust.
Stand the steaks on their fatty edge with tongs until the fat turns golden and crisp. Skip this and the richest bite stays chewy.
Rest the pork on a warm plate while you toss apple with parsley and a pinch of salt. Cutting straight away sends the juices across the board instead of back into the meat.
Slice across the grain, spoon tahini underneath, and pile the apple over the hot pork so it stays bright rather than wilting into the sauce.

note: Use pork shoulder steaks rather than loin; the fat makes the hard griddle heat feel comforting, not dry.

name: Crisp Harissa Carrot Msemen Hash
hook: Shattering bread, sweet carrots, chilli warmth.

steps.t: Squeeze the grated carrot hard in a clean tea towel until it stops dripping. Wet carrot lowers the oil temperature and makes a soft tangle, not a crisp hash.
Stir harissa, cumin, cinnamon and lemon juice together, then loosen with 1 tbsp oil. Mixing the paste first prevents pockets of raw, bitter spice in the pan.
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a wide frying pan until the surface looks thin and shimmering. If the oil is cool, the flatbread drinks it before it crisps.
Fry the torn msemen in a single layer until the edges blister and sound dry when tapped, turning once. Crowding the pan traps steam and leaves leathery patches.
Lift the bread to a plate, then fry the onion and carrot in the same pan until the carrot darkens at the tips and smells sweet rather than raw.
Fold in the harissa mixture and return the crisp bread for the last minute only. Add it earlier and the shards collapse into porridge.
Spoon yoghurt onto plates, pile the hot hash over it, and finish with coriander so the herbs stay leafy rather than blackening in the pan.

note: A vegetable-led breakfast with no eggs needed; the crunch comes from shallow frying the bread properly.

name: Sherry-Pickled Beetroot with Smoked Almond Migas
hook: Glossy beetroot, sharp sherry, smoky crunch.

steps.t: Whisk sherry vinegar, honey, mustard, 30ml olive oil and a good pinch of salt until glossy. If the dressing is split now, it will slide off the beetroot later.
Toss the beetroot and red onion through the dressing while the wedges are at room temperature. Fridge-cold beetroot tastes muted and barely takes the pickle.
Leave the beetroot to pickle, turning once, until the onion softens and stains ruby at the edges. Less time leaves it harsh and raw.
Meanwhile heat the remaining oil in a frying pan and add the sourdough crumbs. Keep them moving until they turn unevenly golden with crisp little spikes; pale crumbs taste dusty.
Stir in smoked almonds and paprika for the final minute only. Paprika scorches fast and turns acrid if it sits on the pan floor.
Spoon the beetroot onto a wide platter, leaving excess dressing behind, then scatter the warm migas over just before serving. Add them too soon and the crunch drinks the pickle.
Finish with parsley and a thin thread of the reserved dressing, enough to shine but not flood the platter.

note: Use vacuum-packed cooked beetroot if you like; the impressive part is the sharp dressing and last-minute migas.

name: Summer Hake Tian with Fennel and Tomatoes
hook: Silky fish, fennel, sun-warmed juices.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Slice the fennel and courgette thinly; thick pieces stay squeaky and underdone by the time the fish is ready.
Toss fennel, tomatoes, courgette, garlic, olive oil and salt in a shallow baking dish, then spread them in an even layer. A piled-up centre steams while the edges dry out.
Bake until the tomatoes slump and the fennel tips take a little colour, giving the dish its sauce before the fish goes in.
Season the hake and nestle it into the vegetables with the thicker ends towards the hotter back of the oven. If the fillets sit on top, they dry before the underside cooks.
Pour the wine around, not over, the fish so the seasoning stays put. Bake until the flakes just separate when pressed at the thickest point.
Rest the dish out of the oven until the bubbling calms. Serve immediately from a violently boiling dish and the fish keeps cooking to chalky.
Finish with lemon zest and torn basil, letting them hit the warm juices rather than baking them dull and brown.

note: Any firm white fish works, but hake stays especially soft in this light one-dish bake.

name: Bourbon-Braised Mushrooms on Skillet Toast
hook: Deep gravy mushrooms, crisp buttery toast.

steps.t: Brown the mushrooms in a wide pan with olive oil and half the butter, working in two batches if needed. If they overlap heavily, they boil in their own water and never build a savoury crust.
Lower the heat and add shallot and garlic, cooking until the shallot turns translucent and sweet-smelling. Burnt garlic makes the whole braise taste metallic.
Pour in the bourbon and let it bubble until the harsh alcohol smell fades. Keep your face back from the steam, and do not leave it tasting raw and hot.
Add stock, soy sauce and maple syrup, then return all mushrooms to the pan. The liquid should come halfway up, not drown them, or the final sauce will be thin.
Cover and braise gently until the mushroom stems are tender all the way through. A hard boil breaks them down and clouds the sauce.
Uncover and simmer until the liquid coats a spoon in a shiny brown glaze. Stop too early and the toast goes soggy; push too far and it turns salty.
Fry the sourdough in the remaining butter until both faces are crisp and nut-brown, then spoon the mushrooms over and scatter with chives. Soft toast cannot hold a shared-plate braise.

note: Serve as small plates with forks, or cut each toast into fingers for passing around.

name: Crisp Gochujang Lamb Jeon
hook: Lacy edges, chilli gloss, juicy lamb

steps.t: Mix lamb, gochujang, soy, garlic, ginger, two spring onions and sesame oil until tacky; if it stays loose, the patties will shed crumbs in the pan.
Beat in the egg, then fold through flour and panko just until no dry patches remain; overworking makes the jeon bouncy instead of juicy.
Flatten into 8 thin patties, about 1 cm thick, with damp hands; thick centres cook slowly and the outside will burn before the lamb is safe.
Heat the neutral oil in a wide frying pan until a breadcrumb fizzes at once; if the oil is only warm, the coating drinks it and turns heavy.
Shallow-fry the patties in one layer until the undersides are lace-brown and crisp, then turn once; crowding drops the heat and steams the crust.
Cook the second side until crisp and the centres are piping hot with no pink lamb left, then drain on kitchen paper; leaving them in the pan softens the edges.
Scatter with the remaining spring onion and serve straight away, while the crust still rasps under a fork.

note: Add quick cucumber slices with rice vinegar if you want a fresher plate without slowing dinner down.

name: Steamed Red Bean Cloud Buns
hook: Soft white buns, glossy bean heart

ingredients.name: plain flour, plus extra for dusting

steps.t: Cover the adzuki beans with water in a pan, bring to a boil, then simmer until they crush easily between finger and thumb; undercooked beans make a gritty filling no sugar can hide.
Drain well, mash with 130 g sugar and oil, then stir over medium heat until the paste pulls from the pan in a glossy mound; stop too wet and it will leak through the dough.
Cool the paste completely, then roll into 16 balls; warm filling wakes the yeast too early and gives wrinkled buns.
Mix flour, yeast, baking powder, 40 g sugar and salt, then add lukewarm water and knead until smooth and elastic; dry cracks now become split seams later.
Cover and prove until puffed and almost doubled, not sagging; overproved dough smells boozy and collapses in the steamer.
Divide into 16 pieces, wrap each around a bean ball, pinch the seam tight and set seam-side down on parchment; a lazy seal opens like a mouth as steam builds.
Rest the buns until they feel marshmallow-light, then steam over a steady simmer with space between them; violent boiling spits water onto the tops and makes blisters.
Turn off the heat and leave the lid closed for 3 minutes before lifting it; sudden cold air shrinks the skins into wrinkles.

note: This is a slow, satisfying project: cook the beans properly and the buns feel bakery-soft.

name: Coal-Grilled Ancho Lime Chicken
hook: Smoke, lime, lean fire-charred protein

steps.t: Butterfly the chicken breasts to an even 1.5 cm thickness; uneven pieces dry at the thin end before the thick end is cooked through.
Rub with lime juice, olive oil, ancho, cumin, oregano, garlic and salt, then leave while the coals settle; longer is fine, but do not reuse raw-chicken marinade on cooked food.
Light the barbecue and wait until the coals are grey-edged with no tall flames; flames scorch the spices before the chicken reaches a safe centre.
Grill the chicken directly over the coals until clear grill marks form and the meat releases without tearing; if it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
Turn and grill until the thickest part reaches 74°C or the juices run clear with no translucent centre; guessing by colour on a smoky grill is risky.
Rest the chicken on a clean plate while you toss black beans, tomatoes and coriander; slicing immediately spills the juices across the board.
Slice across the grain and serve with the bean salad and avocado, spooning any clean resting juices over the top.

note: Lean breast, beans and avocado make it gym-friendly without tasting like punishment.

name: Steamed Mastiha Honey Custards
hook: Silky honey custard, pine-sweet perfume

ingredients.name: Greek thyme honey, plus extra to serve

steps.t: Warm milk, cream, orange zest, salt and mastiha until steaming at the edges, not boiling; boiled dairy dulls the perfume and can split the custard.
Whisk eggs, honey and sugar just until smooth, avoiding froth; foam sets as bubbles and ruins the glassy surface.
Pour the hot milk into the eggs in a thin stream while whisking constantly; adding it fast scrambles the eggs into sweet soup.
Strain into four small heatproof ramekins and skim any bubbles; what you see on top now will set on top later.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil and place in a steamer over a gentle simmer; a hard boil shakes the custard into curds.
Steam until the edges are set and the centre wobbles like thick yoghurt, then remove from the heat; fully firm in the steamer means rubbery on the spoon.
Cool for 10 minutes, then finish with honey and pistachios; serving straight from the steamer hides the floral mastiha under heat.

note: Mastiha is potent, so keep it restrained for a clean Greek finish.

name: Pul Biber Halloumi Sac Tava
hook: Salty squeak, blistered peppers, tomato heat

steps.t: Pat the halloumi dry before it hits the pan; wet cubes steam and squeak sadly instead of taking colour.
Heat a wok or wide frying pan until a drop of water vanishes on contact, then add oil and halloumi; a lukewarm pan makes the cheese weep brine.
Stir-fry the halloumi until two sides are golden and blistered, then lift it to a plate; leave it in too long and it turns tough before the vegetables are ready.
Throw onion and peppers into the same hot pan and keep them moving until the edges char and the middles stay bright; slow cooking makes them limp and sweet.
Add garlic, pul biber and tomato paste, frying until the paste darkens brick-red; if it stays raw, the whole pan tastes tinny.
Tip in the chopped tomatoes and boil hard until the sauce clings to the peppers rather than pooling underneath; watery sauce slides straight out of the flatbread.
Return the halloumi for 30 seconds only, toss with parsley, and eat in warm flatbreads; reheating it for minutes kills the soft, salty centre.

note: Built for one pan, cheap cheese and enough heat to make a student hob feel useful.

name: Weeknight Beef Carbonada with Sweetcorn
hook: Silky beef, squash and paprika warmth

ingredients.name: butternut squash, peeled and 2 cm diced

steps.t: Heat the oil in a wide casserole, add the beef mince with a pinch of salt, and press it down until the underside forms dark little crusts; if you stir straight away, it stews grey and loses the beefy base.
Break up the mince, add the onion and red pepper, and cook until the onion turns glossy and the pepper softens at the edges; if the pan looks wet, keep cooking until the moisture has driven off.
Stir in the garlic, tomato purée and paprika until the purée darkens to brick-red and sticks slightly to the pan; if the paprika scorches, the stew will taste bitter, so keep it moving.
Add the squash and stock, scraping the bottom clean, then simmer uncovered until the squash is tender but not collapsing; a hard boil will smash the cubes and make the stew muddy.
Stir in the sweetcorn and simmer until the kernels are hot and bright yellow; adding them earlier makes them dull and chewy.
Finish with the vinegar, taste for salt, and let the stew sit off the heat until the surface stops bubbling; serving it immediately means the flavours taste separate rather than rounded.

note: A fast, practical nod to Argentine carbonada using mince so the stew tastes slow-cooked on a weeknight.

name: Whole Roasted Mackerel Moqueca with Lime Farofa
hook: Rich fish, coconut, smoky citrus crumbs

ingredients.name: whole mackerel, about 500 g each, gutted and scaled

steps.t: Cut three shallow slashes into each side of the mackerel, then rub with half the lime juice, the zest, garlic and salt; keep the cuts shallow, because deep cuts make oily fish tear open in the oven.
Chill the fish uncovered so the skin dries and the seasoning settles; if the skin goes into the oven wet, it steams before it roasts.
Spread onion, peppers and tomatoes in a roasting tin with palm oil and salt, then roast until the pepper tips blister and the tomatoes slump; pale vegetables underneath the fish will taste boiled.
Pour in the coconut milk, stir the vegetables loose, and lay the mackerel on top; keep the fish sitting proud of the sauce or the skin turns soft.
Roast until the eyes turn opaque, the belly flesh flakes at the thickest point, and the sauce bubbles thickly at the edges; undercooked whole fish clings stubbornly to the bone.
Meanwhile melt the butter, stir in cassava flour and toast until it smells nutty and feels sandy, not dusty; if you rush it, the farofa tastes raw and chalky.
Stir the remaining lime juice and coriander through the sauce, spoon over a little sauce, and serve the whole fish with lime farofa; drowning it on the platter hides the crisp roasted top.

note: Built around Brazilian moqueca flavours, but treated as a whole-fish roast for a slow weekend centrepiece.

name: Dhungar Tofu Tikka Bowl with Green Chutney Beans
hook: Smoke-kissed tofu, sharp chutney crunch

steps.t: Pat the pressed tofu dry until it feels tacky rather than wet; if you leave surface water, the yoghurt marinade slides off and the tofu will not char.
Mix yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, tikka spices, chilli powder, lemon and salt, then fold in the tofu gently; rough mixing breaks the cubes and makes the bowl look like scramble.
