Thread the tofu on skewers or spread it on a lined tray, brush with oil, and grill hot until the corners blister and the marinade sets into rusty patches; if the grill is lukewarm, it bakes pale and sour.
Boil the green beans until bright and just squeaky, then drain hard; overcooked beans turn khaki and make the bowl feel canteen-heavy.
Blend coriander, mint, green chilli, a spoon of yoghurt, water and salt into a loose chutney, then toss through the beans; too little water makes it claggy instead of coating.

For the dhungar smoke, put the cooked tofu in a heatproof bowl, set a foil cup in the middle, add red-hot charcoal, drizzle it with a few drops of oil, cover tightly and smoke until you smell barbecue when you lift the lid; do this away from loose paper and discard the charcoal safely.
Pile rice, smoky tofu and chutney beans into bowls while the tofu is still warm; if it cools fully before serving, the smoke turns flat rather than fragrant.

note: High-protein without heaviness: tofu, yoghurt and beans bring the protein while dhungar smoke gives proper Pakistani grill character.

name: Cà Phê Trứng Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Velvet coffee custard, caramel-bitter finish

steps.t: Whisk eggs, yolks, condensed milk, whole milk, coffee, vanilla and salt until smooth but not frothy; beating in foam leaves little holes through the custard.
Strain the mixture into a jug, then skim off any bubbles; skipped bubbles set as pockmarks on the surface.
Divide between four small heatproof cups and cover each tightly with foil; uncovered cups catch dripping steam and turn watery on top.
Set the cups in a steamer over a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, and steam until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly; fierce steam makes the eggs split and weep.
Turn off the heat and leave the cups covered in the steamer so the residual heat finishes the middle; pulling them out too soon gives a liquid centre under a set skin.
Chill until cool and softly set; warm custard tastes eggier and the coffee bitterness feels sharper.
Dust with cocoa and a little caster sugar just before serving; dusting early dissolves into damp patches instead of a fine bitter-sweet cap.

note: Inspired by Vietnamese egg coffee, reworked as a steamed dessert custard rather than a drink.

name: Coal-Grilled Ceci Spiedini with Lemon Rosemary Oil
hook: Charred chickpeas, rosemary, bright lemon

steps.t: Light the coals and let them burn down until they are white-edged with no tall flames; cooking over flames blackens the outside before the chickpeas warm through.
Pat the chickpeas very dry, then toss with one tablespoon of oil, fennel seeds, chilli and salt; wet chickpeas steam and fall apart when you try to skewer them.
Thread the chickpeas snugly onto soaked wooden skewers, using any split ones for a loose foil tray; forcing broken chickpeas onto skewers just makes them crumble into the coals.
Mix the remaining oil with lemon zest, lemon juice, rosemary and garlic, then keep it away from the grill; brushing garlicky oil on too early burns it bitter.
Grill the chickpea skewers over steady coals, turning when the skins blister and pick up little char spots; turn too soon and they stick, too late and they dry to pellets.
Grill the stale bread until the ridges are dark and the centre is still chewy; thin or fresh bread scorches before it becomes satisfying.
Spoon the lemon rosemary oil over the hot chickpeas, pile with rocket on the grilled bread, and eat at once; if it sits, the bread takes all the oil and the chickpeas lose their crackle.

note: A cheap Italian-style grill meal that treats tinned chickpeas like spiedini, with bread making it filling enough for dinner.

name: Hanoi Winter Hake with Ginger Pickle Dressing
hook: Warm flakes, sharp pickle, gingered steam

steps.t: Toss the daikon and carrot with the rice vinegar, sugar and a good pinch of salt, then scrunch until the matchsticks look glossy and start to bend; if you leave them stiff, the pickle tastes raw rather than bright.
Cook the rice noodles until they bend easily but still have a little spring, then drain and rinse with hot water; if they go soft now, the warm dressing will turn them woolly.

Put the hake in a shallow pan with 2 tbsp water, cover and steam over a low simmer until the flesh turns pearly white and flakes at the thickest point; a hard boil tightens the fish and leaves a dry edge.
Warm the fish sauce with the lime juice, grated ginger, crushed garlic, sliced chilli and 2 tbsp hot water just until it smells gingery; do not boil it, or the lime turns harsh and metallic.
Drain the pickle well, then toss it through the warm noodles with most of the coriander; if the pickle liquid floods the bowl, the dressing gets thin and sour.

Lift the hake on top in large flakes, checking for bones as you go, then spoon over the hot ginger dressing and finish with the remaining coriander; pouring it on cold loses the winter comfort of the dish.

note: Best with a warmed bowl so the noodles and dressing stay steamy.

name: Sicilian Sardine Dawn Bake
hook: Runny eggs, crisp crumbs, briny sardines

ingredients.name: tinned sardines in olive oil, drained

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C and put a small baking dish inside; starting in a cold dish makes the tomatoes stew instead of blister.
Tip the tomatoes, olive oil, fennel seeds and capers into the hot dish and shake once, then bake until the tomato skins split and the juices hiss at the edges.
Fold in the spinach while the dish is still hot, just until it slumps and turns glossy; if you pack it in raw under the eggs, it leaks water and thins the bake.
Make four clear wells, crack in the eggs, then tuck the sardines between them rather than over the yolks; covering the yolks traps heat and overcooks them before the whites set.
Scatter over the ciabatta, Parmesan and lemon zest, keeping some crumbs on the surface so they crisp instead of soaking up tomato juice.
Bake until the whites are set, the yolks still wobble softly and the crumbs are golden at their tips; pull it too early and the whites stay snotty, too late and breakfast turns chalky.

note: Serve straight from the dish with coffee and more lemon if you like it sharper.

name: Black Cardamom Beef Shin
hook: Silky gravy, spoon-tender beef, warm spice

ingredients.name: beef shin, cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Pat the beef dry, salt it, then brown it in ghee in batches until the flat sides have a deep crust; crowd the pan and the meat steams grey, which gives a dull gravy.
Lower the heat and cook the onions in the same pot until they collapse and turn lace-brown at the edges; pale onions taste raw-sweet, while black onions make the whole braise bitter.
Stir in the ginger, garlic, coriander, chilli, garam masala and black cardamom until the spice catches in the fat and smells toasted; if it sticks dry, add a splash of stock before it scorches.
Beat the yoghurt with the tomato purée, then stir it in a spoonful at a time until the sauce looks brick-red and glossy; dumping cold yoghurt into fierce heat makes it split into grains.

Return the beef and any juices, pour in the stock, cover and braise at a lazy bubble until a spoon presses through the shin without resistance; a fast boil squeezes the meat dry before the collagen melts.
Uncover and simmer until the gravy coats the back of a spoon in a smooth sheet; if it still runs like stock, it will look thin on the platter.
Rest the braise off the heat for 15 minutes, then skim the top lightly and serve; skipping the rest leaves the gravy greasy rather than plush.

note: Serve with naan, saffron rice and a sharp cucumber salad for contrast.

name: Sour Pineapple Mackerel Stew
hook: Sour broth, rich mackerel, pineapple snap

steps.t: Cut the mackerel into large pieces and keep it chilled while you build the broth; small pieces overcook before the vegetables are ready.
Crush the shallots, lemongrass and curry paste together in the pot with a splash of water until the paste loosens and smells citrusy; leaving lumps of lemongrass gives woody bites.
Add 750 ml water, tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar, then simmer until the broth tastes sharply sour but rounded at the back; if it tastes flat now, the fish will not fix it later.
Add the pineapple, tomatoes and green beans and simmer until the beans are bright green and the tomatoes start to slump, not collapse.
Slide in the mackerel skin-side up and keep the stew at a gentle tremble until the fish flakes cleanly at the thickest part; a rolling boil breaks the oily fish into grey crumbs.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in lime and tear over Thai basil; boiling after the lime goes in dulls the fresh summer edge.

note: Serve warm rather than piping hot, with jasmine rice if you want it more filling.

name: Miso-Roasted Whole Tofu with Daikon Ponzu
hook: Burnished tofu, sharp daikon, sesame crunch

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in kitchen paper and press it under a light weight until the paper is wet and the block feels firmer; if it stays waterlogged, it steams and the glaze slides off.
Heat the oven to 220°C and line a small tray with baking paper; miso catches fast on bare metal and turns acrid before the tofu warms through.
Mix the miso, mirin, half the soy sauce and sesame oil into a smooth glaze, then score the tofu top in shallow diamonds; cut too deep and the block splits when you lift it.
Set the tofu whole on the tray, brush it generously with glaze and scatter the shiitake around it; keep the mushrooms cut-side up so they roast meaty rather than leak into the glaze.
Roast until the tofu is burnished at the ridges and the mushrooms have curled dark edges; if the glaze is still beige, it has not developed its savoury sweetness.
Stir the grated daikon with the lemon juice and remaining soy sauce, then squeeze it lightly so it is juicy but not swimming; too much liquid washes the roasted crust away.
Move the whole tofu to a sharing plate, spoon daikon ponzu around it and finish with spring onions and sesame seeds; slicing it in the kitchen loses the drama and cools the centre.

note: Put out small spoons so everyone can take a burnished edge and a soft middle.

name: Malai Paneer Kachumber with Saffron Walnuts
hook: Cool paneer, warm spice, winter softness

steps.t: Soak the saffron in the warm milk until the milk turns deep gold; if you scatter it straight into cold yoghurt, the flavour stays trapped in dry threads.
Whisk the yoghurt, cream, saffron milk, cardamom and chaat masala until glossy and spoon-coating; leave lumps now and they cling to the paneer in chalky patches.
Fold in the paneer gently so the cubes stay clean-edged, then let it sit while you cut the vegetables; rough stirring breaks it into a paste rather than a kachumber.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan just until they smell buttery and show darker speckles, then tip them out; keep them in the hot pan and they go bitter fast.
Toss the onion, cucumber, lemon juice and coriander in a separate bowl, squeezing the onion once with your fingers so it softens without becoming wet and limp.
Spoon the chilled malai paneer into shallow bowls, pile the sharp kachumber beside it and finish with warm walnuts; mixing everything too early makes the cucumber bleed into the cream.

note: A barely cooked winter chaat: creamy, cool and soothing rather than fiery.

name: Crackling Mung Bean Pad Krapow Breakfast Rice
hook: Hot wok beans, basil, runny yolk

steps.t: Spread the mung beans on kitchen paper and pat them very dry; wet beans steam in the wok and turn breakfast into sludge.
Stir together the soy sauce, oyster sauce, fish sauce and sugar in a cup so it can hit the wok at once; hunting for bottles later will burn the garlic.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wok until it shimmers hard, then add garlic and chillies for a few seconds until sharp and fragrant; if the garlic goes chestnut before the beans go in, start again.
Throw in the mung beans and press them against the hot metal until some skins split and crackle; constant stirring stops them catching the smoky edges you want.
Add the cold rice and break it up with the back of the spatula until every grain is hot and separate; clumps stay bland inside no matter how much sauce you add.
Pour in the sauce and toss hard until the rice looks stained and dry rather than shiny-wet, then fold through the basil just until it collapses; overcooked basil tastes muddy.
In a separate small pan, fry the eggs in the remaining oil until the whites blister and the yolks still wobble; pale rubbery eggs flatten the whole plate.
Serve the basil mung rice with the crisp-edged eggs and lime wedges, squeezing lime at the table so the rice stays lively rather than damp.

note: Use day-old rice and properly drained pulses for real wok character.

name: Miso-Lacquered Halloumi Yaki with Nori Pear
hook: Glossy salt-sweet slabs, clean pear snap

steps.t: Pat the halloumi dry on both sides until the paper comes away almost clean; surface brine makes the glaze slide off and spit on the griddle.
Whisk miso, mirin, soy, vinegar and honey into a smooth lacquer; unmixed miso burns in salty clumps before the cheese warms through.
Heat a ridged griddle until a drop of water skips away, then oil it lightly; a lukewarm griddle gives you sweaty halloumi with no stripes.
Lay on the halloumi and leave it alone until dark ridges mark the underside and the edges soften slightly; moving it early tears the crust and leaves half on the pan.
Turn the slices, brush the cooked side with glaze, then flip briefly glazed-side down just until sticky and mahogany in spots; leave sugar over the heat too long and it goes acrid.
Brush the second side, flip for a final lacquer, then lift the halloumi to a warm plate before it tightens and squeaks too hard.
Toss the pear with nori, sesame and spring onion at the last moment; salt from the nori pulls juice quickly and dulls the clean crunch.
Serve the glossy halloumi in overlapping slabs with the nori pear scattered over and around it, keeping the stripes visible for the table.

note: A griddle-pan centrepiece with izakaya-style shine and a fresh, sharp garnish.

name: Sesame-Crisp Pork Perilla Cups with Chilled Cucumber
hook: Crackly pork, cold leaves, bright vinegar

ingredients.name: pork tenderloin, sliced into thin medallions

steps.t: Stir the gochujang, soy, vinegar and ginger together, then coat the pork lightly; drown it in marinade and the starch turns gluey instead of crisp.
Leave the pork while you shave the cucumber and chill it with the spring onions; warm cucumber wilts the leaves and makes the plate feel heavy.
Mix potato starch with sesame seeds, then press each pork slice into it until dusted all over, shaking off loose powder; thick patches fry into sandy shells.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of starch sizzles instantly, then add pork in one uncrowded layer; crowding drops the heat and the coating drinks oil.
Fry until the underside is crisp and pale gold at the edges, then turn once; fiddling with it before the crust sets pulls the sesame coat away.
Cook the second side until the pork is firm but still springy, then drain on a rack rather than paper so steam cannot soften the crust.
Toss cucumber and spring onion with sesame oil and a tiny splash of rice vinegar from the bowl if needed; season lightly because the pork brings salt and chilli.
Pile crisp pork into perilla or lettuce cups with the chilled cucumber, serving straight away while hot crust and cold leaves still contrast.

note: Tenderloin cooks quickly and safely; slice evenly so every piece finishes together.

name: Black Vinegar Pickled Eggs with Chilli Sesame Dressing
hook: Jammy yolks, dark tang, sesame heat

steps.t: Lower the eggs into gently boiling water and keep the boil lively but not violent; a hard rolling pan cracks shells and leaks white into the water.
Move the eggs straight into iced water until completely cool to the touch; if they stay warm, the yolks keep cooking past jammy.
Meanwhile simmer the vinegar, soy, sugar, star anise and ginger just until the sugar dissolves and the spices smell rounded, then cool it; hot pickle toughens the egg whites.
Peel the eggs carefully under water, tapping all over first so the membrane loosens; gouged whites absorb unevenly and look ragged on a shared plate.
Submerge the peeled eggs in the cooled pickle, turning once halfway so the colour stains evenly; floating tops stay pale and taste underseasoned.
Stir chilli crisp with sesame oil and a spoonful of the pickling liquid until glossy; straight chilli crisp sits greasy on the eggs rather than dressing them.
Halve the eggs with a wet sharp knife, wiping between cuts so the yolks stay clean, then arrange cut-side up on a shallow plate.
Spoon over the chilli sesame dressing and scatter with spring onions and sesame seeds just before serving; dress too early and the yolks lose their shine.

note: Made for sharing alongside cold greens, peanuts and steamed buns.

name: Salsa Verde Courgette Tortilla Bake
hook: Tangy salsa, soft tortillas, crisp edges

ingredients.name: small corn tortillas, torn into quarters
lime, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Put the oil, pepper and courgette into a small baking dish and toss hard enough to coat the vegetables; dry patches scorch before they soften.
Bake the vegetables on the top shelf until the courgette edges look blistered and the pepper has slumped, not just warmed through.
Stir in the sweetcorn, cumin, lime zest and two-thirds of the salsa verde. Scrape the corners of the dish, because hidden dry cumin tastes dusty after baking.
Fold through the torn tortillas so they are glossy with sauce but not compacted; if you press them flat they turn heavy instead of spoonable.
Spoon the remaining salsa over the top and bake until the exposed tortilla tips are crisp and the sauce bubbles thickly around the sides.
Rest for 3 minutes so the tortillas drink the sauce rather than slide apart on the plate. Finish with coriander and lime wedges.

note: Use a punchy tomatillo salsa verde if you can; a green jalapeño salsa also works.

name: Island Salt Cod Plaki with Cinnamon Onions
hook: Silky onions, sweet tomato, pearly cod

steps.t: Rinse the salt cod, cover it with plenty of cold water and refrigerate, changing the water several times; if you rush this, the finished plaki will be aggressively salty all the way through.
Drain the cod, pat it dry and cut into large pieces, feeling for bones as you go. Small scraps overcook before the sauce has settled around them.
Warm the oil in a wide casserole and cook the onions with a pinch of salt until they collapse into a pale gold tangle; if they catch brown now, the long braise turns bitter.
Stir in the garlic for just a minute, then add passata, potatoes, cinnamon and bay. Keep the heat low enough for lazy plops, because a hard boil breaks the potatoes and spits tomato everywhere.
Cover and braise until the potatoes yield to a knife and the sauce tastes sweet rather than raw-tomato sharp.
Nestle in the cod and olives, spoon sauce over the fish, then cover and barely simmer until the flakes separate when nudged; boiling makes salt cod cottony.
Turn off the heat, add vinegar and parsley, and rest uncovered so the oil rises in orange pools instead of tasting muddy.

note: The soaking day is part of the dish; start on Saturday for a Sunday lunch.

name: Pul Biber Mushroom Lentil Güveç
hook: Earthy mushrooms in a peppery red stew

steps.t: Heat the oil in a deep pan and cook the onion until glossy and soft at the edges; if it stays raw, the stew keeps a harsh onion bite.
Add the mushrooms and spread them out. Let them squeak, darken and give off their water before stirring too much, or they stew grey and bland from the start.
Stir in tomato paste, pepper paste and pul biber until the oil stains brick red; undercooked paste tastes metallic no matter how long the lentils simmer.
Add lentils, chickpeas and stock, scraping the base clean. Simmer with the lid slightly ajar so the lentils soften without the pan reducing to sludge.
Check the lentils: they should be tender with a tiny bite and the broth should coat a spoon. If it is watery, simmer uncovered; if it is tight, splash in hot water.
Take off the heat for 2 minutes, then swirl in half the yoghurt so it enriches rather than splits in the boil.
Serve with the remaining yoghurt and dill on top, keeping the herbs fresh rather than stirring them into the hot stew until dull.

note: Built around lentils, chickpeas and strained yoghurt for a filling post-training bowl.

name: Rose Cardamom Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Wobbling silk with pistachio crunch

steps.t: Warm the milk, cream, sugar and cardamom until steaming at the edges, then turn off the heat; boiling it hard gives the custard a cooked-milk heaviness.
Leave to infuse until the cardamom smells floral rather than sharp, then strain out the pods.
Whisk the eggs in a jug just until smooth, not foamy. Pour in the warm milk slowly while whisking, because hot milk dumped in one go scrambles the eggs.
Stir in the rose water, then strain the custard into four small heatproof cups. Skipping the strain leaves stringy egg bits that ruin the silkiness.
Cover each cup tightly with foil and set in a steamer over barely simmering water. A rolling boil punches holes through the custard and makes it rubbery.
Steam until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly when tapped, then lift them out carefully so water does not slosh under the foil.
Cool for 10 minutes, then chill until cold. Finish with pistachios and a thread of honey just before serving so the nuts stay crisp.

note: Rose waters vary wildly; start measured rather than generous.

name: Smoked Mackerel Chermoula Couscous
hook: Smoky flakes, lemon herbs, warm spice

steps.t: Put the couscous in a bowl with a pinch of salt, pour over the boiling water and cover tightly; a loose cover lets steam escape and leaves hard grains underneath.
Mix the olive oil, cumin, smoked paprika, lemon zest, half the lemon juice and grated garlic into a loose chermoula. If the garlic sits in a dry clump, it bites too harshly.
Fluff the couscous with a fork until no wet lumps remain; stirring with a spoon compacts it into paste.
Fold the chermoula and grated carrot through the warm couscous so the spice blooms and the carrot softens just slightly.
Break the smoked mackerel into big flakes, checking for bones as you go. Mash it too small and the oily fish takes over every mouthful.
Gently turn the mackerel and herbs through the couscous, then sharpen with the remaining lemon juice until it tastes bright rather than oily.

note: Smoked mackerel is already cooked, so this is about warming it gently, not frying it dry.

name: Miso Roasted Whole Mushrooms with Buttered Negi
hook: Deep savoury warmth, glossy and woodsy

ingredients.name: large chestnut or portobello mushrooms, kept whole

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Wipe the mushrooms clean and trim only the dry stem ends; washing them makes the tray flood before the caps can roast properly.
Mix the miso, butter, mirin and soy into a soft paste. If the butter is cold, it will sit in lumps and scorch before the miso glazes the mushrooms.
Put the mushrooms gill-side up on a lined tray and rub the paste over the caps and into the gills. Keep them whole and spaced apart, or they steam into grey sponges.
Roast until the caps sag slightly, the edges are dark and sticky, and the tray juices smell nutty rather than raw.
Spoon the hot tray juices back over the mushrooms, then return them to the oven until the glaze catches in shiny mahogany patches; pull them before the miso turns black and bitter.
Stir the rice vinegar through the sliced spring onions. This cuts the butteriness; skip it and the dish eats heavy rather than comforting.
Serve the whole mushrooms over warm rice with buttered negi, sesame and nori. Pour over every drop of roasting liquor, as that is where the winter depth sits.

note: Use the largest firm mushrooms you can find; small ones overcook before the miso glaze develops.

name: Smoked Samgyeopsal Breakfast Bap with Kimchi Eggs
hook: Smoke, yolk and chilli morning crunch

ingredients.name: oak or apple wood chips, soaked and drained

steps.t: Stir the gochujang, soy and sesame oil together, then coat the pork belly lightly. Do not cake it on, because sugary chilli paste burns fast in smoke.

Set up a barbecue or lidded grill for indirect cooking with a small handful of drained wood chips on the coals. Wait until the smoke smells sweet and woody, not sharp and dirty, before adding the pork.
Smoke the pork belly away from direct heat, lid down, until the fat turns translucent and the edges tighten. Keep it off the flames or the dripping fat will flare and blacken the marinade.
Move the pork briefly over direct heat to crisp the edges until they blister and char in small spots. If you leave it there too long, the glaze goes bitter before the fat renders.

While the pork rests, fry the chopped kimchi in a dry pan until its wet hiss turns to a sharper sizzle. Add the rice and press it down so the bottom freckles gold; stirring constantly stops the crust forming.
Fry the eggs until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble. Undercooked whites make the bap slippery, while hard yolks lose the sauce you want.
Toast the buns cut-side down, pile in the kimchi rice, sliced smoked pork, egg, spring onions and sesame. Build just before eating or the bun steams soft underneath.

note: This is intentionally hearty; serve with iced barley tea or cucumber if you want a fresher breakfast plate.

name: Ginger-Scallion Steamed Mackerel with Sizzling Soy
hook: Silky fish under aromatic hot oil

ingredients.name: whole mackerel, about 450 g each, cleaned and scaled
fresh ginger, cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: Pat the mackerel dry inside and out, then cut three shallow slashes on each side. If the skin stays wet, it tastes steamed-flat rather than clean and glossy.
Put half the ginger and spring onions inside the fish and set them on a heatproof plate that fits your steamer. Do not crowd the plate, or the bellies cook while the thick backs stay glassy.
Bring the steamer to a hard boil before the fish goes in. Starting in lukewarm steam gives oily fish time to leak and smell heavy.
Steam until the eyes turn white, the skin pulls back at the slashes, and the thickest flesh lifts from the bone with a chopstick.
Carefully pour away the cloudy liquid from the plate. Keep it and the final sauce tastes muddy, no matter how good the fish is.
Warm the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine and sugar just until the sugar dissolves, then spoon it around the fish, not over the crisp aromatics you are about to add.

Heap the remaining ginger, spring onions, coriander and white pepper on top. Heat the neutral oil with sesame oil until it shimmers and just begins to smoke, then pour it over the aromatics so they crackle; oil that is not hot enough makes them greasy instead of fragrant.

note: Ask the fishmonger to clean the mackerel but keep the heads on for the most impressive platter.

name: Coal-Grilled Achiote Tofu with Lime Cabbage
hook: Charred edges, cool crunch, bright lime

steps.t: Press the tofu between clean towels with a weight on top until it feels firm and dry at the edges. Wet tofu sticks to the grill and tastes steamed rather than coal-kissed.
Whisk achiote paste with orange juice, half the lime juice, olive oil and cumin. Mash out the red lumps, because pockets of paste taste dusty and over-salted.
Cut the tofu into thick slabs and coat them with the achiote marinade. Keep the slabs broad, not diced, or they fall through the bars when you turn them.
Toss cabbage, red onion, jalapeño, coriander and the remaining lime juice with a pinch of salt. Squeeze the cabbage once with your hands so it bends without collapsing into pickle.
Grill the tofu over medium-hot coals until it releases cleanly and has dark rail marks at the edges. If you force it early, the crust stays behind on the grate.
Turn with a thin spatula and grill the second side until the marinade smells citrusy and toasted, not raw and earthy.
Warm the tortillas at the edge of the grill, then serve the tofu with lime cabbage folded over the top. Keep the slaw off until serving so the tofu stays charred, not soggy.

note: A clean, well-oiled grill grate matters here more than extra oil in the marinade.

name: Ouzo-Cured Sardine Meze with Cucumber and Dill
hook: Cold silver fish, anise and lemon

ingredients.name: very fresh sardine fillets, pin-boned and skin on

steps.t: Use sardines that smell clean and sea-like, and keep them chilled until the moment you work. If they smell fishy before curing, salt and lemon will not rescue them.
Lay the fillets skin-side down and sprinkle the flesh evenly with sea salt. Too much piled in one place gives you hard salty patches while the rest stays soft.
Rinse the fillets quickly under cold water and pat them completely dry. Leaving surface salt or water behind makes the dressing harsh and thin.
Whisk lemon zest, lemon juice, ouzo and olive oil until cloudy. Add the sardines and turn them once; they should go satin-opaque at the edges but stay tender in the centre.
Fold cucumber, shallot, capers and dill together separately. Mixing them in too early draws out water and dilutes the ouzo-lemon gloss.
Arrange the sardines on a cold plate, spoon over the cucumber mixture and a little curing oil. Do not stack the fillets high, or the delicate cure becomes mushy under its own weight.
Serve with grilled sourdough while the bread is still crisp. Soft bread turns this from bright meze into oily toast.

note: For raw-style preparations, buy sardines from a trusted fishmonger and tell them you plan to cure them lightly.

name: Saffron Steam Tofu with Smoky Chickpeas
hook: Silken warmth, paprika, slow winter depth

steps.t: Cut the tofu into 2 cm slabs, pat it dry, and salt both sides lightly; wet tofu steams watery rather than custardy.
Warm the oil in a wide pan, add the onion, and cook until it folds down soft and pale gold at the edges; rush this and the base tastes sharp, not sweet.
Stir in the garlic, paprika and saffron for 30 seconds, just until the oil turns brick-red; let the paprika catch and it goes bitter fast.
Add chickpeas, passata and stock, then simmer until the sauce thickens enough to leave a slow trail when you drag a spoon through it; too loose and it will swamp the tofu.
Set the tofu on a heatproof plate in a steamer, spoon over 3 tablespoons of the chickpea sauce, cover, and steam until the tofu is hot right through and slightly quivering.
Stir sherry vinegar through the remaining chickpeas and taste for salt; add the vinegar before simmering and its brightness disappears.
Spoon the smoky chickpeas into warm bowls, slide the steamed tofu on top, and finish with parsley and a thread of olive oil.

note: Best with crusty bread for catching the paprika-saffron broth.

name: Coal-Grilled Halloumi Croque with Thyme Grapes
hook: Smoke, salt, honeyed grapes, crisp brioche

steps.t: Light the charcoal and wait until the flames have gone and the coals are ash-grey; cooking over flames scorches the brioche before the cheese warms.
Mix Dijon, crème fraîche, lemon zest and plenty of black pepper; keep it thick, because a loose sauce makes the toast slide apart.
Toss the grapes with honey, thyme and a squeeze of lemon, then thread them onto skewers or sit them in a grill basket; loose grapes drop through the bars and burst in the coals.
Butter one side of each brioche slice and spread the mustard cream on the other; butter outside gives crunch, but butter inside turns greasy.
Grill the grapes until their skins split and shine, turning once; pull them before they collapse into jam.
Grill the halloumi until the bars are deep bronze and the centres bend without melting away; move it too early and it tears to the grate.
Toast the brioche butter-side down until the edges are crisp and nut-brown, then sandwich with halloumi and grapes and serve while the cheese still squeaks.

note: A French-leaning coal breakfast: croque structure, thyme, mustard cream and sweet grilled fruit.

name: Cape Cod Fluke Crudo with Buttermilk Snow
hook: Cold silk, apple snap, clean heat

ingredients.name: sashimi-grade fluke or other white fish fillet, skinless and pin-boned

steps.t: Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it below 5°C, and open it only when you are ready; ordinary raw fillets are not a safe shortcut here.
Chill four plates and your serving bowl; warm plates soften the fish and make the buttermilk look tired.
Whisk buttermilk with lemon juice, horseradish and a pinch of salt until it tastes bright but not sour; too much lemon makes the dairy split into grainy flecks.
Slice the fish across the grain into thin, even pieces with a clean sharp knife on a clean board; sawing gives ragged edges and warms the flesh.
Lay the fish in a single layer on the cold plates, then season with flaky salt and olive oil; stacking the slices makes them cure unevenly and look clumsy.
Spoon the buttermilk around, not over, the fish so the surface stays glossy and visible; drowning it hides the clean cut you paid for.
Finish with apple, celery, dill and crushed crisps just before serving; add them early and the crunch goes limp.

note: Serve immediately, and discard any raw fish left at room temperature for more than two hours.

name: Chimichurri Chicken Salteado with Peach Corn
hook: Fast char, green herbs, summer crunch

ingredients.name: chicken breast, sliced into thin strips
ripe but firm peach, cut into wedges

steps.t: Mix parsley, oregano, garlic, vinegar, chilli flakes and 1 tablespoon of olive oil to make a loose chimichurri; if it sits as a dry paste, it will clump instead of coating the chicken.
Pat the chicken dry and season it well; damp strips steam in the wok and never pick up the smoky edges you want.
Heat a wok or large frying pan until a drop of water skitters away instantly, then add the remaining oil; start cooler and the chicken leaks juice.
Stir-fry the chicken in one layer until the outside is browned and the thickest strip is white through with no pink centre; crowding the pan makes it boil, so cook in two batches if needed.
Lift the chicken to a plate, add corn, pepper and onion, and toss until the corn blisters in spots but the pepper still bends with a snap; soft vegetables make the plate heavy.
Return the chicken with the peach wedges and half the chimichurri, tossing only until the peach is warm at the edges; overcook it and it turns jammy.
Spoon onto a wide plate and drizzle with the remaining chimichurri so the herbs stay green and sharp.

note: A hot pan and thin chicken strips keep this bright rather than stew-like.

name: Chapa Prawns with Lime Farofa
hook: Garlic fizz, sweet prawns, sandy crunch

ingredients.name: large raw prawns, shell on, deveined
lime, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry and salt them lightly; wet shells spit hard on the chapa and steam the meat inside.
Melt 25 g butter in a small pan, add half the garlic, and cook until it smells sweet but stays pale; brown garlic makes the farofa taste burnt.
Stir in the cassava flour and lime zest until it looks like coarse golden sand, then take it off the heat; leave it on and it dries into dust.
Heat a flat griddle or cast-iron plate until a prawn shell sizzles the instant it touches; if the chapa is only warm, the prawns turn rubbery before they colour.
Add olive oil and the prawns in a single layer, then griddle until the shells blush deep pink and char in freckles, turning once; pile them up and the top ones stay grey.
Add the remaining butter, remaining garlic, chilli and cachaça off to one side of the griddle, then toss the prawns through the foaming butter until glossy; do not pour alcohol onto an open flame.
Scatter with coriander and serve on a platter with lime wedges and the warm farofa for dipping and sprinkling.

note: Shell-on prawns make the table slow down, which is exactly the point.

name: Lahori Chaat Masala Halloumi Bites
hook: Crackly edges, lime-bright heat

steps.t: Pat the halloumi very dry before you mix anything else; if it goes in wet, the coating slides off and the cheese spits in the pan.

Stir gram flour, cornflour, chaat masala, chilli and ajwain with the yoghurt and lemon to make a thick paste that clings to a spoon; if it is runny, it fries into a dusty skirt instead of a crisp shell.
Fold in the halloumi until every cube is coated, then leave it while the pan heats; if you rush straight in, the flour tastes raw at the centre of the crust.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a tiny dab of batter sizzles instantly and floats; if the oil is only warm, the halloumi softens before the crust sets.
Fry the cubes in one loose layer, turning when the undersides are deep gold with lace-brown edges; crowding the pan steams them and gives you rubbery cheese.
Lift onto kitchen paper, shower with coriander and a pinch more chaat masala, then eat hot; left sitting in a bowl, the crisp crust sweats itself soft.

note: Paneer works too, but salt it lightly before coating because it is milder than halloumi.

name: Saigon Pickled Pork Shoulder Herb Tangle
hook: Sharp pickle, soft pork, crushed peanuts

steps.t: Rub the pork all over with the salt and chill it uncovered for 2 hours; skip this and the slices taste flat no matter how lively the pickle is.
Rinse the pork, put it in a saucepan, cover with fresh water and simmer gently until a knife slides in without tearing; a hard boil tightens the shoulder into stringy meat.
Lift the pork out, cool until the steam stops, then chill until firm; slicing it warm makes ragged fibres that cloud the pickle.
Boil the rice vinegar, fish sauce, sugar and garlic for 2 minutes, then cool completely; hot brine cooks the vegetables dull and makes the pork greasy at the edges.
Slice the cold pork thinly and pack it with the carrot and daikon in a clean container, then pour over the cold brine to cover; anything poking above the liquid will season unevenly.
Refrigerate for 24 hours, turning the container once if the pork is tightly packed; leaving it at room temperature is unsafe and makes the fish sauce harsh.
Drain what you need, toss with cucumber, mint and coriander, and dress with a few spoonfuls of the pickling liquor; overdressing floods the herbs and turns the salad limp.
Finish with crushed peanuts just before serving; add them early and they lose the dry crunch that makes the pork taste brighter.

note: Keep the pork refrigerated while it pickles and eat within three days.

name: Tuscan Ricotta Egg White Traybake
hook: Golden top, clean gym fuel

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C and oil a medium baking dish; if the dish is dry, the lean egg white layer grips like glue.
Tip in the spinach and tomatoes with the olive oil and oregano, then bake until the spinach has collapsed and the tomatoes look glossy; raw vegetables leak water into the eggs.
Whisk the eggs, egg whites, ricotta, half the parmesan and a firm pinch of salt until only small ricotta flecks remain; big lumps bake into chalky pockets.
Stir the beans through the hot vegetables in the dish, then pour over the egg mixture; if the beans sit in one corner, the bake cuts unevenly and feels heavy there.
Scatter over the remaining parmesan and bake until the centre has a gentle wobble, not a wet slosh, and the edges puff golden; overbake it and the egg whites squeak.
Rest for 5 minutes before slicing so the protein sets cleanly; cut straight away and whey runs across the plate.
Tear basil over the top at the table; baked basil goes black and loses its fresh lift.

note: Good hot or cold, and sturdy enough for meal prep.

name: Saffron Elaichi Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Silky wobble, warm cardamom sweetness

steps.t: Warm 3 tablespoons of the milk with the saffron until it stains the milk deep yellow; if you add dry saffron straight to the custard, the flavour stays trapped in brittle threads.
Grease six small heatproof cups with ghee and set up a steamer at a gentle simmer; a roaring steamer blows bubbles through the custard.
Whisk eggs, condensed milk, jaggery, cardamom, the saffron milk and the remaining milk until smooth, but stop before it gets foamy; foam sets as pockmarks on the surface.
Strain the mixture into a jug, then pour into the cups; skipping the sieve leaves stringy egg white that ruins the silkiness.
Cover each cup tightly with foil and steam gently until the custards tremble as one piece when nudged; uncovered cups collect drips and turn watery on top.
Take the cups off the heat and rest for 10 minutes before uncovering; peeling the foil back immediately lets condensed steam fall onto the custard.
Scatter with pistachios and serve warm or chilled; add the nuts too early and they soften into the surface.

note: The texture should be closer to crème caramel than cake: barely set and spoonable.

name: Bangkok Sour Pollock Cabbage Stew
hook: Tamarind broth, tender flakes, cheap comfort

steps.t: Pat the thawed pollock dry and cut it into large chunks; small wet pieces break up and make the broth woolly.
Fry the curry paste in a saucepan with a splash of water until it smells sharp and the colour darkens slightly; if it stays raw, the stew tastes flat and dusty.
Add the water, tamarind, fish sauce and sugar, then bring to a steady simmer and taste for sour-salty balance; boiling hard now just reduces the broth before the vegetables cook.
Add cabbage and carrots and simmer until the cabbage bends but still has a pale bite; undercook it and the stew feels like hot coleslaw.
Stir in the tomatoes and nestle the pollock on top in one layer; if you bury and stir the fish, it sheds flakes before it is cooked.
Simmer gently until the fish turns opaque and separates in big moist flakes; a rolling boil makes cheap white fish tough at the edges.
Finish with lime wedges and coriander in the bowls, not the pan; cooked coriander goes dull and the lime can make the fish taste metallic if boiled.

note: Serve with rice if you have it, but the cabbage makes the stew filling on its own.

name: Charred Aleppo Chickpea Kavurma
hook: Smoky chickpeas, blistered peppers, lemon snap

steps.t: Heat a wide wok or heavy frying pan until a drop of water skitters off at once; if the pan is only warm, the chickpeas will steam and turn woolly instead of catching.
Add the oil and onion with the salt, then stir-fry hard until the onion tips soften and pick up dark freckles; keep it moving or the sugars scorch bitterly.
Add the peppers and garlic, spreading them across the pan so they touch metal; cook until the pepper skins blister in patches, not until they collapse into stew.
Tip in the dry chickpeas and leave them untouched for short bursts between tosses until some skins split and go nut-brown; wet chickpeas will spit, so dry them properly first.
Push everything aside, fry the tomato purée and pul biber in the bare oil for 30 seconds until brick-red and fragrant; if it goes black, scrape it out because it will dominate the dish.
Toss the paste through the chickpeas, squeeze over the lemon and fold in the parsley off the heat; boiling the lemon dulls the sharp lift you need.
Spoon onto warm plates with yoghurt alongside, keeping the yoghurt separate so the hot pan juices streak it rather than turning it grainy.

note: Serve with flatbread if you want it more filling; the high heat is the whole point.

name: Sumac Griddle Chicken Musakhan Wraps
hook: Charred chicken, silky onions, sharp sumac

steps.t: Mix the chicken with 1 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp sumac, allspice, garlic, lemon zest, half the lemon juice, 1 tsp salt and the pepper; coat every fold, because bare patches taste flat after griddling.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours and up to 24; leaving it on the counter is unsafe, and a short marinade will not season the thick thigh meat properly.
Cook the onions in 2 tbsp oil with the remaining salt over medium-low heat until they slump into glossy ribbons and taste sweet; rush this over high heat and the edges burn before the centres soften.
Stir the remaining sumac and lemon juice into the onions, then set aside; adding sumac early makes it dusty rather than bright.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan until patchy gold and nutty-smelling, shaking often; they go from perfect to acrid in seconds if left still.
Heat a ridged griddle until smoking lightly, then lay on the chicken without crowding; if the pieces touch, they leak juice and stew instead of taking dark bars.
Griddle the chicken until well-striped, firm at the thickest point and cooked through, turning once; cut into the largest piece to check there is no pink meat or clear raw-looking centre.
Warm the flatbreads on the griddle, pile with onions, sliced chicken, pine nuts and parsley, then roll while flexible; cold bread cracks and spills the juices.

note: Most of the time is hands-off marinating and slow onions; that is what makes it a weekend project.

name: Crisp Chermoula Prawn Cakes
hook: Crackly edges, clean herbs, lean protein

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry, then roughly chop half and finely chop the rest; if they stay wet or are puréed smooth, the cakes turn bouncy and shed moisture in the pan.
Mix prawns with egg white, breadcrumbs, garlic, spices, herbs, lemon zest and salt until just sticky; overworking makes the protein tighten like a rubber ball.
Shape into 6 small cakes with damp hands and chill on a plate so the crumbs hydrate and the edges firm up; frying loose mix straight away makes it split.
Heat the oil in a non-stick frying pan until a breadcrumb sizzles immediately but does not blacken; oil that is too cool soaks in, too hot burns the outside before the prawns cook.
Lay in the cakes with space between them and shallow fry until the undersides form a crisp amber crust that releases cleanly; forcing them early tears off the crust.
Turn once and fry until the second side is crisp and the centres are opaque, hot and springy; raw prawn should never look glassy in the middle.
Drain briefly on kitchen paper, then serve with lemon wedges; stacking them traps steam and softens the crackle you just built.

note: Use raw prawns, not cooked ones, so the cakes bind and finish juicy without overcooking.

name: Orange Sherry Flan al Vapor
hook: Silky custard, bitter caramel, citrus warmth

steps.t: Put 80 g sugar and the water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup turns deep amber at the edges; stirring crystallises it, and pale caramel tastes only sweet.
Divide the caramel between 4 heatproof ramekins, swirling carefully to coat the bases; caramel burns badly, so keep fingers away from the hot cups.
Warm the milk with orange zest until steaming but not boiling; if it boils hard, the zest turns pithy and the milk can catch on the pan.
Whisk eggs, remaining sugar, sherry and salt just until blended, then slowly whisk in the hot milk; pouring it in fast scrambles the eggs into sweet strands.
Strain the custard into the ramekins and cover each tightly with foil; skipping the strainer leaves chalazae and zest clumps in an otherwise silky flan.
Set the ramekins in a steamer over gently simmering water and steam until the edges are set but the centres tremble like soft jelly; a rolling boil makes bubbles and a tough, pocked custard.
Cool, then chill until cold before unmoulding with a thin knife; warm flan slumps and the caramel runs thin instead of glazing the top.

note: Best made earlier in the day; the chill time is included in the total.

name: Dijon Sausage Lentil Gratin
hook: Mustardy sausages over creamy green lentils

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan and choose a baking dish where the sausages sit in one layer; a crowded dish traps steam and leaves the skins pale.
Toss onion, carrots, garlic, oil, thyme and pepper in the dish, then lay the sausages on top; burying the sausages stops them browning.
Bake until the sausage skins are taut and starting to bronze and the onion edges look soft; if the vegetables are still raw-looking, the lentils will taste harsh later.
Lift the sausages to a plate, then stir lentils, stock, Dijon and crème fraîche through the hot vegetables, scraping the sticky bits from the dish; unmixed mustard leaves fierce yellow pockets.
Nestle the sausages back on top and scatter with breadcrumbs; put crumbs under the sauce and they turn to paste instead of crust.
Bake until the sauce bubbles thickly around the edges, the sausages are cooked through and the crumbs are crisp gold; if the centre is watery, give it a few more minutes rather than serving soup.
Rest for 5 minutes before spooning out, so the lentils absorb the loose sauce; serving straight from the oven makes it run across the plate.

note: A cheap one-dish dinner built from tins, sausages and a little mustardy French swagger.

name: Molasses-Braised Eggs with Buttered Grits
hook: Soft yolks, smoky-sweet winter gravy

steps.t: Melt the butter in a wide lidded pan and cook the onion with a pinch of salt until it slumps into glossy amber ribbons; if the heat is too high it will catch before it sweetens.
Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for a minute, just until the pan smells smoky; if the paprika scorches, the whole braise turns bitter.

Add the tomatoes, molasses and stock, then simmer uncovered until the sauce looks thick enough to leave a clear trail when you drag a spoon through it; watery sauce makes the eggs spread and poach unevenly.
Meanwhile cook the grits or polenta according to the packet with salt, stirring often until they blip like small volcanoes; neglect them and they set into lumps at the bottom.
Beat the Cheddar into the hot grits off the heat until smooth and glossy; boiling it hard after the cheese goes in can make it grainy.

Make four hollows in the braised sauce, crack in the eggs, cover and cook until the whites are set but the yolks still wobble when the pan is nudged; overcook them and you lose the soft winter richness.
Spoon grits into warm bowls, lift an egg and plenty of sauce over each, then finish with spring onion for a sharp edge against the sweetness.

note: A slow, smoky tomato braise gives eggs the heft of a proper cold-weather supper.

name: Matambre Breakfast Egg Stew
hook: Beefy peppers, jammy yolks, bright chimichurri

ingredients.name: chorizo or cured beef sausage, diced

steps.t: Warm the oil in a deep frying pan and render the diced chorizo until the fat stains the oil red and the edges crisp; stop too soon and the stew tastes flat rather than savoury.
Add the pepper and onion and cook until they soften and the onion is sweet, not squeaky; undercooked pepper gives the stew a raw breakfast-café taste.
Stir in the garlic and cumin until fragrant, keeping them moving because both turn harsh if they stick to the hot chorizo fat.
Pour in the passata with a splash of water and simmer until the surface changes from loose bubbles to thick, slow plops; if it is still thin, the eggs will sink and toughen at the base.
Fold in the beans and simmer until they are hot all the way through and slightly stained red; stirring roughly now breaks them into paste.
Crack in the eggs, cover, and simmer gently until the whites turn opaque right to the yolk but the centres still tremble; a hard boil will rubberise the whites before the tops set.
Mix parsley with vinegar and a pinch of salt, then spoon it over the stew with toast alongside; without that sharp green finish the pan eats heavy.

note: Inspired by Argentine breakfast flavours rather than a strict classic, built as a one-pan stew for slow mornings.

name: Moqueca-Roasted Whole Bream
hook: Coconut-slick fish with sunset peppers

ingredients.name: whole sea bream, cleaned and scaled
dendê palm oil or olive oil

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan and line a roasting tray; a cold oven makes the fish steam before the skin has a chance to tighten.
Cut three deep slashes into each side of the bream, then rub with lime juice, grated garlic and salt, pushing it into the cuts; seasoning only the skin leaves the thickest flesh bland.
Scatter the peppers and onion in the tray and sit the fish on top with lime slices in the cavity; burying the fish under vegetables traps moisture and dulls the roast flavour.
Whisk coconut milk with tomato purée and palm oil, then pour it around, not over, the fish so the skin roasts while the sauce bubbles underneath.
Roast until the eye turns opaque, the slashes open and the flesh flakes cleanly from the backbone near the head; pull it early and the centre will cling glassy to the bone.
Rest the tray for five minutes so the juices settle back into the flesh; carving straight away makes the coconut sauce flood the plate and the fish look ragged.
Spoon the roasted pepper coconut sauce onto a platter, lay the fish over it, and finish with coriander and chilli for colour and lift.

note: Use bream, bass or another firm white fish of similar size; ask the fishmonger to scale it well.

name: Dhuaan Mushroom Kachumber
hook: Char-smoked mushrooms, cucumber-cool crunch

steps.t: Toss the mushrooms with oil, ground coriander, chilli and salt, coating the torn edges where flavour clings; dry patches roast pale and taste like plain sponge.
Spread them in one layer in a very hot frying pan or griddle and cook until they squeak less, shrink and take dark freckles; crowding the pan makes them leak and stew.
Tip the hot mushrooms into a heatproof bowl, leaving a little space in the centre for smoking; a plastic bowl can soften, so use metal, ceramic or glass.
Heat the charcoal directly over a gas flame or with tongs under a grill until one edge glows red, then set it in a small foil cup in the bowl; if it is only black-hot, it will not smoke properly.
Drizzle a few drops of oil onto the charcoal and cover the bowl immediately until the mushrooms smell campfire-smoky, not ashy; leaving it too long can make them taste bitter.
Remove and safely extinguish the charcoal, then fold in cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, lemon juice and mint; mixing the salad before smoking wilts the fresh crunch.
Taste for salt and lemon just before serving, because mushrooms drink seasoning as they sit and a flat kachumber loses its summer snap.

note: The dhungar smoke is brief and controlled, giving grill-house aroma without making the salad heavy.

name: Bò Lá Lốt Steamed Cups
hook: Peppery beef parcels, herbs everywhere

ingredients.name: betel leaves or small perilla leaves

steps.t: Soak the rice vermicelli in boiling water until tender but still springy, then rinse cold; leave it hot and it clumps into a sticky mat for the table.
Mix beef, shallot, garlic, fish sauce, sugar and pepper with your hand just until tacky; overworking makes the steamed parcels bouncy rather than tender.
Wipe the leaves clean and place them shiny-side down, then add small walnut-sized logs of beef; overfilling splits the leaves before the beef cooks through.
Fold the sides over and roll into snug cups or parcels, setting them seam-side down on a lightly oiled steaming plate; loose seams open when the steam hits.
Steam over fast-simmering water until the leaves darken and the beef feels firm in the centre with clear juices, not pink juices; lifting the lid repeatedly drops the heat and lengthens the cook.
Rest the parcels for three minutes so the juices settle instead of spilling across the plate at the first bite.
Serve on a shared platter with noodles, carrot, cucumber, herbs and nuoc cham, letting everyone build small mouthfuls rather than heavy rolls.

note: Betel leaves give the classic peppery aroma; perilla is easier to find and still works beautifully when steamed.

name: Black Vinegar Pickle Prawns with Gingered Congee
hook: Sharp prawns over velvet rice warmth

ingredients.name: fresh ginger, half sliced and half finely shredded

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water runs only cloudy, not milky, then put it in a heavy pan with the stock and sliced ginger. If you skip the rinse, the congee can turn gluey instead of soft and flowing.
Bring to a lively boil, then drop to a low simmer and stir right down to the base. A hard boil will spit and catch before the grains have collapsed.
Simmer, stirring every 8 minutes, until the rice grains burst and the surface looks glossy and porridge-like; add a splash of water if the spoon stands up in it.
While it cooks, whisk black vinegar, soy, sugar and chilli oil until the sugar disappears, then fold in the prawns and shredded ginger. Dress them only now, or the prawns go tight and woolly.
Taste the congee and season with a little soy if needed; it should be savoury and gentle, because the prawns are sharp. If both are salty, the bowl tastes flat and harsh.
Ladle the congee into warm bowls and spoon the pickled prawns and their dressing over the top. Finish with spring onions and sesame, keeping them last so they stay crisp and fragrant.

note: Use fully cooked prawns and keep them chilled until dressing; this dish is about bright pickled dressing, not curing raw shellfish.

name: Chipotle Mushroom Breakfast Cazuela
hook: Runny yolks, smoky bubbling mushrooms

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Put the mushrooms, oil and a pinch of salt in a medium baking dish and toss well; crowding them dry and unseasoned makes them steam blandly.
Bake until the mushrooms have shrunk, darkened and left a savoury brown slick in the dish. If they still look pale and spongy, the sauce will taste watery.
Stir in the onion, garlic and chipotle paste, scraping the hot dish so the paste stains the oil brick-red. If the paste sits in lumps, you get harsh smoky pockets.
Add tomatoes and black beans, season, then bake until the sauce bubbles thickly around the edges rather than sloshing when nudged.
Make four shallow hollows and crack in the eggs, keeping the yolks intact; if the hollows are too deep, the whites stay raw underneath while the tops overcook.
Bake until the whites are just set and the yolks still wobble when the dish is tapped.
Scatter with feta and coriander, then rest for 2 minutes before scooping with warm tortillas. Serving straight away burns mouths and breaks the eggs into the sauce.

note: For a milder breakfast, use 2 teaspoons chipotle paste and add smoked paprika for colour.

name: Orange-Oregano Pork Kleftiko Parcels
hook: Fragrant pork collapsing into citrus juices

ingredients.name: pork shoulder, cut into large chunks

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Toss pork, potatoes, onions, garlic, orange zest and juice, lemon juice, oil, oregano, cinnamon, wine, salt and pepper in a large bowl until everything shines; dry corners will braise grey, not golden.

Line a deep roasting tin with two long crossed sheets of baking paper and foil, then tip the mixture into the centre. Keep the potatoes mostly underneath the pork so they drink the juices instead of drying out.
Fold the paper tightly over the filling, then seal the foil into a domed parcel with no gaps. If steam can escape, the pork tightens before it becomes tender.
Braise until a piece of pork gives easily when pressed with a spoon through the opened parcel; it should not spring back like a chop.
Open the parcel carefully away from your face, add the olives, and turn the oven up to 220°C fan. If you tear it open roughly, the juices run into the tin and scorch.
Roast uncovered until the pork edges catch bronze and the potatoes are sticky with reduced citrusy liquor.
Rest for 10 minutes, then shower with feta at the table. Cutting in immediately sends the juices across the platter instead of back through the meat.

note: Serve with a bitter leaf salad; the braise is rich and wants something sharp beside it.

name: Summer Menemen with Courgette and Dill
hook: Silky eggs in tomato-pepper brightness

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat, then add the pepper, courgette and a pinch of salt. Cook until the courgette edges look translucent; rushing this leaves squeaky, raw-tasting pieces in the eggs.
Add the spring onions and pul biber, stirring until the oil smells sweet and peppery. Letting the chilli burn makes the whole stew bitter.
Pour in the grated tomatoes and simmer until the mixture looks loose but not watery, with small orange oil beads at the edge. If it is soupy, the eggs will separate into rags.
Beat the eggs lightly with a pinch of salt, stopping while streaks of white remain. Overbeating makes the menemen uniform and bouncy rather than silky.
Lower the heat and pour in the eggs, stirring slowly in broad folds until soft curds sit in a glossy tomato stew. If you stir fast or cook hard, it turns grainy.
Take the pan off while the eggs still wobble, then fold through half the dill. Residual heat finishes them; waiting until they look fully set means they will be dry on the plate.
Serve with yoghurt, the remaining dill and lemon wedges. Keep the yoghurt on the side so its cool tang stays clean rather than disappearing into the pan.

note: Best with bread for scooping, but still light enough for a hot day.

name: Za’atar Roast Cauliflower with Green Tahini
hook: Charred petals, cool sesame sauce

ingredients.name: cauliflower, leaves trimmed but core kept intact

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan. Sit the cauliflower stem-side down in a snug roasting dish and rub it all over with oil, salt, za’atar and cumin; unseasoned crevices taste like boiled brassica under the crust.
Pour 100 ml water into the dish, then cover tightly with foil. The steam softens the core; without it the outside burns before the centre yields.
Roast covered until a skewer slides into the stem with slight resistance, not a hard crunch.
Remove the foil, spoon the spiced oil from the dish back over the cauliflower, and roast until the top florets are charred at the tips and the sides are deep gold.
Blend tahini, lemon juice, garlic, parsley, mint, a pinch of salt and 70 ml cold water until pale green and pourable. Add the water gradually, or tahini can seize into a stiff paste.
Rest the cauliflower for 5 minutes so it slices into wedges rather than collapsing into crumbs.
Spoon green tahini onto a platter, set the whole cauliflower on top, then scatter with pomegranate and pine nuts. Add the toppings last so they stay bright and crunchy.

note: A strong centrepiece for a mezze table with pickles, flatbreads and olives.

name: Semolina-Crisp Chermoula Cod
hook: Lace-crisp fish, lemony green heat

steps.t: Cut the fish into chunky fingers and pat them very dry; if the surface feels damp, the crust steams and slips off in the pan.
Stir semolina, flour, ras el hanout and salt in a shallow bowl. Beat the egg in a second bowl until no stringy white remains, or it will drag bare patches through the coating.
Dip the fish in egg, then press into the spiced semolina until every side feels sandy. Set pieces on a plate without stacking, because stacked coating turns paste-like.
Finely chop parsley with the garlic, the zest of half the lemon and 1 tbsp lemon juice to make a rough chermoula; keep it bright and loose, not pounded into bitter green mush.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of semolina fizzes at once. If the oil is only shimmering lazily, wait, or the fish will drink oil before it crisps.
Shallow-fry the fish in one layer until the underside is lace-golden and firm at the edges, then turn once; crowding the pan drops the heat and gives you soft crumbs.
Drain on kitchen paper, spoon over the lemony chermoula and serve straight away; the crust is best while it still rasps under a knife.

note: Fast Moroccan-style weeknight fish with a semolina crust that stays crisp better than breadcrumbs.

name: Sherry-Steamed Mushroom Terrine with Almond Picada
hook: Deep woodland slices, glossy with sherry

ingredients.name: mixed mushrooms, such as chestnut, oyster and shiitake

steps.t: Slice the mushrooms thickly, keeping the nicest caps for the top layer. If you slice them too thin, they collapse into a grey paste during steaming.
Cook shallots and garlic in olive oil until soft and sweet-smelling but not browned; scorched garlic will make the whole terrine taste metallic.

Add mushrooms, salt and sherry, cover tightly and steam in their own juices until they slump and release dark liquor. Keep the lid on, because escaping steam means dry mushrooms, not concentrated ones.
Tip into a sieve over a bowl and press gently; save 4 tbsp liquor. If the filling is wet, the terrine weeps and will not slice cleanly.
Whisk eggs, cream, breadcrumbs, Manchego, paprika and the saved liquor, then fold through the mushrooms. Stop mixing once coated, or the caps break and the slice loses its marbled look.

Line a small loaf tin with baking paper, arrange the reserved caps on the base, pack in the mixture and cover tightly with foil. Steam over barely bubbling water until the centre feels set and springy, topping up the pan with boiling water if it runs low.
Cool, weight with tins and chill until firm; cutting warm gives ragged, leaking slices instead of neat terrine.
Toast and crush the almonds to a rough picada, then serve over chilled or room-temperature slices with a spoon of the reduced mushroom liquor if you like.

note: A Spanish-inspired make-ahead mushroom terrine: most of the time is chilling and pressing, which gives clean slices.

name: Coal-Grilled Dijon Bavette with Lentil Herb Salad
hook: Smoke, mustard, lean beef bite

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ashed over with a fierce red core; cooking over flames gives soot, not char.
Pat the bavette dry, season with salt and pepper, then smear with 1 tbsp Dijon. A wet steak steams on the grate and will never pick up those dark grill bars.
Stir lentils with vinegar, olive oil, the remaining Dijon, chopped cornichons, parsley and finely diced shallot. Taste now, because cold lentils mute salt and need a sharp edge.
Grill the bavette directly over the coals until the first side has dark stripes and releases without tearing. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
Flip and grill until the thickest part feels springy with a little give, not hard. Overcook bavette and the long fibres turn chewy even when sliced correctly.
Rest the steak on a board so the juices settle; slicing straight off the fire floods the board and dries the meat.
Slice thinly across the grain, then pile over the lentil herb salad with any resting juices. Cutting with the grain makes even good steak eat like rope.

note: Lean bavette and lentils make this French-leaning coal-grilled plate high in protein without a heavy sauce.

name: Maple-Steamed Egg Custards with Pecan Salt
hook: Silky maple wobble, toasted crunch

steps.t: Butter four small heatproof ramekins. Do this right to the rim, because bare ceramic grabs the custard and tears the edge as it cools.
Whisk eggs, milk, cream, maple syrup, brown sugar, vanilla and salt until smooth but not frothy. Whipping in bubbles gives a pocked, foamy top instead of a satin one.
Strain the mixture into a jug, then divide between the ramekins. Skipping the sieve leaves bits of egg white that set into pale threads.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil and set in a steamer over gently simmering water. If the water boils hard, the custard curdles around the edges before the centre sets.
Steam until the centres tremble like soft jelly when nudged, not like liquid under skin. Keep the lid closed during cooking or the temperature drops and the set turns patchy.
Lift out and rest for 10 minutes; eating immediately makes the texture taste eggy and loose rather than creamy.
Toast pecans in the butter with a pinch more salt until they smell like pie crust and darken at the edges; pale nuts taste dusty against the maple custard.
Spoon the warm pecan salt over the custards and serve warm or chilled.

note: An American-style maple custard dessert, gently steamed so the eggs set smooth rather than baked firm.

name: Chimichurri Tofu Salteño
hook: Hot-pan tofu, sharp green punch

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in kitchen paper and press it under a plate while you chop. If it goes into the pan wet, it spits and steams instead of browning.
Chop parsley and one garlic clove with oregano, vinegar, chilli flakes and 1 tbsp oil to make a rough chimichurri. Keep it coarse; blending makes it muddy and harsh.
Cut tofu into 2 cm cubes, slice the pepper and onion, and mince the remaining garlic. Have everything ready, because high-heat stir-frying punishes rummaging.
Heat a wok or large frying pan until a drop of water skates off, then add the remaining oil and tofu. If the pan is only warm, the tofu sheds water and sticks.
Stir-fry the tofu until two or three sides are golden and the corners look dry and crisp, then splash in the soy sauce. Add it earlier and the sugars catch before the tofu browns.
Add onion and pepper and toss hard over high heat until the onion edges char but the pepper still snaps. Limp vegetables make the bowl taste boiled.
Stir in the minced garlic for the last few seconds only, then take the pan off the heat; burnt garlic will bully the chimichurri.
Fold through half the chimichurri and serve over hot rice with the rest spooned on top.

note: A cheap Argentine-inspired salteado using tofu, rice and a punchy chimichurri-style finish.

name: Coal-Grilled Mackerel with Orange Caper Oil
hook: Charred skin, bright bitter-sweet citrus

steps.t: Light a small chimney of charcoal and let it burn until the top coals are ashed over; cook on black coals and the fish will taste sooty rather than smoky.

Zest half the orange, then cut away the peel and slice the flesh into rounds. Mix the zest with lemon juice, capers, parsley, olive oil and fennel seeds; if you add the orange slices now, they collapse and muddy the oil.
Pat the mackerel skin very dry and salt it lightly. Damp skin welds itself to the grill, so keep wiping until the paper comes away almost clean.
Set the grill over the coals and oil the bars. Lay the mackerel skin-side down where you can hold your hand above the heat for about two seconds; any hotter and the fat flares before the flesh cooks.
Grill skin-side down until the edges blister and the flesh has turned opaque two-thirds up the side, then turn once. Fiddling early tears the skin, so wait for it to release cleanly.
Give the flesh side 30–45 seconds, just until pearly rather than glassy. Spoon over the caper oil and serve with orange rounds and rocket; leave it sitting and oily fish turns heavy fast.

note: Sardines work beautifully too; use 8 butterflied fish and shave a minute off the grill time.

name: Malabar Barely-Poached Prawn Chaat with Dosa Crisps
hook: Cool prawns, hot mustard, sharp mango

ingredients.name: raw king prawns, peeled and deveined

steps.t: Rinse the rice and dal until the water loses its chalkiness, then soak them with the fenugreek. Skimp on rinsing and the batter ferments with a dusty, stale edge.

Drain, blend with just enough fresh water to make a thick cream, then leave covered somewhere warm until bubbled and lightly sour. If it smells harshly alcoholic, it has gone too far and will taste bitter in the crisps.

Spread a ladle of batter thinly in a lightly oiled frying pan and cook until the underside is lace-brown and the edges lift. Soft pale dosas will steam under the prawns, so push them to properly crisp and break into shards.
Toast the mustard seeds in the mustard oil until they pop and smell nutty, then take off the heat. Burnt mustard tastes acrid, so stop as soon as the popping slows.
Bring a pan of well-salted water to a bare simmer, add the prawns and cook until they turn opaque and curl into loose Cs. Grey centres are not safe; tight rings mean you have gone rubbery.
Lift the prawns straight into a chilled bowl and cool quickly. Leaving them in hot water carries on cooking them and loses the barely-poached snap.
Whisk yoghurt with lime juice, chilli, the mustard oil and a pinch of salt, then fold through prawns, green mango, coriander and coconut. Stir hard and the prawns shred, so turn everything gently.
Pile the chaat onto plates and tuck dosa crisps around it at the last moment. Add them early and the fermented crunch turns leathery.

note: Use very fresh prawns from a reputable fishmonger, keep them chilled, and cook them the same day you serve the chaat.

name: Krapao Lamb Power Stir-Fry with Beans
hook: Lean lamb, basil smoke, chilli snap

steps.t: Slice the lamb across the grain into thin strips and pat dry. Cut with the grain and it chews like elastic; leave it wet and the wok cools before it sears.
Crush garlic and chillies to a rough paste, then mix fish sauce, oyster sauce, soy and a squeeze of lime in a cup. Searching for bottles once the wok is hot is how stir-fries overcook.
Blanch the beans until greener and just bendy, then drain hard. Raw beans stay squeaky in the finished dish, but soggy beans dump water into the wok.
Heat the wok until a wisp of smoke rises, add oil, then half the lamb in a single layer. If you crowd it, the meat boils grey instead of catching at the edges.
Stir-fry the lamb until browned in patches but still springy, scrape it out, and repeat with the rest. Waiting for every strip to look dark will take it past juicy.
Add the chilli-garlic paste for a few seconds until sharp and fragrant, then return lamb and beans with the sauce. Toss hard until the sauce clings rather than pools.
Kill the heat and fold in Thai basil until it just wilts. Cook basil on the flame and its perfume disappears into bitterness; finish with extra lime if the lamb tastes heavy.

note: For a bigger training meal, add steamed jasmine rice; the listed calories are for the stir-fry alone.

name: Matcha Steamed Custard with Black Sugar Syrup
hook: Quiet wobble, bitter tea, glossy syrup

steps.t: Put muscovado sugar, mirin, lemon peel and 40 ml water in a small pan and simmer until glossy and lightly thickened. Boil it fiercely and it turns salty-bitter rather than rounded.
Warm the milk until steaming but not bubbling, then whisk matcha with a splash of it to a smooth paste. Dump matcha straight into the bowl and you will chase green lumps forever.
Whisk eggs and caster sugar gently, then stir in the matcha milk. Beating in foam makes a bubbly, pocked custard instead of a clean wobble.
Strain the custard into four small heatproof cups and skim off any surface bubbles. Unstrained egg threads set as little rubbery flecks.
Set the cups in a steamer over low steam, cover with a cloth-wrapped lid and steam until the edges are set and the centres tremble like soft jelly. Hard boiling steam honeycombs the custard.
Turn off the heat and let the cups sit covered so the centres finish gently. Pull them out immediately and the middle can slump into liquid.
Spoon the black sugar syrup over the warm or chilled custards and dust with kinako. Pour syrup too early on hot custard and it sinks instead of glazing the top.

note: The custards are best slightly chilled, but still soft enough to quiver when the spoon touches them.

name: Gochujang Crisp Chicken Rice Plate
hook: Sticky heat, shattering edges, soft rice

steps.t: Cut the chicken into bite-sized chunks, salt lightly and toss with cornflour until every surface looks dusty. Bare patches leak juice into the pan and stop the crust forming.
Stir garlic, gochujang, soy, honey and vinegar with 2 tablespoons water. Make the sauce before frying; if the chicken waits while you mix, steam softens the crust.
Heat the oil in a frying pan until a pinch of cornflour sizzles on contact. If the oil is only warm, the coating drinks it and turns pasty.
Shallow fry the chicken in two batches, turning until the corners are crisp and the thickest pieces are piping hot with no pink juices. Crowd the pan and you get beige steamed chicken.
Drain the chicken on a rack or crumpled paper. A flat plate traps steam underneath and makes the bottom side soggy.
Pour off excess oil, add the sauce to the pan and bubble until it looks shiny and leaves a clear trail when stirred. Stop while watery and it will soak the crust instead of coating it.
Toss the chicken through the sauce for just a few turns, then serve over hot rice with cabbage and sesame seeds. Lingering in the pan turns crisp edges chewy, so plate fast.

note: Chicken thighs stay juicy and are usually cheaper than breast; leftover cooked rice is perfect here.

name: Red Curry Pork & Pumpkin Weeknight Stew
hook: Silky coconut heat, tender pork edges

ingredients.name: pork shoulder steaks, sliced 1 cm thick
pumpkin or butternut squash, peeled and diced
palm sugar or light brown sugar

steps.t: Heat the oil in a wide saucepan over medium-high heat, then fry the curry paste until it darkens slightly and the oil stains orange; if it smells harsh and raw, give it another minute before adding liquid.
Add the pork and toss until every slice is red and glossy; do not try to brown it hard here or the paste will catch and turn bitter.
Pour in the coconut milk and 150 ml water, scraping the base until it feels clean; any paste left stuck down there will scorch during the simmer.
Add the pumpkin, fish sauce and sugar, then simmer uncovered until the pumpkin corners soften but the pieces still hold their shape.
Stir in the green beans and cook until they turn bright green with a slight snap; if they go khaki, they have crossed into limp stew territory.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in lime and tear over the herbs; boiling after the lime goes in flattens the fresh edge.

note: Serve with jasmine rice if you want a bigger dinner; the stew itself is designed to be rich but not heavy.

name: Hojicha Tare-Roasted Weekend Eggs
hook: Jammy centres, smoky lacquered whites

steps.t: Lower the eggs into gently boiling water and cook for set whites with soft centres; a violent boil cracks shells and leaks wispy egg into the pan.
Move the eggs straight into iced water until fully cold; if they stay warm, the yolks keep cooking and lose the fudgy middle.
Simmer soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, hojicha, spring onion and ginger until the steam smells roasted and sweet rather than alcoholic.
Strain the tare, cool it completely, then peel the eggs and submerge them; warm tare toughens the whites before the flavour gets inside.
Chill the eggs in the tare overnight, turning once if they bob above the surface; any exposed patch will stay pale and under-seasoned.
Heat the oven to 220°C, pat the whole eggs dry, brush with sesame oil and roast on baking paper until the outsides blister in mahogany freckles; wet eggs steam instead of lacquer.
Halve to serve and scatter with sesame seeds; use a thin sharp knife, wiping between cuts, or the yolks smear over the shiny whites.

note: The long time is mostly marinating; the roasting is brief so the eggs stay tender rather than rubbery.

name: Smoked Dubu & Edamame Bossam Cups
hook: Cold smoke, crunch, deep soybean savour

ingredients.name: king oyster mushrooms, torn into strips

steps.t: Press the tofu between towels under a heavy pan until the surface feels dry and slightly tacky; wet tofu tastes steamed, not smoked.
Set a lidded barbecue or smoker for indirect low heat, add the drained chips, and wait for thin blue smoke; thick white smoke will make the vegetables acrid.
Smoke the tofu slab, edamame and torn mushrooms on a tray until the mushrooms slump and the tofu smells nutty at the edges.
Whisk doenjang, gochujang, rice vinegar, sesame oil and 2 tbsp water into a spoonable sauce; if it sits like paste, it will clump instead of dressing the filling.
Slice the smoked tofu into chunky batons and toss gently with edamame, mushrooms, spring onions and half the sauce; rough stirring breaks the tofu into chalky crumbs.
