Slice the chicken thickly and spoon over the creamy beans. If the beans look tight, stir in a splash of boiling water to loosen the sauce without cooling it down.

note: Each serving gives roughly 55 g protein, depending on the size of the chicken fillets.

name: Steamed Cardamom Egg Jaggery Custard
hook: Silky wobble, caramel warmth, saffron breath

steps.t: Melt the jaggery with 2 tbsp water in a small pan until syrupy and dark amber. Do not let it smoke, or the custard will taste burnt rather than caramel-warm.
Divide the syrup between six heatproof ramekins and swirl to coat the bases. Work quickly, because jaggery sets sticky and uneven as it cools.
Warm the milk, cream, sugar, cardamom and saffron until steaming at the edge, then take off the heat. Boiling it hard gives the eggs a cooked-milk taste and makes foam that sets pockmarked.
Whisk the eggs in a jug, then slowly whisk in the warm milk. Pour too fast and you scramble the eggs before they reach the steamer.
Strain the custard into the ramekins and cover each with foil. Unstrained custard leaves stringy egg bits, and uncovered cups collect watery drips.
Steam gently over barely simmering water until the centres tremble like soft jelly, not liquid ripples. Fierce steam makes tunnels and a rubbery edge.
Cool for 10 minutes, then chill or serve warm with pistachios. If turning out, loosen the edge first so the caramel runs over the custard instead of tearing it.

note: For food safety, the custards should be fully set with no raw liquid centre.

name: Thai Paneer Potato Coconut Stew
hook: Soft potatoes, salty paneer, curry heat

steps.t: Put the onion and curry paste into a medium saucepan with 2 tbsp of the thick coconut cream from the top of the tin. Fry until the paste darkens and smells roasted; if it stays raw, the stew tastes flat and dusty.
Add the potatoes and stir until their edges are stained red. Bare patches mean bland potatoes later, because the seasoning stays in the broth.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and stock, then simmer with the lid slightly open until a knife slides into the potatoes without crunch.
Stir in the cabbage, soy sauce and sugar. Keep it at a simmer, not a boil, or the coconut splits oily and the cabbage turns sulphurous.
Add the paneer and simmer gently until hot through and slightly swollen. Stir hard and the cubes crumble into the sauce instead of staying chewy.
Turn off the heat and add lime juice and coriander. Boil after adding lime and the stew loses its clean, sharp finish.

note: Serve with rice if you have it, but the potatoes make it filling on their own.

name: Bengali Hot-Mustard Salmon with Ginger Ghee
hook: Silken fish under spiced winter warmth

steps.t: Put two shallow bowls in a warm spot, but keep the salmon in the fridge until the last moment; warm raw fish turns slack and woolly before the ghee ever touches it.
Whisk the yoghurt, kasundi, lemon juice, turmeric and salt until the sauce is smooth and ochre-yellow; if the mustard sits in streaks, some bites will be fierce and others flat.
Slice the salmon across the grain into 1 cm slabs and lay them in the bowls in a single layer; thick overlapping pieces stay fridge-cold underneath instead of turning gently pearly at the edges.
Spoon the mustard yoghurt over the fish, leaving a few orange-pink edges showing; drowning it makes the dish taste like dip rather than warmed fish.

Cut the ginger into fine matchsticks, then heat the ghee with the nigella seeds, chilli and ginger until the seeds crackle and the ginger curls at the tips; stop before the ginger goes dark brown, or the whole bowl tastes bitter.
Immediately spoon the hot spiced ghee over the salmon so the surface turns satin-matte and just opaque in places; if the ghee is only warm, the fish stays raw-cold and greasy.
Scatter over coriander and serve at once; if it sits around, the lemon and residual heat tighten the salmon like leftovers.

note: Use only salmon sold for raw eating, keep it chilled, and serve immediately after dressing.

name: Thai Basil Halloumi Breakfast Wok
hook: Salty squeak, chilli, runny yolk

steps.t: Stir the fish sauce, oyster sauce and palm sugar together until the sugar dissolves; loose grains hit the hot wok and scorch before they season the rice.
Pat the halloumi very dry and cut it into thumb-sized cubes; surface water makes it steam and squeak sadly instead of taking on golden freckles.
Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wok or wide frying pan, crack in the eggs and fry until the whites have lacy brown edges but the yolks still wobble; lift them out before the yolks chalk over.
Turn the heat up until the wok gives off a faint shimmer, then add the remaining oil, garlic, chillies and green beans; if it does not hiss hard, wait, because a cool wok gives you boiled beans.
Add the halloumi and leave it alone until the underside is speckled deep gold, then toss once or twice; constant stirring tears the cheese and squeezes out brine.
Add the cold rice and the sauce, then stir-fry hard until the grains separate and steam smells savoury rather than damp; clumps mean the rice has not had enough direct heat.
Throw in the Thai basil off the heat and fold just until it wilts glossy-dark; cook it longer and the perfume disappears. Serve with the fried eggs and lime wedges.

note: Cold day-old rice fries cleanly; freshly cooked rice turns heavy in the wok.

name: Miso-Yuzu Lamb Cutlets on a Smoking Griddle
hook: Charred edges, glossy citrus miso

steps.t: Trim the lamb so only a thin rim of fat remains; a thick cap melts onto the griddle and gives the meat a sooty flare-up taste.
Mix the miso, mirin, soy sauce, yuzu juice and sugar, then rub it thinly over the cutlets and leave them out of the fridge; fridge-cold lamb chars outside before the centre relaxes.
Scrape off any heavy blobs of marinade and rub the cutlets with the oil; excess miso burns black long before the lamb is ready.
Heat a ridged griddle until it is properly smoking, then lay the cutlets down with space between them; crowding drops the heat and gives grey, wet stripes instead of grill marks.
Griddle the cutlets until dark bars appear and the fat edge turns crisp, then flip and repeat on the second side; press only the fatty edge down if it needs help, not the meat, or the juices run out.
Griddle the spring onions until blistered and slumped, moving them away from fierce hot spots before the green ends turn papery.
Rest the lamb on a warm plate so the juices settle back inside, then scatter with sesame seeds and serve with the charred spring onions; slice too soon and the board gets the sauce, not your guests.

note: For pink lamb, aim for springy meat with a warm rosy centre; cook longer if preferred.

name: Gochugaru Chickpea Jeon with Cucumber Ribbons
hook: Crisp bean lace, cold bright crunch

steps.t: Coarsely grate the courgette, toss it with the salt, then squeeze until it stops dripping; watery courgette makes the pancakes steam-soft in the centre.
Whisk the chickpea flour, cold water and gochugaru into a smooth batter the thickness of single cream; dry pockets of flour taste raw even after frying.
Fold in the squeezed kimchi, courgette and sliced spring onions; if the vegetables sit in a mound instead of being coated, the pancakes will split when flipped.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat, spoon in small pancakes and press them thin; thick jeon brown outside while staying pasty in the middle.
Shallow fry until the edges go lace-brown and the top looks mostly set, then flip; turn too early and the bean batter smears instead of forming a crust.
Fry the second side until it taps crisp with the spatula and smells nutty, not beany; pale patches mean the chickpea flour has not cooked through.
Shave the cucumber into ribbons and dress with rice vinegar, soy sauce and sesame oil, then pile it beside the hot jeon; dressing it too soon makes a puddle that softens the crisp edges.

note: Small pancakes stay lighter and crisper than one large jeon.

name: Black Vinegar Pickled Chicken with Sesame Chilli
hook: Cold shreds, sharp gloss, numbing warmth

steps.t: Slice the ginger, bash the spring onion whites and finely slice the greens; the bashed whites season the poaching water, while the greens stay sharp for the finish.
Put the chicken in a small pan with the ginger and spring onion whites, cover with cold water and bring just to a tremble; a rolling boil tightens the breasts into dry strings.
Simmer gently until the thickest part is cooked through and reaches 75°C, then lift the chicken out; guessing here is not worth it, because undercooked chicken is unsafe.
Cool the chicken until easy to handle, then tear it with the grain into long shreds; chopping makes blunt pieces that shed the dressing instead of catching it.
Mix the black vinegar, soy sauce and sugar, then toss with the chicken and smashed cucumber; leave it until the cucumber darkens at the edges and the chicken tastes sharp all the way through.
Stir the sesame paste with chilli oil and a spoonful of the pickling liquid until glossy and pourable; adding all the liquid at once makes it split and look grainy.

Pile the pickled chicken and cucumber onto a small platter, spoon over the sesame chilli dressing, then finish with Sichuan pepper, sesame seeds and spring onion greens; dress at the last minute so the top stays fragrant, not soggy.

note: This is a cold cooked-chicken dish: poach first, then pickle and dress.

name: Charred Salsa Verde Prawn Enchilada Bake
hook: Zesty prawns under bubbling cheese

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Put the oil and sliced pepper in a shallow baking dish and heat it in the oven until the pepper edges start to hiss; a cold dish makes the bake watery instead of lively.
Pat the prawns very dry on kitchen paper. If they go in wet, the salsa thins out and the prawns steam before they bake.

Stir the salsa verde, black beans, lime zest and half the lime juice into the hot dish, then fold in the prawns in a loose single layer; piled-up prawns cook unevenly and can stay glassy in the middle.
Tear the tortillas into broad strips and tuck them through the sauce, leaving a few corners exposed. Scatter over the cheese; completely buried tortillas turn pasty, fully exposed ones burn.
Bake until the cheese bubbles in bronze spots and the prawns are opaque and curled into loose C-shapes, not tight rubbery rings.
Rest for 2 minutes so the sauce stops spitting, then finish with coriander and the remaining lime juice; serving straight from the oven makes the prawns seem tougher than they are.

note: Use raw prawns, not cooked ones, so they finish safely and stay juicy in the oven.

name: Cinnamon-Wine Paneer Stifado
hook: Silky onions, squeaky golden paneer

steps.t: Brown the paneer in 1 tablespoon of oil in a wide casserole until the cut sides are freckled gold, then lift it out. If you skip this, it sheds moisture later and tastes flat.
Add the remaining oil and the peeled onions. Cook gently until their skins look glossy and patchily caramelised; rushing on high heat scorches the outside while the cores stay sharp.
Stir in the garlic and tomato purée until the purée darkens to brick red and sticks lightly to the pan; if it still smells raw, the finished sauce will taste tinny.
Pour in the wine and scrape the base clean. Let it bubble until the harsh alcohol smell fades and the liquid looks syrupy at the edges.
Add the tomatoes, vinegar, cinnamon, bay and oregano. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and braise at the laziest bubble until the onions yield to a spoon but still hold their shape.
Return the paneer to the casserole and nudge it under the sauce. Simmer gently until the cubes feel springy and seasoned through; a hard boil makes paneer tough at the edges.
Rest off the heat, fish out the cinnamon and bay, then scatter with parsley. Serving immediately misses the point: the sauce needs a short pause to cling to the paneer.

note: Paneer gives the salty, firm bite you want here without halloumi turning rubbery during the long braise.

name: Urfa Pepper Pork & White Bean Stew
hook: Lean pork in smoky red broth

steps.t: Pat the pork dry and season it. Sear it in the oil in two batches until the edges are chestnut brown; crowded pork leaks juice and boils grey.
Lower the heat and add the onion and red pepper. Cook until the onion is soft and sweet-smelling, not just translucent on the surface.
Stir in the garlic, tomato purée, pepper paste and Urfa chilli until the fat turns red and the paste catches slightly on the base; pale paste gives a thin broth.
Return the pork and its juices, then add the tomatoes and stock. Bring just to a simmer, not a rolling boil, because lean pork tightens fast when bullied.
Cover and simmer gently until a cube of pork splits with the side of a spoon but still looks moist inside.
Stir in the beans and simmer uncovered until the broth thickens around them and turns glossy; adding them earlier makes them burst and cloud the stew.
Finish with chopped parsley and a final pinch of Urfa chilli. Let it stand for 5 minutes so the beans settle and the pork fibres relax.

note: Built around lean pork and beans for a filling, high-protein bowl without a creamy sauce.

name: Orange Blossom Steamed Egg Custards with Pistachio Honey
hook: Wobbly custard, floral honey gloss

steps.t: Set a steamer or a wide lidded pan with a rack over barely simmering water. If the water boils hard, the custards puff and turn holey instead of smooth.
Whisk the eggs and sugar just until the sugar dissolves. Do not froth them; bubbles become little craters on the steamed surface.
Warm the milk until it feels hot but not scalding, then whisk it slowly into the eggs with the orange blossom water and vanilla. Pouring boiling milk straight in scrambles the eggs.
Strain into four small ramekins and cover each tightly with foil. Uncovered custards collect condensation and taste watery on top.
Steam gently until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly rather than sloshing like liquid.
Warm the honey with the cardamom until loose, then spoon it over the custards with pistachios. If the honey is cold, it drags and tears the delicate tops.
Serve warm or cool, but give them 5 minutes off the steam first; straight from the pan, the floral aroma is muted by heat.

note: A soft Levantine-style milk-and-egg pudding scented with orange blossom rather than a baked custard.

name: Tea-Smoked Chermoula Vegetable Couscous
hook: Campfire vegetables over fluffy couscous

steps.t: Toss the aubergine, carrots and onion with the oil, cumin and salt. Cut the carrots thinly; thick chunks stay crunchy while the aubergine collapses.
Cook the vegetables in a wide lidded frying pan until the aubergine is silky and the carrot slices bend without snapping. Stir enough to prevent black patches, but not so much that nothing chars.
Meanwhile, pour the hot stock over the couscous, cover and leave until the grains swell. Fluff with a fork; stirring early makes it clump like paste.

Push the vegetables to the sides of the pan. Put the tea, rice and sugar in a small foil cup on a dry bare patch of the pan, then heat until a thin blue smoke appears; thick yellow smoke tastes bitter.
Clamp on the lid, lower the heat and smoke the vegetables, then turn the heat off before lifting the lid. If the smoking mix flares, keep the lid on until it dies down.
Stir lemon zest, lemon juice and parsley through the smoky vegetables, then fold them through the couscous. Adding the herbs before smoking dulls their fresh chermoula snap.

note: No meat, fish, eggs, dairy or pulses added; the character comes from vegetables, smoke and lemony herbs.

name: Snow-Day Cider Braised Chicken
hook: Soft chicken, sweet roots, buttery gravy

steps.t: Season the chicken well, then dust only the skin side with flour. Too much flour turns the braise pasty instead of glossy.
Melt the butter in a wide casserole and brown the chicken skin-side down until the skin is deep gold and releases without tearing; if it sticks, it is not ready.
Lift out the chicken. Add onion, carrots and celery, scraping the brown bits as they soften; if the pan goes dry and black, splash in a spoonful of stock before it burns.
Stir in the garlic, cider, stock, bay and thyme, then bring to a steady simmer. Boiling hard now will make the chicken tighten before it has time to soften.
Nestle the chicken skin-side up, cover with a lid slightly ajar and braise gently until the meat pulls easily from the bone but still holds its shape.
Remove the lid and simmer until the gravy coats the back of a spoon; thin, watery gravy will taste flat no matter how tender the chicken is.
Stir in the cream off the boil, then taste for salt. Boiling the cream hard can split the sauce and dull the cider sweetness.

note: Serve with mashed potatoes or hot biscuits for proper deep-winter comfort.

name: Mushroom Carbonada Breakfast Stew
hook: Earthy mushrooms under yolky golden eggs

steps.t: Put a wide pan over high heat and dry-fry the mushrooms until they squeak and shed their water; adding oil too early makes them spongey.
Add a little oil, then the onion, red pepper and garlic. Cook until the onion smells sweet, not sharp; raw onion will bully the stew.
Stir in the squash, paprika and cumin until the spices stain the vegetables brick-red. If the spices catch black, the whole pot will taste bitter.
Add tomatoes, stock and sweetcorn, then simmer uncovered until the squash is tender and the sauce looks thick enough to cradle an egg.
Make four hollows and crack in the eggs. Keep the stew at a lazy bubble; a rolling boil breaks the whites into rags.
Cover and cook until the whites are set but the yolks still wobble when you shake the pan.
Finish with parsley and a final pinch of salt. Serve straight away, because the eggs keep cooking in the hot stew.

note: Inspired by Argentine carbonada, made meat-free and breakfast-ready.

name: Moqueca-Roasted Whole Halloumi
hook: Bronzed cheese in coconut-lime heat

ingredients.name: dendê palm oil or olive oil

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Soak the halloumi blocks in cold water while the oven heats; skipping this can leave the finished cheese aggressively salty.
Toss peppers, tomatoes and onion with oil, garlic and chilli in a roasting tin. Spread them out, because crowded vegetables steam instead of blister.
Pat the halloumi completely dry and sit the blocks whole on top of the vegetables. Wet cheese will weep and refuse to bronze.
Roast until the tomatoes split, the pepper tips char and the halloumi has a golden crust at the corners.
Whisk coconut milk with lime zest and half the juice, then pour it around, not over, the halloumi. Covering the crust makes it rubbery.
Return to the oven until the coconut sauce bubbles at the edges and turns peachy from the roasted juices.
Mix cassava flour, cashews, coriander and the remaining lime juice into a quick farofa. Spoon it over at the table so it stays sandy-crisp, not soggy.

note: Bring the tin to the table and cut the halloumi like a roast.

name: Dhuwan Pork Tenderloin Kachumber
hook: Cool salad, warm smoke, tender pork

steps.t: Mix yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, half the lemon juice, cumin, coriander, chilli and salt. Coat the pork lightly; a thick blanket of marinade scorches before the meat cooks.
Rest the pork at room temperature while you make the salad, but do not leave it out for more than 30 minutes. Cold pork cooks unevenly; warm pork left too long is unsafe.
Toss cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, mint and the remaining lemon juice with salt. Keep it chilled, because a warm kachumber loses its snap.
Sear the pork in a hot ovenproof pan until the yoghurt crust is speckled brown, not black. Burnt yoghurt tastes acrid and hides the spices.
Roast at 200°C until the thickest part reaches 63°C, then take it out. Guessing by colour is unreliable with pork tenderloin.

Rest the pork under foil. Meanwhile heat the charcoal until ashed over, then place it in a small foil cup beside the cooked pork, add a teaspoon of oil to the coal and cover the pan tightly; never use this smoke step on raw pork as a shortcut.
Slice the pork thinly across the grain and lay it over the cold kachumber. Cutting with the grain makes even perfectly cooked tenderloin chew stringy.

note: A diaspora-style Pakistani plate using dhuwan smoke and summer salad rather than a heavy curry.

name: Nước Mắm Steamed Eggs with Shiitake
hook: Silky savoury custard for passing round

steps.t: Set up a steamer with a gentle simmer, not a furious boil. Violent steam makes egg custard bubble and split.
Whisk eggs, warm stock, fish sauce, sugar and sesame oil until smooth, then strain into a shallow heatproof dish. Straining catches stringy whites that would set into lumps.
Scatter over the shiitake and half the spring onions. Push any floating mushroom slices just under the surface so they cook rather than dry out.
Cover the dish with foil and steam gently until the edges are set and the centre trembles like soft jelly.
Turn off the heat and leave the dish covered in the steamer. Lifting it straight away can shock the custard into weeping watery liquid.
Top with chilli, coriander and the remaining spring onions. Add lime at the table, because squeezing it on early dulls the green herbs.

note: Serve warm with other small plates, rice and dipping sauces.

name: Coal-Charred Courgette Panzanella
hook: Smoky vegetables, torn bread, bright vinegar

steps.t: Light a small, fierce bed of coals and let the flames die back; if you cook over flames, the courgettes scorch before their centres soften.
Toss courgettes and pepper with 1 tbsp olive oil and salt, then grill cut-side down until bar marks are dark and the edges sag, not just striped on the surface.
Put the bread directly on the cooler edge of the grill and turn until crisp at the corners with a little smoke; leave it too long and it turns bitter rather than toasty.
Whisk vinegar, remaining olive oil, oregano, capers and a pinch of salt in a large bowl; under-season this dressing and the bread will make the whole salad taste flat.
Slice the hot grilled vegetables into bite-sized pieces and drop them straight into the dressing so they drink it in; if they cool first, the flavour stays on the outside.
Fold in tomatoes, onion, grilled bread and basil, then rest until the bread is chewy at the centre but still crisp on the edges.
Taste for vinegar and salt just before serving, because tomatoes dilute the seasoning as they sit.

note: Fastest if the coals are already being lit for another meal; a griddle pan works, but you lose the smoke.

name: Kokum-Lime Cured Sea Bass Chaat
hook: Cool fish, sour fruit, crackling spice

ingredients.name: previously frozen sashimi-grade sea bass or cod loin, skinned and pin-boned

steps.t: Soak the kokum in 120 ml just-boiled water until the water turns deep plum and sharply fruity; rush this and the cure tastes like plain lime instead of kokum.
Keep the fish fridge-cold, then slice it 5 mm thick with a clean knife; ragged thick pieces cure unevenly and feel woolly at the edges.
Strain the kokum water and mix it with lime juice, salt and sugar, then pour over the fish in a shallow dish so every slice is touched by the cure.
Cover and chill until the fish turns opaque around the edges but still looks glossy in the centre; if it goes chalk-white all through, you have left it too long.
Stir onion, chilli, cumin and coriander together, then let them sit briefly so the onion loses its harsh raw bite without going limp.
Warm the oil until it shimmers, then drizzle it over the cumin-onion mix; if the oil smokes, it will make the coriander taste scorched rather than fragrant.
Lift the fish from the cure, dab away excess liquid, and plate with yoghurt, the spiced onion mix and sev added at the last second so it stays crackly.

note: Use fish sold for raw eating or fish that has been commercially frozen; keep it cold and eat the dish the same day.

name: Thai Basil Mushroom Tofu Power Stir-Fry
hook: Hot wok, meaty mushrooms, basil snap

ingredients.name: green beans, cut into short lengths
fish sauce or extra soy sauce

steps.t: Mix soy sauce, mushroom sauce, fish sauce and sugar in a small bowl before the wok heats; stopping to measure later makes the mushrooms dump water and stew.
Heat a wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add 1 tbsp oil and the tofu; it should hiss hard, or it will stick and crumble before it browns.
Stir-fry the tofu until the torn ridges turn golden and dry-looking, then scoop it out so it stays chewy rather than soggy.
Add the remaining oil, mushrooms and green beans, spreading them up the sides of the wok; crowding them in a heap traps steam and kills the char.
Add garlic and chillies and toss until the garlic smells sweet and sharp, not dark brown; burnt garlic will dominate the whole bowl.
Return the tofu, pour in the sauce and toss hard until it clings in shiny patches with no puddle at the bottom.
Turn off the heat and fold through Thai basil just until it slumps and perfumes the wok; cook it longer and the leaves turn black and medicinal.
Serve immediately over hot rice, scraping over the wok juices because that is where the salt and mushroom depth have collected.

note: Pressing tofu well is the difference between crisp-edged protein and a watery stir-fry.

name: Matcha Kuromitsu Steamed Egg Purin
hook: Silken custard, bitter tea, dark syrup

steps.t: Set a steamer to a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil; violent steam makes the custard bubble and turn honeycombed.
Warm milk, cream, sugar, matcha and salt until the sugar dissolves and the milk is steaming but not boiling, whisking until no green clumps remain.
Beat the eggs just to loosen them, then slowly whisk in the warm milk; pour too fast and you will scramble the eggs in streaks.
Strain the custard into a jug, then skim off foam because every bubble becomes a pockmark on the finished surface.
Divide into four heatproof cups, cover each with foil and steam gently until the edges are set and the centre trembles like soft jelly.
Turn off the heat and rest the covered cups in the steamer so the centres finish without overcooking at the edges.
Chill until fully cold, then spoon over kuromitsu and sesame; add the syrup earlier and it sinks in instead of glazing the top.

note: If using muscovado syrup, loosen it with a teaspoon of hot water so it pours cleanly.

name: Gochujang Crisp Mackerel Jeon
hook: Crackly fish, chilli glaze, student price

steps.t: Pat the mackerel very dry and cut each fillet into chunky strips; wet skin spits in the pan and stops the coating turning crisp.
Dust the fish lightly with flour, shaking off the excess, then dip in beaten egg; a thick flour blanket turns pasty instead of crackly.
Stir gochujang, soy, vinegar and honey with 1 tbsp water in a bowl, ready for glazing before the fish leaves the pan.
Heat the oil in a frying pan until a fleck of egg sizzles on contact, then lay in the fish skin-side down with space between pieces.
Fry until the skin side is rigid and deep golden at the edges, then turn once; fiddling early tears the coating off the oily flesh.
Cook the second side until the egg coating is crisp and the mackerel flakes at the thickest point, not translucent in the centre.
Spoon off excess oil, lower the heat and brush on the gochujang glaze for the last few seconds; high heat now burns the chilli paste bitter.
Serve over rice with spring onion and sesame, keeping the glazed fish on top so the crisp bits do not steam soft underneath.

note: Tinned mackerel is cheaper, but fresh fillets hold together and crisp far better for jeon.

name: Istanbul Pepper Beef Sac Tava
hook: Hot pan, sweet peppers, juicy beef

ingredients.name: beef rump steak, sliced into 5 mm strips

steps.t: Pat the beef very dry and spread it on a plate; wet strips steam grey before they ever sear.
Heat a wide wok or sauté pan until a drop of water skitters, then add the oil and half the beef in one loose layer; crowding the pan makes juice pool in the bottom.
Stir-fry the beef just until the edges catch dark spots and the centre is still springy, then lift it out and repeat with the rest.
Throw in the onion and peppers and keep them moving over high heat until the onion tips brown and the pepper skins blister; if they soften quietly, the heat is too low.
Add garlic, tomato paste, pul biber and oregano, scraping hard until the paste stains the oil brick-red; raw paste tastes tinny if it only warms through.
Return the beef with the tomatoes and butter, toss until the tomatoes slump but still hold their shape, then finish with parsley and salt.

note: Serve with warm flatbread or quick bulgur to catch the peppery juices.

name: Sumac-Griddled Mackerel Man’oushe
hook: Oily char, soft bread, sharp onions

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, 180 ml warm water, 1 tbsp olive oil and 1 tsp salt to a soft dough, then knead until it stops tearing in shaggy patches.
Cover the dough and let it rise until puffy and almost doubled; if it is still tight, the flatbreads will griddle dense and bready.
Cook the onions in 3 tbsp olive oil with the sumac, allspice and a pinch of salt until they are jammy at the edges, not crisp; burnt sumac turns bitter fast.
Whisk tahini with half the lemon juice, 80 ml cold water and salt until glossy and pourable; stop adding water once it ribbons, or it will taste thin.
Divide the dough into 4, roll into rough ovals and griddle on a hot dry ridged pan until the undersides have charred bars and the tops bubble.
Brush the mackerel with the remaining olive oil and lemon juice, salt it, then griddle skin-side down until the skin releases and the flesh has turned opaque halfway up.
Turn the mackerel for a final flash until it flakes at the thickest part; pulling it early leaves the centre glassy and unsafe to serve.
Spoon onions over the flatbreads, add mackerel, tahini, parsley and pickles while the bread is still warm enough to bend.

note: A long, lazy build: dough, onions, sauce and fish each earn their place.

name: Crisp Chermoula Tofu Power Plate
hook: Crackly edges, lemony chermoula heat

steps.t: Slice the tofu into thick batons and press between clean tea towels until the surface feels tacky-dry; damp tofu spits oil and sheds its crust.
Stir chickpea flour, cornflour, half the ras el hanout, smoked paprika and salt in a bowl, then toss the tofu until every face looks dusty, not clumped.
Mix garlic, lemon zest, lemon juice, herbs, the remaining ras el hanout and 2 tbsp olive oil into a loose chermoula; if it sits as a dry paste, it will not coat the hot tofu.
Heat the remaining oil in a frying pan to a lively shimmer and lay in the tofu with space between pieces; packed tofu lowers the oil and turns leathery.
Shallow fry, turning each baton, until all long sides are deep gold and the corners sound scratchy against the tongs.
Toss lentils, carrot and spinach with a spoonful of chermoula and a pinch of salt; dress it lightly or the salad collapses under the hot tofu.
Pile the lentils onto plates, add the crisp tofu and spoon over the remaining chermoula while the crust is still crackling.

note: Use the firmest tofu you can find; soft tofu will break before it crisps.

name: Seville Orange Steamed Flan Cups
hook: Silky custard under bitter caramel

steps.t: Put 80 g sugar and the water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the caramel is deep amber; pale caramel tastes flat, but black caramel will scorch the custard.
Divide the caramel between 4 ramekins and swirl only the bases, keeping fingers well away because molten sugar burns badly.
Warm the milk with orange zest and vanilla until it steams at the edge, then take it off the heat; boiling milk gives the eggs a cooked-sulphur note.
Whisk eggs, yolks, remaining sugar and salt just until smooth, not foamy, because bubbles set into pockmarks.
Slowly whisk the hot milk into the eggs, strain into a jug, then pour into the ramekins; skipping the sieve leaves stringy bits in a dessert that should be silk.
Set the ramekins in a covered steamer over a bare simmer and steam until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly, not liquid.
Cool, then chill until fully cold before turning out; unmoulding warm flan breaks the custard and smears the caramel.

note: If using sweet oranges rather than Seville, add a teaspoon of lemon juice to sharpen the finish.

name: Dijon Lentil and Bean Gratin
hook: Mustardy beans beneath a golden crust

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C and oil a medium baking dish; a dry dish grips the pulses and leaves a hard crust around the edges.
Tip onion, carrot, garlic and olive oil into the dish, toss well and bake until the onion smells sweet and the carrot edges look slightly shrivelled.
Stir in lentils, beans, hot stock, Dijon, herbes de Provence and black pepper until the mustard has dissolved; streaks of mustard bake into harsh yellow pockets.
Cover tightly with foil and bake until the liquid bubbles right in the centre, not just at the edges.
Mix breadcrumbs with the grated cheese, scatter evenly over the pulses, then press down lightly so the topping touches the sauce; loose crumbs brown while staying dusty underneath.
Bake uncovered until the top is golden and the sauce blips up through the corners; if it looks dry before browning, splash in a little hot water at the side.
Rest the gratin until the bubbling calms, because spooning it straight away makes the sauce run thin across the plate.

note: Built for one baking dish and supermarket tins, with enough savoury depth to feel planned.

name: Yuzu-Miso Whole Roast Pork Shoulder with Daikon Jus
hook: Miso gloss, tender pork, snowy daikon

ingredients.name: daikon, peeled and cut into thick rounds

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Mix the miso, mirin, sake, soy, ginger, garlic and sesame oil into a smooth paste; leave lumps of miso and they scorch into salty freckles rather than glazing.
Pat the pork very dry, then rub the paste into every side of the whole joint. If the surface is wet, the coating slides off and the meat steams pale instead of roasting.
Lay the daikon rounds in a snug roasting tin, pour in the stock and sit the pork on top, fat side up. Keep the liquid below the pork; if it covers the meat, you lose the sticky roasted edges.
Cover tightly with foil and roast until a skewer meets almost no resistance in the centre and the daikon is translucent at the rims.
Remove the foil, baste the pork, raise the oven to 210°C fan and roast until the miso turns mahogany and tacky. Pull it before the glaze goes black, because burnt miso tastes bitter fast.
Rest the pork loosely covered so the juices settle; slicing straight away floods the board and dries the joint.
Stir the yuzu juice through the hot daikon juices, then slice the pork thickly. Serve over the daikon with the jus spooned round and spring onions scattered on top.

note: A cold-weather centrepiece with the sweetness of mirin, the depth of miso and soft daikon that drinks up the pork juices.

name: Sesame-Smoked Gyeran over Crackling Kimchi Rice
hook: Smoky eggs over crackling kimchi rice

steps.t: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook until the whites are set but the yolks stay fudgy. Go shorter and they tear when peeled; go much longer and the yolks turn dusty.
Chill the eggs in cold water, peel them and dry them thoroughly with kitchen paper. Damp eggs taste boiled, not smoked, because the smoke clings in streaks.

Line an old lidded wok or heavy pan with foil, add the uncooked rice, tea and brown sugar, then set a rack above it. Heat until a steady curl of smoke appears, add the eggs, cover and smoke; use extraction and avoid a non-stick pan unless it is rated for this heat.
Lift the smoked eggs out and keep them warm. If they sit in the closed smoker too long, the tea smoke turns acrid and tannic.
Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan, add the kimchi and cook until it darkens to brick red and smells sharp-savoury rather than cabbagey. Pale kimchi leaves the rice wet.
Stir in the gochujang, soy and chilled rice, then press the rice flat so the underside crackles. Constant stirring gives you hot rice, not breakfast crust.
Fold through the sesame oil and half the spring onions. Halve the smoked eggs over the rice and finish with the remaining spring onions.

note: Best with day-old rice; fresh rice is too steamy to crisp properly.

name: Coal-Grilled Lime-Chile Sea Bass with Cucumber Radish Salad
hook: Charred lime fish, cucumber-cool and bright

ingredients.name: small red onion, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no licking flames. Flames blacken the lime and leave the fish tasting sooty before it is cooked.
Toss the cucumber, radishes, red onion, coriander, jalapeño, juice of one lime and a pinch of salt. If you dress it too early, the cucumber slumps and puddles the plate.
Mix the ancho, grated garlic, olive oil, zest of one lime and the remaining salt. Rub it over the fish, especially the skin side; thick clumps of chilli burn instead of perfuming the fish.
Scrub the grill bars clean and oil them well, then place the fish skin-side down over the coals. Leave it until the skin firms, blisters and releases when nudged; moving it early tears the fillet.
Turn the fish once and grill the flesh side just until it turns opaque in thick flakes. If you wait for it to feel firm all the way through, it will be dry by the time it reaches the table.
Squeeze over the remaining lime, plate with the cucumber-radish salad and scatter with pumpkin seeds for crunch.

note: Skin-on fillets are much easier over coals than skinless white fish, which sticks and breaks quickly.

name: Ouzo-Cured Sardines with Caper, Dill and Lemon Oil
hook: Silver sardines, ouzo, lemon and herbs

ingredients.name: sardine fillets, sashimi-grade or commercially frozen and thawed
barley rusks or crispbread, to serve

steps.t: Keep the sardines cold while you check for pin bones and trim ragged edges. Warm oily fish turns metallic and soft, which no amount of lemon can fix.
Mix the lemon juice, ouzo and salt until dissolved. Lay the sardines skin-side down in a shallow dish and spoon the cure over them evenly.
Chill until the edges turn opaque and the centres still look glossy. Leave them too long and the flesh tightens into chalk rather than staying silky.
Soak the red onion in cold water to take off the raw burn, then drain it very well. Wet onion thins the olive oil dressing on the plate.
Lift the sardines from the cure and pat the surface lightly; do not rinse them, or you wash away the ouzo and sea-salt seasoning.

Arrange the sardines on a shared plate, drizzle with olive oil and scatter over onion, capers, dill, oregano and Aleppo pepper. Let them stand briefly so the oil loses its fridge chill, but do not leave raw fish sitting warm.
Serve with barley rusks or crispbread for scooping up the lemony oil.

note: Use only fish sold for raw preparation or commercially frozen first; acid curing is not the same as cooking.

name: Black Vinegar Snow Tofu with Pickled Mustard Greens
hook: Hot silk, sour crunch, chilli warmth

ingredients.name: Chinese pickled mustard greens, finely chopped

steps.t: Slide the tofu into a shallow heatproof bowl in one piece if you can; if it tears, keep the pieces snug so they warm evenly rather than weeping into the dressing.
Steam the tofu over gently bubbling water until it trembles like custard and is hot in the centre; fierce boiling makes silken tofu split and turn watery.
Meanwhile rinse the pickled mustard greens briefly, then squeeze them hard in your fist; if you skip the squeeze, the whole bowl tastes briny instead of bright.
Stir black vinegar, soy, sesame oil, chilli oil, sugar and ginger until the sugar disappears; undissolved grains sit harshly on the tofu.
Lift the hot bowl out carefully and spoon away the clear liquid around the tofu; leaving it there dilutes the glossy dressing into soup.
Scatter the mustard greens over the tofu, spoon the dressing into the cracks and finish with spring onion and sesame; dress at the table if you want the greens to stay snappy.

note: Serve with plain steamed rice or a small bowl of congee for proper cold-weather comfort.

name: Sardine Chilaquiles Sunrise Bake
hook: Crisp tortillas under molten salsa

ingredients.name: tinned sardines in olive oil, drained lightly

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan and oil a small baking dish; a cold oven leaves the chips soggy before the eggs set.
Spread half the tortilla chips in the dish, spoon over half the salsa and beans, then repeat; do not crush the chips flat or you lose the crisp ridges chilaquiles need.
Flake the sardines into large pieces over the top, keeping some silver skin visible; mashing them makes the bake taste heavy and fish-pastey.
Bake until the salsa bubbles hard at the edges and the top chips darken at their tips, not until everything is soft.
Make two hollows with a spoon and crack in the eggs; if the hollows are too shallow, the whites run to the edges and overcook before the yolks warm.
Return to the oven until the whites are just opaque and the yolks still wobble when the dish is nudged.
Finish with cheese, soured cream, onion, coriander and lime; add the fresh toppings after baking or they turn dull and sweaty.

note: Use sardines packed in olive oil rather than tomato sauce, which fights the salsa verde.

name: Orange Saffron Gigantes with Feta Crust
hook: Velvet beans in golden tomato oil

ingredients.name: cooked gigantes or large butter beans, drained

steps.t: Heat the oven to 170°C fan. Warm the olive oil in a wide ovenproof pan and soften the onion until it collapses and turns sweet at the edges; rushing this leaves raw onion sharpness in the braise.
Add the garlic and stir only until it smells nutty, not brown; burnt garlic will bitter the whole pot for the next hour.
Stir in passata, orange zest and juice, saffron, oregano, vinegar and 150ml water, scraping the base clean so no onion catches during the long bake.
Fold in the beans gently until every one is lacquered; broken beans thicken nicely, but smashing too many turns the dish pasty.
Bake uncovered until the sauce reduces to a glossy red oil around the edges and the top beans wrinkle slightly.
Scatter over the feta and bake again until the cheese freckles gold and the sauce no longer looks loose in the centre.
Rest for 10 minutes, then shower with parsley; serving straight from the oven hides the saffron and makes the beans taste flat-hot rather than deep.

note: Bring to the table in the pan with bread for swiping through the orange-saffron oil.

name: Lemon Courgette Tavuk Stew with Dill
hook: Brothy chicken, soft summer vegetables

ingredients.name: skinless boneless chicken thighs, cut into large pieces

steps.t: Season the chicken, then warm the oil in a shallow pan and seal the pieces until they lose their raw pink outside; browning hard makes this light stew taste roasted instead of clean.
Add the onion and cook until translucent and soft enough to fold around the chicken; if it stays crunchy now, it will taste harsh in the broth.
Stir in garlic and pul biber until fragrant, keeping the heat moderate because scorched chilli turns dusty and bitter.
Add grated tomato and cook until it darkens slightly and the watery foam disappears; adding stock too early gives a thin, raw tomato broth.
Pour in the stock, cover and simmer gently until the chicken is tender enough to split with a spoon; a rolling boil tightens the meat.
Add courgettes and lemon zest, then simmer uncovered until the courgettes bend but still hold their green edges; overcooked courgette muddies the stew.
Turn off the heat, stir in lemon juice and dill, and serve with yoghurt spooned on top; boiling after the lemon goes in dulls the fresh finish.

note: Good warm rather than piping hot, with rice or flatbread and a cucumber salad.

name: Za’atar Roasted Whole Prawns with Lemon Tahini
hook: Shells crackle, butter runs green

steps.t: Heat the oven to 230°C fan and put a large tray in to get hot; a cool tray steams the prawns before the shells can roast.
Pat the prawns very dry, especially under the heads, because surface water stops the shells turning crisp and fragrant.
Mix olive oil, za’atar, garlic, lemon zest, softened butter and Aleppo pepper, then rub it over the whole prawns; keep the lemon juice out for now or it starts curing the flesh.
Tip the prawns onto the hot tray in a single layer, with space between them; piling them up gives grey, rubbery prawns instead of blistered shells.
Roast until the shells are coral, the heads smell sweet and roasted, and the flesh is just opaque at the thickest part.
Whisk tahini with lemon juice, cold water and a pinch of salt until pale and pourable; add the water gradually or it can seize into a stiff paste.
Scatter parsley over the prawns and serve on the tray with lemon tahini and warm flatbreads; waiting too long makes the shells soften and the butter congeal.

note: Put out finger bowls and a bowl for shells; this is meant to be eaten messily.

name: Chermoula-Crisp Halloumi Couscous
hook: Salty crunch, orange-bright couscous

steps.t: Put the couscous in a bowl with the orange zest, a pinch of salt and 150 ml boiling water. Cover it tightly; if steam escapes, the grains stay gritty instead of swelling soft.
Mix the flour with the ras el hanout. Dip the halloumi in flour, then egg, then panko, pressing firmly; loose crumbs fall off and burn before the cheese crisps.
Fluff the couscous with the orange juice, grated carrot and coriander. Taste now, because once the halloumi is hot and salty it will dominate a flat salad.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a breadcrumb fizzes at once. If the oil is merely warm, the coating drinks it and turns heavy.
Shallow fry the halloumi in one layer until the undersides are lace-gold and crisp, then turn once; crowding the pan steams the crust off.
Drain on kitchen paper for a minute, then serve over the orange couscous while the crust still cracks under the knife.

note: Halloumi varies in saltiness; if yours is very salty, keep the couscous seasoning restrained.

name: Asturian Cider-Steam Pork Hock
hook: Silky pork, cider-sweet steam

steps.t: Rub the pork hock with salt and smoked paprika, getting into the folds of skin. Leave uncovered in the fridge; if it sits wet and wrapped, the seasoning stays on the surface.
Set onions, garlic and bay in a large steamer base with the cider and 500 ml water. Bring to a steady simmer, not a violent boil, or the liquid spits up and washes flavour from the meat.

Place the hock in the steamer basket, cover tightly and steam until a skewer slides into the thickest part with almost no resistance. Top up with boiling water if the base gets low; a dry pan scorches bitter.
Add the potatoes around the pork, cover again and steam until their edges look satin rather than chalky. If they are stacked in a tight mound, the centres lag behind.
Lift the pork to a board and rest it. Steam the cabbage wedges until bright and bendy but not khaki; overdone cabbage will drag the whole dish into sulphur.
Boil the cider juices hard until glossy and salty-sweet, then sharpen with sherry vinegar and olive oil. If it tastes flat, reduce more before adding extra salt.
Pull the pork into large pieces and spoon over the cider glaze with the potatoes and cabbage.

note: The first step is passive curing time; it turns this into a relaxed weekend project rather than a rushed braise.

name: Coal-Grilled Provençal Egg-White Omelette
hook: Smoke-edged, lean and herby

steps.t: Light the barbecue and let the coals burn until they are grey and pulsing, not flaming; flames scorch the base before the eggs set.
Whisk egg whites, whole eggs, cottage cheese, mustard, herbs and a good pinch of salt until just broken up. Do not whip to foam, or the omelette rises then collapses watery.
Squeeze the grated courgette hard in a clean cloth. If you skip this, it leaks into the pan and the eggs steam rather than grill at the edges.
Set a small cast-iron pan over the coals and heat the oil until it shimmers. Add courgette and tomatoes; cook until the tomato skins wrinkle and the courgette smells nutty.
Pour in the eggs and scatter parsley over the top. Move the pan to a slightly cooler patch of coals and cover with the barbecue lid; fierce heat gives a leathery bottom and raw top.
The omelette is ready when the centre trembles like set custard and no clear egg runs from a knife tip. Rest it briefly, because slicing immediately forces out the curds.
Serve with lemon wedges for squeezing over the smoky, herb-speckled top.

note: Use a pan with a metal handle only; plastic or rubber handles do not belong over coals.

name: Steamed Maple Bourbon Custard Pots
hook: Warm satin, maple and vanilla

steps.t: Set four ramekins in a wide pan on a folded tea towel. The towel matters: without it, the pots rattle and the custard can split at the edges.
Warm milk, cream, maple syrup and salt until steaming at the rim, not boiling. Boiling dairy scrambles the eggs the moment it hits them.
Whisk eggs and yolks just until smooth, then slowly pour in the hot dairy while whisking. Rush this and you get sweet scrambled egg specks.
Strain the custard into a jug, stir in bourbon and vanilla, then divide between the ramekins. Straining catches the stringy bits that ruin the satin texture.
Pour boiling water into the pan to come halfway up the ramekins, cover with a lid wrapped in a clean cloth, and steam over the gentlest simmer. Hard bubbling makes holes like a sponge cake.
Check one pot: the centre should wobble softly, not slosh. If it is liquid, cover and steam a little longer rather than turning up the heat.
Rest for 10 minutes, then finish with toasted pecans. Serve warm so the maple smells round and buttery.

note: The bourbon is gentle; leave it out for an alcohol-free finish and add another teaspoon of vanilla.

name: Chimichurri Hake Noodle Saltado
hook: Hot wok fish, sharp green herbs

ingredients.name: frozen hake fillets, thawed and patted dry

steps.t: Cook the noodles in salted boiling water until just bendy with a firm centre. Drain and rinse briefly; fully soft noodles collapse in the wok.
Cut the hake into large chunks and pat it very dry. Wet fish chills the pan and sheds flakes before it can sear.
Mix parsley, oregano, vinegar, chilli flakes, half the garlic and a pinch of salt into a rough chimichurri. Keep it raw; frying it too early kills the bright green bite.
Heat a wok or large frying pan until a drop of water skitters away, then add the oil. If the pan is only medium-hot, the fish stews and smells tired.
Stir-fry the onion and pepper until blistered at the tips but still snappy, then add the remaining garlic for the last few seconds so it perfumes rather than burns.
Add the hake and toss gently until the outside turns opaque and the thickest pieces flake with a nudge. Keep the spatula broad and calm; aggressive stirring shreds the fish.
Add noodles and toss over high heat until they pick up glossy patches, then take off the heat and fold through the chimichurri. Serve immediately before the herbs dull.

note: Frozen hake is cheap and works well here, but thaw it fully and dry it properly for high-heat cooking.

name: Coconut Lime Red Lentil Stew
hook: Creamy heat, sharp lime, soft lentils

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide saucepan, then fry the curry paste until it darkens slightly and smells roasted; if it stays raw and bright, the stew will taste flat and pasty.
Stir in the rinsed lentils so every grain is stained red; dry patches clump later and cook unevenly.
Pour in the coconut milk and stock, scraping the base straight away; any paste left stuck there will catch and turn bitter.
Simmer gently, not hard, until the lentils slump and thicken the liquid like loose porridge; a rolling boil splits the coconut and gives a gritty finish.
Add the tomatoes and soy sauce, then simmer until the tomato skins wrinkle but the halves still hold shape; cook them to collapse and the stew turns too sweet and muddy.
Fold in the spinach off the heat until just wilted and glossy; boiling it makes it khaki and stringy.
Finish with lime zest, lime juice and coriander, tasting before you add more salt; lime added too early disappears into the stew.

note: Red lentils give the pulse body without needing soaking, so this eats like a stew in under half an hour.

name: Miso Sake Weekend Roast Chicken
hook: Bronzed skin, sake steam, savoury juices

steps.t: Pat the chicken very dry, including the creases at the thighs; damp skin steams first and never becomes properly bronze.
Mix miso, sake, mirin, soy, oil and ginger, then rub it over the bird and lightly under the breast skin without tearing it; thick clumps burn before the meat is cooked.
Set the chicken uncovered in the fridge on a tray for 4 hours, so the surface goes tacky rather than wet; skip this and the glaze slides off into the tin.
Take the chicken out while the oven heats to 200°C fan, then tuck the spring onions inside the cavity; roasting fridge-cold gives tight breast meat before the legs catch up.
Toss the potatoes with sesame oil in the roasting tin, sit the chicken on top breast-side up, and roast until the glaze is deep chestnut, not black at the wing tips.
Turn the heat down to 170°C fan and keep roasting until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 74°C and the juices run clear; guessing by colour alone is where whole chickens go wrong.
Rest the chicken on a board, uncovered, until the juices settle and the skin stays crisp; foil traps steam and softens the best part.
Spoon the miso chicken juices through the potatoes, carve cleanly through the joints, and serve while the potatoes are sticky at the cut edges.

note: A dry, tacky miso cure is the weekend work here; the oven does the rest.

name: Pine-Smoked Gochujang Mussels and Prawns
hook: Clean smoke, chilli gloss, briny protein

ingredients.name: raw king prawns, peeled and deveined
food-safe hardwood or fruitwood chips, soaked

steps.t: Check the mussels: tap any open ones and discard those that do not close, plus any cracked shells; dead mussels are not worth negotiating with.
Stir gochujang, soy, vinegar, sesame oil and garlic into a loose glaze; if it looks like paste, it will scorch on the shellfish instead of coating it.
Light a small charcoal barbecue for indirect heat and add the drained wood chips when the coals are glowing, not flaming; flames give acrid soot rather than clean smoke.
Put the mussels in a perforated grill tray over the cooler side, close the lid and smoke until most shells yawn open; leaving the lid up wastes the smoke and delays safe cooking.
Add the prawns, brush everything with half the glaze, then close the lid until the prawns curl into a C and turn opaque; tight O-shaped prawns are already overcooked.
Discard any mussels that stayed shut, then toss the hot shellfish with the remaining glaze, spring onions and sesame seeds; forcing shut shells open is the unsafe shortcut.
Spoon over warm rice, keeping the smoky juices from the tray; without those juices this eats lean rather than satisfying.

note: Shellfish cooks fast, so set up the smoke first and only then bring the mussels and prawns to the heat.

name: Steamed Ginger Osmanthus Egg Custards
hook: Silky wobble, warm ginger, floral syrup

steps.t: Warm the milk with the ginger until it steams at the edge but does not boil; boiled milk tastes cooked and makes the custard foam harder to control.
Cover and let the ginger steep until the milk smells warm and spicy, not harsh; too short and the custard tastes only of egg and sugar.
Whisk eggs, sugar and salt just until the whites disappear; beating hard traps bubbles that steam into little craters.
Strain the ginger milk into the eggs slowly while whisking, then strain again into four small bowls; skipping the second strain leaves stringy chalazae in a dessert that should be glassy.
Cover each bowl tightly with foil and set in a steamer over a gentle simmer; a fierce boil makes the surface pockmarked and watery.
Steam until the custards tremble like set jelly at the centre when nudged; if the middle sloshes, they will collapse when spooned.
Rest for 5 minutes, then warm the honey with osmanthus and spoon it over the tops; pouring cold honey on hot custard drags the surface.

note: The double strain and gentle steam are what give the custard its soft restaurant wobble.

name: Coal-Grilled Achiote Pork Tacos
hook: Charred pork, sour orange, hot tortillas

steps.t: Mash achiote paste with orange juice, lime juice, garlic and oregano until smooth; lumps stick to the grill and leave bare pork behind.
Coat the pork slices thoroughly and leave them while the coals burn down; grilling over flames burns the marinade before the shoulder has softened.
Set the barbecue for a hot direct zone and a cooler edge, then oil the grate lightly; a dirty dry grate steals the best charred crust.
Grill the pork over the hot coals until the edges blister and the marinade goes brick-red with black freckles, moving pieces to the cooler edge if they flare.
Turn and cook until the pork is firm but still juicy, with no raw pink at the thickest point; shoulder sliced thin forgives heat, but undercooked pork does not.
Rest the pork, then chop it across the grain into taco-sized bites; chopping straight off the fire spills the juices onto the board.
Warm the tortillas on the grate until they puff in spots and smell like toasted corn; cold tortillas crack and make cheap tacos feel cheaper.
Fill with pork, onion, coriander, cabbage and jalapeño, spooning over any resting juices so the tortillas catch the smoky achiote oil.

note: Pork shoulder steaks are cheaper than loin and better over coals when sliced thin.

name: Farofa Butter Mushroom Chapa
hook: Smoke, butter and cassava crunch

ingredients.name: mixed mushrooms, large ones torn in half

steps.t: Heat a heavy griddle or cast-iron pan until a drop of water skitters away at once; if the pan is only warm, the mushrooms will steam and turn woolly.
Toss the mushrooms with olive oil and a good pinch of salt, then lay them down with space between pieces; crowding them makes them leak water instead of taking on dark chapa stripes.
Griddle the mushrooms without fiddling until the cut edges are mahogany and the caps have collapsed slightly, then turn once; moving them early tears them and leaves the flavour pale.
Push the mushrooms aside, add half the butter, onion, garlic, paprika and cumin, and stir until the onion smells sweet rather than raw; let the garlic go chestnut and it will taste bitter.
Add the black beans and a splash of water, scraping the pan until the beans are glossy and hot; too much water turns the dish soupy instead of winter-thick.
Melt the remaining butter in a small pan, stir in the cassava flour and toast until it looks like damp golden sand; stop before it darkens past hazelnut or the farofa will taste scorched.
Spoon the beans and mushrooms into warm bowls, shower over the farofa, lime zest, lime juice and coriander; add the lime at the end or its brightness disappears into the heat.

note: Use the widest pan you own, or griddle the mushrooms in two batches for proper char.

name: Lahori Crisp Aloo Methi Parathas
hook: Flaky edges, spiced potato steam

ingredients.name: plain flour, plus extra for rolling
fresh fenugreek leaves or spinach, chopped

steps.t: Mix the flour with a pinch of salt and the warm water to make a soft dough, then knead until it springs back gently; if it feels dry now, the parathas will crack when stuffed.
Cover the dough while you cook the potatoes in salted water until a knife slides through without resistance; undercooked cubes tear holes through the bread.
Drain the potatoes very well, then mash with onion, chilli, fenugreek, cumin, coriander, turmeric, lemon juice and salt until rough but not wet; watery filling bursts in the pan.
Divide the dough and filling into four, flatten each dough ball, enclose the filling and pinch shut with no trapped air; air pockets puff, split and spill potato into the oil.
Roll each parcel gently to about 18 cm, dusting lightly; pressing hard at the edges pushes the filling out and leaves a thick raw rim.

Heat a thin film of oil in a frying pan until a pinch of flour sizzles softly, then shallow fry each paratha until the underside is blistered with crisp brown freckles; oil that is smoking scorches the flour before the centre warms.
Turn, drizzle a little more oil round the edge, and fry until both sides feel crisp under the spatula; stacking them too soon traps steam and steals the crunch.

note: Serve with achar and sweet milky tea for a proper savoury breakfast.

name: Saigon Pickled Mackerel Mango Plate
hook: Bright pickle over smoky silver fish

ingredients.name: firm green mango, cut into matchsticks
daikon or mooli, cut into matchsticks

steps.t: Stir the rice vinegar, sugar and a pinch of salt until the grains vanish; undissolved sugar leaves harsh sweet patches in the pickle.
Add mango, daikon, carrot and shallot, toss hard with your hands, and leave until the vegetables bend but still snap; leave them too long and the plate goes limp.
Whisk fish sauce, lime juice, chilli and 2 tablespoons of the pickling liquid into a sharp dressing; if it tastes flat now, the oily fish will smother it.
Flake the hot-smoked mackerel into generous pieces, checking carefully for pin bones; shredding it too finely makes it look like leftovers rather than a guest dish.
Drain the pickles well and pat away the obvious drips; excess brine will flood the platter and dilute the dressing.
Layer herbs, pickles and mackerel on a wide plate, then spoon the dressing over just before serving; dressing too early dulls the herbs and softens the fish.
Finish with crushed peanuts and a few chilli rings, keeping the rim clean; messy edges make even a beautiful pickle look careless.

note: Hot-smoked mackerel gives richness without asking guests to navigate raw fish.

name: Amalfi Tofu Courgette Bake
hook: Lemon-slick courgettes, soft basil tofu

ingredients.name: firm tofu, drained and patted dry

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C and put a shallow baking dish inside; starting in a cold dish makes the courgettes leak before they roast.
Tear the tofu into rough chunks and pat every face dry with kitchen paper; wet tofu tastes steamed and refuses to catch the lemon oil.

Toss courgettes, tomatoes, onion, garlic, oregano, capers, olive oil, lemon zest, salt and pepper in the hot dish until they hiss lightly; if nothing sizzles, the dish was not hot enough for a summer roast.
Nestle the tofu among the vegetables, keeping some pieces exposed; burying it completely leaves it pale and spongey.
Bake until the tomatoes split, the courgette edges wrinkle and the tofu corners turn faintly gold; pull it too soon and the bake will taste watery.
Scatter breadcrumbs over the top and bake until they are sandy-golden, not dark brown; burnt crumbs make the whole dish taste stale.
Rest for 5 minutes, then spoon over lemon juice and torn basil; adding basil in the oven turns it black and muddy.

note: Eat warm or at room temperature with bitter leaves and chilled white wine.

name: Nihari Lamb Shank Pinch Pots
hook: Silky spice, marrow-rich gravy

steps.t: Salt the lamb shanks, then brown them in hot ghee until the knobbly edges are deep walnut; pale meat gives a thin, boiled-tasting gravy.
Lift out the lamb, add the onions and cook until they slump and turn copper at the tips; rushing this leaves the braise sharp and oniony.
Stir in ginger and garlic until the raw sting disappears, then add flour, coriander, chilli, fennel and nutmeg; flour that is not cooked for a minute will taste dusty in the sauce.
Pour in the stock little by little, scraping the base until no spice paste is stuck; any paste left behind will catch during the long braise.
Return the lamb, cover with a tight lid and braise very gently until the meat can be teased from the bone with a spoon; a hard boil tightens the lamb instead of making it silky.
Lift the shanks out, skim the glossy fat you do not want, then simmer the gravy uncovered until it coats the back of a spoon; if it is thin, it will run straight off the small plates.
Pull the lamb into large flakes, fold it back through the gravy with a squeeze of lime, and serve in small warm bowls with extra lime wedges; shredding it to threads loses the luxurious bite.

note: Make it a day ahead if you can; the gravy sets richer and reheats beautifully.

name: Snowy Halloumi with Warm Thyme Honey
hook: Salty, glossy, winter-soft comfort

steps.t: Take the halloumi out of its packet, pat it dry and slice it 5 mm thick; if you leave it wet, the honey slides off and the plate turns briny.
Cut the peel and white pith from the oranges, then slice into rounds over the serving plate so the juice lands where you need it; leaving pith on makes the whole dish bitter.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until they smell warm and the skins look a shade darker; walk away and they turn acrid before they look burnt.
Warm the honey, olive oil and thyme in the same pan over low heat until loose and glossy, not bubbling hard; boiled honey tastes flat and sticky rather than floral.
Lay the raw halloumi over the oranges, tuck in the olives and walnuts, then spoon the warm thyme honey over while it is still runny; cold honey clumps and gives you sweet patches.
Finish with lemon zest and plenty of black pepper, then serve straight away while the cheese is cool and firm against the warm dressing.

note: Use good halloumi here: the dish depends on its squeaky saltiness rather than cooking technique.

name: Pul Biber Chickpea Breakfast Kavurma
hook: Hot pan, soft chickpeas, bright peppers

steps.t: Drain the chickpeas well and rub them dry in a tea towel; wet chickpeas steam, and you lose the nutty edges that make this breakfast worth it.
Heat a wide frying pan until a drop of water skitters, then add the oil, onion and pepper; if the pan is timid, the vegetables slump instead of catching at the tips.
Stir-fry hard until the onion edges bronze and the pepper skins blister in little shiny patches, keeping everything moving so the onion does not scorch black.
Add the tomato paste, pul biber and cumin, and smear them through the oil until the paste darkens to brick red; undercook it and the pan tastes metallic.
Tip in the chickpeas and stir-fry until they look drier, slightly wrinkled and stained red; if you crowd them in a small pan, cook in two batches or they will boil.
Add the grated tomatoes and salt, then toss until the tomato clings rather than pools at the bottom; too much liquid turns kavurma into stew.
Scatter with chopped parsley and eat hot with bread, scraping up the oily red bits before they harden on the pan.

note: A cast-iron or carbon-steel pan gives the best high-heat flavour, but any wide heavy pan works.

name: Za’atar Griddled Cod with Pomegranate Tahini
hook: Charred spice, silk sauce, jewelled crunch

steps.t: Pat the cod very dry and season it with salt, za’atar, 1 tablespoon of olive oil and a little lemon zest; damp fish sticks and tears before it ever gets impressive.
Whisk tahini, yoghurt, grated garlic, the juice of half the lemon and enough cold water to make a slow ribboning sauce; add water gradually or it will go thin and chalky.
Heat a ridged griddle pan until it is properly hot and faintly smoking, then oil the ridges lightly; a lukewarm griddle gives grey fish and no char lines.
Lay the cod on the griddle and do not prod it until the underside releases and the spice crust smells toasted; moving it early rips off the best bit.
Turn with a thin fish slice and cook until the flakes just separate under gentle pressure and the centre is opaque, not dry and splitting wide open.
Spoon the tahini sauce onto a platter, set the cod on top, then finish with pomegranate seeds, torn mint, the remaining olive oil and a squeeze of lemon.

note: Cod loin is easier for guests because the thick pieces cook evenly and hold their shape.

name: Crisp Chermoula Oyster Mushrooms
hook: Lacy mushrooms, cool cucumber, green spice

steps.t: Tear the oyster mushrooms into broad strips, keeping some frilly edges; chopping them too small makes them fry into crumbs rather than crisp pieces.
Mix the flour with cumin, paprika, coriander and salt, then toss the mushrooms lightly and shake off the excess; thick flour pockets turn pasty in the oil.
Grate the cucumber, squeeze it firmly, then mix with lemon juice, chopped coriander, grated garlic and a pinch of salt; unsqueezed cucumber floods the plate.
Heat the sunflower oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of flour sizzles instantly, then add the mushrooms in a single loose layer; crowding drops the heat and makes them leathery.
Shallow fry until the undersides are crisp and lace-golden, then turn once; constant turning knocks off the coating and greases the mushrooms.
Lift onto kitchen paper and salt while hot, when the surface is still tacky enough to hold seasoning.
Spread the cucumber chermoula on a platter and pile the mushrooms over it just before serving; if they sit on the wet dressing, the crunch disappears.

note: Oyster mushrooms stay lighter than button mushrooms because their frilled edges crisp quickly.

name: Seville Escabeche Beef with Peppers
hook: Sharp vinegar, rosy beef, smoky oil

steps.t: Season the steak generously and leave it at room temperature while you slice the vegetables; fridge-cold beef overcooks at the edges before the middle warms.
Sear the steak in 1 tablespoon of hot olive oil until a dark crust forms on both sides and the centre is still springy; pale steak tastes boiled once it meets vinegar.
Rest the steak on a board so the juices settle; slice too soon and the dressing turns muddy with meat juices.
Lower the heat, add the remaining olive oil, pepper and onion, and cook until just softened but still bright; take them too far and the pickle feels heavy.
Stir in sherry vinegar, smoked paprika, bay leaf, sugar and a pinch of salt, simmering until the vinegar smells sharp but not raw in the throat.
Slice the rested beef thinly across the grain; cutting with the grain makes even good steak chewy on a tapas fork.
Layer the beef with the warm escabeche vegetables, capers and parsley, then leave for 10 minutes so the edges pickle lightly while the centre stays rosy.
Serve at room temperature with the smoky vinegar oil spooned over the top; fridge-cold beef tastes dull and waxy.

note: This is designed for sharing, so the beef is lightly pickled rather than submerged for days.

name: Ginger Coconut Steamed Mussels with Dill Rice
hook: Briny shells in soft winter steam

ingredients.name: fresh ginger, cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water is only faintly cloudy, then cook with 220 ml water and a pinch of salt; unrinsed rice turns gluey and heavy under the mussels.
While it cooks, check the mussels: discard cracked shells and any open ones that do not close when tapped, because dead mussels are not worth the risk.
Set a wide lidded pan over medium heat with a spoonful of coconut milk, then add ginger, garlic and chilli until the garlic smells sweet but has not browned; burnt garlic will make the broth harsh.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and fish sauce, bring to a firm simmer, then add the mussels and clamp on the lid; a lazy simmer will steam them unevenly.
Shake the pan once or twice until the shells gape wide and the mussels look plump; throw away any that stay shut, rather than forcing them open.
Fold dill and spring onions through the hot rice, then spoon into deep bowls before it clumps; cold rice will drink the broth instead of cushioning it.
Finish the mussel broth with lime juice, taste for salt, and ladle shells and coconut steam over the rice while everything is still roaring hot.

note: A winter-leaning Vietnamese bowl built around mussels, coconut, ginger and dill.

name: Coal-Grilled Halloumi Breakfast Piadina
hook: Smoke, salt, yolk-soft tomato

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are mostly grey with a steady red glow; flames will scorch the halloumi before the centre softens.
Toss the tomatoes with olive oil, vinegar, oregano and a pinch of salt in a small foil tray; too much vinegar makes them wet rather than jammy.
Grill the tomato tray at the cooler edge until the skins split and the juices turn syrupy at the corners.
Put the halloumi directly over the hot coals and turn once when the bars are dark and the edges sag slightly; move it too early and it tears, too late and it toughens.
Warm the piadine briefly on the grill until bendy and smoke-marked; if they crisp fully, they will crack when folded.
Fry the eggs in a small pan on the grill or hob until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble; underdone whites make the whole breakfast slippery.
Pile rocket, tomatoes, halloumi and eggs onto the warm piadine, squeeze over lemon and fold while the cheese is still squeaky-hot.

note: Italian in spirit, with breakfast built around smoke, tomato and salty grilled halloumi.

name: Lime-Cured Sea Bass Chutney Chaat
hook: Cool fish, sharp chutney, crisp sev

ingredients.name: sashimi-grade sea bass fillet, skinless and pin-boned

steps.t: Chill your serving plates and keep the fish cold; warm raw fish loses its clean texture and smells tired fast.
Slice the sea bass across the grain into 5 mm pieces with one long stroke of the knife; sawing ragged edges makes the cure grab unevenly.
Stir lime juice, salt, sugar and chilli, then spoon over the fish in a shallow dish so every slice is glossy, not drowning.
Leave until the edges turn opaque white but the centres still look pearly; take it too far and the sea bass becomes chalky.
Blend coriander, mint, yoghurt and crushed cumin into a pale green chutney; if it sits too long, the herbs dull and the yoghurt weeps.
Lift the fish from the cure and blot lightly on kitchen paper; plating it wet will flood the chutney and soften the crunch.
Swipe chutney onto cold plates, lay on the cured bass, then finish with red onion and sev at the last second so the crisp bits stay crisp.

note: Use only fish sold for raw consumption, and keep it refrigerated until curing.

name: Wok-Kissed Egg and Basil Larb
hook: Frilly egg, lime heat, soft herbs

ingredients.name: palm sugar or light brown sugar

steps.t: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt just until streak-free; overbeating makes them foamy and dry in the wok.
Mix lime juice, fish sauce and sugar until the grains disappear; undissolved sugar gives random sweet bites rather than balance.
Heat the wok until a drop of water skitters away instantly, then add oil; a timid wok makes pale scrambled egg, not frilly edges.
Pour in the eggs and push them out into a thin sheet, letting the edges puff and blister before folding; stirring too soon turns them into curds.
Add shallot and chilli, toss hard for just long enough to take the raw edge off; if the shallot collapses, the plate stops feeling summery.
Take the wok off the heat, splash in the dressing and scatter over toasted rice powder; cooking the lime dressing makes it bitter and flat.
Tumble through basil and mint, then serve with cucumber while the egg is warm and the herbs are still standing up.

note: A light Thai-style egg larb where high heat gives the eggs texture without heaviness.

name: Miso-Butter Griddled Kabocha with Sesame Salt
hook: Sweet squash, charred edges, nutty salt

ingredients.name: kabocha or crown prince squash, deseeded and cut into 1 cm wedges

steps.t: Steam or microwave the squash wedges until a knife meets slight resistance at the centre; fully soft squash collapses on the griddle.
Mash miso, butter and mirin into a smooth paste; lumps of miso catch and burn before the squash chars.
Heat a ridged griddle until it smokes lightly, then oil the squash rather than the pan; oil in the grooves burns and tastes dirty.
Lay the wedges down with space between them and press gently until the ridges mark dark lines and the edges smell caramel-sweet.
Turn once and brush the cooked side thinly with miso butter; coating too early glues the squash to the pan.
Crush sesame seeds with flaky salt, stopping while some seeds stay whole; grinding to a paste loses the little pops of nuttiness.
Arrange the squash on a shared plate, flick with rice vinegar, then finish with sesame salt and spring onions so the rich glaze stays lively.

note: A vegetable-led Japanese small plate, made for passing around with other dishes.

name: Crackle Gochugaru Cod Jeon
hook: Lacy edges, soft pearly fish

steps.t: Cut the fish into 4 cm pieces and pat them dry until the paper comes away almost clean; wet fish steams inside the coating and the crust slides off.
Whisk flour, cornflour, egg, gochugaru, salt and 60 ml cold water to a thin cream, then fold in half the spring onions; a thick batter turns bready instead of crisp.
Stir soy, rice vinegar, honey and the remaining spring onions in a small bowl; if you leave this until after frying, the fish cools while you fiddle.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a drip of batter fizzes hard and floats straight back up; if it only sighs, the fish will drink oil.
Dip the fish, let excess batter fall back, then fry in one uncrowded layer until the undersides are lace-brown and set.
Turn once and fry until the second side crackles when tapped and the fish flakes cleanly; constant turning knocks off the fragile crust.
Drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, then spoon over a little dipping sauce at the table; piling the pieces traps steam and softens the edges.

note: Use any firm white fish, but avoid very thin fillets as they overcook before the coating crisps.

name: Black Vinegar Weekend Mushrooms
hook: Cool, chewy, electric with ginger

ingredients.name: mixed mushrooms, such as shiitake, oyster and wood ear

steps.t: Trim the mushrooms and tear large caps into bite-sized pieces, keeping them chunky; slices that are too thin collapse into a slippery tangle after pickling.
Blanch the mushrooms in a large pan of boiling water until they darken, soften and smell nutty rather than raw; undercooked mushrooms stay squeaky and resist the pickle.
Drain very well, then spread on a tray until no steam is rising; hot, wet mushrooms dilute the brine and turn the jar cloudy.
Bring vinegar, soy, sugar, salt, ginger, garlic, Sichuan pepper and chilli flakes just to a simmer, stirring until the grains disappear; a hard boil drives off the vinegar’s lift.
Pack mushrooms into a clean jar, pour over the warm brine so everything is submerged, cool, then refrigerate; exposed pieces dry out instead of pickling.
Leave for two days, turning the jar whenever you pass the fridge; rushing it gives seasoned outsides and bland centres.
Drain what you need, dress with sesame oil, spring onions and coriander, and serve cold; drowning it in brine at the table makes the dressing harsh.

note: This is a refrigerator pickle, not a shelf-stable preserve; keep chilled and eat within one week.

name: Chipotle Beef Fridge Bake
hook: Molten beans, beef, clean heat

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan and put the beef in a deep baking dish, spreading it out thinly; a mound of mince steams grey instead of browning.
Bake the beef until the top has browned patches and there is sizzling fat at the edges, then break it up with a spoon; stirring too early gives you boiled crumbs.
Mix in onion, garlic, chipotle paste and cumin until the beef is stained brick-red; dry spices left on the surface scorch bitterly in the oven.
Stir in tomatoes, black beans, rice and sweetcorn, scraping the corners so no plain rice is hiding there; unmixed pockets bake dry and chalky.
