Level the mixture, cover tightly with foil and bake until it bubbles steadily in the centre, not just around the sides.
Remove the foil, scatter over cheddar and bake until the cheese blisters and the tomato edges look thick and jammy; taking it out pale makes it watery on the plate.
Rest for 5 minutes, then serve with yoghurt and lime squeezed over; cutting straight in sends the juices running across the dish.

note: Built for meal prep: cool portions quickly and refrigerate for up to three days.

name: Mastiha Honey Egg Clouds
hook: Silky custard, thyme-honey shine

steps.t: Warm the milk with sugar, lemon zest, mastiha and salt until steaming and the sugar has dissolved; boiling it makes the eggs taste cooked before they are even mixed.
Let the milk cool until it feels warm, not hot, on a fingertip, then remove the zest; hot milk scrambles the eggs into flecks.
Beat the eggs gently in a jug, then whisk in the warm milk without making a foam; bubbles steam into pockmarks instead of a glassy surface.
Strain into four small heatproof bowls and cover each tightly with foil; unstrained chalazae and uncovered drips both ruin the silkiness.
Set the bowls in a steamer over barely simmering water and steam until the centres wobble like soft jelly; a rolling boil makes tunnels and rubbery edges.
Turn off the heat and leave the covered custards in the steamer so the centres finish softly; lifting them out at once can leave a loose puddle underneath.
Spoon over thyme honey and pistachios while just warm or chilled; adding nuts too early makes them leathery.

note: Mastiha gives a Greek resinous lift, but vanilla keeps the dessert easy to shop for.

name: Tomato Pepper Tofu Yahni
hook: Soft tofu in oily red comfort

steps.t: Press the tofu between plates while you chop the vegetables, then tear it into rough chunks; wet cubes shed water into the stew and taste blank inside.
Heat the oil in a saucepan and cook onion and pepper until the onion is floppy and sweet at the edges; rushing this leaves the stew sharp and thin.
Add garlic, tomato paste and pul biber, stirring until the paste darkens to rusty red and sticks slightly; if it stays raw, the sauce tastes tinny.
Stir in tomatoes, potatoes and stock, scraping the base clean; paste left on the bottom catches and turns bitter.
Simmer with the lid ajar until the potato edges round off and a knife slides in without crunch; boiling hard breaks the potatoes before they thicken the stew.
Fold in the tofu and simmer gently until the chunks are stained red and hot through; aggressive stirring crumbles them into curds.
Finish with parsley and lemon juice, then rest 2 minutes before eating; skipping the acid makes the cheap tomatoes taste flat.

note: Serve with bread, rice or bulgur if you need to stretch it further.

name: Provençal Mackerel Bean Bake
hook: Tomato juices, salty olives, crisp fish

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Use a wide roasting dish, not a cramped one; if the tomatoes sit in a deep pile they stew instead of blistering.
In the dish, toss the beans, tomatoes, fennel, garlic, olives, capers, olive oil, lemon zest, salt and black pepper. Spread everything to the corners so the fennel edges can catch.
Bake until the tomato skins split and the fennel tips look lightly singed, not pale and floppy.
Pat the mackerel dry, then lay it skin-side up on the hot vegetables. If the skin is wet or buried in sauce, it will turn rubbery rather than crisp.
Bake until the skin is taut and lace-gold at the edges and the thickest part flakes under a fork; leave it longer and oily fish turns cottony fast.
Squeeze over lemon juice and scatter with parsley. Spoon the bean juices around the fish, not over the skin, so the crisp top stays crisp.

note: Fast, briny and very French in spirit: everything bakes in one dish while the mackerel oils season the beans.

name: Hickory Molasses Braised Tofu and Beans
hook: Sticky edges, smoky beans, deep patience

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in a clean tea towel, weight it with a pan and press until it feels firm rather than spongey; skip this and the braise tastes watery.
Cut the tofu into thick slabs. Sear in oil in a heavy casserole until the faces are nut-brown and dry to the touch; pale tofu will shed water into the sauce.
Lift out the tofu. Add the onion and cook until it smells sweet and the edges turn amber; rushing this leaves the sauce sharp and raw.
Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika, mustard, molasses and cider vinegar. Let it bubble until glossy, because unboiled vinegar sits harshly on top of the braise.
Add passata, stock, beans and liquid smoke, then return the tofu in a single layer. The slabs should be mostly covered; exposed tofu dries before it absorbs flavour.
Cover and braise in a 150°C oven until the sauce is dark and the tofu yields like slow-cooked meat when pressed with a spoon.
Uncover and cook until the top is tacky and the beans are thickly lacquered, then rest before serving; straight from the oven it tastes flatter and burns mouths.

note: A barbecue-house style weekend tofu braise: low, slow and smoky without pretending to be meat.

name: Chimichurri Lamb Lentil Guiso
hook: Lean lamb, earthy lentils, sharp herbs

steps.t: Pat the lamb dry and salt it. Brown it in the oil in a wide casserole until the corners form a dark crust; crowded, damp lamb boils grey and tastes thin.
Add the onion to the same pan and cook until it softens into the lamb fat and turns golden at the edges, scraping up the browned bits before they burn.
Stir in the garlic, tomato purée, paprika and cumin until the purée darkens brick-red; if it stays raw and bright, the stew will taste tinny.
Pour in the stock and return the lamb. Simmer gently, with only lazy bubbles breaking the surface, until the meat starts to soften; a hard boil tightens lean lamb.
Add the lentils and squash. Keep simmering until the lentils are tender but still hold their shape and the squash thickens the broth at the edges.
Check the lamb by pressing a cube against the side of the pan; it should split with a spoon, not spring back.
Stir parsley with red wine vinegar, then fold most of it through the guiso and spoon the rest on top. Add it at the end, or the herbs turn khaki and dull.

note: Built for protein without heaviness: lamb, lentils and a bright chimichurri-style finish.

name: Silky Brazilian Pudim with Burnt Caramel
hook: Cool custard under bitter caramel

steps.t: Put the sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the caramel is deep amber and smells toasty; pale caramel tastes flat, black caramel tastes acrid.
Immediately pour the caramel into a 20cm ring mould or pudding basin and tilt to coat the base. Work quickly, because caramel sets hard as soon as it cools.
Blend the eggs, condensed milk, whole milk, vanilla and salt just until smooth. Do not whip it foamy, or the pudim will steam with little bubbles instead of a satin texture.
Strain the custard into the caramel-lined mould, then cover tightly with foil. Loose foil lets condensed steam drip in and pockmark the top.
Set the mould on a trivet in a large covered pan with simmering water halfway up the sides. Steam gently, not furiously, until the edges are set and the centre wobbles like soft jelly.
Lift out and cool until the mould is no longer hot, then chill thoroughly; unmoulding warm pudim makes it slump and tear.
Run a thin knife around the edge, dip the base briefly in warm water and invert onto a lipped plate so the caramel pours over the custard, not onto the worktop.

note: Classic Brazilian pudim is an egg custard dessert steamed low and slow, then served cold.

name: Dhungar Chicken Chana Rice
hook: Charcoal smoke over spiced student comfort

steps.t: Put the rice on to cook by your usual absorption method; if it finishes early, keep it covered so the grains steam dry instead of turning claggy.
Fry the onion in the oil in a lidded pan until the edges are deep gold. Stop at pale yellow and the curry will taste sweet but flat; go black and it will taste bitter.
Add the chicken, garlic-ginger paste, garam masala, chilli powder and salt. Stir until the chicken loses its raw shine and the spices cling to the oil, not the pan.
Add tomatoes and chickpeas, then simmer with the lid slightly ajar until the sauce thickens and the chicken is fully cooked through with no pink centre.
Turn the heat low and stir in the yoghurt a spoonful at a time. If the sauce is boiling hard, the yoghurt splits into grainy flecks.

Heat the charcoal until glowing and grey at the edges. Sit a small foil cup on top of the cooked curry, place the coal in it, spoon over a few drops of oil and cover fast; the smoke should season the food, not leave ash in it.
Remove the foil cup and charcoal, stir through coriander and serve over the rice. Do not leave the coal in the pan, or the smoke turns harsh and sooty.

note: Dhungar gives a cheap chicken-and-chickpea pan the smoky aroma of a much longer cook.

name: Black Cardamom Beef Nihari
hook: Slow, dark gravy for icy nights

ingredients.name: beef shin, cut into large chunks

steps.t: Heat the ghee in a heavy casserole and fry the onions over a medium heat until they collapse into deep bronze strands; stop at tan and the gravy will taste flat, push to black and it will turn bitter.
Add the beef shin and turn the pieces until the outside loses its raw red sheen; if the pan is crowded and watery, fry in two batches or the meat will stew before it has any roasted flavour.
Stir in ginger, garlic, flour, coriander, chilli, fennel and black cardamom for one minute, scraping the base; if the spices sit dry and catch, splash in a spoonful of stock before they scorch.
Pour in the stock, bring to a quiet bubble, then cover with the lid slightly ajar; a hard boil will tighten the beef before the collagen melts.
Braise gently until the shin gives way when pressed with a spoon and the sauce looks glossy rather than dusty, stirring every so often so the flour-thickened base does not stick.

Lift out the cardamom pods, shred a few pieces of beef back into the gravy, and simmer uncovered until it coats the back of a spoon; leave it thin and it will eat like soup, reduce too far and it will salt up.
Rest off the heat for ten minutes, then serve with lemon wedges; serving it straight from the boil hides the spice and burns the tongue before the richness lands.

note: Best with naan or basmati rice, and even better reheated the next day.

name: Coconut Chilli Egg Khai Palo Stew
hook: Jammy eggs in fragrant morning broth

ingredients.name: palm sugar or light brown sugar

steps.t: Lower the eggs into simmering water and cook until the yolks are softly set; guessing here gives either chalky centres or whites too fragile for the stew.
Cool the eggs under cold running water, peel carefully and set aside; peel them hot and you will tear craters into the whites that leak yolk later.
Warm the oil in a small saucepan and fry shallots until their edges turn golden and papery, then add garlic; if garlic goes in first, it burns before the shallots sweeten.
Stir in the curry paste until the oil stains red and smells rounded rather than raw; undercooked paste tastes harsh even after simmering.
Add coconut milk, stock, fish sauce and sugar, then simmer gently until the surface trembles and the broth tastes joined-up; boiling hard can split the coconut milk into greasy flecks.
Add tomatoes and the peeled eggs, simmering just until the tomatoes slump and the eggs warm through; too long here turns the yolks grey at the edge.
Fold in spinach until just wilted, squeeze in lime to sharpen the broth, and serve in bowls; if the greens cook to khaki, the breakfast loses its lift.

note: Serve with jasmine rice or toast for a breakfast that feels generous without being heavy.

name: Miso-Lacquered Whole Tofu with Ginger Leeks
hook: A golden centrepiece, soft as custard

ingredients.name: firm tofu, in one large block if possible

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in a clean tea towel, set it on a plate and weight it lightly until it feels firmer and sheds a shallow puddle; skip this and the glaze slides off into the tray.
Heat the oven to 220°C fan and line a roasting tin with baking paper; without lining, the miso sugars weld themselves to the metal.
Whisk miso, mirin, soy, sesame oil, vinegar and ginger into a smooth paste, pressing out lumps; lumps scorch in bitter freckles while the rest stays pale.
Put leeks and shiitake in the tin, set the tofu whole on top, and brush it all over with half the glaze; keep the coating thin or it burns before the tofu heats through.
Roast until the tofu edges begin to bronze and the leeks soften at their cut faces; if the vegetables are piled under the tofu, they steam instead of sweetening.
Brush on the remaining glaze and roast again until the top is lacquered, chestnut-gold and lightly blistered; leave it too long after this point and miso turns acrid fast.
Rest for five minutes, scatter with sesame seeds and spring onions, then carry it to the table whole; cutting too soon makes the block slump and weep.

note: Slice with a broad knife at the table and spoon the roasted leeks and mushrooms around it.

name: Smoked Lamb Ssam with Watermelon Radish
hook: Cool leaves, smoke and bright crunch

ingredients.name: boneless lamb leg steak or thick lamb rump
watermelon radish or breakfast radishes, thinly sliced

steps.t: Mix gochujang, soy, vinegar, sesame oil, honey and garlic, then rub two-thirds over the lamb; if the marinade is left in thick clumps, the sugar burns rather than glazing.
Leave the lamb at room temperature while you set up a covered barbecue or smoker for indirect heat at about 120°C; putting fridge-cold lamb into smoke gives a grey band before the centre warms.
Smoke the lamb away from the coals until the outside is mahogany and the centre reaches 58°C for pink; relying on colour alone is risky because smoke darkens the crust early.
Brush with the remaining marinade for the last few minutes only; add it too early and the honey-blackened edges taste burnt, not smoky.
Rest the lamb loosely covered until the juices settle and the surface stops hissing; slicing straight away floods the board and leaves the meat dry.
Slice thinly across the grain, watching for the muscle lines and cutting across them; cut with the grain and even good lamb eats stringy.
Arrange lettuce, radish, cucumber, mint, sesame and lamb on a cool platter; overloading each leaf hides the fresh crunch that makes this a summer plate.

note: If using a kettle barbecue, add one small chunk of fruit wood and keep the smoke pale, not billowing.

name: Steamed Garlic Black Bean Chickpeas
hook: Glossy little bites for chopsticks

ingredients.name: fermented black beans, rinsed and chopped

steps.t: Put a steamer on to boil with enough water that it will not run dry; a sputtering dry pan gives the chickpeas a scorched, metallic taste.
Toss chickpeas with black beans, garlic, ginger, soy, Shaoxing wine, sugar, cornflour and oil in a shallow heatproof dish; if the cornflour stays in white clumps, the sauce will set gluey in patches.
Spread the chickpeas in a single shallow layer so steam can move through them; a deep mound heats unevenly and leaves the centre tasting tinny.
Steam over a lively boil until the chickpeas are hot all the way through and the black bean sauce turns glossy at the edges of the dish.
Stir once from the outside in, then steam briefly again so the sauce coats rather than pools; skipping this leaves the top dry and the bottom over-salty.
Finish with spring onions and a thin ribbon of chilli oil while still steaming; add them before steaming and the onion dulls to a tired, boiled flavour.

note: Serve as one of several small plates with greens, rice rolls or steamed fish.

name: Coal-Kissed Lime Achiote Chicken Tacos
hook: Smoke, citrus, chilli, crisp cabbage

steps.t: Light a small chimney of charcoal first; if you start cooking over black coals the chicken tastes sooty instead of smoky.
Mash the achiote, lime juice, oil, garlic, cumin and salt into a loose brick-red paste, then coat the chicken thoroughly; dry patches scorch before the meat cooks.
Tip the cabbage and coriander together with a pinch of salt and a squeeze from the spent lime halves; unsalted cabbage stays squeaky and flat.
Grill the chicken over glowing coals, turning when the underside has dark grill bars and releases without tearing; move pieces away from flare-ups or the paste will burn bitter.
Check the thickest piece is piping hot with clear juices, or 74°C on a probe; guessing with thigh meat is how you serve pink centres.
Rest the chicken on a warm plate so the juices settle; slice too soon and the board gets the sauce instead of the tacos.
Warm the tortillas directly on the grill until spotted and flexible, then fill with sliced chicken and cabbage; cold tortillas crack before the first bite.

note: A fast charcoal dinner works best with a small, very hot fire rather than a full barbecue load.

name: Ouzo-Lime Barely Poached Prawn Plate
hook: Chilled prawns, anise, sharp herbs

steps.t: Peel and devein the prawns, keeping the shells; leaving the dark vein in makes a supposedly clean plate taste muddy.
Simmer the shells with 500ml water, half the ouzo and half the salt until the liquid smells sweet and marine, not raw and tinny.
Strain the stock, bring it back to a lively simmer, then slide in the prawns for a brief poach until they curl into loose Cs and turn just opaque; tight rings mean rubber.
Lift the prawns straight into a tray over ice, then chill them uncovered; if they sit in hot liquor they keep cooking past tender.
Toss fennel and cucumber with vinegar, lemon juice and the remaining salt, then weight lightly so they slump but still snap; drowning them makes salad, not pickles.
Whisk lime zest, lime juice, olive oil and the remaining ouzo until glossy, then taste for salt; raw spirit without citrus tastes harsh.
Fold the chilled prawns through the dressing with dill and mint, and leave in the fridge until cold all the way through; warm shellfish dulls the anise and feels heavy.
Serve the prawns over the drained fennel and cucumber with a spoonful of the dressing; piling on the pickle liquid washes out the ouzo.

note: Keep the prawns refrigerated after poaching and serve the same day; this is barely cooked, not raw.

name: High-Heat Hellim Pepper Sac Tava
hook: Salty cheese, charred peppers, hot pan

steps.t: Pat the halloumi very dry; wet cheese steams and squeaks instead of taking on a bronze crust.
Heat a wide wok or sauté pan until a drop of water skitters and vanishes; a polite pan will make the vegetables leak juice.
Add the oil and halloumi in one layer, then leave it alone until the undersides freckle deep gold; stirring early tears the crust off.
Flip the halloumi onto a plate, then throw peppers and onion into the same hot pan; if the pan looks crowded, cook in two goes or you will boil them.
Add garlic, tomato paste and pul biber, smearing the paste against the metal until it darkens brick-red; pale paste tastes sweet and raw.
Toss in the chickpeas until their skins blister in spots, then return the halloumi only to heat through; overcooked halloumi tightens and turns leathery.
Finish with parsley and lemon off the heat; adding them early kills the green lift you need against the salty cheese.

note: Plenty of protein without feeling like a plain meal-prep bowl.

name: Rose Cardamom Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Silky wobble, floral syrup, pistachio crunch

steps.t: Set a steamer over a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil; violent steam makes custard pockmarked and eggy.
Warm the milk, cream, sugar, cardamom and salt until the sugar dissolves and the mixture feels hot but not scalding; boiling it will scramble the eggs on contact.
Whisk the eggs just until no streaks remain, then slowly pour in the warm dairy while whisking; dump it in fast and you get sweet scrambled egg.
Stir in the orange blossom water, then strain into four small heatproof bowls; unstrained chalazae and spice clumps ruin the silk.
Cover each bowl tightly with foil and steam gently until the centres wobble like set jelly, not liquid milk; uncovered bowls collect drips that crater the tops.
Rest the custards off the heat so the carry-over heat finishes the centre; spooning them immediately makes them slump and weep.
Drizzle with rose syrup and scatter pistachios just before serving; add nuts too early and they soften into the surface.

note: Serve warm after dinner, or chill for a firmer, cleaner cut.

name: Crisp Harissa Fried Eggs on Msemen Crisps
hook: Runny yolks, fiery edges, flaky bread

steps.t: Tear the msemen into big shards; neat little pieces brown too quickly and taste like burnt crackers.
Heat half the oil in a frying pan and fry the bread until the layers blister and the corners turn crisp mahogany; soft bread underneath will sag under the eggs.
Stir harissa, cumin, paprika, garlic, lemon juice and a pinch of salt in a cup; adding dry spices straight to the pan makes gritty hot spots.
Add the remaining oil to the pan and heat until it shimmers, then spoon in the harissa mix and let it foam dark red; cold oil gives greasy eggs with no lace.
Crack the eggs in one at a time, spooning the spiced oil over the whites until the edges frill and crisp while the yolks stay glossy; blast the yolks with oil and they turn chalky.
Slide the crisp bread onto plates and lift the eggs on top, leaving excess oil behind; pouring it all over makes the bread heavy.
Finish with coriander and a squeeze more lemon if needed; without the fresh hit the harissa tastes flat and salty.

note: Cheap, fast and filling, especially with yesterday’s flatbread.

name: Date-Molasses Whole Lamb Shoulder
hook: Sticky spice, falling lamb, winter warmth

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the lamb very dry and slash the fat in shallow diamonds; wet skin steams instead of roasting and the spice paste slides off.
Mix the oil, cumin, coriander, cinnamon, garlic, 1½ teaspoons salt and plenty of black pepper, then rub it into every cut. If the paste sits only on top, the meat underneath tastes flat.
Spread the onions, carrots and chickpeas in a deep roasting tin, pour in the stock, then set the lamb on top fat-side up. Keep the liquid below the fat cap or you will boil the surface pale.
Cover tightly with baking paper and foil, then roast until a fork twists easily in the thickest part and the onions have collapsed into the stock.
Uncover, spoon over the date molasses and return to the oven until the shoulder is lacquered dark mahogany at the edges; pull it earlier and the glaze tastes sugary rather than roasted.
Rest the lamb loosely covered so the juices settle back into the fibres; carve too soon and the board gets the sauce, not the meat.
Skim excess fat from the roasting tin, crush some chickpeas into the juices to thicken them, then shower the lamb with torn mint at the table. The mint goes on last, or it bruises black in the heat.

note: Serve with warm flatbreads or buttery rice for a proper cold-night centrepiece.

name: Harissa Smoked Pork Breakfast Skillet
hook: Crisp potatoes, smoky pork, molten yolks

ingredients.name: waxy potatoes, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: Simmer the potato cubes in salted water until the corners just give to a knife; take them further and they break into mash when they hit the pan.
Drain the potatoes well and let them steam dry in the colander. If they go into the skillet wet, the pork fat spits and the edges stay waxy.
Fry the smoked pork belly in the olive oil over a medium heat until the fat runs clear and the edges look bronze and crisp, not merely grey.
Add the onion and pepper and cook until the onion is sweet and floppy; rushing this leaves a raw onion bite under the spices.

Stir in the potatoes, chickpeas, ras el hanout and harissa, pressing the potatoes against the pan until patches turn crusty. Add the tomatoes only after the spice smells toasted, or it will taste dusty.
Spoon in the tomatoes, bubble until thick enough to leave a trail, then make four hollows and crack in the eggs. Cover and cook until the whites set but the yolks still wobble.
Finish with coriander and a squeeze of lemon. The acid matters here; without it the smoke and pork fat sit heavy at breakfast.

note: Moroccan-spiced rather than traditional; the smoked pork makes it unapologetically brunchy.

name: Saffron-Steam Chicken with Clams
hook: Sherry steam, golden chicken, briny clams

steps.t: Check the clams: discard any cracked ones, and any open ones that do not close when tapped. A dead clam can ruin the whole pot.
Season the chicken well and set it skin-side down in a wide lidded pan over a medium heat until the skin releases its own fat and turns deep gold. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
Lift the chicken out and soften the shallots and garlic in the chicken fat until glossy, not brown; burnt garlic will make the saffron steam bitter.
Crumble in the saffron, pour in the sherry and let it boil hard until the sharp alcohol smell fades. If you skip this, the sauce tastes raw and boozy.
Add the stock and peppers, return the chicken skin-side up, cover tightly and steam at a gentle bubble until the thickest thigh reaches 75°C and the juices run clear.
Scatter in the clams and peas, cover again and steam until the clams spring open and the peas are bright green. Discard any clams that stay shut.
Transfer to a warmed platter, spoon over the saffron liquor, then finish with almonds, parsley and lemon. Add the nuts at the end so they stay crisp against the soft steamed chicken.

note: Bring the whole pan to the table and lift the lid there; the saffron and sherry steam does the theatre.

name: Coal-Grilled Langoustines with Pastis Fennel
hook: Sweet shells, anise smoke, lemon brightness

steps.t: Light the barbecue and wait until the coals are ashed over and glowing, not flaming. Flames scorch shells before the meat turns pearly.
Split the langoustines lengthways with a heavy knife and remove the dark vein. Wipe, don’t rinse, or water pools in the shell and dulls the grill heat.
Mix the butter with pastis, garlic, half the herbs and a pinch of salt. Keep it soft rather than melted; melted butter runs straight through the shells into the coals.
Toss the fennel with olive oil, lemon juice and a little salt, then spread it on the platter. Dress it early enough to bend but not so early that it collapses.
Set the langoustines shell-side down over the coals and dot the flesh with the pastis butter. Cook until the flesh turns opaque at the edges and just firm at the tail.
Turn them flesh-side down for a brief kiss of smoke, no longer than needed for light grill marks. Leave them there and the sweet meat tightens like rubber.
Pile the hot langoustines over the fennel and finish with the remaining herbs, lemon wedges and flaky salt. Serve at once while the shell heat is still perfuming the fennel.

note: If buying frozen langoustines, thaw overnight in the fridge and pat them very dry before grilling.

name: Buffalo Halloumi Watermelon Bites
hook: Cold crunch, hot sauce, salty cheese

ingredients.name: pasteurised halloumi, cut into 2 cm cubes
seedless watermelon, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: Chill a serving plate before you start. Warm watermelon sheds juice fast on a room-temperature plate and makes the cheese slide around.
Cube the halloumi and watermelon to the same size, then pat both dry. Surface moisture thins the Buffalo glaze and turns the bites slippery.
Warm the hot sauce, butter, honey and vinegar in a small pan just until glossy and combined; do not boil it, or the butter splits into an oily slick.
Let the sauce cool until warm rather than hot, then toss it with the halloumi only. If the sauce is too hot, the raw halloumi sweats and loses its clean salty bite.
Thread watermelon, Buffalo halloumi and celery onto cocktail sticks, keeping the watermelon at the bottom so the juiciest piece anchors each bite.
Arrange on the cold plate and scatter with blue cheese and spring onions. Add these last, or the blue cheese smears into the glaze instead of landing in sharp little hits.

note: Use pasteurised halloumi because this is served uncooked, with only a warm Buffalo glaze.

name: High-Heat Chimichurri Pork with Charred Peppers
hook: charred peppers, garlic vinegar, juicy pork

ingredients.name: pork tenderloin, cut into thin strips

steps.t: Pat the pork very dry, then toss with smoked paprika, half the garlic, 1 tbsp oil and a firm pinch of salt. If it goes into the pan wet, it will steam grey instead of catching at the edges.
Stir parsley, oregano, vinegar, remaining garlic and 1 tbsp oil into a sharp chimichurri. Keep it raw and bright; cooking it now would flatten the green, grassy bite.
Heat a wide frying pan or wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add the last 1 tbsp oil. If the pan is only warm, the pork will leak juice before it browns.
Stir-fry the pork in one loose layer until the edges are browned and the centres are just cooked through with no raw pink. Work in two batches if needed, because crowding gives you boiled strips.

Tip the pork onto a plate, then throw in the pepper, onion and potato. Let them sit between tosses until the pepper skins blister and the potato faces turn bronze; constant stirring stops the char forming.

Return the pork and any resting juices, toss for 30 seconds, then take the pan off the heat and spoon over the chimichurri. Leaving it on the burner after the herbs go in makes the vinegar harsh and the pork tight.

note: Serve straight from the pan with extra vinegar at the table if you like it sharper.

name: Weekend Tapioca Beiju with Coalho Eggs
hook: chewy tapioca, salty cheese, satin eggs

steps.t: Sprinkle the water over the tapioca starch with the salt, rubbing it through your fingers until it feels like damp beach sand. Pouring the water in one place makes gluey clumps that will not griddle evenly.
Cover and rest the starch until it hydrates all the way through, then rub and sieve it into a snowy, slightly damp flour. Skip the rest and the beiju cracks before it can turn chewy.
Mix tomato, spring onions, coriander, lime juice and black pepper. Keep it juicy but not watery; a wet filling will turn the tapioca wrapper leathery.
Heat a flat griddle or heavy frying pan over medium-high heat and sear the queijo coalho until it has dark stripes and a squeaky centre. Move it too early and it tears instead of releasing cleanly.
Whisk the eggs with a pinch of salt, then scramble in butter over low heat until glossy curds slowly fold over each other. If they go dry in the pan, they will eat rubbery once wrapped.

For each beiju, scatter a thin, even layer of hydrated tapioca over the dry hot griddle and cook until the grains fuse into a flexible white sheet with dry edges. Too thick a layer stays powdery in the middle.

Fill each beiju with eggs, griddled cheese and tomato salsa, then fold and press briefly on the griddle until the outside is warm and faintly crisp. Pressing hard squeezes out the eggs and makes the seam burst.

note: Hydrated tapioca keeps covered in the fridge for two days, so the slow part can be done the day before.

name: Steamed Vietnamese Coffee Caramel Flan
hook: silky custard under bitter coffee caramel

steps.t: Put sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup turns the colour of dark honey and smells faintly bitter. Stirring throws crystals up the sides and makes a sandy caramel.
Pour the caramel into six ramekins, swirling quickly to coat the bases. Hesitate too long and it sets in one thick puddle that will not sauce the flan evenly.
Whisk eggs and yolk gently with condensed milk, whole milk, coffee, vanilla and salt until combined, not foamy. Beating in bubbles gives the custard a pitted, bread-like texture.
Strain the custard into the ramekins over the caramel. Do not skip this; the sieve catches egg threads that would cook into rubbery flecks.

Set the ramekins in a steamer, cover with a clean tea towel under the lid, and steam on the lowest steady heat until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly. Hard boiling makes tunnels and scrambled edges.
Lift the ramekins out and cool to room temperature, then chill until the caramel loosens into a syrup. Unmoulding warm flan breaks it before the custard firms.
Run a thin knife around each flan and invert onto plates, letting the coffee caramel spill over the top. If it sticks, hold the base in warm water for 10 seconds rather than shaking it apart.

note: A gentle steam is the whole trick; the water should murmur, never roar.

name: One-Dish Mushroom Orzo al Forno
hook: bubbling orzo with deep mushroom edges

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Tip mushrooms, onion, garlic, oregano, olive oil and a pinch of salt into a deep baking dish and spread them out; piled mushrooms stew instead of roasting.
Bake until the mushrooms shrink, darken at the edges and leave glossy juices in the dish. Pull them too early and the whole bake tastes watery.
Stir in the orzo, chopped tomatoes and hot stock, scraping the roasted bits from the base. If dry pasta sits above the liquid, it bakes hard rather than tender.
Cover tightly with foil and bake until the orzo is almost tender and the sauce is still looser than you want. A loose middle matters because it thickens as it stands.
Uncover, stir well from the corners, then scatter over mozzarella and hard cheese. Miss the corners and you will find clumps of dry orzo hiding there.
Bake uncovered until the cheese blisters and the surface bubbles slowly like lava. Stop before the edges turn black, or the orzo at the sides becomes chewy.
Rest for 5 minutes before serving so the sauce settles around the pasta. Spoon it out immediately and it runs like soup across the plate.

note: Built for one dish, one cheap bag of pasta, and mushrooms doing most of the flavour work.

name: Warm Escabeche Winter Roots
hook: Sherry-bright roots under smoky golden oil

ingredients.name: waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into thick coins

steps.t: Put the potatoes in salted cold water, bring to a steady simmer, then add the carrots and parsnips after 8 minutes; if the water boils hard the potatoes crack before the roots soften.
Cook until a knife slides through the thickest carrot with just a little resistance and the potato edges still hold their shape; mushy roots drink the dressing like paste.
Meanwhile warm the olive oil, garlic and sliced onion in a wide pan until the garlic is pale gold and the onion has slackened; if the garlic goes chestnut-brown the escabeche will taste bitter.
Pull the pan off the heat and stir in the smoked paprika, sherry vinegar, orange zest and orange juice; paprika burns in direct heat, so it must hit warm oil, not a frying pan.
Drain the roots well and let them steam-dry for 2 minutes; wet vegetables dilute the vinegar and leave the dressing sliding off.
Fold the hot roots through the escabeche with the parsley, then rest until warm rather than boiling-hot so the vinegar settles into the vegetables.
Serve in a shallow dish with the smoky oil spooned back over the top; if you leave the oil behind, you lose the comfort.

note: A winter vegetable dish in the Spanish escabeche spirit, served warm rather than fridge-cold.

name: Comté Mushroom Oeufs Cocotte Gratin
hook: Runny yolks beneath a mushroom crust

steps.t: Heat the oven to 190°C fan and butter a 22 cm baking dish; if the dish is too deep, the eggs overcook at the edges before the centre warms.
Fry the mushrooms in the butter over a lively heat until their water disappears and the edges smell nutty; if you crowd them or stop early, the gratin bakes watery.
Stir in the shallot for 1 minute, then add the Dijon and cream, scraping the pan until the sauce coats the mushrooms rather than pooling thinly.
Spread the mushrooms in the baking dish and make four shallow hollows; without hollows the eggs skate about and set unevenly.
Crack an egg into each hollow, keeping the yolks whole, then scatter over Comté and breadcrumbs, mostly around the whites so the yolks stay visible.
Bake until the crumbs are gold, the whites wobble softly and the yolks still tremble when the dish is nudged; a fully firm wobble means the breakfast has gone hard.
Rest for 3 minutes, finish with chives and serve with toast for scooping; straight from the oven the cream is too fierce and can split on the plate.

note: A one-dish breakfast gratin with the comfort of oeufs cocotte and the savoury pull of mushrooms.

name: Bourbon-Braised Short Ribs with Mushroom Gravy
hook: Glossy ribs, deep mushroom smoke

steps.t: Soak the porcini in 250 ml just-boiled water for 15 minutes, then lift them out and keep the gritty last spoonful of liquid behind; pouring it all in makes the sauce sandy.
Season the ribs, dust lightly with flour and brown them in oil until the meaty sides form a dark mahogany crust; pale ribs give you grey gravy, not dinner-party depth.
Remove the ribs and fry the cremini mushrooms in the same pot until they squeak and take colour at the corners; if they are still spongy, they will taste boiled later.
Add the onion, garlic and tomato purée, cooking until the purée darkens brick-red on the base of the pot; raw tomato purée leaves a tinny finish.
Pour in the bourbon off the heat, return to the hob and bubble until the harsh alcohol smell turns sweet and oaky; leaving it raw makes the braise sharp.
Add stock, porcini, strained soaking liquor, Worcestershire and thyme, then nestle in the ribs so the liquid comes halfway up, not over, the meat.
Cover and braise gently in a 160°C oven until a fork twists into the meat and the bones loosen without tugging; a rolling boil tightens the beef fibres.
Skim excess fat, reduce the sauce uncovered until it coats the back of a spoon, then spoon it over the ribs; thin sauce makes the plate look tired.

note: Serve with mashed potatoes or buttered noodles if you want a fuller plate.

name: Summer Carbonada Beef Stew
hook: Lean beef, sweetcorn and bright tomato broth

ingredients.name: lean braising beef, cut into 2 cm pieces
ripe tomatoes, grated or finely chopped

steps.t: Pat the beef dry and season it, then brown in olive oil in a wide pan until the corners are caramel-dark; damp beef steams and makes a dull broth.
Add onion and red pepper, cooking until the onion is glossy and sweet-smelling; if it is still crunchy now, it will stay harsh in the finished stew.
Stir in garlic and cumin for 30 seconds, just until fragrant; burnt cumin turns dusty and dominates the tomatoes.
Add the tomatoes and scrape the base until the red juices pick up every browned bit; leaving the fond stuck to the pan leaves flavour behind.
Pour in the stock, bring to a quiet simmer, cover partly and cook until the beef yields when pressed with a spoon but still holds neat cubes.
Add corn and courgette and simmer uncovered until the courgette is tender at the centre but still green at the skin; overcooking makes the stew heavy and khaki.
Fold in the peach for the final 2 minutes so it warms and perfumes the broth without collapsing into jam.
Finish with parsley and a small splash of water if the broth has reduced too far; it should eat with a spoon, not sit like a winter casserole.

note: Inspired by Argentine carbonada, kept lighter with summer vegetables and a clean tomato broth.

name: Lahori Crisp Tofu Katori
hook: Crackly tofu, hot chaat-shop edges

ingredients.name: firm tofu, pressed and torn into bite-size chunks

steps.t: Pat the tofu properly dry, then tear it rather than cutting it; wet cubes spit in the oil and smooth sides do not catch enough crunchy coating.
Mix gram flour, cornflour, chaat masala, chilli and cumin in a bowl, then toss the tofu through until every torn ridge looks dusty; bare patches fry leathery instead of crisp.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of flour sizzles at once but does not blacken; if the oil is shy, the tofu drinks it, and if it smokes, the spices scorch.
Fry the tofu in one loose layer, turning only when the undersides are deep golden and rough-crusted; crowding the pan steams the coating off.
Lift onto kitchen paper and salt lightly while hot, because cold tofu will not hold the seasoning on its crust.
Spoon yoghurt into bowls, ripple with tamarind chutney, then pile over the tofu, onion and coriander; serve immediately before the yoghurt softens the crackle.

note: Fast, sharp and filling; add warm naan if you want a bigger dinner.

name: Hanoi Lotus-Steamed Lamb Parcels
hook: Perfumed lamb, soft rice, fragrant steam

ingredients.name: boneless lamb shoulder, trimmed and cut into 3 cm pieces
glutinous rice, soaked overnight and drained
lotus or banana leaves, thawed if frozen

steps.t: Marinate the lamb with fish sauce, soy, palm sugar, garlic, lemongrass and ginger, massaging until glossy; a dry stir leaves salty pockets and bland centres.
Chill the lamb for at least 2 hours, or overnight if you can; rushing this leaves the shoulder tasting separate from the aromatics.
Blanch the lotus or banana leaves until floppy and bright, then wipe them dry; stiff leaves split when folded and leak rice into the steamer.
Lay two leaves crossed, scatter on a thin bed of soaked rice, add lamb, then cap with more rice and fold into tight parcels; loose parcels swell open and cook unevenly.

Set the parcels seam-side down in a large steamer over steadily boiling water, topping up with boiling water as needed; letting the pan run dry scorches the leaves and perfumes the lamb with bitterness.
Rest the parcels off the heat until they stop hissing fiercely; opening them straight away releases the steam that finishes softening the rice.
Unwrap at the table and finish with herbs and lime; if the rice still has a chalky core, rewrap and steam another 15 minutes rather than serving it gritty.

note: A slow, aromatic project with sticky rice that catches the lamb juices.

name: Coal-Grilled Lentil Salsiccia Skewers
hook: Smoky lentil patties with gym-bag power

ingredients.name: cannellini beans, drained, 240 g drained weight

steps.t: Mash half the lentils with the cannellini beans until sticky, leaving the rest whole; if everything stays loose, the skewers crumble through the grill bars.
Mix in parmesan, oats, egg, garlic, tomato purée, fennel, lemon zest and salt until the mixture holds when squeezed; if it smears like paste, add a spoonful more oats.
Shape into 8 short sausage-like patties around flat skewers, then chill so the oats hydrate and the surface firms; warm patties tear when turned over coals.
Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no licking flames; flames burn the oats before the middle heats through.
Brush the patties with olive oil and grill over the coals, turning only when the underside has dark grill marks and releases cleanly; forcing them early leaves half the crust behind.
Move to the cooler edge for a final firm-up until the centres feel springy rather than soft; pulling them too soon gives a mushy bite.
Serve with rocket and lemon wedges, squeezing the lemon on at the table so the crust stays smoky, not soggy.

note: Built for protein without pretending pulses behave exactly like meat.

name: Saffron Steamed Egg Malai Pudding
hook: Silky custard, cardamom, warm saffron

steps.t: Warm the milk, cream, saffron, cardamom and salt until steaming at the edge, not boiling; a hard boil dulls the saffron and can split the dairy.
Whisk the eggs and sugar just until smooth, avoiding a thick foam; foamy custard sets with bubbles instead of a glassy surface.
Pour the hot milk into the eggs slowly while whisking, then stir in rosewater; dumping it in fast gives sweet scrambled egg.
Strain into four small heatproof bowls and skim off surface bubbles; leaving them there makes pockmarks on the finished pudding.
Cover each bowl tightly with foil and steam over the gentlest simmer, where the lid trembles but does not rattle; violent steam honeycombs the custard.
Check one pudding: the edges should be set and the centre should wobble like soft jelly; if it sloshes, steam in 3-minute bursts, but do not chase a firm centre or it will curdle.
Cool for 10 minutes, then scatter with pistachios and serve warm or chilled; nuts added too early sink and lose their snap.

note: A finish-on dessert with the texture of crème caramel and the perfume of kulfi.

name: Bangkok Chilli Mussel Noodles
hook: Briny mussels, basil, wok smoke

ingredients.name: Thai basil or regular basil leaves

steps.t: Soak the rice noodles in hot water until bendy but still a little firm, then drain; fully soft noodles collapse into clumps once they hit the wok.
Check the mussels and discard any cracked ones or any open ones that do not close when tapped; bad mussels are not worth gambling dinner on.
Heat a wok until a drop of water vanishes on contact, then add oil, garlic and chilli; if the wok is only warm, the garlic sweats instead of flashing fragrant.
Add the mussels and green beans, toss hard, then cover briefly until the mussels open and the beans turn glossy green; keep the heat high or they leak water and stew.
Remove and discard any mussels that stay closed, because forcing them open does not make them safe to eat.

Add noodles, fish sauce, oyster sauce and sugar, tossing until the noodles are stained brown at the edges and the pan sounds dry again; if sauce pools underneath, keep tossing over heat, not stirring off the hob.
Tear in basil and serve with lime wedges; basil cooked for longer than a few seconds turns black and medicinal.

note: Frozen mussels work too; thaw and drain them well, then stir-fry for less time.

name: Miso-Butter Griddled Halloumi with Winter Cabbage Udon
hook: Salty crust, buttery noodles, deep warmth.

ingredients.name: savoy cabbage, cut into thick wedges

steps.t: Whisk the miso, butter, mirin, soy and ginger in a small bowl; if the butter is fridge-hard it will smear rather than glaze, so soften it until it takes the miso smoothly.

Heat a ridged griddle pan until a drop of water skitters away. Oil the cabbage wedges lightly with sesame oil and griddle them cut-side down until the ridges turn dark and the leaves smell nutty; move too early and they steam instead of sweeten.
Add the mushrooms to the hot ridges and press them down for firm contact. Cook until their faces are chestnut-brown and no longer squeak against the pan; pale mushrooms will make the noodles watery.
Dip the halloumi slabs lightly in half the miso butter, then griddle until the edges blister and the underside releases cleanly. If you force them, the crust tears off and stays on the pan.
Loosen the udon with a splash of boiling water in a wide frying pan, just until the strands separate; boil them hard for longer and they turn flabby.
Toss the udon with the remaining miso butter, cabbage and mushrooms until the noodles look glossy and the sauce clings rather than pools. If it looks dry, add one spoon of hot water, not more butter.
Pile into warm bowls, lay the griddled halloumi on top, and finish with spring onions and sesame seeds so the fresh bite cuts through the salty richness.

note: Best eaten straight away, while the halloumi crust is still squeaky and hot.

name: Crisp Gochugaru Mackerel with Sesame Breakfast Rice
hook: Crackling skin, hot rice, sharp kimchi.

steps.t: Pat the mackerel very dry, especially the skin side; any shine of water will spit in the oil and soften the crust before it forms.
Mix the potato starch, gochugaru and salt on a plate, then coat the fillets thinly and shake off the dusty excess. A thick coat tastes chalky and falls into the pan.
Warm the rice with a spoonful of water until steamy, then fold through the sesame oil and half the spring onions. Keep it covered; uncovered rice dries at the edges before the fish is ready.
Heat the rapeseed oil in a frying pan until a pinch of starch fizzes immediately. Lay the mackerel skin-side down and do not prod it until the skin audibly crackles and the edges turn bronze.
Turn the fillets once and fry just until the flesh flakes at the thickest part. Cook it past that point and oily fish becomes dry and metallic rather than lush.
Stir the soy and rice vinegar together, spoon over the hot rice, then add kimchi, crisp mackerel, seaweed and the remaining spring onions. Serve while the fish is still snapping at the edges.

note: Use yesterday’s rice if you have it; it reheats fluffy and makes this feel properly breakfast-ready.

name: Chinkiang Pickled Eggs with Cucumber Ribbons
hook: Glossy eggs, sharp bite, red oil.

steps.t: Bring a pan of water to a gentle boil, lower in the eggs and keep the bubbles steady rather than violent; a rolling boil knocks the shells and gives ragged whites.
Lift the eggs straight into cold water until fully cool to the touch. Peel them under water, because dry peeling pulls divots from the surface you want glossy.
Simmer the vinegar, soy, water, sugar, ginger and star anise until the sugar disappears and the steam smells warm and sour. Do not reduce it hard, or the pickle becomes too salty.
Cool the pickle to room temperature before adding the eggs; hot liquid keeps cooking the yolks and gives a grey ring instead of a clean centre.
Submerge the peeled eggs in the cooled pickle, turning once halfway so the colour stains evenly. If any egg sits above the liquid, that pale patch will show on the platter.
Shave the cucumber into ribbons and pat them dry; wet cucumber thins the dressing and leaves a puddle around the eggs.
Halve the eggs with a wiped knife, set them on cucumber ribbons, then spoon over chilli crisp, sesame and coriander. Dress at the last moment so the red oil stays bright.

note: For a stronger stain, pickle the eggs overnight in the fridge, then bring them towards room temperature before serving.

name: Summer Calabacitas Salsa Verde Bake
hook: Green heat, sweet corn, blistered edges.

ingredients.name: corn tortillas, torn into rough pieces

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Put the courgettes, corn, tomatoes, onion and green pepper into a wide baking dish; if the dish is crowded into a deep heap, the vegetables stew instead of blister.
Toss the vegetables with olive oil and a good pinch of salt until every cut face shines. Dry patches scorch before the tomatoes have time to collapse.
Bake until the tomatoes slump and the courgette edges pick up brown freckles. Pulling it early leaves the bake watery and raw-tasting.
Stir in the salsa verde and half the torn tortillas, scraping the sticky tomato juices from the dish into the sauce. If the tortillas stay on top only, they crisp but do not thicken the base.
Scatter the remaining tortilla pieces and jalapeño over the top, then bake until the tortilla tips curl and the sauce bubbles at the corners.
Rest the dish briefly so the juices settle back around the vegetables; spooning straight away makes it look thin on the plate.
Finish with lime juice and coriander at the table, because their brightness disappears if baked into the dish.

note: Serve warm rather than piping hot; the salsa verde tastes cleaner once the heat drops slightly.

name: Sicilian Skillet Baked Eggs with Mozzarella Crumbs
hook: Jammy eggs in a briny red sauce

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Put the oil and onion in a 24 cm ovenproof dish or skillet over medium heat; cook until the onion is glossy and collapsing, not browned hard or it will taste sharp.
Add the garlic and chilli flakes and stir for 30 seconds, just until the garlic smells sweet; if it turns biscuit-brown now, it will keep burning in the oven.
Tip in the cherry tomatoes, passata, capers and olives. Bubble briskly until the sauce leaves a clear trail when you drag a spoon through it; watery sauce gives you loose, floating eggs.
Taste the sauce before the eggs go in, then make four deep hollows. Crack in the eggs close to the surface so the yolks stay whole; dropping them from high up spreads the whites everywhere.
Scatter over the mozzarella and bake until the whites are set at the edges but the yolks still wobble when you nudge the dish; overbaking gives chalky yolks and rubbery cheese.
Rest for 2 minutes, then tear over basil. Spoon from the edges first, where the sauce is thickest, so the eggs do not break before they reach the plate.

note: Best with toasted ciabatta, but still a complete fast dinner without it.

name: Kashmiri Dum Aloo with Slow-Braised Cauliflower
hook: Silky potatoes under a brick-red gravy

ingredients.name: small cauliflower, cut into large florets

steps.t: Prick the potatoes all over and simmer them in salted water until a skewer meets slight resistance in the centre; fully cooked potatoes will collapse during the long braise.
Drain the potatoes and let them steam-dry until their skins look dusty. If they go into the oil wet, they spit and never take on that firm, wrinkled skin.
Heat the oil in a heavy casserole and fry the potatoes and cauliflower in batches until the potato skins blister and the cauliflower edges spot gold; crowding the pan steams the vegetables instead.
Lower the heat and cook the onions in the same oil until deep amber and sticky at the edges. Stop at tan and the gravy tastes flat; push to dark brown and it turns bitter.
Stir in the garlic-ginger paste, chilli, coriander and salt until the oil stains red and the raw garlic smell disappears; spices left dry on the base will scorch fast.
Whisk the yoghurt with the passata, then add it a spoonful at a time, stirring until each addition looks glossy. Dump it in cold and it can split into grainy curds.
Return the vegetables, add 200 ml water, cover with a tight lid and braise on the lowest heat until the potatoes are creamy inside and the cauliflower stems yield to a spoon.
Uncover, stir in garam masala and kasuri methi, then simmer until the oil beads at the rim. If it still looks soupy, the spices will taste separate from the vegetables.

note: A proper weekend curry: better after a 20-minute rest, excellent the next day.

name: Lemongrass Cod Green Curry Stew
hook: Lean flakes in a citrusy coconut broth

ingredients.name: skinless cod or haddock fillet, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.t: Pat the fish dry and season it lightly. Wet fish dilutes the stew and sheds flakes before it has even cooked.

Put 3 tablespoons of the thick coconut cream from the tin into a pan with the curry paste. Fry until the paste darkens slightly and tiny green oil spots appear; if it stays raw, the broth tastes grassy and harsh.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and stock, then add lemongrass and ginger. Bring to a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, or the coconut can look split and greasy.
Add fish sauce, lime zest and the fish pieces. Keep the surface barely trembling until the fish turns opaque around the edges; hard boiling knocks the chunks into shreds.
Add mangetout and spinach, pressing them under the broth until the spinach wilts and the mangetout stays bright green. Cook them dull and they lose the clean crunch this stew needs.
Turn off the heat, squeeze in lime juice and scatter coriander over the top. Add lime off the heat so the broth stays fragrant rather than bitter.

note: Serve with jasmine rice if you need more carbs; the stew itself is protein-forward.

name: Black Sesame Steamed Purin Cups
hook: A wobbling custard with nutty caramel

steps.t: Put 50 g sugar and the water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the caramel is the colour of strong tea; pale caramel tastes flat, but mahogany caramel will turn bitter fast.
Divide the caramel between four heatproof cups, swirling just enough to cover the bases. Leave it alone once poured, because overworking it makes strings and bare patches.
Warm the milk, cream, remaining sugar, sesame paste, vanilla and salt until steaming and smooth. Do not boil it, or the eggs will scramble on contact.
Beat the eggs gently in a bowl, then whisk in the hot sesame milk a little at a time. Vigorous beating traps bubbles that steam into a pitted surface.
Strain the custard into a jug and pour into the cups. Skipping the sieve leaves sesame grit and egg threads in what should be silk-smooth.
Set the cups in a steamer over barely simmering water, cover with a cloth-wrapped lid and steam until the centres wobble like set jelly, not liquid milk.
Cool for 10 minutes, then chill until fully cold before turning out. Unmoulding warm custard tears the sides and leaves caramel stuck in the cup.

note: Run a thin knife round each cup and invert onto small plates to serve.

name: Tea-Smoked Gochujang Beef Rice
hook: Charred-sweet beef with campfire edges

steps.t: Mix the beef with gochujang, soy, garlic, 1 tablespoon brown sugar and sesame oil. Work it just until sticky; kneading hard makes the mince springy rather than crumbly.
Fry the beef in a hot pan, pressing it into a thin layer first, until the underside forms dark, lacquered patches. Stir too early and you get grey steamed mince.
Break the beef into rough nuggets and cook until no pink remains and the edges look crisp. The beef must be fully cooked before smoking, because the smoke stage is for flavour, not safety.

Line a wok or deep pan with foil. Put the uncooked rice, tea and remaining brown sugar in the centre, then set a small rack or foil ring above it. If the beef touches the smoking mix, it will taste acrid.

Place the cooked beef on a small plate on the rack, cover tightly and heat until you see wisps of smoke escaping. Keep a window open; if smoke pours out heavily, the heat is too high and the tea will burn.
Smoke gently, off the highest heat, until the beef smells toasty and the edges deepen in colour. Longer is not better here: over-smoked mince turns bitter.
Pile hot rice into bowls, spoon over the smoked beef, then add kimchi, cucumber and spring onions. Keep the cucumber raw and cold so the bowl does not eat like one heavy, salty note.

note: Use an old lidded pan or foil-lined wok rather than a non-stick pan you care about.

name: Istanbul Peppered Mushroom Stew
hook: Silky mushrooms in a red pepper broth

steps.t: Heat the oil in a wide pan, then add the onion and peppers with a pinch of salt. Cook until they look glossy and bend easily; if they brown hard now, the stew tastes harsh rather than sweet.
Stir in the garlic, tomato paste and pul biber. Fry until the paste turns brick-red and stains the oil; stop too soon and it keeps that raw, tinny edge.
Add the mushrooms and spread them out. Let them hiss before stirring, cooking until they slump and leave tan streaks on the pan; if you cover them, they flood the stew with grey liquid.
Tip in the chickpeas and stock, scraping the base so the red peppery oil dissolves into the broth. Keep it at a steady bubble, not a wild boil, or the chickpeas split and go woolly.
Crush a spoonful of chickpeas against the side of the pan to thicken the juices. The stew should coat a spoon lightly; if it runs like soup, give it another two minutes uncovered.
Rub the dried mint between your fingers, stir it in with the parsley, and taste for salt. Add herbs at the end or they turn dull and grassy.

note: Good with plain yoghurt or bread, but the stew is complete without either.

name: Sumac Pomegranate Whole-Roast Brisket
hook: Sticky bark, sour-sweet juices, soft beef

steps.t: Mix the baharat, sumac, salt, pomegranate molasses and oil into a dark paste. Rub it all over the brisket, keeping the joint whole; if you slash it deeply, the lean parts dry before the centre softens.
Cover and refrigerate for 12 hours. This is not just waiting: without it, the spice sits on the surface and the middle tastes like plain boiled beef.
Take the beef out for 1 hour before roasting. Cold brisket tightens in the oven and cooks unevenly, leaving a stubborn firm seam through the middle.
Heat the oven to 150°C. Lay the onions and garlic in a roasting tin, set the brisket on top, pour in the stock, then cover tightly with foil so no steam escapes at the corners.

Roast until a skewer slides in with only a little resistance and the onions have collapsed into the stock. If the tin smells dry or scorched, add a splash of water immediately or the glaze will burn bitter.

Uncover, spoon the juices over the beef, and roast again until the top is lacquered and almost black at the edges, not dusty or charred. Spoon over more juices halfway through so the bark stays sticky.
Rest the brisket under loose foil, then slice across the grain and brighten the tray juices with lemon. Cut with the grain and even perfect beef chews like rope.
Scatter with parsley and serve with the onions and garlicky pomegranate juices spooned over the slices.

note: The beef is roasted as one whole joint, then sliced only after resting.

name: Chermoula Tea-Smoked Sardines
hook: Clean smoke, lemon herbs, oily fish

steps.t: Pat the sardines dry and check for bones with your fingertips. Wet fish steams before it smokes, and stray bones ruin the clean, quick eating.

Mix the coriander, garlic, lemon zest, half the lemon juice, cumin, harissa and olive oil. Spoon a little over the sardines and fold the rest through the lentils and cucumber; if you drown the fish now, the herbs scorch in the smoker.
Line a wok or deep pan with foil and add the tea, rice and sugar. Set a rack above it, open a window, and heat until thin blue wisps appear; thick yellow smoke tastes acrid.

Lay the sardines skin-side down on the rack, cover tightly, and smoke over medium heat until the flesh turns opaque and flakes at the thickest point. If it is still glassy, cover and cook a little longer.
Lift the fish out gently with a fish slice. Tugging at the tail end breaks the oily fillets into shreds, so support each piece from underneath.
Pile the chermoula lentils into bowls, top with the smoked sardines, and squeeze over the remaining lemon juice. Add the final acid at the table or the lentils go flat and muddy.

note: Use a pan you can ventilate well; the sardines must be fully opaque before serving.

name: Seville Steam-Kissed Honey Flan
hook: Silky custard, orange and amber honey

steps.t: Divide the honey between four heatproof ramekins and tilt to coat the bases. If the honey sits in one thick puddle, the flans release unevenly.
Warm the milk with the orange zest and cinnamon until steam rises at the edge, then turn off the heat. Do not boil it, or the zest tastes pithy and the milk forms a skin.
Whisk the eggs, yolks, sugar and salt just until smooth, not foamy. Froth becomes little holes in the finished custard.
Pour the warm milk into the eggs in a thin stream, whisking constantly, then strain into a jug. Skip the strainer and cooked egg threads show up in every spoonful.

Fill the ramekins, cover each with foil, and set them in a wide pan on a folded tea towel. Pour in hot water to halfway up the sides; without the towel, the bubbling pan rattles the custards into curds.
Cover the pan and steam at a very gentle tremble until the edges are set and the centres wobble like soft jelly. A rolling boil makes the flan rubbery and pocked.
Cool, then chill until fully cold before unmoulding. Run a small knife around the edge and invert; warm flan slumps instead of landing cleanly.

note: A quiet steam gives the smooth texture; the eggs should never meet fierce heat.

name: Dijon Charcoal Lamb Breast Baguettes
hook: Smoky lamb fat, sharp mustard crunch

ingredients.name: boneless lamb breast, sliced into thin strips
baguettes, split and cut in half

steps.t: Light the charcoal and let it burn down until the coals are grey with no tall flames. If you cook over fresh flames, lamb breast fat catches and tastes like paraffin smoke.
Mix the mustard, vinegar, garlic, rosemary and oil. Toss with the lamb strips, keeping them thin and flat; thick chunks burn outside before the breast has time to soften.
Mash the white beans with a spoonful of the mustard marinade from the bowl before it touches raw lamb, then stir in some onion and cornichons. Do not use marinade after the meat has been in it.

Grill the lamb over medium coals, turning often, until the edges crisp, the fat looks translucent and bubbling, and the meat is cooked through. Move pieces away from flare-ups or they blacken before rendering.
Toast the baguette halves cut-side down for the final minute. Leave them longer and the crumb turns brittle, so pull them when the cut face is striped and warm.
Spread the bean mash into the baguettes, pile in the lamb, then finish with the remaining onion and cornichons. The sharp bits matter; without them the lamb fat feels heavy.

note: Lamb breast is inexpensive but fatty, so patient medium coals are the trick.

name: Winter Ginger-Soy Steamed Mackerel
hook: Hot ginger steam, soft oily flakes

ingredients.name: fresh ginger, cut into fine matchsticks

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water is no longer chalky, then cook it with 225ml water; if you skip the rinse, the bed under the fish turns gummy rather than soft-grained.
Set a steamer over a steady simmer, not a violent boil; hard bubbling throws water onto the fish and makes the skin ragged.
Lay the mackerel skin-side up on a heatproof plate, spoon over the Shaoxing wine, and scatter half the ginger beneath and over it; ginger only on top will perfume the room, not the flesh.
Steam until the thickest part opens in moist flakes and the skin looks glossy, not split and dry.
Warm the soy, vinegar, sesame oil and chilli crisp together just until fragrant; boiling the sauce makes the soy taste harsh and salty.
Lift the plate out carefully, pour away the fishy steaming liquor, then cover the mackerel with spring onion and the remaining ginger; leaving the liquor in the plate dulls the clean soy finish.

Heat the rapeseed oil until it shimmers and just whispers, then pour it over the aromatics so they hiss and curl; lukewarm oil leaves raw onion bite instead of that winter-hot fragrance. Serve over the rice.

note: Best with very fresh mackerel; ask the fishmonger to pin-bone it if you can.

name: Ember Black Bean Molletes
hook: Charred beans, molten cheese, bright dawn salsa

ingredients.name: bolillo rolls or small crusty rolls, split
Oaxaca cheese or low-moisture mozzarella, shredded

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no licking flames; cooking over black coals gives you soot outside and cold beans inside.
Put the tomatoes and onion half directly over the coals until the skins blister and the onion edges blacken in patches, not all over; fully burnt salsa tastes bitter, not smoky.
Chop the charred tomato and onion with lime juice, coriander and salt; keep it chunky, because a watery salsa soaks the bread before the cheese melts.
Set a cast-iron pan on the grill, melt the lard, then mash in the black beans and chipotle until thick enough to hold a spoon trail; loose beans slide off the rolls into the fire.
Toast the split rolls cut-side down until the edges are crisp and coal-striped, then turn them over; if the cut side stays pale, it will steam under the beans.
Spread on the beans, mound with cheese, and cover loosely with a metal bowl or lid until the cheese slumps and shines; uncovered cheese dries before it melts.
Fry the eggs in the same hot pan until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble, then slide them onto the molletes with the salsa; under-set whites make the whole plate slippery.

note: Use a barbecue grate or a heavy griddle over the coals; the bread needs direct dry heat.

name: Aegean Sea Bass Crudo with Lemon Oil
hook: Cold white slices, lemon-bright and glossy

ingredients.name: sashimi-quality sea bass fillet, skinless and pin-boned

steps.t: Keep the sea bass in the fridge until the board, knife and plates are ready; warm raw fish softens fast and slices raggedly instead of cleanly.
Zest half the lemon into the olive oil and let it stand while you prepare the vegetables; grating into the fish later clumps the zest in bitter little patches.
Shave the fennel and cucumber as thinly as you can, then pat them dry; wet vegetables leave puddles that wash the oil off the fish.
Slice the sea bass across the grain into thin, even pieces with one long pull of the knife; sawing crushes the flesh and makes it look tired on the plate.
Arrange the fish on chilled plates with slight overlaps, then season with flaky salt; salting in a bowl cures the edges before your guests see it.
Spoon over the lemon oil, add a small squeeze of lemon, then scatter fennel, cucumber, capers and oregano; too much lemon too early turns the fish opaque and tight.

note: Only use fish sold for raw eating, ideally previously frozen by the supplier, and keep it properly chilled.

name: Sumac-Sizzled Chickpeas with Courgette and Dill
hook: Fast chickpeas, sharp sumac, cool herbs

ingredients.name: tin chickpeas, drained and patted dry

steps.t: Pat the chickpeas very dry on a tea towel; damp chickpeas steam and shed their skins instead of catching in the hot pan.
Heat a wide frying pan or wok until a drop of water flicks away instantly, then add the oil; starting cool makes the courgette leak and slump.
Stir-fry the chickpeas and courgette hard until the chickpeas take golden freckles and the courgette edges turn glassy, not mushy.
Add the green pepper and onion and keep everything moving; if the pan looks crowded and wet, pause stirring for a few seconds so the heat can climb again.
Add the garlic, sumac and pul biber for the last minute only; scorched sumac tastes dusty and garlic goes bitter fast over this heat.
Fold in the tomatoes just until their cut faces gloss and soften at the edges; fully collapsed tomatoes turn the plate into stew, not a summer stir-fry.
Finish off the heat with lemon juice, dill and a little salt; herbs cooked in the pan lose their cool, aniseed lift.

note: Serve warm or just above room temperature with yoghurt or bread if you want a fuller plate.

name: Za’atar Griddle Chicken Bites with Garlic Tahini Yoghurt
hook: Smoke-striped chicken for tearing and dipping

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-size pieces

steps.t: Mix the chicken with olive oil, half the garlic, za’atar, cumin, allspice, lemon zest and salt; bare patches on the meat scorch before the spices bloom.
Rest the chicken while the griddle heats until it is smoking lightly; a merely warm griddle gives you grey chicken and a pan full of juice.
Stir the yoghurt with tahini, the remaining garlic, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt; adding all the lemon at once can split the yoghurt, so loosen it gradually.
Lay the chicken on the griddle with space between pieces and do not move it until dark stripes form; crowding traps steam and wipes out the char.
Turn the pieces and cook until the centres are piping hot and the juices run clear, with no pink at the thickest point; guessing by colour outside is unsafe with thigh meat.
Flash the flatbreads on the griddle until warm and marked, not crisp; brittle bread cracks instead of scooping the yoghurt.
Pile the chicken onto a warm plate, scatter with parsley and finish with lemon juice; lemon added before griddling burns onto the pan and tastes metallic.

note: Set out with pickles, olives and sliced cucumber for an easy mezze-style spread.

name: Maple Waldorf Halloumi Plate
hook: Salty squeak, maple warmth, apple crunch

steps.t: Tear the rye into rough crumbs and toast it with the pecans in a dry frying pan until the nuts smell buttery and the crumbs darken at the tips; stop before the pecans go shiny-black, because they turn bitter fast.
Slice the halloumi as thinly as you can, about 3 mm, and lay it on the serving plate; thick slabs stay fridge-cold in the middle and make the salad feel clumsy.
Whisk maple syrup, cider vinegar, Dijon and olive oil in a small pan, then warm just until it loosens and steams at the edge; if it boils, the mustard splits and the dressing tastes harsh.
Quarter the radicchio, shave out the hard core, then slice it with the celery; leave the leaves chunky enough to hold dressing, or the plate collapses into slaw.
Cut the apple last into thin wedges and toss it with a spoon of the warm dressing; cut it too early and the edges brown before the halloumi softens.

Pile radicchio, celery, apple and cranberries over the halloumi, spoon over the warm dressing, then scatter pecans and rye crumbs; add the crumbs last or they drink the dressing and lose their winter crunch.

note: Use pasteurised halloumi and keep it chilled until slicing; the warm dressing barely softens it rather than cooking it.

name: Coconut Lime Griddled Prawns with Cashew Farofa
hook: Charred prawns, coconut gloss, lime smoke

ingredients.name: raw king prawns, peeled and deveined

steps.t: Pat the prawns dry, then toss with coconut milk, lime zest, grated garlic, half the dendê oil and salt; leave them glossy, not swimming, or the marinade will burn before the prawns char.
Toast the cashews in a dry pan until they smell sweet and show tan patches, then chop them roughly; take them too dark and the farofa tastes scorched.
Melt the butter in the same pan, add cassava flour and stir until it turns sandy and pale gold; stop while it still flows, because over-toasted farofa becomes dusty on the plate.
Stir the cashews, chopped chilli and half the coriander through the farofa, then keep it warm off the heat; covering it traps steam and softens the grains.
Heat a ridged griddle until fiercely hot and lightly oil the bars; if the griddle is only warm, the prawns leak juice and boil instead of taking stripes.
Griddle the prawns in a single layer until the undersides are marked and the flesh has turned opaque halfway up, then flip once; repeated turning tears them and squeezes out their sweetness.
Finish with lime juice and the remaining coriander, then serve over warm farofa with extra lime wedges; prawns should be firm and opaque all the way through, never glassy in the centre.

note: Dendê oil gives the Brazilian moqueca-like aroma; olive oil works if you want a lighter finish.

name: Lahori Crisp Paneer with Cucumber Mint Kachumber
hook: Crackly paneer, cold cucumber, lemon spice

steps.t: Cut the paneer into thumb-size batons and blot them dry; if the surface is wet, the batter slides off and spits in the oil.
Whisk gram flour, rice flour, half the chaat masala, chilli powder and sparkling water to a thick cream; a thin batter gives a leathery coat instead of a crisp shell.
Dice cucumber, halve tomatoes and finely slice the onion, then toss with mint, lemon juice and the remaining chaat masala; salt it too early and the cucumber floods the plate.
Heat the oil in a frying pan until a drip of batter rises with tiny, eager bubbles; if it sinks, the paneer will drink oil before it crisps.

Dip paneer batons, let excess batter fall back into the bowl, then shallow fry with space between pieces until the bottoms turn deep gold at the corners; crowding drops the heat and makes the coating heavy.
Turn once and fry the second side until the paneer feels light under the tongs and the crust rasps against the pan; keep flipping and the crust cracks away.
Drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, then serve immediately beside the cold kachumber; paper traps steam underneath and steals the crunch you just made.

note: Paneer stays neat and mild here; halloumi also works, but reduce the chaat masala slightly because halloumi is saltier.

name: Nuoc Cham Pickled Pork Cups
hook: Cool pork, sharp pickle, peanut crunch

steps.t: Poach the pork tenderloin in barely simmering salted water until it reaches 63°C in the thickest part, then rest it; a hard boil tightens the meat and a guess risks undercooking.
While the pork rests, cut carrot, daikon and cucumber into fine matchsticks; chunky pieces do not pickle quickly enough for a small-plate salad.
Stir rice vinegar, fish sauce, lime juice, sugar and sliced chilli until the sugar is fully dissolved; gritty sugar sits at the bottom and leaves the top of the salad flat.
Shred the warm pork across the grain into bite-size strands, discarding any silverskin; long fibres tangle in the lettuce cups and make guests fight the plate.
Toss pork, carrot, daikon and cucumber with the dressing and leave until the vegetables bend but still snap; pickle it much longer and the cucumber goes limp.
Separate the lettuce leaves, wash and dry them thoroughly; wet leaves dilute the nuoc cham and collapse in the hand.
Fold herbs through the dressed pork at the last moment, spoon into lettuce leaves and finish with crushed peanuts; add herbs earlier and their cut edges blacken in the acid.

note: The pork is safely cooked first, then pickled and dressed for the bright Vietnamese small-plates feel.

name: Lace-Crisp Chermoula Prawns
hook: Cumin heat, crackling edges, cold lemon

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry with kitchen paper; if they go into the coating damp, the crust steams off instead of frying crisp.

Finely chop the coriander and garlic, then mix with lemon zest, half the lemon juice, cumin, paprika, cayenne and a pinch of salt; keep it rough and fragrant, not watery, or it will loosen the coating.

Beat the egg in one bowl. Mix semolina and flour in another. Toss the prawns through the chermoula, dip in egg, then press into the semolina mix until every curve looks sandy; bare patches turn leathery in the pan.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of semolina fizzes instantly and floats; if the oil only sulks, wait, because prawns cook before a cold crust can crisp.
Fry the prawns in one loose layer until the edges go lace-brown and the centres turn opaque, about 75 seconds per side; crowding drops the heat and gives you bouncy prawns with a greasy coat.
Drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, so steam can escape instead of softening the underside. Stir the remaining lemon juice into the yoghurt with a pinch of salt.
Serve the prawns immediately with the lemon yoghurt; leave them sitting and the semolina crust loses its crackle fast.

note: Use raw prawns, not cooked ones; cooked prawns will overcook before the crust colours.

name: Saffron Escabeche Halloumi with Almond Dressing
hook: Silky peppers, sharp cheese, smoky gold

steps.t: Grill the whole peppers until the skins are black and blistered all over; patchy charring makes them hard to peel and leaves papery bits in the pickle.
Seal the peppers in a bowl for 10 minutes, then peel, deseed and tear into wide strips; rinse nothing, or you wash away the sweet roasted juices.

Warm the sherry vinegar, 80 ml olive oil, garlic, bay, smoked paprika, saffron, orange zest and 60 ml water until the garlic just softens and the saffron stains the oil gold; boiling hard makes the vinegar harsh.

Slice the halloumi into thick fingers and put them in a clean container with the pepper strips. Pour over the warm escabeche; if the cheese is not mostly covered, turn it once or use a narrower container.
Cool, cover and refrigerate for 24 hours, turning once halfway if you remember; serving it too soon gives you salty cheese with pickle on the outside, not through it.
Toast the almonds until they smell like warm marzipan and show darker freckles, then chop with the olives and parsley; pale nuts taste flat and dusty here.

Lift the halloumi and peppers from the escabeche, spoon over a little pickling liquor and the remaining olive oil, then scatter with the almond dressing; drown it and the smoky saffron flavour disappears.

note: Keep refrigerated and eat within three days; the texture is best after one full day of pickling.

name: Dijon Pork Fillet and Haricot Bake
hook: Mustard steam, lean pork, creamy beans

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan. Put the potatoes, leeks, garlic, thyme, olive oil and a good pinch of salt in a deep baking dish and toss well; dry unseasoned potatoes stay waxy and bland underneath the pork.
