Bake until the leek edges slump and the potatoes start to take golden corners; if they are still raw-hard now, the pork will be done before the base catches up.
Whisk the stock, crème fraîche and Dijon until smooth, then stir in the haricot beans and green beans around the potatoes; blobs of mustard scorch if they sit uncovered on top.
Season the pork fillet, lay it over the beans and spoon a little sauce over the top. Keep it in one piece so it stays juicy rather than drying into medallions.
Bake until the sauce bubbles at the edges and the pork reaches 63°C in the thickest part; guessing is where you get dry ends or an undercooked centre.
Rest the pork on a board while the dish sits uncovered; cutting straight away spills the juices and thins the sauce.
Slice the pork thickly and return it to the creamy beans, spooning sauce over the cut faces so they stay glossy.

note: Designed as a high-protein main: pork fillet plus haricot beans without a heavy gratin topping.

name: Maple Steam Custard Cups
hook: Warm maple wobble with nutmeg

steps.t: Set a lidded wide pan with 2 cm water over a low heat and put a folded tea towel in the base; ramekins rattling on bare metal cook unevenly and can crack.
Whisk the eggs, milk, cream, maple syrup, brown sugar, vanilla, nutmeg and salt gently until the sugar dissolves; frothing it hard traps bubbles that set into a pocked custard.
Strain the mixture into four ramekins and skim any foam from the surface; skip this and the tops turn speckled instead of satin-smooth.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil, place in the pan, then cover the pan. Keep the water at a quiet tremble, not a rolling boil, or the eggs curdle around the edges.
Check one custard: it should wobble as one piece and read about 75°C in the centre; if it ripples like milk, steam for a little longer.
Lift the cups out carefully and rest for 5 minutes so the centres finish setting; spooning in immediately breaks the soft gel into sweet scrambled egg.
Serve warm with blueberries and a small extra thread of maple syrup if liked; cold berries keep the dessert from feeling heavy.

note: A gentle steam gives diner-style egg custard without needing an oven bain-marie.

name: Mendoza Squash Carbonada
hook: Sweet squash, smoky tomato, soft potatoes

steps.t: Heat the oil in a large saucepan and cook the onion with a pinch of salt until it turns soft and shiny; if it browns hard now, the stew tastes harsh instead of sweet.
Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika and oregano for a few seconds until the pan smells smoky; leave them dry for too long and the paprika goes bitter.
Add the squash, potatoes and red pepper, turning them through the spiced oil so the cubes are stained orange; unstirred vegetables cook in separate layers and season unevenly.
Pour in the tomatoes and stock, scrape the base clean, then simmer with the lid half on until the potato edges are soft but not collapsing.
Add the sweetcorn and raisins, then simmer uncovered until the squash partly melts into the broth and the stew thickens enough to mound on a spoon; watery carbonada feels like soup, not supper.
Taste for salt and rest off the heat for 5 minutes; serving straight from the boil hides the sweetness and burns mouths before the flavours settle.
Ladle into bowls with plenty of the thick orange broth; if it has tightened too much, loosen with a splash of hot water rather than more oil.

note: No meat, beans or cheese: just cheap vegetables stretched into a filling Argentine-style stew.

name: Moqueca-Roasted Sea Bass with Coconut Farofa
hook: Coconut-rich, golden and winter-warm

ingredients.name: whole sea bass, scaled and gutted

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C. Cut three deep slashes on each side of the fish, then rub it inside and out with lime, garlic and salt; if the cuts are shallow, the seasoning sits on the skin and the thick back tastes flat.

Lay the onion and pepper in a roasting tin and set the fish on top. Pour the coconut milk around, not over, the fish, then spoon the dendê and paprika into the sauce; coating the skin too heavily stops it roasting and turns it leathery.
Roast until the sauce bubbles hard at the edges and the flesh pulls cleanly from the backbone at the thickest slash.

While the fish roasts, melt the butter in a frying pan and stir in the cassava flour. Keep it moving until it smells nutty and turns pale gold; if it catches dark brown, it will taste bitter instead of toasted.
Spoon a little hot coconut sauce over the fish and return it to the oven just until the top looks glossy and the exposed flakes are opaque; leave it longer and the belly meat dries first.
Rest the fish in the tin so the juices settle rather than flooding the plate when you lift it.
Finish with coriander and a warm shower of farofa. Serve from the bone with the thick coconut-pepper sauce underneath.

note: Use any firm whole white fish of similar weight, such as bream, bass or snapper.

name: Dhungar Halloumi Anda Paratha Skillet
hook: Smoky salt, soft eggs, crisp bread

steps.t: Brown the halloumi in 1 tbsp ghee over a medium-high heat until the corners blister and squeak against the pan; if the pan is cool, it leaks brine and stews.
Lift out the halloumi. Add the remaining ghee, cumin and onion, cooking until the onion edges turn tea-brown; pale onion makes the masala taste raw and sweet.
Stir in ginger-garlic paste, chilli, tomatoes and garam masala. Cook hard until the tomatoes collapse into a shiny paste and the ghee freckles the surface; watery masala will make the paratha soggy.
Return the halloumi, then fold through torn crisp paratha pieces so some stay exposed and crunchy; burying every piece makes the whole skillet heavy.
Make four hollows and crack in the eggs. Cover and cook until the whites are set but the yolks still wobble slightly; under-set whites are unpleasant, overcooked yolks lose the breakfast richness.

Heat the charcoal directly over a gas flame or with a blowtorch until ashed and glowing. Put it in a small heatproof cup in the skillet, spoon on a few drops of ghee, cover immediately and smoke briefly; too long turns the dairy acrid.
Remove the charcoal cup, scatter coriander over the top and eat straight from the pan while the halloumi is still bouncy.

note: If using paneer instead, salt it lightly before frying because it lacks halloumi’s briny punch.

name: Steamed Lemongrass Beef Betel Parcels
hook: Fragrant parcels with glossy dipping sauce

ingredients.name: betel leaves or large spinach leaves

steps.t: Mix beef, lemongrass, garlic, 1 tbsp fish sauce, sugar and toasted rice powder until the mixture turns tacky; stop while it is just cohesive, because overworking makes the parcels rubbery.
Wipe the leaves dry and place them shiny-side down. Add a thumb-sized log of beef to each and fold in the sides before rolling; wet leaves slide open in the steamer.
Set the parcels seam-side down in a lined steamer with a little space between them. Crowding traps juice and makes the leaves tear when lifted.
Steam over briskly boiling water until the leaves darken and the beef is cooked through to the centre with no pink mince visible.
Meanwhile, stir lime juice, the remaining fish sauce, chilli and 2 tbsp water into a sharp dipping sauce. Taste for salty-sour balance; if it is only salty, the beef will feel heavy.
Rest the parcels uncovered for a minute so the surface stops sweating; plating them straight away leaves a puddle on the serving dish.
Arrange with cucumber, mint and peanuts, then spoon over a little sauce at the table so the leaves stay glossy rather than waterlogged.

note: Betel leaves give the deepest aroma; spinach leaves work when betel is unavailable.

name: Coal-Grilled Sardines with Fennel Agrodolce
hook: Charred skin, sweet-sharp summer crunch

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are glowing with a thin grey ash; flames will scorch sardine skin before the flesh warms through.
Toss fennel with vinegar, honey, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Scrunch it until it bends without snapping; unsqueezed fennel tastes raw and bulky beside the fish.
Pat the sardines completely dry, then rub with olive oil, lemon zest and salt. Damp skin sticks to the bars and tears away the best char.
Grill the sardines over direct heat until the skin blisters and releases cleanly when nudged, not before.
Turn once and grill until the belly slit shows opaque flesh and the tail edges are crisp; repeated turning breaks the delicate oily fish.
Fold capers, pine nuts, parsley and the remaining lemon juice through the fennel. If you dress it too early with the nuts, they soften and lose their snap.
Serve the sardines immediately on the fennel agrodolce, spooning any sharp juices around rather than over the crisp skin.

note: Mackerel fillets work too, but give them a little longer over a slightly cooler part of the grill.

name: Mustard-Lime Mackerel Kachumber
hook: Cold, bright, mustard-hot silver bites

ingredients.name: previously frozen sashimi-grade mackerel fillets, skinned and pin-boned

steps.t: Keep the mackerel chilled while you prepare everything else. Raw oily fish warms quickly, and once it smells strong rather than clean and marine, the dish is lost.
Whisk lime juice, mustard, turmeric, mustard oil and salt until glossy. If the mustard stays in lumps, some bites will be harsh and others flat.
Dice onion and cucumber very small, then blot them dry. Wet vegetables dilute the dressing and make the fish look grey.
Slice the mackerel across the grain into 5 mm pieces with a sharp knife; sawing crushes the flesh and brings out oiliness.

Fold fish through the dressing just until every piece is lacquered, then chill briefly so the edges tighten but the centre stays silky. Lime is not a safety cook, and leaving it too long makes the fish chalky.
Fold in onion, cucumber, chilli and coriander at the last moment. Adding them earlier draws out water and slackens the clean mustard bite.
Spoon onto a cold plate and finish with sev for crunch. Serve immediately as a shared small plate.

note: Only use fish sold for raw consumption and previously frozen to control parasites; keep it refrigerated until serving.

name: Green Peppercorn Basil Lamb
hook: Hot wok lamb, basil, peppercorn bite

ingredients.name: lamb leg steaks, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Pat the lamb dry and slice it across the grain as thinly as you can; wet, thick slices stew before they sear.
Stir the fish sauce, oyster sauce and sugar together in a small bowl so the wok time stays fast; hunting for bottles later will overcook the lamb.
Heat a wok until a bead of water skitters and vanishes, then add the oil. If the oil smokes hard before the lamb goes in, pull the wok off the heat for a breath or the garlic will scorch.
Add lamb in one loose layer and leave it alone until the underside catches dark at the edges, then toss hard; crowding the pan gives you grey meat and lamb juice.
Add garlic, chillies, green peppercorns and red pepper, tossing until the garlic smells sharp and sweet and the pepper still has snap; burnt garlic turns the whole dish bitter.
Pour in the sauce and toss until it lacquers the lamb rather than pooling in the wok; if it looks watery, keep it moving over fierce heat for a few more seconds.
Kill the heat, fold through the Thai basil until just wilted, and serve over hot jasmine rice; cooking the basil hard makes it black and dull.

note: Put the lamb in the freezer for 10 minutes before slicing if it feels too soft to cut thinly.

name: Miso Adzuki Oyaki
hook: Charred dumplings with savoury bean heart

ingredients.name: plain flour, plus extra for dusting
neutral oil, plus extra for the griddle

steps.t: Soak the adzuki beans in plenty of cold water overnight; if the beans are barely covered, the top layer stays hard and cooks unevenly.
Drain, cover with fresh water by 5 cm and simmer until the beans squash easily between finger and thumb but still mostly hold shape; stopping at chalky centres gives a gritty filling.
Drain the beans well, then mash half with miso, soy, mirin and sesame oil. Fold through the whole beans, spring onions and sesame seeds; a wet filling leaks and burns on the griddle.
Mix the flour with hot water and 2 tbsp oil, then knead until smooth and elastic rather than shaggy; undermixed dough cracks when you seal it.
Cover the dough and rest it until soft and relaxed; rolling it straight away makes it spring back and tear around the beans.
Divide dough and filling into 8 pieces. Flatten each dough piece, spoon filling into the centre and pinch closed firmly, keeping flour off the seams or they will open in the pan.
Oil a heavy griddle lightly and cook the oyaki seam-side down until the bases are freckled deep brown and smell toasted, not pale and floury.
Flip, splash in 3 tbsp water and cover until the skins turn slightly translucent and springy; skip this steam and the outside chars before the dough cooks through.

note: These reheat well on a dry griddle, which is why the weekend batch is worth making.

name: Gochugaru Crisp Chicken Cutlets
hook: Lean chicken, crackling crust, chilli warmth

ingredients.name: skinless chicken breasts, about 360 g total

steps.t: Split each chicken breast horizontally into two thin cutlets and pat them dry; thick centres stay bland while the crust over-browns.
Mix gochujang, soy, vinegar and egg white, then coat the chicken evenly; clumps of paste burn before the meat is cooked.
Combine cornflour, panko and gochugaru on a plate, press the chicken in hard, and shake off dusty excess; loose crumbs fall into the oil and turn bitter.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a breadcrumb sizzles immediately but does not blacken; too cool makes a greasy crust, too hot leaves raw chicken inside.
Shallow fry the cutlets without crowding until the underside is brick-red and crisp at the thinnest edges.
Flip and cook until the second side crackles under tongs and the thickest part is piping hot throughout; do not guess with pink chicken.
Rest the cutlets on a rack, not kitchen paper, so steam escapes instead of softening the crust.
Slice and serve with cucumber and rice; cutting straight from the pan spills juice and makes the coating slump.

note: For a stricter gym plate, swap half the rice for extra cucumber or steamed greens.

name: Ginger Rock Sugar Steamed Custard
hook: Silky spoonfuls, warm ginger perfume

steps.t: Warm the milk, rock sugar, ginger and salt until the sugar dissolves and the milk smells gingery; boiling it hard skins the milk and dulls the custard.
Leave the ginger to steep off the heat, then strain and cool until just warm to the touch; hot milk scrambles the eggs on contact.
Beat the eggs gently with the vanilla, keeping the whisk low; foamy eggs steam into a pitted, bubbly surface.
Pour the warm ginger milk into the eggs in a thin stream, stirring constantly, then strain into four small heatproof bowls; unstrained chalazae set as rubbery white flecks.
Cover each bowl tightly with foil and set in a steamer over a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil; aggressive steam makes tunnels instead of silk.
Steam until the custards tremble like soft jelly at the centre when nudged; if they wave like liquid, they need longer, if they dome, they are overdone.
Scatter over goji berries, cover again for a brief softening, then serve warm or chilled; dry berries on top stay chewy and sharp.

note: A folded tea towel under the steamer lid catches drips before they spot the custard.

name: Chipotle Paneer Rice Bake
hook: Smoky rice, squeaky cheese, student budget

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan and choose a snug baking dish; a dish that is too wide dries the rice at the edges before the centre cooks.
Tip in the rice, beans, tomatoes, sweetcorn, onion, chipotle, cumin and stock, then stir right into the corners; dry pockets of rice stay hard no matter how long you bake.
Nestle the paneer cubes on top and press them halfway under the liquid; fully exposed paneer turns leathery before the rice is tender.
Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake until the rice has absorbed most of the liquid and looks swollen, not soupy.
Peel back the foil carefully, stir once from the edges into the middle, and check a few grains; if they are chalky, add a splash of boiling water before the final bake.
Scatter over the cheddar and bake uncovered until the top bubbles and the paneer corners go golden; leaving it covered now gives melted cheese with no crust.
Rest for 5 minutes, then squeeze lime over the top; serving straight away makes the rice collapse into wet spoonfuls.

note: Paneer keeps its shape better than most cheap cheeses, so the bake stays chunky rather than greasy.

name: Cretan Orange-Braised Pork with Chestnut Potatoes
hook: Citrus steam, soft pork, winter depth

ingredients.name: pork shoulder, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.t: Salt the pork well, then brown it in the olive oil in a heavy casserole until the corners form a dark honey crust; if the pan is crowded it will boil grey instead of building the base of the sauce.
Lift out the pork and soften the onions in the same fat until they slump and catch lightly at the edges; if they scorch black, the braise will taste bitter rather than sweet.
Stir in the garlic for just a minute, then pour in the wine and scrape hard at the sticky base; leave those brown bits behind and you leave half the flavour behind.

Return the pork with the orange zest, orange juice, oregano, bay and stock, bring to a quiet simmer, then cover and braise gently until a spoon can press into the meat without effort; a rolling boil tightens the pork.
Tuck in the potatoes and chestnuts, re-cover and cook until the potatoes take a knife cleanly but have not collapsed into the sauce.
Uncover and simmer until the liquid turns glossy and clings to the pork; if it still looks watery, it will taste thin on the plate.
Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, skim only the obvious surface fat, then serve with the orange-scented sauce spooned over everything; rushing the rest makes the meat shed juice into the pot.

note: Deeply Greek in its oregano, citrus and wine, with chestnuts giving the braise a proper winter sweetness.

name: Pul Biber Pork Breakfast Stew with Soft Eggs
hook: Peppery pork under molten yolks

steps.t: Brown the pork mince in olive oil, breaking it into small nuggets until the fat runs clear and the edges look crisp; if you stop while it is still pink or wet, the stew tastes heavy and raw-edged.
Add the onion and peppers and cook until the peppers soften but still hold their green shape; if they blacken now, they will dominate the tomatoes.
Stir in the garlic, pul biber and cumin until the pan smells warm and peppery; spices left dry for too long turn dusty and harsh.

Add the tomatoes and water, scrape the base clean, then simmer until the sauce thickens enough to leave a trail when a spoon passes through it; too much liquid means the eggs will sink and overcook unevenly.
Make four shallow hollows, crack in the eggs, cover and simmer gently until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble; a hard boil gives rubbery whites and chalky yolks.
Scatter with parsley and leave for 2 minutes off the heat so the eggs finish gently; serving straight away can leave a slippery ring of unset white.
Spoon into warm bowls with toast for dragging through the porky pepper sauce; cold bread dulls the fat and makes the stew feel greasy.

note: A Turkish-style pepper and tomato breakfast stew, made intentionally with pork for the brief rather than tradition.

name: Oak-Smoked Hake with Fennel, Orange and Green Olive
hook: Cool citrus against warm smoke

ingredients.name: large fennel bulb, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Pat the hake dry, rub with olive oil, ras el hanout and salt, then chill while you set up the smoker; wet fish steams before it smokes and the spice slides off.
Line a wok or deep pan with foil, add the oak chips, set a rack above them and keep a tight-fitting lid ready; gaps leak smoke and leave the fish tasting merely baked.
Heat until the chips give a steady pale smoke, then lay the hake on the rack, cover and reduce to medium; thick yellow smoke makes the fish acrid.
Smoke until the hake is opaque and flakes in large moist petals at the thickest point; underdone fish looks glassy, overdone fish breaks into dry shreds.
Lift the fish to a plate and rest uncovered for 5 minutes so the smoke softens; covering it traps steam and ruins the clean flakes.
Toss fennel, orange segments, reserved orange juice, olives, lemon juice and coriander until glossy and bright; dressing too early wilts the fennel into a limp tangle.
Serve the warm smoked hake over the cool salad, spooning over any orange-olive juices; mixing the fish through the salad breaks it up and muddies the plate.

note: Use a kitchen with strong ventilation for stovetop smoking, and cook the fish until fully opaque at the centre.

name: Manzanilla-Steamed Mushrooms with Almond Picada
hook: Sherry steam, garlic gloss, almond bite

steps.t: Choose a wide pan with a lid so the mushrooms sit in one loose layer; if they are piled high, the bottom turns watery before the top sees steam.
Warm the olive oil and garlic until the slices turn pale gold at the edges; dark brown garlic will make the whole tapa taste burnt.
Add the mushrooms, salt, smoked paprika and manzanilla, then clamp on the lid so the sherry becomes the steaming liquid rather than evaporating away.
Steam until the mushrooms look glossy, have relaxed but still spring back when pressed; take them too far and they shrink into slippery scraps.
Meanwhile crush the toasted almonds with sherry vinegar, parsley and lemon zest into a rough picada; a smooth paste disappears, but coarse crumbs give the dish its bite.
Uncover the pan and bubble the juices until they coat the mushrooms like a light glaze; leaving a puddle dilutes the sherry and washes the picada off.
Spoon into a warm shallow dish and scatter the picada over just before serving; adding it in the pan softens the almonds and loses the contrast.

note: Built for sharing with bread and cold fino, but still light enough to sit beside other small plates.

name: Phở Gà Pickle Pot
hook: Star anise steam, bright winter crunch

steps.t: Put the carrots and red onion in a bowl with the rice vinegar, sugar and a pinch of salt. Scrunch briefly, then leave until the onion turns glossy pink; if you skip the scrunch, the pickle stays harsh and stiff.
Toast the star anise in a dry casserole until it smells sweet and liquorice-like. Add the stock, ginger and chicken thighs; do not boil hard or the broth will turn cloudy and the meat tight.
Simmer gently, skimming once or twice, until the chicken pulls cleanly from the bone and the skin has given the broth a rounded sheen.
Lift out the chicken and rest it until you can handle it. Tear off the meat in generous strips; avoid shredding it too fine or it will disappear into the noodles.
Soak or cook the rice noodles according to the packet until bendy but not mushy. Rinse briefly in warm water; cold noodles will flatten the broth as soon as they meet it.
Season the broth with fish sauce and a squeeze of lime until it tastes savoury first, then bright. If it tastes only salty, it needs lime rather than more fish sauce.
Divide noodles and chicken between bowls, ladle over the hot broth, then pile on the drained pickle, herbs and lime wedges. Dress at the last second so the herbs stay leafy, not blackened.

note: A dressed, pickle-bright chicken noodle bowl with enough broth depth for winter.

name: Eggs al Forno with Tomato, Ricotta and Crisp Sage
hook: Runny yolks under bubbling tomato

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Warm the oil in a medium baking dish on the hob, then sizzle the garlic and sage until the sage darkens and stiffens; if the garlic goes chestnut-brown, start again because it will bitter the sauce.

Scoop the crisp sage onto a plate. Add passata, oregano, chilli flakes, salt and pepper to the dish, then simmer until the sauce leaves a brief trail when stirred; watery sauce makes the eggs slide and overcook unevenly.
Dot in spoonfuls of ricotta, keeping some white patches visible. Do not stir it smooth; those pockets are what make the bake feel generous.
Make eight shallow hollows and crack in the eggs one at a time. If a yolk breaks, keep it near the edge where it will set fastest rather than clouding the whole dish.
Scatter over parmesan and bake until the whites are set at the edges but the yolks still wobble when the dish is nudged.
Rest for 3 minutes; cutting in immediately turns the sauce loose and the eggs chalky at the edges.
Finish with the crisp sage and serve with toasted sourdough dragged through the tomato and yolk.

note: One baking dish, no fuss, but it eats like a proper Italian breakfast spread.

name: Saffron Halloumi Dum Braise
hook: Golden cheese in velvet spice gravy

ingredients.name: saffron threads, soaked in 2 tbsp warm water

steps.t: Soak the halloumi slabs in just-boiled water for 10 minutes, then drain and pat dry. This pulls back the salt; skip it and the finished gravy tastes seasoned twice.
Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a heavy casserole and fry the onions slowly until deep gold and jammy at the edges. Pale onions give a thin gravy; scorched black tips make the whole pot taste burnt.
Add garlic and ginger and cook until the raw sharp smell turns mellow. Stir in coriander, cumin and chilli for 30 seconds only; powdered spices burn fast once the pan is dry.
Lower the heat and whisk in the yoghurt a spoonful at a time until glossy. If it boils before it is blended, it will split into grains instead of becoming a smooth sauce.
Stir in ground almonds, saffron water and 200 ml hot water, then slide in the halloumi. The liquid should come halfway up the cheese, not drown it, or you lose the braised texture.
Cover with a tight lid and braise on the lowest heat until the gravy thickens to velvet and the halloumi yields to a spoon without squeaking aggressively.
Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, then spoon the saffron oil from the edges back over the top. Finish with coriander leaves; adding them earlier turns their fragrance muddy.

note: Built for the centre of the table with naan, pulao and a quiet flourish.

name: Lemongrass Pork and Green Papaya Stew
hook: Clean broth, tender pork, lime lift

ingredients.name: pork tenderloin or lean pork shoulder, cut into 3 cm pieces
lemongrass, bruised and cut into lengths
green papaya, peeled and cut into batons
palm sugar or light brown sugar

steps.t: Put the stock, lemongrass, lime leaves and galangal in a wide pan and bring to a gentle simmer. Do not hard-boil the aromatics; they turn woody and medicinal instead of bright.
Add the pork and keep the surface barely trembling, skimming any grey foam. A rolling boil squeezes lean pork dry before it has time to soften.
Add the green papaya and simmer until the batons look slightly translucent at the edges but still hold their shape. If they collapse, the stew loses its clean summer bite.
Stir in tomatoes, fish sauce and palm sugar. Cook just until the tomato skins relax; bursting them completely muddies the broth.
Turn off the heat, then add lime juice a little at a time until the broth tastes sharp, salty and lightly sweet in that order. Boiling lime juice dulls it, so keep the pan off the heat.
Fish out the lemongrass, lime leaves and galangal. Leaving them in looks rustic but gives guests tough, fibrous mouthfuls.
Ladle into shallow bowls with chilli and herbs scattered over the top. Serve warm rather than boiling hot, so the lime and basil stay vivid.

note: A clear Thai-style stew that keeps pork gentle rather than heavy.

name: Miso-Roasted Scotch Eggs with Sesame Cabbage
hook: Jammy eggs, savoury crust, crisp cabbage

steps.t: Boil 4 eggs for 6 minutes 30 seconds, then plunge them into iced water. Guessing this step is risky: underdone eggs tear when wrapped, overdone eggs lose the jammy centre.
Peel the eggs carefully under water, rubbing rather than picking at the shell. Gouges in the white become weak spots where the meat pulls away during roasting.
Mix pork mince with miso, soy sauce, ginger and 25 g panko until sticky. Stop once it clings to your fingers; overworking makes the casing bouncy instead of tender.
Beat the remaining 2 eggs in a bowl. Wrap each boiled egg completely in a thin layer of pork, then dip in beaten egg and roll in the remaining panko; any bare patch will leak juices and split.
Set on an oiled tray, drizzle with sesame oil and roast at 210°C fan until the crumb is deep gold and the pork feels firm all the way round.
Toss cabbage with rice vinegar, sesame seeds and a pinch of salt, squeezing once to soften it. If you dress it too early without squeezing, it weeps into a puddle.
Stir mayonnaise with mustard. Halve the roasted eggs with a sharp knife, wiping between cuts so the yolks stay clean, then serve on the cabbage with the sauce for dipping.

note: Roasted whole eggs for sharing, with Japanese seasoning and no deep-frying.

name: Lotus Leaf Steamed Cod with Weekend Chilli Crisp
hook: Silky fish under fragrant red oil

ingredients.name: thick cod loin or other firm white fish, skin removed
fermented black beans, rinsed and chopped

steps.t: Soak the lotus leaf in hot water until floppy and tea-scented, and soak the glass noodles in a separate bowl; if the leaf stays stiff it tears, and dry noodles steal moisture from the fish.
Pour the oil into a small pan with the sliced garlic and half the ginger, then heat gently until the garlic turns pale straw-gold; if it reaches chestnut brown, it will taste bitter after cooling.
Take the pan off the heat, stir in the dried chillies, black beans, sugar and 1 tbsp soy sauce, then leave the chilli crisp to settle; rushing it while scorching-hot burns the chilli flakes black.
Cut the cod into four even blocks, pat them dry, and rub with Shaoxing wine and 1 tbsp soy sauce; wet fish leaks albumen and gives the sauce a cloudy, boiled look.

Line a steamer tray with the softened lotus leaf, lay in the drained noodles, then place the cod on top with the remaining ginger and spring onions; burying the fish under noodles makes it cook unevenly.
Steam over a rolling boil until the cod flakes in thick pearly sheets and reaches 63°C in the centre; a lazy simmer leaves the middle glassy while the outside overcooks.
Warm the remaining soy sauce with a spoonful of the chilli crisp oil, spoon it over the fish, then finish with extra crisp at the table; drowning it early masks the clean sweetness of the cod.

note: The chilli crisp makes more than you need, which is the point of the weekend project.

name: Coal-Grilled Adobo Mushroom Bean Plates
hook: Smoky mushrooms, beans, lime bite

ingredients.name: large portobello or king oyster mushrooms
tin black beans, drained and rinsed
queso fresco or firm low-fat feta, crumbled
dried ancho chillies, stems and seeds removed

steps.t: Light the charcoal and let it burn down until the coals are mostly grey with a few red seams; cooking over flames coats the mushrooms in soot before they soften.
Toast the ancho chillies briefly on the hot grate until they smell like raisins and tobacco, then soak in boiling water; if they blacken, the marinade turns acrid.
Blend the softened chillies with garlic, cumin, oregano, juice of 1 lime, olive oil and a pinch of salt into a brick-red paste; leaving chilli skins whole makes the coating patchy.
Toss the mushrooms with most of the adobo and keep the beans separate with the remaining spoonful; beans on the grill fall through and dry out, so they only need seasoning.
Grill the mushrooms over the coals until they sag, darken at the ridges and stop leaking watery juice; pull them too early and they eat spongy, not meaty.
Warm the beans in a small pan at the edge of the grill or on the hob until glossy and hot all the way through; lukewarm beans make the whole plate feel like a salad.
Char the tortillas for a few seconds per side, then pile with sliced mushrooms, beans, cheese, yoghurt, coriander and lime wedges; over-charring makes them crack instead of fold.

note: Beans plus cheese and yoghurt keep the plate properly substantial after training.

name: Mastiha Steamed Honey Custards
hook: Cool wobble, piney honey perfume

ingredients.name: Greek thyme honey, plus extra to serve
mastiha crystals, crushed with a little sugar

steps.t: Warm the milk, cream, honey, lemon zest, salt and crushed mastiha until steaming at the edges, not boiling; boiling drives off the mastiha aroma and can split the dairy.
Cover and infuse off the heat until the milk smells piney and lemony; a short infusion leaves the custards tasting merely sweet.
Whisk the eggs just until the yolks and whites disappear together; frothing them fills the custard with bubbles that set into pockmarks.
Strain the warm milk into the eggs slowly while whisking, then strain again into four heatproof cups; skipping the second strain leaves stringy egg and lemon zest in the finished wobble.
Cover each cup tightly with foil and set in a steamer over barely simmering water; a hard boil makes the eggs curdle around the edges before the centres set.
Steam until the custards tremble as one piece when nudged and a knife comes out clean, then uncover away from your face so condensation does not drip back in.
Chill until cold, then finish with honey and pistachios; serving warm makes the sweetness flat and the texture loose.

note: Mastiha is powerful, so keep the pinch small rather than medicinal.

name: High-Heat Sardine Bulgur Tava
hook: Peppery sardines, sharp sumac onions

ingredients.name: sardines in oil, about 120 g drained weight each

steps.t: Cover the bulgur with 220 ml boiling water and a pinch of salt, clamp on a lid and leave until swollen; stirring it like risotto makes it claggy.
Drain the sardines, saving 2 tbsp of their oil, and split them into large pieces; mashing them now turns the stir-fry muddy.
Heat the saved sardine oil in a wok or wide frying pan until it shimmers, then add onion and green pepper; if the pan is timid, the vegetables sweat instead of blister.
Stir-fry hard until the onion edges char in spots and the pepper turns glossy but still bends; pale vegetables make the final dish taste boiled.
Add tomato paste, pul biber and cumin, then scrape and fry until the paste darkens brick-red; if it stays raw, it tastes tinny.
Tip in the fluffed bulgur and toss over high heat until grains separate and pick up red oil; overcrowded, wet bulgur sticks in lumps, so break it up before it hits the pan.
Fold in the sardines only at the end and shake the pan until just hot; aggressive stirring breaks them into salty crumbs.
Finish with lemon juice, parsley and sumac, then eat straight from bowls while the fish is still glossy; leaving it in the pan dries the sardines fast.

note: Tinned sardines keep it cheap while still giving the oily-fish richness.

name: Coal-Kissed Bavette à l’Échalote
hook: Smoky steak, sharp shallot butter

steps.t: Light a small chimney of charcoal; cook over it only when the coals are ash-grey and the black smoke has gone, or the steak will taste sooty rather than smoky.
Mash the butter with the shallot, Dijon, vinegar and parsley until it looks speckled and spreadable; if the butter is fridge-hard it will sit in lumps and slide off the hot beef.
Pat the bavette dry, rub with olive oil, salt and pepper, then leave it beside the grill while the coals settle; wet beef steams before it chars.
Grill the steak directly over the coals until the first side has dark bars and the edges tighten, then turn; move it away from flare-ups or the fat will taste burnt.
Grill the second side until the thickest part springs back but still gives under a finger; if it feels firm all the way through, you have gone past juicy.
Rest the steak on a warm plate with the shallot butter on top, then slice across the grain into thin ribbons; cut with the grain and even a perfect bavette eats chewy.

note: Fast, smoky and best served with a bag of crisp leaves or bread for the butter.

name: Maple Pastrami-Cured Salmon Board
hook: Silky salmon with deli spice

ingredients.name: previously frozen salmon fillet, skin on, suitable for raw eating

steps.t: Check the salmon for pin bones, keep the skin on, and pat the flesh dry; if it goes into the cure wet, the surface turns sludgy instead of cleanly seasoned.
Toast the peppercorns and coriander seeds in a dry pan until they smell like a deli counter, then crush them coarsely; powdery spice makes the cure muddy.
Mix salt, sugar, maple syrup, smoked paprika and the crushed spices, then pack it over the salmon flesh in an even blanket; bare patches cure unevenly and slice blotchy.
Wrap the salmon tightly, set it skin-side down in a tray, weight it with a tin, and refrigerate; turn it halfway so one end does not become saltier than the other.
Rinse the cure off quickly under cold water, pat absolutely dry, then chill uncovered on a rack until the surface feels satin-dry; skip this and the knife drags through the fish.
Simmer the cider vinegar with the mustard seeds until they swell and pop softly between your teeth; if they still feel like grit, give them longer.
Slice the salmon thinly at a shallow angle, stopping before the skin, and lay it on toasted rye bagels with the pickled mustard seeds; thick slices eat sticky rather than silky.

note: Use fish sold for raw eating, keep it refrigerated throughout, and eat within two days of slicing.

name: Buenos Aires Chimichurri Tofu Salteado
hook: Charred tofu, punchy green heat

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in a clean tea towel and press it under a pan; if it still feels damp on the surface, it will shed water and refuse to sear.
Stir parsley, garlic, oregano, vinegar, chilli flakes, half the salt and 1 tablespoon of olive oil into a rough chimichurri; making it too early and smooth turns it dull and grassy.
Tear the pressed tofu into large craggy pieces and dust with smoked paprika and the remaining salt; neat cubes brown less because they have fewer rough edges.
Heat a wok or wide frying pan until a drop of water skitters, then add 1 tablespoon oil and the tofu; if the pan only whispers, wait, or the tofu will stew.
Stir-fry the tofu until the torn ridges are chestnut-brown and crisp in places, then lift it out; keep it moving but not constantly, or the crust never forms.
Add the last tablespoon of oil, the pepper and onion, and stir-fry until the onion edges char and the pepper stays bright; limp vegetables make the whole bowl feel canteen-soft.
Return the tofu with the white beans and toss hard for a minute, then take off the heat and spoon over the chimichurri; boil the herbs in the pan and their fresh punch disappears.

note: High protein without heaviness; good with a squeeze of extra vinegar after training.

name: Rio Steamed Coconut Pudim Cups
hook: Wobbling caramel, cool coconut custard

steps.t: Put the sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup is amber like runny honey; stir it and the caramel may crystallise into sandy clumps.
Divide the caramel between six heatproof ramekins, swirling fast before it sets; if it pools thickly in one spot, the pudim will unmould with a bitter shard.
Blend eggs, yolk, condensed milk, coconut milk, whole milk and lime zest just until smooth; over-blending whips in bubbles that leave holes in the custard.
Strain the mixture into a jug, then pour into the caramel-lined ramekins; skip the sieve and little egg threads show up in every spoonful.
Cover each ramekin tightly with foil and set in a steamer over gently bubbling water; a fierce boil rattles the cups and makes the custard split at the edges.
Steam until the centres wobble like soft jelly, not liquid milk, then lift the cups out carefully so water does not drip under the foil.
Chill until fully cold, run a thin knife around each edge, and invert onto plates; unmould warm and the caramel runs while the custard slumps.

note: A small steamed version of Brazilian pudim, rich enough to finish a meal neatly.

name: Lahori Masoor Dal Tikki Chaat
hook: Crisp lentil cakes, cold yoghurt

steps.t: Rinse the lentils until the water is less cloudy, then soak them in fresh water; unsoaked lentils blend gritty and fry with a raw chalky centre.
Drain the lentils hard in a sieve, then blitz with ginger and green chilli to a coarse paste with a few whole bits; add water and the batter will spit in the pan.
Fold in onion, coriander, cumin seeds, chilli powder and gram flour until the mix holds when squeezed; if it slumps through your fingers, add a pinch more flour.
Heat the oil in a frying pan to a shallow shimmer and drop in a lentil crumb; it should fizz at once, not sink silently or smoke black.
Shape small flat tikkis and shallow fry without crowding until the undersides are deep golden and the edges look frilly-crisp, then turn once.
Fry the second side until tapping a tikki sounds crisp rather than dull, then drain on a rack; kitchen paper traps steam and softens the crust.
Spoon over cold yoghurt, chaat masala and lemon juice just before eating; dress them too early and the student-budget crunch disappears.

note: Red lentils keep it cheap, fast and filling without needing a long soak.

name: Za’atar Griddled Tofu with Silky Tahini Lentils
hook: Charred edges, lemony warmth, soft winter comfort

steps.t: Slice the tofu into thick slabs and press them hard between kitchen paper for 5 minutes; if the surface stays wet, it will steam on the griddle instead of catching.
Rub the tofu with 1 tbsp olive oil, za’atar, cumin and a good pinch of salt, getting spice into the corners; bare patches taste flat once seared.
Warm the remaining oil in a small pan and cook the onion with a pinch of salt until soft and honey-coloured at the edges; rush this and the lentils taste sharp and raw.
Stir in the garlic for 30 seconds, then add lentils and stock; let them bubble until glossy and spoonable, not soupy, or the tahini will turn thin and dull.
Take the lentils off the heat and beat in tahini, lemon zest and half the juice; boiling tahini makes it seize and taste dusty.
Heat a ridged griddle until a drop of water spits away, then cook the tofu until dark bars form and the edges feel firm; move it too soon and the crust tears off.
Spoon the tahini lentils into warm bowls, top with tofu, parsley and the remaining lemon juice; the final acid keeps the dish from eating heavy.

note: Deep winter comfort without heaviness: warm lentils, nutty tahini and properly charred tofu.

name: Crisp Chermoula Mushrooms with Harissa Yoghurt
hook: Crunchy caps, smoky yoghurt, runny-morning energy

steps.t: Mix yoghurt, harissa, lemon juice and half the coriander, then season; if you leave the yoghurt plain until the end, the fried mushrooms taste one-note.
Pat the mushrooms completely dry, especially under the caps; moisture under batter spits badly and turns the coating leathery.
Whisk the egg with 1 tbsp water in one bowl, and mix flour, cumin, paprika, coriander and salt in another; uneven spice means some mushrooms taste dusty while others taste bare.
Dip mushrooms in egg, then flour, pressing the coating into the gills; a loose dusting falls off as soon as it hits the oil.
Heat 1 cm oil in a frying pan until a pinch of flour fizzes instantly but does not blacken; oil that is too cool makes greasy mushrooms, too hot burns the spices before the centre warms.
Fry the mushrooms in two batches until the coating is crisp and walnut-brown, turning once; crowding the pan drops the heat and gives you soggy caps.
Drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, then fry the serving eggs in the same pan until the whites set and the edges frill; paper traps steam and softens the crust you worked for.
Plate the harissa yoghurt, pile on the crisp mushrooms, add the eggs and scatter the remaining coriander; serve at once while the crust still crackles.

note: A breakfast plate with the crunch of fritters and the deep savouriness of mushrooms.

name: Sherry-Pickled Chickpeas with Orange Almond Dressing
hook: Bright pulses, glossy oil, dinner-party poise

ingredients.name: small red onion, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Warm the chickpeas gently in a pan with a splash of water, then drain well; cold chickpeas resist the pickle and taste chalky in the middle.
Toss the warm chickpeas and red onion with sherry vinegar and salt, then leave until the onion turns brighter pink and the chickpeas smell nutty-sour.
Whisk olive oil, orange zest, smoked paprika and honey until glossy; if the honey sits in a lump, the dressing lands sweet in patches.
Drain off and keep 2 tbsp of the pickling vinegar, then fold the dressing through the chickpeas; adding everything makes the salad harsh rather than lively.
Add orange segments, capers, roasted pepper and parsley with gentle hands; rough mixing breaks the orange and muddies the plate.
Taste and sharpen with the reserved vinegar only if the chickpeas have gone mellow; acidity should lift the oil, not sting the throat.
Spoon onto a wide platter and finish with almonds just before serving; add them earlier and their expensive crunch disappears.

note: Looks composed, travels well, and gives pulses the polished treatment they deserve.

name: Provençal Baked Chicken with Courgette, Tomatoes and Vermouth
hook: Herby juices, tender chicken, sunlit restraint

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan and choose a baking dish that holds everything in one snug layer; if the dish is cramped, the vegetables boil in chicken juices instead of roasting lightly.
Whisk vermouth, olive oil, Dijon, herbes de Provence, lemon zest, half the lemon juice, salt and pepper; unblended mustard clings in hot pockets.
Toss courgettes, tomatoes, onion and garlic in the dish with half the dressing, then spread them flat; piled courgettes turn watery and bland.
Season the chicken and nestle it among the vegetables, spooning over the remaining dressing; leave the tops uncovered so they roast rather than poach.
Bake until the chicken is cooked through, the tomatoes have slumped and the pan juices are clear and fragrant; undercooked chicken is unsafe, so check the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Rest the dish for 8 minutes so the juices settle back into the meat; cut too soon and the plate floods.
Finish with basil and the remaining lemon juice just before serving; baked basil goes black and lemon added early tastes cooked instead of bright.

note: A one-dish chicken supper built for warm evenings: juicy, herbal and deliberately light.

name: Bourbon-Braised Prawns with Old Bay Butter
hook: Sweet shells, peppered butter, messy fingers

steps.t: Keep the prawns chilled while you start the sauce; shellfish warms quickly and loses its clean snap before it reaches the pan.
Melt half the butter in a wide sauté pan and soften the onion until translucent and sweet-smelling; browned onion pushes the sauce bitter against the bourbon.
Add garlic for 30 seconds, then pour in pale ale and bourbon, scraping the base; let the raw alcohol smell fade or the finished braise tastes hot and thin.
Stir in Old Bay, Worcestershire and brown sugar, then simmer until the liquid looks slightly syrupy around the bubbles; if it stays watery, it will slide off the shells.
Turn the heat low, add the prawns in one layer and cover; cook gently until the shells turn pink and the flesh is just opaque, because hard boiling makes prawns rubbery.
Lift the prawns to a warm shallow bowl, then whisk the remaining butter into the braising liquor off the heat; boiling after the butter goes in splits the sauce greasy.
Pour the glossy sauce over the prawns, scatter with chives and serve with lemon wedges; the lemon belongs at the table so each person can cut the richness to taste.

note: A slow, buttery shell-on braise for passing round with napkins and bread.

name: Mendoza Halloumi Carbonada
hook: Tomato-sweet stew with squeaky golden cheese

ingredients.name: butternut squash, peeled and diced small

steps.t: Pat the halloumi very dry, then fry it in the oil in a wide pan until the corners turn deep gold; if it goes in wet, it steams and sheds salty water into the stew.
Lift the cheese out, add the onion and pepper, and cook until the onion is glossy and sweet-smelling; if you rush this, the stew tastes sharp rather than round.
Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for 30 seconds, just until the pan smells smoky; longer than that and the paprika catches bitterly.
Add the squash, potato, tomatoes and stock, scraping the base clean so the browned cheese bits dissolve into the sauce.
Simmer hard enough to blur the surface, not boil violently, until the potato edges soften but still hold their shape; too fierce a boil breaks the vegetables into paste.
Stir in the sweetcorn and halloumi for the last few minutes, just until the cheese warms and squeaks when bitten; simmering it too long makes it rubbery.
Taste before salting, because halloumi carries plenty, then finish with parsley and spoon into shallow bowls.

note: Carbonada-inspired rather than traditional, built for a fast pan and a cold evening.

name: Bahian Pururuca Whole Pork Shoulder
hook: Crackling skin, lime, garlic and cachaça

ingredients.name: skin-on bone-in pork shoulder, kept whole

steps.t: Score the pork skin in finger-width lines without cutting into the meat; cut too deep and the juices climb through the skin, stopping it from crackling.

Rub the meat side with garlic, lime zest, lime juice, cachaça, pepper, cumin and bay, then rub the skin with the salt and leave uncovered in the fridge; uncovered is the point, as damp skin roasts leathery.
Take the pork out while the oven heats to 150°C, wipe any wet patches from the skin, and set it skin-side up in a snug roasting tin.
Roast until a skewer slides into the shoulder with almost no resistance and the meat is at least 88°C in the thickest part; pulling it early gives neat slices but tough chewing.

Spoon off most of the fat into a frying pan, raise the oven to 240°C, and return the pork until the skin blisters into hard little bubbles; if the oven is not fierce, you get bubbles of grease instead of pururuca crackle.
Rest the pork uncovered so the crackling stays crisp; foil traps steam and softens the work you just did.
Toast the cassava flour in the reserved pork fat with the butter until it smells nutty and looks like damp sand, not pale dust.
Carve by lifting away shards of crackling first, then pulling the shoulder meat into generous pieces and serving it with the hot farofa.

note: Ask the butcher for an unrolled shoulder with the skin left on; rolled joints cook unevenly here.

name: Lahori Dhuan Egg Bhurji Bowl
hook: Charcoal smoke over spiced, protein-heavy eggs

steps.t: Beat the eggs with the egg whites and a pinch of salt until streak-free but not foamy; foam makes the bhurji puff up and turn watery as it settles.
Cook the onion in ghee until the edges are tea-brown and the middle is soft; pale onion leaves a raw bite that smoke will only make harsher.
Add tomato, ginger-garlic paste, cumin, chilli and garam masala, then cook until the tomato collapses and the fat starts to glisten at the edge of the pan.
Lower the heat, pour in the eggs and fold slowly with a spatula, dragging from the edge to the centre; high heat gives dry curds before the whites set safely.
Fold in the spinach and keep cooking until the eggs are softly set with no liquid running through them; stopping glossy-wet is not safe with added raw egg white.
Nestle a small heatproof foil cup in the pan, put a red-hot piece of charcoal in it, drip on a little ghee, cover the pan, and let the smoke sit; leave it too long and the eggs taste ashy, not smoky.
Remove and discard the charcoal cup, then spoon the bhurji over yoghurt so the hot eggs loosen it into a tangy sauce.

note: Use metal tongs for the charcoal and keep it in the foil cup, never loose in the food.

name: Saigon Cà Phê Sữa Steamed Flan
hook: Silky caramel custard with coffee warmth

steps.t: Cook the sugar and water in a small pan without stirring until the bubbles slow and the caramel turns copper; stirring crystals the sugar, and dark brown caramel tastes burnt in steam.
Divide the caramel between four ramekins and tilt quickly to coat the bases before it sets into thick glassy puddles.
Whisk eggs, yolks, milk, condensed milk, coffee, vanilla and salt gently until combined; beating hard traps bubbles that become little holes in the finished flan.
Strain the custard twice into a jug, then pour over the caramel; skipping the sieve leaves ropey egg strands that steaming will not hide.
Cover each ramekin with foil and steam over barely trembling water, not a rolling boil, until the centres wobble like soft jelly.
Lift the ramekins out and cool until no longer hot to the touch; putting hot custard straight into the fridge makes condensation drip onto the surface.
Chill until fully cold, then run a thin knife around each flan and invert onto plates so the coffee caramel spills over the top.

note: A low steamer is the difference between satin custard and a bubbled, eggy sponge.

name: Calabrian Coal-Grilled Pollock Cartoccio
hook: Cheap white fish, smoke, lemony crumbs

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are mostly grey with no tall flames; flames scorch the parcels before the fish has warmed through.
Pat the pollock dry, then season with salt and half the lemon juice; wet fillets leak into the parcel and turn the crumbs pasty.
Mix bread crumbs, lemon zest, garlic, olive oil, capers, parsley and chilli until the crumbs feel damp and clump lightly; dry crumbs burn over coals, oily crumbs fry properly.
Lay courgette coins on two double layers of foil, sit the fish on top, and pack the crumbs over the fish so they protect it from the heat.
Seal the foil into loose parcels with headroom above the crumbs; tight wrapping glues the topping to the foil and squeezes the fish.
Grill the parcels over medium coals, turning once, until the foil hisses quietly and the fish flakes in thick white petals when checked.
Open the parcels away from your face, splash with the remaining lemon juice, and eat straight from the foil before the steam softens the crumb crust.

note: Pollock keeps this cheap, but any firm white fish fillet of similar thickness works.

name: Rioja Steam-Baked Eggs with Paprika Chickpeas
hook: Soft yolks under smoky tomato warmth

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide lidded sauté pan over a medium heat, then cook the onion with a pinch of salt until it slumps and turns translucent; if it catches brown now, the sauce will taste harsh rather than sweet.
Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for 30 seconds, just until the oil turns brick-red; let the paprika scorch and it will go bitter fast.
Add the tomatoes, chickpeas and peppers, then simmer until the sauce is thick enough to leave a brief trail when stirred; if it is still watery, the eggs will poach unevenly and taste flat.
Make four shallow hollows, crack in the eggs, and season the whites, not the yolks; breaking yolks into the sauce gives you scrambled tomato rather than soft-centred eggs.
Scatter over the Manchego, cover tightly, and steam on a low heat until the whites are just set and the yolks still wobble when the pan is nudged; fierce heat gives rubbery whites and chalky yolks.
Rest off the heat for 2 minutes, then finish with parsley and a thread of olive oil; serving straight from the boil makes the eggs keep cooking on the plate.

note: Serve with toasted country bread for scooping through the smoky sauce.

name: Charcoal Leek and Mushroom Tartines with Dijon Crème
hook: Smoke, butter and morning crunch

ingredients.name: small leeks, trimmed and halved lengthways

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no licking flames; cooking over flames blackens the leeks outside before the centres soften.
Toss the leeks and mushrooms with olive oil and salt, keeping the leek layers intact; loose layers fall through the bars and turn to bitter scraps.
Grill the leeks cut-side down until striped dark and soft at the thick end, turning only once; too much moving stops the sweet char forming.
Grill the mushrooms in a grill basket or on a fine rack until their edges wrinkle and smell nutty; if they sit crowded, they steam and go squeaky.
Brush the sourdough with melted butter and grill until the ridges are crisp and golden; leave it pale and the crème will make it soggy in minutes.
Stir the Dijon into the crème fraîche with lemon juice and chives, then taste for salt; over-mustarding hides the smoke you worked for.
Spread the toast with Dijon crème, pile on the smoky leeks and mushrooms, and finish with sea salt flakes while everything is still warm.

note: Best cooked on a small morning fire, but a barbecue chimney of coals is enough.

name: Citrus Fluke Crudo with Buttermilk and Chilli Oil
hook: Silky fish, sharp citrus, cold cream

ingredients.name: sashimi-grade fluke or other sushi-grade flat white fish, skinless and pin-boned

steps.t: Chill the serving plates and keep the fish in the fridge until the last moment; warm fish turns soft and loses the clean slice you need for crudo.
Segment the grapefruit over a bowl, catching the juice, then squeeze in the lime; pith left on the segments makes the whole plate taste medicinal.
Slice the fish across the grain into thin, even pieces with a long sharp knife; sawing at it tears the flesh and makes an expensive fish look ragged.

Whisk 2 tablespoons grapefruit-lime juice with the buttermilk, olive oil and a pinch of salt until it tastes bright but not puckering; too much acid will start curing the fish before it reaches the table.
Arrange the fish in a single layer on the cold plates, then spoon over the buttermilk dressing lightly; puddling the dressing drowns the delicate sweetness.
Top with grapefruit segments, shaved fennel, capers, dill and dots of chilli oil; heavy garnish hides the fish, so leave some slices bare and glossy.
Serve within 5 minutes while the fish is cold and satin-textured; let it sit and the acid tightens the edges to opaque.

note: Use only fish sold as suitable for raw consumption by a trusted fishmonger.

name: Mendoza Wok Mushrooms with Green Olive Chimichurri
hook: Hot seared mushrooms, cool herb bite

ingredients.name: mixed mushrooms, torn or thickly sliced

steps.t: Mix the olives, parsley, oregano, vinegar, garlic, chilli flakes and 1 tablespoon olive oil to make a loose chimichurri; if it tastes dull now, it will not wake up the mushrooms later.
Pat the mushrooms dry and tear large ones into bite-size pieces; wet mushrooms spit hard and boil instead of searing.
Heat a wok or heavy frying pan until a drop of water skates and vanishes almost at once; start too cool and the mushrooms leak their juice into a grey stew.
Add the remaining oil, then the mushrooms in one layer, leaving them untouched until the undersides go bronze and the edges curl.
Stir-fry hard for another 2 minutes, tossing rather than stirring slowly; gentle shuffling breaks them before they brown properly.
Add the red onion for the final minute so it loses its raw sting but stays crisp and purple; cook it longer and the whole plate turns sweet and heavy.
Take the pan off the heat, spoon over the green olive chimichurri and squeeze with lemon; adding the herbs over heat makes them khaki and muddy.

note: Eat warm or just off-room-temperature with grilled bread or chilled tomatoes.

name: Picanha Chapa Bites with Lime Farofa Crumb
hook: Salty beef, crisp cassava, lime

ingredients.name: picanha or rump cap steak, fat cap left on
lime, zested and cut into wedges
red chilli, deseeded and finely sliced

steps.t: Cut the picanha with the grain into thick strips, then salt all over and leave while you make the crumb; slicing this way now means the final bites can be cut across the grain and stay tender.
Melt the butter in a small pan, stir in the cassava flour and toast until it smells nutty and feels sandy, not greasy; pale farofa tastes dusty rather than crisp.
Stir lime zest and a pinch of salt into the farofa off the heat; zest added over heat loses its clean citrus snap.
Heat a cast-iron griddle until faintly smoking, then rub with oil; a lukewarm chapa gives you grey beef before the fat cap renders.
Lay the beef fat-side down first until the fat turns golden and glassy at the edge; skip this and every bite will chew waxy.
Griddle the cut sides until a dark crust forms while the centre still gives softly under tongs, turning once; constant flipping stops the crust building.
Rest the beef on a board so the juices settle instead of flooding the farofa, then slice across the grain into small shared bites.
Toss shallot, coriander, chilli and vinegar together, spoon over the beef, and shower with lime farofa; adding the crumb too early lets it drink the juices and go soft.

note: Serve with cocktail sticks and extra lime wedges for a proper shared table.

name: Salsa Verde Black Bean Tortilla Bake
hook: Tangy beans under blistered cheddar

ingredients.name: tinned black beans, drained and rinsed
small corn tortillas, torn into rough pieces

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Oil a medium baking dish; if the dish is too large the bake dries at the edges before the middle bubbles.
Tip in the black beans, sweetcorn, salsa verde and tomatoes, then fold until everything looks glossy and loose. Dry patches of bean will turn chalky rather than saucy.
Tuck the torn tortillas through the beans so some pieces sit underneath and some poke up. If they all sit on top, you get crisps instead of soft, saucy layers.
Scatter over the cheddar and jalapeños, keeping a few tortilla corners exposed so they catch and crisp.
Bake until the sauce is bubbling hard at the sides and the cheese has amber freckles, not just melted pale yellow.
Rest for 5 minutes so the beans settle; spooning straight away makes the bake slump into soup.
Finish with coriander and lime at the table, because baked coriander turns dull and lime loses its snap in the oven.

note: Use a jarred tomatillo salsa verde for the quickest version; green enchilada sauce also works.

name: Greek Orange-Olive Braised Chicken
hook: Silky chicken in citrusy pan juices

ingredients.name: chicken legs and thighs, bone-in and skin-on
waxy potatoes, cut into thick wedges

steps.t: Salt the chicken all over and leave it uncovered while you slice the vegetables; damp skin steams in the pan and never gives you a proper bronze base.
Heat the olive oil in a heavy casserole and brown the chicken skin-side down until the skin is deep gold and releases without tearing. If you tug too early, the best flavour stays welded to the pot.

Lift out the chicken, then add onions and potatoes. Cook until the onion edges look translucent and the potato corners have picked up chicken fat; raw onion under a long braise tastes flat and boiled.
Stir in garlic and oregano for 30 seconds, just until the oregano smells warm. Let it go black and the whole pot turns bitter.
Pour in the wine and scrape until the sticky brown layer dissolves into the liquid. If those patches remain stuck, the sauce tastes thin while the pot tastes burnt.
Add stock, orange zest and juice, lemon juice and olives, then nestle the chicken skin-side up with the skin above the liquid. Submerged skin goes rubbery instead of lacquered.
Cover and braise very gently at 150°C until the meat pulls from the bone with a spoon and the potatoes are satin-edged, not collapsing into mash.
Uncover for the final 25 minutes until the top is glossy and the pan juices taste rounded rather than wine-sharp.

note: A proper weekend braise: it is even better after 20 minutes resting in the warm pot.

name: Istanbul Prawn, Mussel & Bean Stew
hook: Tomato heat with briny shellfish

ingredients.name: lemon, half juiced and half wedged

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide pan, then soften onion and red pepper until the onion is shiny and the pepper has lost its raw crunch. Rushing this leaves hard, sweet chunks in an otherwise soft stew.
Stir in garlic, pepper paste and pul biber until the paste darkens a shade and stains the oil red. If it sits in a lump, the stew tastes harsh in pockets.
Add passata and 150 ml water, scrape the base clean, then simmer until the bubbles look thick and lazy rather than watery and sharp.
Fold in the beans and simmer until a few skins start to split; underheated beans stay separate and do not thicken the sauce.
Add the prawns in one layer and simmer gently until they curl into loose Cs and turn opaque. Tight Os mean they have gone bouncy and overcooked.
Stir in the cooked mussel meat only until piping hot; boiling it hard makes it shrink and taste tinny.
Finish with lemon juice and dill off the heat, then serve with lemon wedges. Dill boiled in the stew loses its bright, aniseed lift.

note: Use chilled or fully defrosted shellfish and keep it refrigerated until it goes into the pan.

name: Rose-Cardamom Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Soft wobble, rose, toasted pistachio

steps.t: Set a steamer over a low simmer, not a rolling boil. Violent steam riddles the custard with holes before the centre has set.
Warm the milk with sugar and cardamom until the sugar dissolves and the milk feels hot but not scalding. Boiling milk gives the eggs a cooked edge the moment they meet.
Whisk the eggs in a bowl just until no streaks remain; frothing them hard traps bubbles that set as pockmarks.
Pour the hot milk into the eggs slowly while whisking, then stir in rosewater and orange blossom water. Dumping it in at once scrambles the bottom of the bowl.
Strain into four small ramekins and cover each tightly with foil. Skipping the strain leaves white threads, and uncovered pots drip with watery condensation.
Steam gently until the edges are set and the centre gives a slow, soft wobble when nudged.
Rest off the heat for 8 minutes; cutting in straight away makes the custard weep around the spoon.
Spoon over honey and pistachios just before serving so the nuts stay crisp against the warm custard.

note: Serve warm for the cleanest rose aroma, or chill for a firmer make-ahead dessert.

name: Harissa Smoked Pork Couscous Pan
hook: Smoky, lemony, built for leftovers

steps.t: Put the lardons in a cold frying pan and set over medium heat so the fat renders before the edges scorch. Starting hot burns the outside while the centres stay chewy.
Add onion and carrot and cook until the onion turns glossy and the carrot softens into the fat. If the vegetables stay raw, the couscous tastes like a garnish rather than dinner.
Stir in harissa and ras el hanout until the pan smells smoky and the spice paste clings to the pork. Leaving it raw gives a dusty chilli taste.
Add passata, chickpeas, the crumbled stock cube and 250 ml boiling water, scraping the base until the red sauce looks even. Undissolved stock leaves salty bites.
Stir in the couscous, turn off the heat, cover tightly and leave it to swell until the grains are plump. A loose lid lets steam escape and leaves crunchy centres.
Fluff with a fork, not a spoon, so the grains separate instead of compacting into paste.
Fold through lemon zest and parsley, then serve with wedges. Adding them earlier mutes the fresh lift that balances the smoked pork.

note: Moroccan-spiced rather than traditional; smoked pork is used here as the cheap, smoky protein.

name: Yuzu Miso Butter Roasted Whole Crab
hook: Sweet crab under bubbling miso butter

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C. Put the crab belly-up on a board, twist off the legs and claws, then lift off the main shell; keep every drop of brown meat and juice in the shell because rinsing it away makes the butter taste flat.
Crack the claws and legs with the back of a heavy knife, just enough to open the shell. Do not smash them to shards or guests will be picking grit from the meat.
Mash the butter with miso, mirin, yuzu juice and ginger until glossy and even. If you leave streaks of miso, they scorch into salty patches under the grill heat.

Spoon half the miso butter into the crab shell with the brown meat, and rub the rest over the cracked legs and claws. Arrange everything in a roasting tin so the cut sides face up; hidden cuts steam instead of roast.
Roast until the butter is bubbling hard and the panko sprinkled over the shell turns pale gold at the edges.
Scatter with spring onions and sesame, then rest for 3 minutes so the butter thickens around the crab juices rather than running straight onto the plate.
Serve with lemon wedges and small forks, making sure the shell of brown meat sits in the centre; that is the warm, savoury dip for the sweet claw meat.

note: Buy a crab that is already cooked by the fishmonger; this recipe reheats and roasts it, rather than cooking a live crab.

name: Smoked Doenjang Breakfast Beans
hook: Oak smoke, soft beans, chilli warmth

ingredients.name: spring onions, whites and greens separated, sliced
tin butter beans, drained and rinsed

steps.t: Soak the oak chips in water while you start cooking; dry chips flare and make the beans taste like an ashtray rather than breakfast smoke.
Warm the oil in a small heavy pan and fry the spring onion whites until they smell sweet and the cut faces turn translucent. If they brown hard now, the paste will taste bitter.
Stir in doenjang and gochugaru for 30 seconds, pressing the paste into the oil until it darkens slightly and smells nutty; leave it clumped and the stew will have salty lumps.
Add the butter beans and stock, then simmer until the liquid looks creamy and coats the back of a spoon. Stir gently from the bottom so the beans thicken the sauce without collapsing into mash.

Set a small foil cup of drained wood chips in the pan, away from the beans. Heat until it begins to smoke, cover tightly, then turn the heat off; if the lid leaks, you will smoke the kitchen and not the beans.
Remove the smoking cup, fold in sesame oil and spinach, and stop as soon as the leaves slump glossy green. Cook them longer and the whole bowl turns dull and mineral.
Spoon over hot sourdough toast and finish with spring onion greens, keeping some sauce pooled around the bread so it softens at the edges but stays crisp in the middle.

note: Use a pan you can cover tightly, or seal the lid edge with foil for a cleaner smoke.

name: Lotus Leaf Steamed Pork Belly Parcels
hook: Silky pork wrapped in tea fragrance

ingredients.name: pork belly, skin on, cut into 2 cm slices

steps.t: Soak the lotus leaves in hot water until pliable and olive-green, then wipe both sides. If you fold them while brittle, they crack and the pork juices escape into the steamer.
Mix soy sauces, Shaoxing wine, hoisin, five-spice, sugar, sesame oil and cornflour into a shiny marinade. The cornflour must disappear fully or it cooks into chalky specks on the pork.
Coat the pork belly, ginger and spring onions in the marinade, turning every slice so the skin edge is covered too; dry exposed pork steams grey and plain.
Line a shallow heatproof bowl with overlapping lotus leaves, glossy side inward, then layer in the pork neatly. Keep the fattier edges facing up so they baste the leaner meat as they soften.
Fold the leaves over into a tight parcel and set the bowl in a steamer over steadily boiling water. Top up the kettle now; letting the pan boil dry gives scorched steam and tough edges.
Steam until a chopstick slides through the pork skin with only gentle resistance and the leaf smells like warm tea.
Rest the parcel for 10 minutes before opening at the table. Open it too soon and the sauce is thin and furious; rested, it clings glossily to each slice.

note: Lotus leaves are available dried from Chinese supermarkets; banana leaf works, but gives a different, greener aroma.

name: Coal-Grilled Huevos with Nopal Salad
hook: Jammy eggs, charred cactus, lime

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are covered with grey ash; cooking over flames blackens the nopales before their slippery centre has a chance to dry out.
Brush the nopales, tomatoes and jalapeño with a little oil and season with salt. Keep the tomatoes on a grill tray or skewers, because once they split they will drop straight through the bars.
Grill the nopales until they show dark stripes and the cut edges stop weeping clear gel. Turn them only when they release easily; forcing them early tears the surface.
Grill the tomatoes and jalapeño until the tomato skins blister and the chilli softens with black freckles, not until everything collapses into sauce.

Set a small cast-iron pan over a cooler part of the grill with the remaining oil, crack in the eggs and cover with a lid or metal bowl. Cook until the whites are set and the yolks still wobble when the pan is nudged; fierce heat gives rubbery skirts and raw tops.
Slice the nopales and jalapeño, then toss with tomatoes, red onion, lime juice and coriander. Taste before adding more salt, as cactus seems bland until the lime wakes it up.
Warm the tortillas quickly over the coals until they puff in spots, then plate with the salad and eggs on top. If the tortillas go crisp, they will crack instead of scooping the yolk.

note: If fresh nopales are hard to find, use thick courgette planks; the dish becomes less traditional but keeps the same light, charred feel.

name: Lemony Courgette Caper Lathes
hook: Cool ribbons with sharp island bite

steps.t: Shave the courgettes lengthways into wide ribbons, stopping when you reach the seedy core. If you use the watery centre, the platter floods before it reaches the table.
Toss the ribbons with salt and leave until they bend softly but still look bright, then drain off the greenish liquid. Skip this and the dressing slides straight off.
Whisk lemon zest, lemon juice, olive oil, garlic and oregano until the dressing turns cloudy and smells sharp. If the garlic sits in one clump, someone gets a raw, hot mouthful.
Pat the courgettes lightly with kitchen paper, then dress them with your hands so every ribbon is glossed without being crushed.
Fold through capers, torn olives and mint. Add the mint last, because heavy mixing bruises it black and muddy.
Scatter broken barley rusks on the platter and pile the courgettes over them just before serving. Put them in too early and they turn to paste; a few crisp corners are the point.

note: This is intentionally protein-free and vegetable-led, built for a table of olives, breads and other small plates.

name: Crisp Lahori Mackerel Fry
hook: Crackly masala skin, sharp lemon heat

steps.t: Pat the mackerel very dry, especially the skin; if it goes into the masala damp, the coating steams off instead of frying crisp.
Mix gram flour, rice flour, spices, salt, lemon juice and ginger-garlic paste into a rough paste. It should smear like wet sand; if it is runny, it will slide into the pan and burn.
Rub the paste over the fish and leave it while the pan heats. Do not marinate for ages: lemon will tighten oily fish and make it taste chalky.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of flour fizzes straight away. Lay the fillets skin-side down, away from you; crowding the pan drops the heat and gives you soft skin.
Fry until the edges go lace-brown and the skin feels rigid when nudged, then turn once. If you keep flipping, the crust tears before it sets.
Cook the flesh side just until the thickest part flakes and looks opaque, then lift onto kitchen paper. Leaving mackerel in the hot pan after this makes the oil taste heavy and metallic.
Scatter with sliced onion and a squeeze of lemon at the table; the raw crunch cuts the fish oil rather than fighting it.

note: Serve with warm chapati or a bagged salad for a properly fast dinner.

name: Three-Day Pickled Tofu Bún Chay
hook: Cool tang, herbs, peanut crunch

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in a clean tea towel, weight it with a plate and tins, and press until it feels dense rather than spongey. If you skip this, the pickle flavours sit on the outside only.
Cut the tofu into 2 cm blocks and pack into a clean lidded container. Keep the pieces even so they pickle at the same pace; ragged crumbs turn sour and woolly.
Heat rice vinegar, 300 ml water, sugar and soy just until the sugar dissolves, then cool until lukewarm. Pouring hot brine over tofu gives it a rubbery edge.

Cover the tofu with brine, chill it, and turn the container when you remember. After two days it should smell sharp, savoury and clean; any fizz or mustiness means it has gone wrong and should be discarded.
Add daikon and carrot to a bowl with 120 ml of the tofu brine and leave until bendy but still snappy. If they collapse completely, the salad loses its bite.
Soak or boil the vermicelli according to the packet, then rinse under cold water until the strands feel slippery and cool. Warm noodles drink the dressing and clump into a block.

Whisk lime juice with 5 tbsp tofu brine, chilli and 2 tbsp water. Toss noodles, pickles, cucumber, herbs and tofu gently, then finish with peanuts; heavy mixing breaks the tofu you spent all weekend seasoning.

note: Start on Friday night for Sunday lunch; the tofu keeps refrigerated for three days once pickled.

name: Rosemary Lamb, Lentil and Ricotta Al Forno
hook: Lean lamb, molten ricotta, deep tomato

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan and put a deep baking dish in to warm. A cold dish makes the lamb leak water before it has a chance to roast.
Add oil, lamb, garlic, rosemary and salt to the hot dish, breaking the meat into small nuggets. Roast until the top smells savoury and the corners are browned, not grey.
Stir in lentils, passata, stock and courgette, scraping the browned lamb from the base. If the lentils are left in dry patches, they bake into hard little pebbles.
Cover tightly with foil and bake until the lentils are swollen and the sauce bubbles thickly at the edges. Loose foil lets the liquid evaporate before the lentils soften.
Fold in the spinach while the dish is still steaming. Stop as soon as it wilts; overworking turns the bake muddy and green.
Dot over ricotta, sprinkle with Parmesan and bake uncovered until the cheese has golden freckles and the sauce no longer looks soupy.
Rest for a few minutes before scooping. If you serve it straight from the oven, the protein-rich sauce runs across the plate instead of sitting like a proper bake.

note: Built for protein: lamb, lentils and ricotta make it filling without needing pasta.

name: Saffron Elaichi Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Silky wobble, caramel warmth

steps.t: Put four ramekins in a steamer basket to check they fit with the lid closed. If steam cannot circulate, the custards set at the edges and stay liquid in the middle.
Melt the caramel sugar in a small pan until amber and smelling like toasted honey, then divide between the ramekins. Take it off before it smokes; burnt caramel will bully the saffron.
Warm the milk with saffron just until it steams at the surface, then let it stand so the colour blooms. Boiling milk dulls the perfume and can scramble the eggs later.
Whisk eggs, condensed milk, cardamom and rosewater gently, then whisk in the warm saffron milk. Keep the whisk low; froth gives pockmarked custards.
Strain into the ramekins over the caramel. Do not skip the sieve, because even tiny egg threads steam into rubbery flecks.
Steam over a low, steady simmer until the centres wobble like soft jelly and a knife near the edge comes out clean. Fierce boiling makes holes and a curdled texture.
Cool, then chill until the caramel loosens into a sauce. Run a thin knife round each custard and turn out; forcing it while warm tears the sides.
Finish with pistachios just before serving so they stay crisp against the soft custard.

note: A make-ahead dessert with Indian mithai flavours and a classic steamed custard texture.

name: Red Curry Chicken and Potato Stew
hook: Coconut broth, soft potatoes, chilli hum
