steps.t: Heat the oil in a saucepan and fry the curry paste until it darkens slightly and smells roasted. If it only warms through, the stew tastes flat and pasty.
Add the onion and stir until the slices soften at the edges. Letting them catch now makes the coconut broth taste bitter, not smoky.
Pour in coconut milk plus 400 ml water, then crumble in the stock cube. Stir until the paste dissolves fully; red lumps on the spoon mean red lumps in the stew.
Add chicken thighs, potatoes and carrots, keeping everything just submerged. Simmer gently, not violently, or the chicken tightens before the potatoes cook.
Lift out the chicken when it is cooked through and the meat pulls easily from the bone. Strip the meat with two forks and discard the bones; leaving bones in a student bowl is cheap in the wrong way.

Return the chicken with fish sauce and sugar, then simmer until the potatoes crush slightly against the spoon and thicken the broth. If the stew looks oily and thin, it needs a few more minutes, not more coconut milk.
Serve with lime wedges and squeeze at the table. Adding lime too early makes the coconut taste sharp and split.

note: Potatoes make it filling without rice, but leftover rice turns it into a bigger second meal.

name: Hot Ghee Paneer Snow Chaat
hook: Warm spice, cold cream, buttery paneer

steps.t: Take the paneer out first and let it lose its fridge chill while you prep; ice-cold paneer makes the hot ghee seize on the surface instead of softening the edges.
Whisk the yoghurt with lime juice and a good pinch of salt until smooth; if it looks grainy, stop whisking and loosen with a teaspoon of water rather than beating it thinner.
Spoon the yoghurt onto a shallow bowl, tumble over the paneer, raisins and coriander, and leave the top uneven so the spiced ghee has places to pool.
Warm the ghee with the walnuts and cumin over medium heat until the nuts smell toasted and the cumin crackles, not smokes; burnt cumin will turn the whole bowl harsh.

Pull the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chilli and garam masala, then pour it straight over the paneer while it is still foaming; if the chilli hits a smoking pan it will go bitter in seconds.
Eat immediately, while the paneer is barely warmed at the edges and creamy in the centre.

note: Comforting rather than heavy: the paneer stays essentially uncooked, with the winter warmth coming from the hot spiced ghee.

name: Bangkok Dawn Mackerel Krapao Rice
hook: Charred fish, basil steam, morning fire

ingredients.name: mackerel fillets, pin-boned and cut into 3 cm pieces
palm sugar or light brown sugar
holy basil or Thai basil leaves

steps.t: Break the cold rice up with your fingers before the wok goes on; clumps stay cold inside and make you stir too long, which shreds the fish later.
Mix the fish sauce, oyster sauce and sugar in a small bowl until the sugar mostly dissolves; hunting for bottles over a smoking wok is how breakfast burns.
Crush the garlic and chillies to a rough paste, not a purée; too fine and it catches before the beans have even hit the pan.

Heat a wok until a drop of water vanishes on contact, add the oil, then lay in the mackerel skin-side down. Leave it until the skin blisters and the thickest flakes turn opaque, then lift it out gently.

Throw in the chilli-garlic paste and beans, toss for a few seconds, then add the rice and sauce. Keep everything moving over fierce heat until the grains look glossy and start jumping; if they sit still, they steam and go soft.
Return the mackerel with the basil and fold only twice or three times, just until the basil collapses and the fish is hot through; over-mixing breaks it into paste. Serve with lime.

note: Use cooked rice from the fridge: dry grains fry hard and fast, which suits oily mackerel.

name: Miso-Lacquered Saba Negiyaki
hook: Glossy fish, smoke-sweet spring onions

ingredients.name: saba or mackerel fillets, skin on and pin-boned

steps.t: Run your fingers over the mackerel and pull any pin bones, then pat the skin very dry; damp skin welds itself to the griddle and tears before it crisps.
Mix the miso, mirin, soy, sugar and ginger, then spread it thinly over the flesh side only. Leave it just long enough to season, not cure hard.
Heat a ridged griddle until properly hot, rub the spring onions with sesame oil, and griddle them until they soften with dark stripes and sweet, smoky edges.
Scrape any thick blobs of glaze from the fish, then lay the fillets skin-side down and press lightly for the first few seconds; if the skin arches away from the pan, it cooks patchy.

Turn the fish once, brush on a thin final slick of glaze, and cook until the flesh is opaque at the thickest point and flakes under gentle pressure; black, sticky patches mean the glaze is too thick or the heat too savage.
Plate the saba over the charred spring onions, scatter sesame seeds and serve with lemon wedges for guests to squeeze at the table.

note: The trick is restraint with the miso glaze: a thin lacquer looks elegant and does not scorch.

name: Crisp Dubu Yuja Cucumber Plate
hook: Cool cucumber under crackling tofu

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in kitchen paper, weight it lightly, and let it shed water; if you skip this, the starch turns gummy and spits in the pan.
Shave the cucumber into ribbons, salt lightly, and leave it in a bowl while you fry; it should bend and glisten, not collapse into watery threads.
Stir the soy, rice vinegar, yuja-cheong and gochugaru until glossy, then fold in the spring onions; undissolved yuja sits in sweet lumps instead of dressing the plate.
Cut the tofu into thick rectangles and dust every side with potato starch, tapping off the snowy excess; loose starch burns in the oil and tastes dusty.
Heat the oil in a frying pan and shallow fry the tofu until the bottoms are crisp and pale gold, then turn carefully and repeat; moving it too early rips off the crust.
Drain the tofu on a rack, not paper, so steam can escape; trapped steam softens the crackle you just made.
Squeeze the cucumber gently, toss it with half the dressing, then top with tofu, the remaining dressing and sesame seeds. Serve while the tofu is hot against the chilled cucumber.

note: Lightness comes from contrast: crisp tofu, cold cucumber and a sharp citrus-soy dressing.

name: Black-Vinegar Pickled Cumin Lamb
hook: Cold slices, smoky cumin bite

steps.t: Pat the lamb dry, rub it with Shaoxing wine and salt, and let it sit while you make the pickle; wet lamb steams grey instead of searing cleanly.
Stir the black vinegar, soy, sugar and garlic until the sugar dissolves, then add the smashed cucumber and spring onions; if the cucumber is sliced too neatly, the dressing slides off it.
Heat the oil in a small frying pan until shimmering, sear the lamb on all sides, and cook until the centre reaches 63°C before resting; guessing here risks either raw cold slices or dry woolly meat.
Rest the lamb on a board so the juices settle clear rather than flooding the vinegar bowl.
In the same pan, toast the cumin seeds and chilli flakes just until the cumin smells smoky and the oil stains red; black specks mean bitterness, so pull it off early.
Slice the rested lamb thinly across the grain and lay it in the vinegar pickle for a short, sharp soak; thick slices stay bland in the middle.
Lift the lamb, cucumber and spring onions onto a small platter, spoon over the cumin chilli oil, and serve cool or at room temperature.

note: This is a cooked lamb dish finished like a pickle: sharp black vinegar, crunchy cucumber and warm cumin oil.

name: Bourbon Cider Lamb Shanks with Winter Roots
hook: Sticky gravy, spoon-tender lamb, cold-night warmth

steps.t: Heat the oven to 160°C. Season the lamb and dust it lightly with flour; if the flour sits in clumps, it will scorch before the meat browns.
Brown the shanks in the oil in a heavy casserole until the knobbly edges are deep chestnut, turning patiently; pale meat gives you thin, flat gravy.
Lift out the lamb, add onions, carrots and parsnips, and cook until the onion edges turn golden and the pan smells sweet, not raw; rush this and the braise tastes boiled.
Stir in the garlic for 30 seconds, then pour in cider and bourbon, scraping until the sticky brown layer dissolves; leave that layer behind and you leave the flavour behind.
Add stock, maple syrup and thyme, return the lamb, then cover and braise in the oven until a fork twists into the meat with almost no resistance.
Uncover and cook until the gravy clings glossily to the back of a spoon; if it still runs like stock, the dish will feel watery on the plate.
Rest the shanks in the sauce for 10 minutes, skim excess fat from the surface, then serve with the roots and plenty of gravy.

note: Best with buttered mash or cornbread to catch the cider-bourbon gravy.

name: Sunrise Criollo Paneer Guiso
hook: Tomato-rich stew with soft-set eggs

ingredients.name: ají molido or mild chilli flakes

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion and red pepper until the pepper bends easily and the onion is translucent; crunchy onion will stay harsh in the finished stew.
Add garlic, ají molido and oregano, stirring until the pan smells toasty and sweet; let the garlic catch and it turns bitter fast.
Pour in the tomatoes, add the potatoes and 250 ml water, then season. Simmer with the lid ajar until the potato corners are tender but not collapsing.
Fold in the paneer and simmer gently until the cubes swell slightly and take on the red sauce; a hard boil makes them rubbery at the edges.
Make four hollows, crack in the eggs, cover and cook until the whites are just set and the yolks still wobble under the lid steam.
Finish with parsley and red wine vinegar, tasting for salt after the paneer has seasoned the stew; adding salt too early can push it over.
Spoon into warm shallow bowls, keeping each egg intact so the yolk breaks into the guiso at the table.

note: Serve with toast or warm rolls for a proper slow breakfast.

name: Bahia Coconut Roast Chicken with Lime Farofa
hook: Golden skin, coconut juices, bright crunch

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C. Pat the chicken very dry, especially around the thighs; damp skin steams and never reaches that lacquered roast finish.

Mix coconut milk, lime zest, half the lime juice, garlic, dendê oil, paprika, cumin, chilli and salt. Rub a little under the breast skin and the rest over the bird; tearing the skin loses the self-basting pocket.
Set the orange slices in a roasting tin and place the chicken on top, breast-side up. Roast until the skin starts to blister and turn deep gold at the wing tips.
Lower the oven to 180°C and roast, basting with the coconut pan juices, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 74°C and the juices run clear, not pink.
Move the chicken to a board and rest it uncovered; cover it tightly and the crisp skin softens in its own steam.
Meanwhile melt the butter in a frying pan, add cassava flour and stir until it smells nutty and looks sandy-golden, not grey and dusty.
Stir coriander and remaining lime juice into the farofa, carve the chicken, and spoon the coconut roasting juices over the meat just before serving.

note: If you cannot find dendê oil, olive oil works; the flavour will be softer but still good.

name: Lahori Smoked Prawn Kachumber Plates
hook: Charcoal perfume, cool crunch, lime heat

steps.t: Toss the prawns with oil, Kashmiri chilli, cumin and salt. Keep them cold while you prepare the salad; warm raw prawns shed water and cook unevenly.
Mix cucumber, tomatoes, red onion, lime juice, mint and coriander in a bowl, then chill it; if it sits warm, the tomatoes collapse and flood the plate.
Sear the prawns in a hot frying pan in a single layer until they curl into loose Cs and turn opaque right through; tight Os mean they have gone tough.
Transfer the cooked prawns to a heatproof bowl. Heat the charcoal over a gas flame or with a kitchen torch until one edge glows red and ashy; black unlit charcoal gives soot, not clean smoke.
Set a small foil cup in the prawn bowl, place the hot charcoal inside, drizzle on a few drops of oil, and cover immediately so the smoke stays trapped around the cooked prawns.
Remove the charcoal cup, sprinkle the prawns with chaat masala, and toss gently; scraping the ash into the food will ruin the clean lime finish.
Pile the cold kachumber onto plates and top with the warm smoked prawns, serving straight away before the salad wilts.

note: Use a heatproof bowl and tongs for the charcoal; the prawns are fully cooked before smoking.

name: Saigon Steamed Paneer Cups with Ginger Nuoc Cham
hook: Soft curds, sharp dressing, herb lift

steps.t: Line a steamer basket with pak choi leaves, leaving gaps for steam; a fully covered base traps water and makes the paneer soggy rather than plush.
Sit the paneer cubes on the leaves with a little space between them. Steam over lively simmering water until the paneer feels hot and slightly springy, not dry at the corners.
Meanwhile stir fish sauce, lime juice, sugar, garlic, ginger, chilli and 2 tbsp warm water until the sugar fully dissolves; gritty sugar sinks and gives harsh final spoonfuls.
Lift the steamer lid away from you so condensation does not drip back over the paneer; excess water dilutes the dressing on contact.
Spoon the ginger nuoc cham over the hot paneer and pak choi, letting it run into the steamer juices for a minute so the cubes drink a little seasoning.
Scatter with spring onions, herbs and crushed peanuts just before serving; add them early and the herbs blacken against the heat.
Serve as small shared cups or on one platter, with extra dressing at the side for spooning over each piece.

note: For a vegetarian version, replace fish sauce with light soy sauce plus a pinch of salt.

name: Istanbul Pepper Hake Kavurma
hook: Flash-hot peppers, pearly fish, lemon smoke

ingredients.name: skinless hake fillets, cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Pat the hake very dry and season it with salt; if it goes into the pan wet, it steams and flakes before it ever sears.

Heat a wide frying pan or wok until a drop of water skitters away, then add the olive oil, onion and pepper. Stir-fry hard until the pepper skins blister in spots and the onion edges catch brown, not until they collapse soft.
Add the garlic, pul biber and cumin and toss for just long enough to smell toasted; if the garlic goes chestnut-brown here, it will taste bitter by the end.
Push the vegetables aside, add the butter, then lay in the hake in one layer. Leave it alone until the underside turns opaque halfway up the pieces; poking early tears it into flakes.
Add the tomatoes and sumac, then fold everything with a wide spatula until the fish is just opaque and the tomatoes have slumped but still hold their skins.
Take the pan off the heat, shower with parsley and lemon juice, and serve at once; left sitting in the hot pan, the hake carries on cooking and turns cottony.

note: Serve with warm flatbread or quick bulgur if you want the juices caught.

name: Sumac-Griddled Mushroom Musakhan Flatbreads
hook: Smoky mushrooms over sweet sumac onions

ingredients.name: mixed oyster and chestnut mushrooms, torn chunky

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, salt, 1 tbsp olive oil and 220 ml lukewarm water into a soft dough; if it feels stiff now, the flatbreads will griddle like crackers instead of puffing.
Knead until smooth and elastic, then cover and leave until doubled and domed; under-risen dough stays dense in the centre no matter how hot the griddle is.
Meanwhile cook the onions in 3 tbsp olive oil with a pinch of salt over low heat until bronze, jammy and sweet, stirring whenever the edges threaten to scorch.
Stir 2 tbsp sumac and the allspice into the onions off the heat; frying the sumac hard dulls its bright, lemony snap.
Toss the torn mushrooms with 1 tbsp olive oil, 0.5 tbsp sumac and salt, then leave them to season while the dough finishes rising; salting too late leaves bland, watery centres.

Divide the dough into 4 balls, roll into thin ovals and griddle on a smoking-hot dry griddle until dark blisters appear and the bread puffs in pockets; if the pan is only warm, the bread dries before it chars.
Griddle the mushrooms in batches until the ridges are mahogany and the torn edges look crisp; crowding the pan makes them leak and stew grey.
Spread each flatbread with sumac onions, pile on mushrooms, drizzle with tahini loosened with lemon juice and water, then finish with pine nuts and parsley.

note: Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan until patchy gold; they burn fast once fragrant.

name: Crisp Chermoula Beef Kefta Coins
hook: Lean beef, crackled edges, cool yoghurt

steps.t: Mix the beef, egg, chickpea flour, garlic, coriander stalks, ras el hanout, paprika, lemon zest and salt with your hand until tacky; if you barely mix it, the coins split in the oil.
Shape into 12 flat coins about 1.5 cm thick, pressing the edges smooth; ragged edges burn before the middle cooks through.
Stir the yoghurt with the squeezed cucumber, harissa, half the lemon juice, chopped coriander leaves and salt; watery cucumber makes the sauce loose enough to run off the plate.

Heat the olive oil in a wide frying pan until a small pinch of mixture sizzles immediately, then lay in half the kefta with space between them; a crowded pan drops in heat and gives you soft meatballs, not crust.
Shallow fry until the underside is deep brown and crisp, then turn once; repeated flipping knocks off the crust you are trying to build.
Cook the second side until the coins feel firm and the centre is piping hot with no pink raw mince remaining; if in doubt, cut one open rather than guessing.
Rest the kefta on kitchen paper for 3 minutes, then squeeze over the remaining lemon and serve with the cool yoghurt; serving straight from the oil makes the crust taste greasy.

note: Add a bagged salad or microwaved lentils if you want a larger post-training plate.

name: Seville Steam-Set Caramel Flan
hook: Silky custard under bitter amber caramel

steps.t: Put 100 g sugar in a small pan with 2 tbsp water and cook without stirring until it turns clear amber, swirling only when the edges colour; stirring makes crystals that turn the caramel sandy.
Pour the caramel into a 1 litre heatproof pudding basin or six ramekins and tilt to coat the base; wait too long and it sets in a thick puddle instead of a thin bitter layer.
Warm the milk with the orange zest and cinnamon until steam rises and the edge trembles, then take it off the heat; boiling the milk gives the custard a cooked-skin flavour.
Whisk the eggs, yolks, remaining 60 g sugar, vanilla and salt until combined but not foamy; froth leaves little bubbles in the finished flan.

Strain the warm milk slowly into the eggs, whisking constantly, then strain again into the caramel-lined dish; skipping the second strain leaves chalazae and zest threads in a dessert that should cut clean.
Cover tightly with foil and steam gently over barely simmering water until the centre wobbles like soft jelly, not liquid; a hard boil makes tunnels and rubbery edges.
Cool, then chill until thoroughly cold before unmoulding; warm flan breaks at the caramel line and spills instead of sliding out glossy.

note: Run a thin knife round the edge and dip the base briefly in warm water before turning out.

name: Dijon Tofu Potato Gratin
hook: Creamy mustard potatoes, golden tofu corners

ingredients.name: firm tofu, drained and torn into chunks

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200°C fan and oil a medium baking dish; an unheated oven delays the potatoes and leaves the tofu drying out on top.
Toss the potato slices, onion, garlic, thyme, salt and pepper directly in the dish, separating the slices with your fingers; stuck-together potato stacks stay hard in the middle.
Whisk the milk, crème fraîche and Dijon until smooth, then pour it over the potatoes and shake the dish so the sauce slips between the layers.
Cover tightly with foil and bake until a knife meets only slight resistance in the centre; loose foil lets the liquid evaporate before the potatoes soften.
Toss the torn tofu with a pinch of salt and nestle it into the top, leaving craggy corners exposed; bury it completely and it turns pale and spongey instead of golden.
Scatter over the Emmental and bake uncovered until the top is bubbling, the cheese is freckled brown and the tofu edges are crisp.
Rest for 5 minutes before scooping; if you serve it straight away, the mustard cream runs to the bottom of the plate.

note: A green salad with vinegar dressing cuts through the gratin if budget allows.

name: Winter Black-Vinegar Beef with Pickled Mustard Greens
hook: Warm vinegar, soft beef, winter-deep savour.

steps.t: Rinse the pickled mustard greens for 10 seconds, then squeeze them hard; soaking them longer steals the sour bite the beef needs.

Put the brisket in a snug pan with the ginger, garlic, star anise, soy sauce and enough water to cover by 2 cm. Bring just to a shiver, not a rolling boil, or the meat tightens and the broth turns muddy.
Cover and simmer until a skewer slides through the thickest part with almost no push; if it still grips, the slices will chew like rope.
Lift the beef out and rest it for 10 minutes, then slice across the grain into thick coins; cutting with the grain makes even tender brisket stringy.
Boil the noodles until springy in the centre, then rinse briefly under hot water; cold rinsing makes this winter dish feel flat and greasy.
Bubble 120 ml of the beef broth with the black vinegar, brown sugar, chilli oil and mustard greens until glossy and sharp-smelling; if it tastes dull, add a splash more vinegar before dressing.
Toss the hot noodles through the dressing, lay over the beef and spoon on extra broth. Finish with spring onions so their bite stays clean, not stewed.

note: Comforting like a braise, but lifted by sour greens and black vinegar.

name: Chorizo Salsa Verde Breakfast Tortilla Bake
hook: Crisp edges, runny yolks, bright salsa.

ingredients.name: small corn tortillas, cut into wedges

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan and oil a medium baking dish; a cold dish steams the tortillas before they can crisp.
Scatter in the tortilla wedges and bake until the points curl and the edges look toasted, not pale and leathery.
Crumble over the pork chorizo and add the onion, breaking the meat into small nuggets so no raw pockets hide underneath.
Bake until the chorizo is sizzling, the onion has slumped and there is no pink pork visible when you nudge the thickest bits apart.
Stir in the black beans and salsa verde, keeping some tortilla corners above the sauce; bury them all and you lose the breakfast crunch.
Make four hollows, crack in the eggs and sprinkle over the cheese. Bake until the whites are set but the yolks still wobble when the dish is tapped.
Rest for 3 minutes, then top with avocado, coriander and lime; cutting straight away sends the yolks racing into the corners.

note: Everything happens in the baking dish, including cooking the pork safely.

name: Aegean Tofu Stifado with Pearl Onions
hook: Wine-dark onions, silken tofu, quiet drama.

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in a clean tea towel and weight it lightly; skip this and the braise tastes watery no matter how good the sauce is.
Cut the tofu into large blocks and brown them in olive oil until the faces are honey-gold and firm; pale tofu will shed crumbs into the stifado.
Lift out the tofu, add the pearl onions and cook until their skins blister in patches; if they only steam, the finished sauce will taste boiled.
Add the garlic for 30 seconds, then pour in the red wine and scrape the pan until the sticky brown bits dissolve; leave them stuck and you leave flavour behind.
Stir in passata, vinegar, cinnamon, bay and oregano, then return the tofu. The liquid should come halfway up the blocks, not drown them.
Cover and braise gently until the onions are spoon-tender and the sauce clings in slow streaks; a hard boil breaks the tofu and turns the wine harsh.
Fold in the olives and rest uncovered for 10 minutes so the sauce settles glossy around the tofu. Scatter with parsley just before serving.

note: Serve in a wide shallow dish so the tofu blocks look deliberate and generous.

name: Summer Lamb Türlü with Courgettes and Dill
hook: Tomato broth, tender lamb, garden freshness.

steps.t: Pat the lamb dry and season it; wet cubes spit, steam and never give the stew its clean savoury base.
Brown the lamb in olive oil in one layer until the corners are chestnut-coloured, working in batches if needed; crowding the pan makes grey meat.
Add the onion and cook until it turns translucent and sweet-smelling, then add the garlic and tomato paste; raw paste leaves a tinny edge.
Stir in the grated tomatoes and pul biber, scraping the base until the sauce looks rust-red and loose.
Add 300 ml water, cover and simmer gently until the lamb yields when pressed with a spoon; a furious boil toughens lean summer cuts.
Add the green beans and courgettes and simmer uncovered until just tender, with the courgettes still holding their shape; cook them to collapse and the stew turns heavy.
Finish with dill and a squeeze of lemon off the heat, because boiled dill tastes grassy and dull rather than bright.

note: Light enough for warm weather, especially with yoghurt and flatbread.

name: Whole-Roasted Cauliflower with Lemon Chickpeas
hook: Golden cauliflower, creamy tahini, crunchy chickpeas.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan and trim the cauliflower stalk so it sits flat; cut too deeply and the head falls apart before it reaches the table.
Lower the whole cauliflower into salted boiling water until a knife enters the stalk with slight resistance; roasting from raw leaves a burnt outside and chalky heart.
Drain well and steam-dry upside down for 5 minutes, because trapped water stops the spices clinging and makes the tray soggy.
Mix olive oil with cumin, coriander and Aleppo pepper, then rub it all over the cauliflower and chickpeas; dry patches roast pale instead of turning fragrant.
Roast the cauliflower in the centre of a tray with chickpeas scattered around until the crown is deep gold and the chickpeas rattle when shaken.
Whisk tahini with lemon juice, garlic, pomegranate molasses and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce; add the water slowly or it seizes into paste.
Spoon tahini onto a platter, set the cauliflower on top and tumble the chickpeas around it. Finish with lemon zest, parsley and pine nuts while everything is still warm.

note: Bring it out whole, then carve at the table for mezze-style sharing.

name: Coal-Grilled Pork Lemon-Sage Spiedini
hook: Smoke, lemon, crackling sage

steps.t: Light a small chimney of charcoal first; you want a tight bed of coals with a pale ash skin, not tall flames that will scorch the pancetta before the pork cooks.

Cut the pork into 3 cm chunks, then toss with grated garlic, olive oil, crushed fennel, salt and the finely grated zest of half the lemon. If the pieces are much smaller, they dry out before they char.
Thread the pork onto metal skewers, tucking pancetta folds and sage leaves between the pieces. Keep everything snug but not compressed, or the inner faces steam instead of grilling.
Rake the coals into one even layer and grill the skewers, turning when the pancetta edges fizz and the sage goes dark green and crisp rather than black.

Move any aggressively flaring skewers to the cooler edge and keep turning until the pork feels just firm and the thickest piece reaches 63°C, then rest it; skipping the rest leaves the juices on the board.

Halve the tomatoes, dress them with a squeeze of lemon and a spoon of the pork resting juices, then pile with rocket. Serve the skewers over the salad so the hot fat wilts the leaves slightly, not into a soggy heap.

note: Fast if the pork is cut evenly and the coal bed is small, hot and controlled.

name: Kokum-Cured Scallop Bhel with Green Mango
hook: Cold scallop, sour crunch, chilli

steps.t: Rinse the kokum, cover with 200 ml just-boiled water, cool, then chill overnight. If the infusion is warm when it touches the scallops, their texture turns woolly rather than cleanly cured.
Simmer the tamarind paste, dates and 120 ml water until the dates collapse into a glossy chutney; stop while it still drops from a spoon, because a stiff paste will clump through the bhel.
Keep the scallops fridge-cold, remove any tough side muscles, and slice each one into three coins. They should smell sweet and sea-clean; if they smell sour or ammoniacal, do not serve them raw.
Toss the green mango, red onion, chilli, juice of one lime and chaat masala, then leave it until the onion loses its raw bite but still snaps.

Strain the kokum infusion and mix it with the juice of the second lime. Lay the scallop slices in it for just long enough that the rims turn satin-opaque while the centres stay translucent; longer curing makes them chalky.
Spoon tamarind-date chutney onto cold plates, lift the scallops out of the cure, and season them with a pinch more chaat masala. Do not pour over the cure or the plate will taste thin and metallic.

Fold puffed rice, coriander and mint through the mango mixture at the very last second, then scatter it over the scallops. If the puffed rice waits in the dressing, the whole point of the bhel disappears.

note: Use only scallops sold for raw eating, keep them below 4°C, and serve immediately after curing.

name: Steamed Black Sesame Purin with Kinako Dust
hook: Silky custard, toasted sesame hush

steps.t: Warm the milk, cream, sugar, sesame paste and salt until the sugar dissolves and the liquid smells nutty; do not boil it, or the eggs will scramble on contact.
Whisk the eggs just until the whites disappear, then slowly pour in the warm sesame milk while whisking. Be gentle: froth becomes pockmarks in the finished purin.
Strain the custard through a fine sieve into four heatproof cups, then skim off any bubbles. Unstrained sesame flecks sink into gritty patches rather than a smooth set.
Cover each cup tightly with foil and set them in a steamer over barely trembling water. A rolling boil is the enemy here; it makes the custard honeycombed instead of silken.
Steam until the edges are set and the centres wobble as one soft piece when nudged, not as liquid ripples.
Lift the cups out and cool for 15 minutes before chilling. Put hot cups straight into the fridge and they sweat water back onto the custard.
Chill until cold and settled, then dust with kinako just before serving. Dusting early turns the kinako into damp beige paste.

note: A calm steamer gives the glossy, spoon-sinking texture.

name: Crisp Oyster Mushroom Kimchi Jeon
hook: Frilly mushrooms, spicy brittle edges

steps.t: Tear the oyster mushrooms into long strips, keeping some frilly edges. Knife-cut chunks sit heavy in the batter and never crisp properly.
Squeeze the kimchi lightly over a bowl and keep the juices; soaking-wet kimchi makes the pancake gummy, but completely dry kimchi tastes flat.
Mix flour, potato starch, egg, ice-cold water, gochugaru and 2 tablespoons kimchi juice into a loose batter. Stop while a few tiny lumps remain, because overmixing makes it bready.
Fold in the mushrooms, kimchi and spring onions until everything is just coated. If batter pools in the bowl, leave some behind rather than frying a stodgy centre.
Heat half the oil in a frying pan and spread in half the mixture as a thin, ragged pancake. Press the mushrooms down so the edges touch the pan; piled-up mushrooms steam instead of crisping.
Fry until the underside is deep golden with lace-brown edges, then flip and cook the second side until it taps crisp with the spatula.
Repeat with the remaining oil and batter, then cut into wedges and serve with soy sauce for dipping. Stack the wedges only at the table, or their own steam softens the crust.

note: Potato starch is the cheap shortcut to a shattering edge.

name: Chapa Mandioca with Winter Couve
hook: Buttery cassava, smoky greens, lime heat

ingredients.name: peeled cassava, cut into thick chips
butternut squash, peeled and cut into 2 cm wedges
cavolo nero or spring greens, shredded

steps.t: Boil the cassava in well-salted water until a knife slides through the thickest piece with no chalky core; undercook it now and it will stay woody however hard you griddle it later.
Add the squash wedges for the final 8 minutes, lifting them out when the edges are tender but not collapsing; if they go mushy they will smear across the chapa instead of charring.
Drain everything thoroughly and steam-dry on the tray for 5 minutes; wet cassava spits and stews, so wait until the surfaces look matte rather than shiny.

Heat a large griddle or heavy frying pan until a drop of water skips across it, then add the oil and cassava in one layer; crowding the pan gives you pale softness, not the deep bronze crust you want.

Turn the cassava and squash only when the contact sides are freckled dark brown, then add butter, garlic, paprika and chilli; if the garlic goes in too early it burns bitter before the roots are crisp.
Fold in the shredded greens and toss until they turn glossy and collapse at the edges but keep a little chew; take them too far and the whole dish tastes boiled.
Finish with lime zest, lime juice and coriander off the heat, tasting for salt; boiling the lime on the griddle flattens its brightness.

note: Cassava is also sold frozen in many European supermarkets; boil it from frozen until fully tender.

name: Lahori Lacy Masala Eggs
hook: Crisp skirts, jammy yolks, spiced butter

ingredients.name: small red onion, very finely sliced
small tomato, deseeded and finely chopped

steps.t: Crack the eggs into two small bowls, two per bowl, so they slide in cleanly; cracking straight into hot oil leaves shell hunting while the whites overcook.
Heat the oil and butter in a wide frying pan until the butter foam thins and the fat shimmers; if it is only warm, the eggs absorb grease instead of forming lacy edges.
Add the onion with a pinch of salt and fry until the tips turn golden and frilled; stop at pale onion and the masala tastes raw, go dark brown and it will dominate the eggs.
Stir in chilli, tomato, cumin, coriander and turmeric, cooking until the tomato loses its watery shine; wet masala stops the egg edges crisping.

Push the masala into two rough nests, slide in the eggs and spoon hot spiced fat over the whites until they bubble and set with brittle brown rims; avoid spooning over the yolks if you want them soft.

Take the pan off the heat when the whites are just opaque and the yolks still wobble under a thin film; carry-over heat finishes them, so waiting for firm yolks in the pan means chalky eggs on the plate.
Scatter with fresh coriander and a squeeze of lemon, then serve at once; the crisp skirts soften fast if they sit in the pan.

note: Serve with hot paratha or buttered toast for scooping up the spiced fat.

name: Pickled King Oyster Gỏi with Tamarind Dressing
hook: Silky mushrooms, sharp herbs, peanut crunch

ingredients.name: king oyster mushrooms, torn into long strips
small cucumber, deseeded and cut into matchsticks

steps.t: Whisk the rice vinegar, sugar, salt and 120 ml warm water until clear; undissolved sugar clings in gritty patches rather than seasoning the vegetables evenly.
Put carrot and cucumber into half the pickle liquid and chill until bendy but still snappy; leave them too long and the cucumber turns floppy and dull.
Sear the torn mushrooms in a dry, very hot frying pan until they squeak, shrink and show chestnut patches; if the pan is cool they leak juice and taste steamed.
Pour the remaining pickle liquid over the hot mushrooms and let them soak until silky and seasoned through; adding it cold to cold mushrooms only flavours the outside.
Whisk tamarind, soy sauce, chilli and 2 tablespoons of the mushroom pickling liquid into a glossy dressing; too much pickle liquid makes it thin and sour, so add it gradually.
Drain the vegetables and mushrooms well, then toss with the dressing and herbs using your hands; excess brine puddles on the platter and washes the herbs flat.
Pile onto a chilled plate and finish with peanuts and fried shallots at the last second; add them early and their crunch disappears before guests sit down.

note: King oyster mushrooms give the most elegant ribbons, but oyster mushrooms work if torn thickly.

name: Amalfi Beef and Courgette Teglia
hook: Lemon beef, sweet tomatoes, basil air

ingredients.name: lemon, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan and oil a wide baking dish; a cramped dish traps steam, leaving grey beef and watery courgettes.
Toss courgettes, tomatoes and onion with 1 tablespoon oil, oregano, salt and pepper directly in the dish until everything glistens; dry slices scorch before they soften.
Mix beef with garlic, lemon zest, breadcrumbs, Parmesan, salt and pepper, using your fingertips just until combined; kneading makes the beef tight and bouncy instead of tender.
Pinch the beef into small rough nuggets over the vegetables, leaving gaps so the heat can reach the courgettes; one solid layer of meat turns this heavy and steamy.
Drizzle with the remaining oil and bake until the tomatoes slump, the courgette edges curl and the beef nuggets are browned and cooked through with no pink centre.
Rest the teglia for 8 minutes so the tomato juices settle into a light sauce; spooning straight away leaves a flood on the plate.
Tear over basil and squeeze lemon at the table; baking the basil would turn it black and mute the summer lift.

note: Good warm rather than piping hot, with a peppery rocket salad alongside.

name: Malabar Tamarind Mackerel Braise
hook: Tangy oil-slicked fish, curry-leaf depth

ingredients.name: mackerel fillets, pin-boned and cut into large pieces

steps.t: Salt the mackerel pieces lightly and chill while you start the masala; leaving fish unsalted until the end makes the flesh taste seasoned only on the surface.
Warm the coconut oil in a shallow pan and cook the onion until soft gold and sticky at the edges; rush this stage and the braise tastes sharp rather than rounded.
Add garlic, ginger and curry leaves, stirring until the leaves crackle and the raw garlic smell disappears; if the garlic catches dark brown, the whole sauce turns harsh.
Stir in chilli powder, coriander and turmeric with a splash of water to make a brick-red paste; dry spices burn in oil in seconds, so keep them moving and damp.
Whisk tamarind, coconut milk, green chilli and 150 ml water into the pan, then simmer gently until the oil beads at the edges and the sauce tastes tangy rather than raw.
Nestle in the mackerel skin-side up, spoon sauce over it and keep the pan at a lazy tremble; a rolling boil breaks the oily fish into flakes before it has braised.
Turn off the heat when the thickest piece flakes with gentle pressure, then rest covered so the sauce settles around the fish; serving immediately makes the coconut oil look split and aggressive.

note: Serve as a small plate with appam, neer dosa or plain rice, plus lime wedges for brightness.

name: Crispy Chermoula Chicken Cutlets
hook: Crisp edges, lemon, cumin warmth

steps.t: Slice the chicken horizontally into thin cutlets, then bash between baking paper to about 1 cm thick; if they are uneven, the thick end stays pale while the thin end dries out.

Mix garlic, lemon zest, half the lemon juice, coriander, parsley, cumin, paprika, turmeric, chilli flakes and a good pinch of salt. Rub it over the chicken; do not leave wet clumps, or they scorch before the crust crisps.
Put the beaten egg in one shallow dish and the semolina in another. Dip each cutlet in egg, then press into semolina until sandy all over; bare patches turn leathery in the pan.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of semolina fizzes at once. If the oil is only warm, the coating drinks it and goes heavy.
Fry the cutlets in a single layer until the underside is deep gold with little lace-brown edges, then turn once and finish the second side; crowding the pan steams the crust soft.
Drain on a rack, not kitchen paper, for 2 minutes, then squeeze over the remaining lemon juice. Paper traps steam underneath and steals the crunch you just made.

note: Serve with chopped cucumber, yoghurt and warm flatbread if you want to stretch it.

name: Saffron Sherry Steamed Mariscada
hook: Saffron steam, briny shells, patient depth

ingredients.name: fennel bulb, finely diced, fronds kept

steps.t: Soak the clams and mussels separately in very cold salted water, then scrub and debeard the mussels. Throw away any cracked shells or any open ones that do not close when tapped; no sauce rescues bad shellfish.

Peel the prawns, keeping the meat chilled, and put the shells in a pan with 700 ml water and the fennel trimmings. Simmer gently until the stock smells sweet and marine, not muddy; a hard boil makes it bitter and cloudy.
Strain the stock through a fine sieve, pressing lightly, and stop before any grit at the bottom goes through. Grit in the broth ruins the whole pot.

Warm the olive oil in a broad lidded casserole and cook onion and fennel until soft, glossy and reduced, then add garlic. If the vegetables still look raw and separate, the final broth will taste thin.
Add grated tomatoes and saffron and cook until the sofrito darkens to brick red and the oil shows at the edges; rush this and you get sharp tomato water instead of depth.
Pour in the sherry and bubble until the alcoholic sting has gone, then add 500 ml prawn stock and bring to a lively simmer. Taste now, because shellfish will add salt fast.
Add clams and mussels, cover and steam until most shells gape wide, then add prawns for the last few minutes until pink and just firm. Overcooked prawns curl tight and squeak.
Discard any shells that stay shut, fold through parsley and fennel fronds, and serve with lemon wedges. Do not dig through the sandy bottom of the pot when ladling.

note: This is built for a slow afternoon: purge carefully, make the stock, then steam everything right before serving.

name: Provençal Coal-Grilled Halloumi with Puy Lentils
hook: Smoke, herbs, squeaky salt, serious protein

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are ash-grey with no tall flames. If you grill halloumi over flames, the outside blisters black before the centre warms.
Whisk Dijon, vinegar, 2 tbsp olive oil, herbes de Provence, garlic, lemon zest and a squeeze of juice. Keep it punchy, because lentils flatten timid seasoning.
Toss the lentils, tomatoes, rocket and chives with half the dressing. If the lentils are wet from the packet, drain them well or the salad tastes sludgy.
Brush halloumi and courgette with the remaining oil. Oil the bars too; dry cheese welds itself to the grill and tears when you turn it.
Grill courgette until striped and floppy at the edges, then move it to the cooler side. Pull it too early and it eats raw and squeaky rather than smoky.
Grill the halloumi until the bars leave dark stripes and the edges soften without collapsing, turning once only. Constant fiddling breaks the slabs and loses the crust.
Pile lentils onto plates, add courgette and hot halloumi, then spoon over the remaining dressing. Dress after grilling as well, or the smoke tastes dry rather than savoury.

note: Use a firm halloumi and thick slices; thin ones melt through the bars before they char.

name: New England Maple Steamed Custard Pots
hook: Silky maple custard, warm and quiet

steps.t: Set four 150 ml ramekins in a wide lidded pan on a folded tea towel, then pour in hot water to come halfway up their sides. Without the towel, the cups rattle and the custard cooks unevenly.
Warm the milk, cream, maple syrup and brown sugar until steaming and the sugar dissolves, but do not let it boil. Boiled dairy makes the eggs seize into sweet scrambled bits.
Whisk eggs, vanilla, salt and nutmeg just until smooth, not foamy. Too much froth sets as bubbles and spoils the silkiness.
Pour the hot dairy into the eggs in a thin stream while whisking, then strain into a jug. If you dump it in quickly, the bottom of the bowl cooks before you can save it.
Divide the blueberries between the ramekins and pour in the custard. Cover each ramekin with foil, crimped loose enough for a little expansion; uncovered pots drip with condensation.
Bring the pan water to the gentlest simmer, cover and steam until the custards wobble like set jelly with no liquid centre. A rolling boil gives tunnels and a rubbery rim.
Lift the pots out and rest for 8 minutes before serving warm. Spoon in too soon and the centre slumps before it finishes setting.

note: They are also good chilled, but warm is the soft diner-style finish.

name: Buenos Aires Crisp Potato Revuelto
hook: Crisp potatoes, glossy eggs, rent-week comfort

steps.t: Rinse the potato matchsticks in cold water, then dry them hard in a tea towel. Damp potatoes steam and stick instead of catching crisp edges.
Beat the eggs with oregano, a pinch of salt and plenty of black pepper until streak-free. Half-mixed eggs cook into separate white rubber and yellow curds.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok until it shimmers, then stir-fry the potatoes over high heat until the tips are golden and the centres are tender. If the pan is not hot, they collapse into oily mash.
Add onion and red pepper and keep tossing until the onion edges char in spots and the pepper softens but still shines. Let them sit too long and the sugars burn bitter.
Stir in garlic and ham for a final blast until the ham curls and the garlic smells nutty. Garlic goes from fragrant to acrid fast at this heat.
Lower the heat slightly, pour in the eggs and fold quickly through the potatoes until glossy curds cling to everything with no raw egg pooling. Walk away now and you get a dry omelette rubble.
Finish with parsley and eat straight from hot plates. Revuelto keeps cooking in the pan, so leaving it there turns the eggs chalky.

note: Inspired by revuelto Gramajo, but pared back for a cheap hob and one battered pan.

name: Velvet Beetroot Halloumi Horiatiki
hook: Salt, honey and winter-bright beetroot

steps.t: Slice the red onion into thin half-moons and toss it with the vinegar and a pinch of salt; if the slices are thick they stay harsh and shout over the halloumi.
Cut the peel and white pith from the oranges, then slice the flesh into rounds over a bowl to catch the juice; leaving pith on makes the whole plate bitter.
Cut the beetroot into wedges and pat it dry with kitchen paper; wet beetroot bleeds into the cheese and turns the salad muddy rather than jewel-bright.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until they smell warm and the skins look slightly darker; take them off before they blacken, because burnt walnut bitterness lingers.
Slice the halloumi about 5 mm thick and let it sit at room temperature while you finish the dressing; fridge-cold halloumi tastes rubbery and closed.
Warm the olive oil, honey, oregano and 1 tbsp orange juice in the walnut pan just until loose and glossy; do not boil it or the honey will taste scorched.
Layer beetroot, orange, halloumi, olives and softened onion on a platter, then spoon over the warm dressing and scatter with walnuts; dressing too early stains everything pink.

note: Use halloumi you enjoy uncooked: it should smell milky and briny, not sour.

name: Sizzling Sucuk-Spiced Mushroom Menemen
hook: Breakfast mushrooms with peppery pan heat

ingredients.name: simits or crusty rolls, to serve

steps.t: Get a wide frying pan very hot before adding oil; if the pan is only warm the mushrooms leak water and stew instead of catching.
Add the mushrooms in one layer and leave them alone until the undersides squeak and go chestnut-brown; stirring too soon pulls out moisture.
Add onion, green pepper, butter, cumin and pul biber, then stir-fry hard until the pepper softens at the edges but still looks green; if it dulls to olive, you have lost the fresh breakfast bite.
Pour in the grated tomatoes with a pinch of salt and cook until the pan sounds like frying again, not simmering; watery tomato makes the eggs loose and soupy.
Beat the eggs lightly, pour them in, and fold with a spatula until glossy curds sit between the mushrooms; hard scrambling makes the dish dry and grainy.
Kill the heat while the eggs still wobble, scatter parsley over, and rest for one minute; carry-over heat finishes them, so waiting for dryness in the pan overcooks them.
Serve straight from the pan with torn simit or rolls for scooping; plating too neatly loses the steam and sizzle that make it worth waking for.

note: The sucuk idea comes from the spice profile, not sausage, keeping the mushrooms in charge.

name: Za’atar Griddled Egg Knafeh Breads
hook: Crisp threads, molten yolks, lemony herbs

steps.t: Toss the kadaif with melted butter and a pinch of salt, separating clumps with your fingers; tangled lumps brown outside while staying pasty inside.
Mix labneh, feta, lemon zest, parsley and mint into a thick spread; if it is loose, it will slide out when the bread hits the griddle.
Heat a large flat griddle or heavy frying pan over medium-high heat and brush with olive oil; too fierce a heat burns the fine pastry before the egg sets.
Lay four loose nests of kadaif on the griddle, pressing each into a thin round with a shallow well in the centre; a deep well leaves raw pastry under the yolk.
Spoon the labneh mixture around the wells, crack an egg into each centre, and sprinkle with za’atar and sesame; crack into a cup first if serving guests, because a broken shell ruins the reveal.
Cover with a lid and cook until the pastry edges are lace-golden and the whites are just opaque; if the whites are still glassy, they are not safe or pleasant to eat.
Slide each bread onto a warm plate and serve at once; stacking them traps steam and softens the crisp threads you worked for.

note: Kadaif gives drama without deep-frying; keep the nests thin so the griddle can do its job.

name: Crisp Courgette Chermoula Coins
hook: Green, crackly, lemon-cumin summer bites

steps.t: Slice the courgettes into 7 mm coins, then salt them lightly and spread them on a tray; if they sit in a heap, they sweat unevenly and fry limp.
Pat the courgettes very dry with a tea towel; surface water spits in the oil and stops the crust clinging.
Mix flour, semolina, cumin, paprika and turmeric in a shallow bowl; semolina gives the sandy crunch, so do not replace it all with flour.
Toss the courgettes through the spiced flour and shake off the excess; a thick dusty coat falls into the pan and burns before the vegetables crisp.
Heat 5 mm olive oil in a wide frying pan until a pinch of flour fizzes immediately; if the oil is quiet, the courgettes drink it and turn greasy.
Fry in single-layer batches until the rims curl and the faces are crisp gold, turning once; crowding drops the heat and gives you soft coins.

Stir lemon juice, lemon zest, coriander, parsley, garlic and 2 tbsp of the warm frying oil into a loose chermoula, then spoon it over the hot courgettes; dressing them cold makes the crust chewy instead of fragrant.

note: Serve with tomato wedges or olives, but keep the courgettes uncovered so they stay crisp.

name: Hake en Escabeche with Orange-Olive Dressing
hook: Cool white fish, sharp golden oil

steps.t: Cut the hake into chunky 4 cm pieces and season with the salt; tiny pieces flake apart in the pickle and look tired on a shared plate.
Warm 2 tbsp olive oil with the garlic and bay leaf until the garlic turns pale straw, not brown; browned garlic makes the escabeche bitter.
Stir in the smoked paprika off the heat, then immediately add vinegar and water; paprika scorches in seconds if it sits in hot oil alone.
Bring the pickle to a gentle simmer, slide in the hake, and keep it barely bubbling until the fish turns opaque and flakes in large moist pieces; boiling makes it cottony.
Lift the fish into a shallow dish and pour the hot pickle over it, including the garlic and bay; leave until cool, because rushing this gives flavour only on the surface.
Zest half the orange, then cut away the peel and dice the flesh; leaving membrane on the orange adds stringy bitterness to the dressing.
Spoon the fish onto a platter, dress with remaining olive oil, orange, olives, parsley and orange zest, then add a few spoonfuls of the pickle; drowning the plate hides the clean white fish.

note: The hake is cooked before pickling, so it is safe for a relaxed tapas table.

name: Coconut-Lime Tofu Jungle Stew
hook: coconut steam, lime snap, soft tofu

steps.t: Pat the tofu very dry and cut it into fat cubes; wet tofu waters down the stew before the coconut has a chance to cling.
Heat the oil in a wide saucepan and fry the curry paste until it darkens to brick-red and smells toasted; if it only warms, the stew tastes harsh and raw.
Pour in a third of the coconut milk and stir until the oil freckles the surface, then add the rest with the stock, soy and sugar; dumping everything in at once leaves the paste in lumps.
Add mushrooms, beans and baby corn, then simmer until the beans bend but still squeak slightly; if they go khaki, you have lost the fresh Thai snap.
Slide in the tofu and simmer gently until the cubes puff at the edges; a hard boil breaks them into curds.
Finish with lime juice, torn herbs and a little lime zest; adding the lime earlier makes it flat instead of bright.

note: Use a vegetarian curry paste if you want the dish fully plant-based.

name: Yuzu-Miso Whole Lamb Leg Roast
hook: burnished miso crust, spoon-soft lamb

steps.t: Score the lamb fat in shallow diamonds, then mix miso, shio koji, mirin, soy, ginger, garlic and yuzu and rub it into every cut; without the scoring, the flavour sits on the surface.
Set the lamb on a tray, cover loosely and refrigerate; a tight wrap smears off the marinade and a crowded tray leaks salty cure everywhere.
Take the lamb out of the fridge about an hour before roasting and wipe off any thick drips of marinade; cold lamb cooks unevenly, while wet miso burns before the meat is tender.
Heat the oven to 220°C, spread daikon, potatoes and whole spring onions in a roasting tin, and sit the lamb on top; if the vegetables are piled up, they steam instead of catching the lamb fat.
Roast hot until the miso crust goes dark mahogany at the ridges but not black; this first blast is what gives the roast its lacquer.
Lower to 150°C and roast, basting with the tin juices, until a probe near the bone reads 60–65°C; guessing by colour wastes a weekend on either raw pockets or dry slices.
Rest the lamb loosely covered before carving across the grain, then spoon over the miso-fat juices; carving straight away sends the juice across the board instead of through the meat.

note: Shio koji tenderises deeply, so avoid salting the lamb separately.

name: Oak-Smoked Gochujang Three-Bean Jjim
hook: smoke, chilli, proper post-lift ballast

steps.t: Spread the lentils, black beans and edamame on a clean tea towel and blot them dry; damp pulses taste steamed and block the smoke from sticking.
Line a wok or heavy pot with foil, add the oak chips, set a rack above them and open a window; if the chips touch the food, you get ash instead of clean smoke.
Put the pulses on perforated foil on the rack, cover tightly, heat until smoke appears, then lower the heat and smoke until they smell like a barbecue stall; longer makes the skins bitter.
Whisk gochujang, doenjang, soy, honey, garlic and 120 ml water in a frying pan; leaving the pastes unmixed gives salty clumps later.
Bubble the sauce until glossy, then fold in the smoked pulses and turn them until every bean is red and sticky; high heat at this point scorches the chilli paste.
Turn off the heat and stir through sesame oil and spring onions; boiling sesame oil flattens its nutty smell.

note: Eat hot, or chill for a dense lunchbox bowl with plenty of protein from the pulses.

name: Ginger-Rock Sugar Steamed Egg Custard
hook: warm silk with gingered sugar

steps.t: Simmer the water, rock sugar and ginger until the sugar disappears and the syrup smells warm and peppery; a fierce boil reduces it too far and makes the custard oversweet.
Let the syrup cool until just warm, then remove the ginger; hot syrup scrambles the eggs on contact.
Beat the eggs gently, then stir in milk, syrup and salt without whipping foam into it; bubbles become pockmarks on the finished surface.
Strain into four small bowls and cover each with foil or a plate; skipping the sieve leaves stringy egg bits that spoil the silk.
Steam over barely trembling water until the centres wobble like soft jelly; a rolling boil makes the custard crater and split.
Rest covered, then scatter with osmanthus; spooning in straight away breaks the set and makes it weep.

note: Serve warm rather than fridge-cold so the ginger perfume stays open.

name: Coal-Grilled Mussel Esquites Tacos
hook: briny mussels, charred corn, lime

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are grey with a steady glow; yellow flames soot the tortillas and scorch the mussel shells before they open.
Scrub the mussels and pull away beards, discarding any cracked shells or open mussels that do not close when tapped; bad shellfish is not worth saving money on.
Oil the corn and grill it in a basket or heavy pan over the coals until speckled brown and sweet-smelling; pale corn tastes tinned, black corn tastes dusty.
Put the mussels in a grill-safe tray, cover with foil and set over the coals, shaking once, until the shells open wide; discard any that stay shut.
Mix mayonnaise, juice of one lime, chilli powder, garlic, coriander, cheese, salt and the charred corn; adding extra salt before the cheese goes in can make the topping harsh.
Warm the tortillas directly on the grill until flexible with a few char spots; leave them too long and they turn into brittle crisps.
Pile mussels and esquites into the tortillas and finish with the second lime cut into wedges; if the mussels sit too long in the hot tray, they shrink and go rubbery.

note: Mussels are usually one of the cheapest shellfish at European fish counters; keep them chilled until cooking.

name: Ginger Mung Bean Steamed Pots
hook: Soft beans, ginger heat, winter steam

ingredients.name: split mung beans, soaked 2 hours and drained
glutinous rice, rinsed until the water runs mostly clear

steps.t: Mix the soaked mung beans and rinsed rice in a heatproof dish that fits your steamer; if the rice is still cloudy, the finished pots turn gluey instead of softly sticky.
Warm the oil in a small pan, then stir in ginger and garlic until the smell turns rounded and sweet; stop before the garlic freckles brown or it will taste bitter after steaming.
Stir the ginger oil, stock, coconut milk and soy into the beans and rice, then level the surface so everything hydrates evenly; mounds left above the liquid stay chalky.
Cover the dish tightly with foil and steam over steadily bubbling water until the centre has swollen and the grains squash easily between finger and spoon; a lazy simmer gives you hard pockets.
Rest, still covered, off the heat so the starch settles rather than smearing when spooned.
Fold through most of the spring onions, then spoon into warm bowls; stir too hard and you will break the beans into paste.
Finish with coriander and the remaining spring onions for a cold snap of freshness against the steam.

note: Inspired by Vietnamese xôi textures, made savoury and bowl-friendly for cold weather.

name: Coal-Grilled Sardines with Fennel Toast
hook: Smoky skins, bright fennel, hot toast

ingredients.name: small fennel bulb, very thinly sliced

steps.t: Light the coals and wait until they are glowing with a thin grey ash; grilling over flames scorches the sardine skin before the flesh warms through.
Toss fennel with lemon juice, capers, parsley, one tablespoon of oil and a pinch of salt; if it is dressed too early and drowned, it collapses instead of staying crisp.
Pat the sardines dry inside and out, then rub with oil, fennel seeds, chilli and salt; wet skin welds itself to the grill.
Grill the bread first until the ridges are dark and the centre is still chewy, then rub one side with garlic; overdo it and breakfast becomes a scraper of charcoal.
Lay the sardines across the bars and leave them alone until the skin releases with blistered silver patches; moving them early tears away the best crisp bits.
Turn once and grill until the belly flesh is opaque and flakes from the backbone; a second round of flipping only breaks the fish.
Pile fennel onto the garlic toast, set the sardines on top, and finish with lemon zest and the remaining oil.

note: Best with very fresh sardines and coffee strong enough to meet the smoke.

name: Coconut Lime Scallop Kachumber
hook: Silky scallops, lime snap, coconut cool

ingredients.name: green chilli, deseeded and finely sliced

steps.t: Chill the serving plates and keep the scallops cold until the last moment; warm shellfish loses its clean sweetness fast.
Slice each scallop into three thin coins with a sharp knife; sawing with a blunt blade bruises the flesh and makes it look ragged on the plate.
Heat coconut oil and mustard seeds in a small pan until the seeds pop and smell nutty, then tip into a cool bowl; leave them on the heat after popping and they turn acrid.
Whisk coconut milk, lime juice and a pinch of salt into the mustard oil until glossy; if it splits, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water before adding the scallops.
Fold in cucumber, onion, chilli and coriander, then add the scallops for just long enough for the edges to turn satin-white while the centres stay pearly.
Arrange on the chilled plates with the coconut dressing spooned around, not flooded over; too much sauce hides the scallops you paid for.
Serve straight away with poppadoms for scooping, because lime will keep curing the scallops as it sits.

note: Use only scallops sold for raw eating; otherwise briefly sear them and chill before dressing.

name: Wok-Charred Halloumi Larb
hook: Squeaky cheese, lime, herb crunch

ingredients.name: halloumi, patted dry and cut into 2 cm cubes
fish sauce or light soy sauce
palm sugar or light brown sugar

steps.t: Whisk lime juice, fish sauce and sugar until the grains disappear; undissolved sugar leaves sweet grit at the bottom of the bowl.
Set a wok over high heat until a drop of water skitters and vanishes, then add oil; if the wok is only warm, halloumi sweats brine instead of charring.
Add the halloumi in one layer and leave it until the underside has deep bronze blisters; stirring straight away gives pale rubbery cubes.
Toss hard for another minute until the corners char and the centres stay springy; cook too long and the cheese tightens into squeaky salt blocks.
Tip the hot halloumi into the dressing with shallot and chilli, tossing so the sharp sauce hits the cheese while it is still open and sizzling.
Fold in mint, coriander and toasted rice powder just before serving; add the herbs early and the heat turns them black.
Spoon into baby gem leaves, keeping the plate loose and juicy rather than piled into a heavy salad.

note: Toasted rice powder gives the classic larb nuttiness and keeps the dish bright rather than oily.

name: Miso Butter Pork Okonomiyaki Coins
hook: Crisp edges, savoury pork, sweet glaze

ingredients.name: cold dashi or light chicken stock
thinly sliced pork belly, cut into short strips

steps.t: Whisk flour, eggs and cold dashi just until no dry patches remain; beating it smooth like cake batter makes the coins bready and tough.
Fold in cabbage and spring onions so every shred is lightly coated; if batter pools at the bottom, the centres cook heavy and wet.
Mash miso into the butter and keep it by the griddle; adding plain miso later in clumps gives salty bites instead of a savoury gloss.
Heat a flat griddle or heavy pan over medium-high heat and lay down small nests of pork; if the pan is cold, the fat leaks out without crisping.
Spoon cabbage batter over each pork nest into palm-sized coins and press lightly; smash them flat and you squeeze out the steam that cooks the cabbage.
Flip when the pork edges are crisp and the batter rim looks set and matte, then griddle until the second side is mottled golden and the centre springs back.
Brush with miso butter while hot, then stripe with okonomiyaki sauce and mayonnaise; sauce before the butter slides off and tastes flat.
Scatter with pickled ginger and serve in the middle of the table while the edges still crackle.

note: Small coins are easier to share than one large pancake and stay crisper at the edges.

name: Crispy Kimchi Egg Jeon
hook: Lacy edges, jammy heat, fast rice

steps.t: Squeeze the kimchi hard over a bowl, then chop it; wet kimchi makes the batter steam instead of crackle.
Whisk eggs, flour, cornflour, gochujang, sesame oil and 2 tbsp kimchi juice until just smooth; over-whisking turns the jeon bready rather than tender.
Fold in kimchi and most of the spring onions; the mix should drop from a spoon in thick ribbons, not run like beaten egg.
Heat half the neutral oil in a wide frying pan until a dab of batter sizzles instantly; if the oil is only warm, the first jeon drinks it and goes heavy.
Spoon in half the batter and spread it thin. Fry until the edges go lace-brown and the centre looks set, then flip before the underside turns bitter-dark.
Fry the second side until it sounds scratchy when nudged with a spatula, then repeat with the remaining oil and batter.
Serve over hot rice with sesame seeds and the remaining spring onions; cutting it too early traps steam and softens the crisp rim.

note: Use older, sour kimchi if you can; it gives the cleanest savoury punch.

name: Sichuan Weekend Pickle Ribbon Salad
hook: Cold crunch under scarlet chilli oil

ingredients.name: Chinese leaf, cut into wide ribbons

steps.t: Toss Chinese leaf, daikon and carrots with the salt in a large bowl; miss this salting step and the pickle liquor gets watery and dull.
Leave until the vegetables slump and shine, then squeeze them firmly in handfuls; if they still drip freely, the finished salad will taste thin.
Stir rice vinegar, sugar, garlic and ginger until the sugar dissolves, then pack everything into a clean jar, pressing the ribbons below the liquid.
Chill for 48 hours, turning the jar whenever you remember; exposed vegetable edges dry out and taste salty rather than pickled.
Drain the pickle well and pick out any large garlic slices if they taste too fierce; dressing wet ribbons makes the chilli oil slide straight off.
Dress with Chinkiang vinegar, chilli oil and crushed Sichuan pepper until every ribbon is glossy and flecked red.
Fold through coriander just before serving; add it earlier and it bruises into dark, grassy clumps.

note: This keeps for four days after pickling, but dress only what you plan to eat.

name: Salsa Verde Cod Black Bean Bake
hook: Lean flakes, bright sauce, serious protein

ingredients.name: cod loin or other firm white fish
tin black beans, drained and rinsed
lime, zested and cut into wedges

steps.t: Heat the oven to 210°C fan and oil a medium baking dish; a cold dish slows the bake and leaves the fish sitting in thin liquid.
Toss black beans, salsa verde, tomatoes, red pepper, cumin, smoked paprika and lime zest in the dish until evenly coated.
Bake the bean base until it bubbles at the edges and the pepper begins to soften; if it still looks raw, the cod will overcook before the vegetables catch up.
Pat the cod dry, season it lightly, then nestle it into the hot beans; wet fish sheds water and turns the sauce soupy.
Return to the oven until the cod flakes in thick pearly pieces and is opaque through the centre; push it too far and it tightens into cottony strands.
Scatter over feta and rest the dish so the bubbling settles back into the beans rather than flooding the plate.
Finish with coriander and lime wedges; add the herbs before baking and they lose their clean green bite.

note: Swap cod for hake or pollock if that is better value, keeping the fillets thick.

name: Honey Mastiha Steamed Egg Custards
hook: Silky spoonfuls, piney honey perfume

ingredients.name: Greek honey, plus extra to serve

steps.t: Set four small heatproof cups in a steamer basket and bring the water to a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil; violent steam makes custards bubble and split.
Warm the milk with honey, sugar, mastiha, orange zest and salt until steaming at the edges; boiling it drives off the perfume and can scramble the eggs on contact.
Whisk the eggs in a jug, then slowly pour in the warm milk while whisking; adding it all at once leaves yellow cooked threads.
Strain the custard into the cups and skim off foam; bubbles left on top set into a pocked surface.
Cover each cup with foil and steam gently until the custards wobble like soft jelly in the centre, not liquid under the skin.
Lift out and rest for 10 minutes; spooning in immediately breaks the delicate set and releases watery whey.
Serve warm or chilled with extra honey and pistachios; nuts added too early soften and lose their snap.

note: If using mastiha crystals, crush them with a little of the sugar before adding.

name: Turkish Beef Bulgur Student Stew
hook: Tomato-rich bowls with peppery warmth

ingredients.name: Turkish pepper paste or mild chilli paste

steps.t: Heat the oil in a large saucepan, add the beef mince and spread it out; stirring too soon makes it grey and watery instead of savoury.
Cook until the underside browns in patches, then break it up and add onion and green pepper; stop while the onion is still harsh and the stew tastes canteen-flat.
Stir in garlic, tomato purée and pepper paste until the paste darkens brick-red and clings to the meat; if it stays raw, it tastes metallic.
Add tomatoes, chickpeas, bulgur, stock and dried mint, scraping the base so no browned bits burn during the simmer.
Simmer uncovered, stirring often near the end, until the bulgur is swollen and the stew drops slowly from the spoon; ignore it and the grains catch on the bottom.
Rest off the heat so the bulgur finishes thickening without boiling into paste.
Taste for salt and loosen with a splash of water if it stands up like porridge; a good stew should mound softly, not slice.

note: Bulgur stretches a small amount of beef while keeping the stew filling and properly savoury.

name: Dijon Mushroom Croque Gratin
hook: Mushrooms under bubbling Gruyère and mustard cream

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Put the mushrooms, oil and salt in a medium baking dish and spread them in one layer; if they are piled up they steam grey instead of roasting nutty.
Bake the mushrooms until they have dropped their water and the edges are chestnut-brown, not just beige and wet.
Stir in the garlic, crème fraîche, Dijon and milk directly in the dish, scraping the browned juices into the sauce; leaving them stuck to the dish wastes the best flavour.
Fold in the baguette chunks so they are glossy but still poking up in places; fully submerging them makes a heavy bread pudding instead of crisp-topped gratin.
Scatter over the Gruyère and bake until the sauce bubbles hard at the edges and the cheese has lace-brown spots.
Rest for 3 minutes, then finish with tarragon; serving straight from the oven makes the cream runny and burns out the herb’s perfume.

note: A green salad with sharp vinaigrette keeps the richness in check.

name: Coffee-Molasses Chuck Roast
hook: Dark gravy, spoon-tender beef, slow Sunday heat

steps.t: Heat the oven to 150°C. Pat the beef dry, season with salt and dust with flour; damp meat boils on contact and leaves you with pale gravy.
Sear the beef in the oil in a heavy casserole until a dark crust forms on all broad sides; move it too soon and the crust tears off into the pan.
Lift out the beef, add onions and carrots, and cook until the onion edges turn deep gold; if they stay raw-white, the braise tastes flat and boiled.
Stir in the garlic for a minute, then pour in coffee and scrape the base until it feels smooth under the spoon; any stuck black patches will turn the gravy bitter.
Add stock, molasses, Worcestershire and thyme, return the beef, cover tightly and braise in the oven until a fork slides in with almost no push.
Turn the beef once during cooking and check the liquid sits about halfway up the meat; if it dries below a few centimetres, top up with hot water before the sugars scorch.
Rest the beef in the covered pot for 20 minutes, then slice or pull into big pieces; cutting immediately squeezes the juices into the gravy instead of keeping them in the meat.
Skim excess fat from the surface and simmer the gravy uncovered until it coats the back of a spoon; stop too early and it tastes watery beside the beef.

note: Best with mash, buttered noodles or soft white bread for the gravy.

name: Mackerel Butter Bean Chupín
hook: Tomato warmth wrapped around oily, firm fish

steps.t: Warm the oil in a wide pan, then soften the onion and red pepper until the onion bends easily and the pepper smells sweet; rushing this leaves the stew harsh.
Add the garlic and paprika and stir until the oil turns brick-red; let the paprika sit dry on the pan and it catches bitter in seconds.
Pour in the tomatoes and stock, then add the potatoes and a pinch of salt. The potatoes need to be just covered, otherwise their tops stay chalky.
Simmer with the lid ajar until a knife slips into the potatoes without cracking them apart; a hard boil breaks the tomato sauce greasy and rough.
Stir in the butter beans and simmer until they are hot and creamy at the edges; adding the fish before this point means overcooked mackerel while the beans are still cold.
Nestle the mackerel skin-side up, spoon sauce over it, cover and simmer gently until the flakes separate when nudged at the thickest point.
Finish with vinegar and parsley off the heat; boiling after the vinegar goes in dulls the lift that makes oily fish feel clean.

note: Use fresh mackerel if possible; sardine fillets also work with a shorter final simmer.

name: Steamed Coconut Pudim
hook: Silky caramel custard with a coconut hush

steps.t: Put the sugar and water in a small pan and cook without stirring until the syrup is deep amber; stirring now crystallises it into sandy lumps.
Immediately pour the caramel into a 1 litre heatproof pudding basin and tilt to coat the base; wait too long and it sets in one thick bitter puddle.
Whisk the eggs, yolk, condensed milk, coconut milk, whole milk, vanilla and salt until smooth but not frothy; whipping in air gives the pudim little holes instead of a satin slice.
Strain the custard into the caramel-lined basin and cover tightly with foil; loose foil lets steam drip in and waters down the top.
Set the basin on a trivet in a lidded pot with simmering water halfway up the sides, then steam gently until the edges are set and the centre wobbles like soft jelly.
Check the water level halfway and top up with boiling water if needed; cold water drops the steam and a dry pot can crack the basin.
Cool uncovered until no longer hot, then chill until fully cold so the caramel loosens and the custard cuts cleanly.
Run a thin knife around the edge and invert onto a rimmed plate; using a flat plate risks losing the caramel sauce across the counter.

note: Make it the morning of dinner or the day before for the cleanest texture.

name: Dhungar Lamb Masoor
hook: Smoky lamb stretched through velvety red lentils

steps.t: Heat the oil in a wide saucepan and fry the onion until the tips are deep brown and the middle is soft; pale onion makes the finished daal taste thin, while black onion turns it acrid.
Add the lamb mince and break it up hard with a spoon until no pink patches remain and the fat runs clear; leaving clumps gives you boiled meatballs in the lentils.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste, cumin, ground coriander and chilli powder until the mince smells roasted; if the spices look dry, splash in water before they scorch.
Add the tomatoes, lentils and water, then scrape the base clean. Simmer gently until the lentils collapse and the surface looks creamy, not gritty.
Beat the stew with the spoon for a minute to thicken it, then adjust salt; if it is catching on the base, loosen with hot water rather than turning up the heat.

Heat the natural charcoal until ashy all over, set it in a small foil cup on top of the cooked stew, drizzle a few drops of oil onto the coal and cover the pan at once; unlit or treated charcoal gives dirty smoke, not barbecue aroma.
Remove the foil cup carefully, stir through most of the coriander and rest for 3 minutes; stirring while the coal is still inside risks ash in the food.
Serve with rice, roti or toast and the remaining coriander; without something plain alongside, the smoke and chilli feel louder than the lamb.

note: A little lamb mince carries the flavour, while red lentils keep it filling and affordable.

name: Chimichurri Prawn Chapa Sizzle
hook: Garlicky prawns, charred peppers, sharp herbs

ingredients.name: small red onion, sliced into wedges

steps.t: Pat the prawns very dry and salt them lightly; if they go into the pan wet, they steam grey instead of catching sweet char.
Mix garlic, parsley, oregano, vinegar, chilli flakes and 1 tbsp olive oil in a bowl; keep it raw and bright, because frying all the herbs makes the chimichurri taste muddy.
Heat a wok or heavy frying pan until a drop of water skitters and vanishes, then add 1 tbsp oil; if the oil only gently shimmers, wait, or the vegetables will stew.
Throw in pepper and onion and stir-fry hard until the onion tips scorch and the pepper skins blister in spots.
Add the prawns in one layer and leave them alone until the undersides turn coral with tiny toasted edges; constant stirring makes them rubbery before they brown.
Flip and toss for another minute, just until the thickest prawn is opaque through the centre; overcooked prawns curl tight and squeak against your teeth.
Take the pan off the heat, fold through the chimichurri and squeeze over lemon; adding it off the heat keeps the parsley grassy and the garlic punchy.

note: Serve with warm bread or quick rice if you want a fuller dinner.

name: Griddled Halloumi Baião Stack
hook: Smoky cheese, slow beans, lime-bright crunch

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water and simmer until creamy inside but still holding their skins; if they burst into sludge now, the stack eats heavy.
Sweat onion, garlic and green pepper in 1 tbsp oil until soft and sweet-smelling, not browned; burnt garlic will make the whole pot bitter.

Stir in smoked paprika, rice, cooked beans and 450 ml bean cooking liquid, then cover and cook until the rice is tender and the surface has little steam holes; lifting the lid often leaves hard grains on top.
Rest the covered pot off the heat so the rice finishes gently; skipping this gives you wet beans underneath and chalky rice above.
Toast cassava flour in a dry pan with 1 tbsp oil until it smells nutty and turns pale gold; take it too dark and it tastes dusty-bitter rather than buttery.
Heat a ridged griddle until fierce, then press the halloumi slabs on until deep bronze stripes form and the edges sag; a lukewarm griddle makes the cheese leak water and stick.
Fork coriander, lime zest and a squeeze of lime through the bean rice, then layer with hot halloumi and cassava farofa; lime added too early dulls before serving.

note: The long cook is in the beans and resting, making this a relaxed weekend plate.

name: Lahori Crisp Pork Cutlets
hook: Lean pork, crackly gram-flour spice crust

steps.t: Beat the pork between baking paper to an even 1 cm; thick patches cook slowly and thin patches dry out before the crust crisps.
Mix yoghurt, lemon, garlic, ginger, cumin, chilli, turmeric and salt, then coat the pork and leave it until the surface looks stained and tacky.
